Just as other embryos lie with their backs against the stomach, pushing up the stomach, placing the abdominal wall behind the spine, crouching on their haunches, placing their chins on their fists like monkeys sitting in a tree hollow when the gods send rain, the Bodhisattva does not do that. The Bodhisattva, however, with his spine behind the spine, sits cross-legged facing east, like a speaker of the Dharma on a Dharma seat.

His previous meritorious actions purify his womb, and in the purified womb, a subtle, smooth, and distinctive complexion arises. Then, the impure skin is unable to conceal him, and he appears as if he is outside to the one who is looking. Explaining this matter with an analogy, the Blessed One said, "*Seyyathāpi*," and so forth.

However, the Bodhisattva inside the womb does not see his mother. For eye-consciousness does not arise inside the womb.

mula_pali: 24. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, sattāhajāte bodhisatte bodhisattamātā kālaṅkaroti tusitaṃ kāyaṃ upapajjati. Ayamettha dhammatā.
mula_english: ‘‘This is the natural law ( *dharmatā eṣā*), monks, that the Bodhisattva’s mother, seven days after the Bodhisattva's birth, dies and is reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. This is the rule (*ayamettha dhammatā*).’
commentary_pali: 24.Kālaṅkarotīti na vijātabhāvapaccayā, āyuparikkhayeneva. Bodhisattena vasitaṭṭhānañhi cetiyakuṭisadisaṃ hoti, aññesaṃ aparibhogārahaṃ, na ca sakkā bodhisattamātaraṃ apanetvā aññaṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapetunti tattakaṃyeva bodhisattamātu āyuppamāṇaṃ hoti, tasmā tadā kālaṅkaroti. Katarasmiṃ pana vaye kālaṃ karotīti? Majjhimavaye. Paṭhamavayasmiñhi sattānaṃ attabhāve chandarāgo balavā hoti, tena tadā sañjātagabbhā itthī gabbhaṃ anurakkhituṃ na sakkoti, gabbho bahvābādho hoti. Majjhimavayassa pana dve koṭṭhāse atikkamma tatiye koṭṭhāse vatthu visadaṃ hoti, visade vatthumhi nibbattadārakā arogā honti, tasmā bodhisattamātāpi paṭhamavaye sampattiṃ anubhavitvā majjhimavayassa tatiye koṭṭhāse vijāyitvā kālaṃ karotīti ayamettha dhammatā.
commentary_english:
24. *kālaṅkarotī* *iti* [means]: <page break ed="v" number="2.0026"/> not because of the condition of being born, but merely due to the exhaustion of lifespan.

The place resided in by a *bodhisattva* is similar to a *cetiya* shrine; it is not fit for the enjoyment of others, and it is not possible to remove the *bodhisattva*'s mother <page break ed="p" number="2.0437"/> and install another in the position of chief queen, because the lifespan of the *bodhisattva*'s mother is only that long; therefore, then she dies.

In which period of life does she die? In middle age.

For, in early life, the desire and lust of beings is strong in their own existence; therefore, at that time, a woman who has conceived is not able to protect the fetus; the fetus is subject to many ailments.

But in middle age, having passed two parts, in the third part the physical base is clear; in a clear physical base, the children born are healthy; therefore, the *bodhisattva*'s mother also, having experienced prosperity in early life, gives birth in the third part of middle age and then dies. This is the natural law here.

mula_pali: 25. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yathā aññā itthikā nava vā dasa vā māse gabbhaṃ kucchinā pariharitvā vijāyanti, na hevaṃ bodhisattaṃ bodhisattamātā vijāyati. Daseva māsāni bodhisattaṃ bodhisattamātā kucchinā pariharitvā vijāyati. Ayamettha dhammatā.
mula_english: It is the rule (*dhammatā*), monks, that whereas other women carry the child in their womb (*gabbhaṃ kucchinā pariharitvā*) for nine or ten months before giving birth (*vijāyanti*), it is not so with the *bodhisattva*; the *bodhisattva*'s mother gives birth (*vijāyati*) after carrying him in her womb (*kucchinā pariharitvā*) for exactly ten months. This is the natural law (*dharmatā*).
commentary_pali: 25.Nava vā dasa vāti ettha vā saddassa vikappanavasena satta vā aṭṭha vā ekādasa vā dvādasa vāti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo. Tattha sattamāsajāto jīvati, sītuṇhakkhamo pana na hoti. Aṭṭhamāsajāto na jīvati, avasesā jīvanti.
commentary_english:
25. It should be understood that here, the word "or" (vā) includes groupings such as seven, eight, eleven, or twelve, according to the options.

There, one born in the seventh month lives, but is not resistant to cold and heat.

One born in the eighth month does not live, but the rest live.

mula_pali: 26. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yathā aññā itthikā nisinnā vā nipannā vā vijāyanti, na hevaṃ bodhisattaṃ bodhisattamātā vijāyati. Ṭhitāva bodhisattaṃ bodhisattamātā vijāyati. Ayamettha dhammatā.
mula_english: ‘This, monks, is the natural law: just as other women give birth sitting or lying down, the Bodhisattva’s mother does not give birth in that way. The Bodhisattva’s mother gives birth standing up. This is the natural law (dharmatā).’

mula_pali: 27. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, devā paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti, pacchā manussā. Ayamettha dhammatā.
mula_english: ‘This is the rule (dhammatā), monks (bhikkhave), that when a Bodhisattva (bodhisatto) issues from his mother’s womb (mātukucchimhā nikkhamati), devas (devā) welcome (paṭiggaṇhanti) him first (paṭhamaṃ), and then (pacchā) humans (manussā). This is the natural law (ayamettha dhammatā).’
commentary_pali: 27.Devā paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhantīti khīṇāsavā suddhāvāsabrahmāno paṭiggaṇhanti. Kathaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti? ‘‘Sūtivesaṃ gaṇhitvā’’ti eke. Taṃ pana paṭikkhipitvā idaṃ vuttaṃ – ‘tadā bodhisattamātā suvaṇṇakhacitaṃ vatthaṃ nivāsetvā macchakkhisadisaṃ dukūlapaṭaṃ yāva pādantā pārupitvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassā sallahukagabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi, dhamakaraṇato udakanikkhamanasadisaṃ. Atha te pakatibrahmaveseneva upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamaṃ suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggahesuṃ. Tesaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno ajinappaveṇiyā paṭiggahesuṃ. Tato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena paṭiggahesuṃ’. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘devā paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti, pacchā manussā’’ti.
commentary_english:
27. "devā paṭhamaṃ paṭiggaṇhantīti" means the *khīṇāsava* pure abode (*śuddhāvāsa*) Brahmās receive [him].

How do they receive [him]? "Having taken the appearance of childbirth," say some.

However, rejecting that, this was said: "Then the mother of the Bodhisattva, having dressed in a golden-ornamented cloth, stood having covered herself with a fine linen cloth similar to a fish's eye down to her feet. Then she had an easy emergence from the womb, like water flowing from a water filter. Then they, in their natural Brahmā appearance, approached and first received [him] in a golden net. From their hands, the Four Great Kings (*mahārājāno*) received [him] on antelope skin. Then humans received [him] on a fine cloth."

Therefore, it was said, "First the gods receive [him], then humans."

mula_pali: 28. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, appattova bodhisatto pathaviṃ hoti, cattāro naṃ devaputtā paṭiggahetvā mātu purato ṭhapenti – ‘attamanā, devi, hohi; mahesakkho te putto uppanno’ti. Ayamettha dhammatā.
mula_english: It is the natural law (dharmatā) , monks, that when a Bodhisattva emerges from his mother's womb (mātukucchimhā nikkhamati), he does not touch the earth (pathaviṃ). Four divine beings (devaputtā) receive him, and placing him before his mother, they say: “Rejoice (attamanā), O queen (devi), a son of great power (mahesakkho) has been born to you!” This, monks, is the rule (ayamettha dhammatā).
commentary_pali: 28.Cattāro naṃ devaputtāti cattāro mahārājāno. Paṭiggahetvāti ajinappaveṇiyā paṭiggahetvā. Mahesakkhoti mahātejo mahāyaso lakkhaṇasampanno.
commentary_english:
28. "catāro naṃ devaputtā" means the Four Great Kings ( *cattāro mahārājāno*).

"paṭiggahetvā" means having accepted with an antelope hide (*ajinappaveṇiyā paṭiggahetvā*).

"mahesakkho" means of great power (*mahātejo mahāyaso lakkhaṇasampanno*).

mula_pali: 29. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, visadova nikkhamati amakkhito udena uddena (syā.), udarena (katthaci) amakkhito semhena amakkhito ruhirena amakkhito kenaci asucinā suddho visuddho (syā.) visado. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, maṇiratanaṃ kāsike vatthe nikkhittaṃ neva maṇiratanaṃ kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ makkheti, nāpi kāsikaṃ vatthaṃ maṇiratanaṃ makkheti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Ubhinnaṃ suddhattā. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, visadova nikkhamati amakkhito, udena amakkhito semhena amakkhito ruhirena amakkhito kenaci asucinā suddho visado. Ayamettha dhammatā.
mula_english: ‘It is the rule, *bhikkhus*, that when the *bodhisatta* issues from his mother’s womb, he issues forth stainless, not defiled by water (*udena*), mucus, blood or any impurity, pure and spotless (*visado*). Just as when a jewel (*maṇiratanaṃ*) is laid on muslin from Kasi, the jewel does not stain the muslin, or the muslin the jewel. Why is that? Because both are pure (*suddhattā*). In the same way, *bhikkhus*, when the *bodhisatta* issues from his mother’s womb, he issues forth stainless, not defiled by water, mucus, blood or any impurity, pure and spotless. This is the natural law (*dhammatā*).’
commentary_pali:
29.Visadova nikkhamatīti yathā aññe sattā yonimagge laggantā bhaggavibhaggā nikkhamanti, na evaṃ nikkhamati, alaggo hutvā nikkhamatīti attho udenāti udakena. Kenaci asucināti yathā aññe sattā kammajavātehi uddhaṃpādā adhosirā yonimagge pakkhittā sataporisaṃ narakapapātaṃ patantā viya, tāḷacchiddena nikkaḍḍhiyamānā hatthī viya mahādukkhaṃ anubhavantā nānāasucimakkhitāva nikkhamanti, na evaṃ bodhisatto. Bodhisattañhi kammajavātā uddhapādaṃ adhosiraṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti. So dhammāsanato otaranto dhammakathiko viya, nisseṇito otaranto puriso viya ca dve hatthe ca dve pāde ca pasāretvā ṭhitakova mātukucchisambhavena kenaci asucinā amakkhitova nikkhamati.

Udakassa dhārāti udakavaṭṭiyo. Tāsu sītā suvaṇṇakaṭāhe patati uṇhā rajatakaṭāhe. Idañca pathavitale kenaci asucinā asammissaṃ tesaṃ pānīyaparibhojanīyaudakañceva aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ kīḷāudakañca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ, aññassa pana suvaṇṇarajataghaṭehi āhariyamānaudakassa ceva haṃsavattakādipokkharaṇīgatassa ca udakassa paricchedo natthi.

Udakassa dhārā
commentary_english:
29. "Visadova Nikkhamatīti" Just as other beings exit stuck in the birth canal, broken and shattered, he does not exit like that, un-stuck. Therefore, *udenā* means by water (udakena).

"Kenaci Asucinā" Just as other beings, tossed into the birth canal by winds of karma, head downwards, experiencing great suffering like an elephant being dragged out through a hole made by a palm leaf, covered in various impurities, they exit; the Bodhisattva does not exit like that.

Indeed, the winds of karma cannot make the Bodhisattva head downwards.

He descends from the Dharma seat like a preacher, he descends from a ladder like a man, and having stretched out both his hands and both his feet, he stands, unsoiled by any impurity arising from his mother's womb, and exits.

"Udakassa Dhārā" means water circles.

Cool water falls in a golden bowl, warm water in a silver bowl.

And it is said that on the surface of the earth, unmixed with any impurity, there is water for drinking and eating, water for playing that is uncommon to others, but there is no limit to the water which is brought in golden and silver pots, nor to the water in ponds inhabited by swans, ducks, etc.

Udakassa Dhārā

mula_pali: 30. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, dve udakassa dhārā antalikkhā pātubhavanti – ekā sītassa ekā uṇhassa yena bodhisattassa udakakiccaṃ karonti mātu ca. Ayamettha dhammatā.
mula_english: “This is the rule, monks, that when a *bodhisatta* emerges from his mother's womb, two streams of water appear from the sky, one cold and one warm, with which they perform the water ritual for the *bodhisatta* and his mother. This is the natural law.

mula_pali: 31. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, sampatijāto bodhisatto samehi pādehi patiṭṭhahitvā uttarābhimukho uttarenābhimukho (syā.) uttarenamukho (ka.) sattapadavītihārena gacchati setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāne, sabbā ca disā anuviloketi, āsabhiṃ vācaṃ bhāsati ‘aggohamasmi lokassa, jeṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, seṭṭhohamasmi lokassa, ayamantimā jāti, natthidāni punabbhavo’ti. Ayamettha dhammatā.
mula_english: ‘This is the rule, monks, that as soon as he is born, the *bodhisattva* takes a firm stance with both feet, faces north, and proceeds with a stride of seven steps (*sattapadavītihārena*), while a white parasol is held over him. He surveys all directions and utters a bull-like speech (*āsabhiṃ vācaṃ bhāsati*): “I am the chief (*aggo*) in the world (*lokassa*), the eldest (*jeṭṭho*) in the world (*lokassa*), the best (*seṭṭho*) in the world (*lokassa*). This is my last birth (*antimā jāti*); now there is no more rebirth (*punabbhavo*)”. This is the natural law (*dharmatā*).’
commentary_pali:
31.Sampatijātoti muhuttajāto. Pāḷiyaṃ pana mātukucchito nikkhantamatto viya dassito, na evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nikkhantamattañhi naṃ paṭhamaṃ brahmāno suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, tesaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno ajinappaveṇiyā, tesaṃ hatthato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena. Manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhito. Setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāneti dibbasetacchatte anudhāriyamānamhi. Ettha ca chattassa parivārāni khaggādīni pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍānipi āgatāneva. Pāḷiyaṃ pana rājagamane rājā viya chattameva vuttaṃ. Tesu chattameva paññāyati, na chattaggāhako. Tathā khaggatālavaṇṭamorahatthakavāḷabījanīuṇhīsamattāyeva paññāyanti, na tesaṃ gāhakā. Sabbāni kira tāni adissamānarūpā devatā gaṇhiṃsu. Vuttañcetaṃ –

‘‘Anekasākhañca sahassamaṇḍalaṃ,

Chattaṃ marū dhārayumantalikkhe;

Suvaṇṇadaṇḍā vipatanti cāmarā,

Na dissare cāmarachattagāhakā’’ti. (su. ni. 693);

Sabbā ca disāti idaṃ sattapadavītihārūpari ṭhitassa viya sabbadisānuvilokanaṃ vuttaṃ, na kho panevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahāsatto hi manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā paṭhaviyaṃ patiṭṭhito puratthimaṃ disaṃ olokesi. Anekāni cakkavāḷasahassāni ekaṅgaṇāni ahesuṃ. Tattha devamanussā gandhamālādīhi pūjayamānā – ‘‘mahāpurisa, idha tumhehi sadisopi natthi, kuto uttaritaro’’ti āhaṃsu. Evaṃ catasso disā, catasso anudisā, heṭṭhā, uparīti dasa disā anuviloketvā attanā sadisaṃ adisvā – ‘‘ayaṃ uttarā disā’’ti uttarābhimukho sattapadavītihārena agamāsīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Āsabhinti uttamaṃ. Aggoti guṇehi sabbapaṭhamo. Itarāni dve padāni etasseva vevacanāni. Ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavoti padadvayena imasmiṃ attabhāve pattabbaṃ arahattaṃ byākāsi.

Sabbā ca disā Āsabhi Aggo Ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo

Ettha ca samehi pādehi pathaviyā patiṭṭhānaṃ caturiddhipādapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, uttarābhimukhabhāvo mahājanaṃ ajjhottharitvā abhibhavitvā gamanassa pubbanimittaṃ, sattapadagamanaṃ sattabojjhaṅgaratanapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, dibbasetacchattadhāraṇaṃ vimuttivarachattapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, pañcarājakakudhabhaṇḍānaṃ paṭilābho pañcahi vimuttīhi vimuccanassa pubbanimittaṃ, sabbadisānuvilokanaṃ anāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ, āsabhivācābhāsanaṃ appaṭivattiyadhammacakkappavattanassa pubbanimittaṃ, ‘‘ayamantimā jātī’’ti sīhanādo anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbānassa pubbanimittanti veditabbaṃ . Ime vārā pāḷiyaṃ āgatā, sambahulavāro pana nāgato, āharitvā dīpetabbo.

Mahāpurisassa hi jātadivase dasasahassilokadhātu kampi. Dasasahassilokadhātumhi devatā ekacakkavāḷe sannipatiṃsu. Paṭhamaṃ devā paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, pacchā manussā. Tantibaddhā vīṇā cammabaddhā bheriyo ca kenaci avāditā sayameva vajjiṃsu. Manussānaṃ andubandhanādīni khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ chijjiṃsu. Sabbarogā vūpasamiṃsu, ambilena dhotatambamalaṃ viya vigacchiṃsu. Jaccandhā rūpāni passiṃsu. Jaccabadhirā saddaṃ suṇiṃsu. Pīṭhasappī javasampannā ahesuṃ. Jātijaḷānampi eḷamūgānaṃ sati patiṭṭhāsi. Videsapakkhandā nāvā supaṭṭanaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Ākāsaṭṭhakabhūmaṭṭhakaratanāni sakatejobhāsitāni ahesuṃ. Verino mettacittaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Avīcimhi aggi nibbāyi. Lokantaresu āloko udapādi. Nadīsu jalaṃ nappavattati. Mahāsamudde madhurasaṃ udakaṃ ahosi. Vāto na vāyi. Ākāsapabbatarukkhagatā sakuṇā bhassitvā pathavigatā ahesuṃ. Cando ativiroci. Sūriyo na uṇho, na sītalo, nimmalo utusampanno ahosi. Devatā attano attano vimānadvāre ṭhatvā apphoṭanaseḷanacelukkhepādīhi mahākīḷakaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Cātuddīpikamahāmegho vassi. Mahājanaṃ neva khudā na pipāsā pīḷesi. Dvārakavāṭāni sayameva vivariṃsu. Pupphūpagaphalūpagā rukkhā pupphaphalāni gaṇhiṃsu. Dasasahassilokadhātu ekaddhajamālā ahosi.

Tatrāpi dasasahassilokadhātukampo sabbaññutaññāṇapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Devatānaṃ ekacakkavāḷe sannipāto dhammacakkappavattanakāle ekappahāreneva sannipatitvā dhammaṃ paṭiggaṇhanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ devatānaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ catunnaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ paṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Pacchā manussānaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ catunnaṃ arūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ paṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Tantibaddhavīṇānaṃ sayaṃ vajjanaṃ anupubbavihārapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Cammabaddhabherīnaṃ vajjanaṃ mahatiyā dhammabheriyā anussāvanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Andubandhanādīnaṃ chedo asmimānasamucchedassa pubbanimittaṃ. Mahājanassa rogavigamo catusaccapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Jaccandhānaṃ rūpadassanaṃ dibbacakkhupaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ . Badhirānaṃ saddassavanaṃ dibbasotadhātupaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Pīṭhasappīnaṃ javasampadā caturiddhipādapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Jaḷānaṃ satipatiṭṭhānaṃ catusatipaṭṭhānapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Videsapakkhandanāvānaṃ supaṭṭanasampāpuṇanaṃ catupaṭisambhidādhigamassa pubbanimittaṃ. Ratanānaṃ sakatejobhāsitattaṃ yaṃ lokassa dhammobhāsaṃ dassessati, tassa pubbanimittaṃ.

Verīnaṃ mettacittapaṭilābho catubrahmavihārapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Avīcimhi agginibbāyanaṃ ekādasaagginibbāyanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Lokantarikāloko avijjandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ñāṇālokadassanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Mahāsamuddassa madhuratā nibbānarasena ekarasabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Vātassa avāyanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatabhindanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Sakuṇānaṃ pathavigamanaṃ mahājanassa ovādaṃ sutvā pāṇehi saraṇagamanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Candassa ativirocanaṃ bahujanakantatāya pubbanimittaṃ. Sūriyassa uṇhasītavivajjanautusukhatā kāyikacetasikasukhappattiyā pubbanimittaṃ. Devatānaṃ vimānadvāresu ṭhatvā apphoṭanādīhi kīḷanaṃ buddhabhāvaṃ patvā udānaṃ udānassa pubbanimittaṃ. Cātuddīpikamahāmeghavassanaṃ mahato dhammameghavassanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Khudāpīḷanassa abhāvo kāyagatāsatiamatapaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Pipāsāpīḷanassa abhāvo vimuttisukhena sukhitabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Dvārakavāṭānaṃ sayameva vivaraṇaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikamaggadvāravivaraṇassa pubbanimittaṃ. Rukkhānaṃ pupphaphalaggahaṇaṃ vimuttipupphehi pupphitassa ca sāmaññaphalabhārabharitabhāvassa ca pubbanimittaṃ. Dasasahassilokadhātuyā ekaddhajamālitā ariyaddhajamālamālitāya pubbanimittanti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ sambahulavāro nāma.

Ettha pañhaṃ pucchanti – ‘‘yadā mahāpuriso pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā uttarābhimukho padasā gantvā āsabhiṃ vācaṃ abhāsi, tadā kiṃ pathaviyā gato, udāhu ākāsena; dissamāno gato, udāhu adissamāno; acelako gato, udāhu alaṅkatapaṭiyatto; daharo hutvā gato , udāhu mahallako; pacchāpi kiṃ tādisova ahosi, udāhu puna bāladārako’’ti? Ayaṃ pana pañho heṭṭhālohapāsāde samuṭṭhito tipiṭakacūḷābhayattherena vissajjitova. Thero kira ettha niyatipubbekatakammaissaranimmānavādavasena taṃ taṃ bahuṃ vatvā avasāne evaṃ byākari – ‘‘mahāpuriso pathaviyā gato, mahājanassa pana ākāsena gacchanto viya ahosi. Dissamāno gato, mahājanassa pana adissamāno viya ahosi. Acelako gato, mahājanassa pana alaṅkatapaṭiyatto viya upaṭṭhāsi. Daharova gato, mahājanassa pana soḷasavassuddesiko viya ahosi. Pacchā pana bāladārakova ahosi, na tādiso’’ti. Parisā cassa – ‘‘buddhena viya hutvā bho therena pañho kathito’’ti attamanā ahosi. Lokantarikavāro vuttanayo eva.

Imā ca pana ādito paṭṭhāya kathitā sabbadhammatā sabbabodhisattānaṃ hontīti veditabbā.

Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
31. *Sampatijāto* means born at that very moment. In the Pāḷi, however, it is shown as just having come out of the mother's womb; it should not be seen like that. For, immediately after he came out, the *Brahmās* received him in a golden net; from their hands the Four Great Kings ( *cattāro mahārājāno*) [received him] on antelope skins (*ajinappaveṇiyā*), from their hands men [received him] on a roll of fine cloth (*dukūlacumbaṭakena*). Having been freed from the hands of men, he stood on the earth. *"While a white umbrella was being held over [him]"* means while a divine white umbrella was being held over [him]. And here, the paraphernalia of the umbrella, swords and the like, and the five royal emblems came into being. In the Pāḷi, however, in the case of a king's procession, only the umbrella is mentioned as being like a king. Among these, only the umbrella is evident, not the umbrella-holder. Likewise, swords, palm-leaf fans, peacock-feather fans, hand fans, whisks, and head-dresses are evident, but not their holders. It is said that all those deities, whose forms are invisible, took [them]. And it was said: "And an *anekasākha* with a thousand circles, An umbrella the *Maruts* held in the sky; Golden rods and chowries fall, Chowrie and umbrella bearers are not seen." (Su. Ni. 693); *"And all directions"* means this looking around in all directions is said to be like [something] standing above the seven strides. However, it should not be seen like that. For the Great Being ( *mahāsatto*), having been freed from the hands of men and standing on the earth, looked at the eastern direction. Innumerable world-systems (*cakkavāḷasahassāni*) became a single courtyard. There, gods and men, honoring [him] with fragrant garlands and the like, said: "Great man (*mahāpurisa*), there is no one here equal to you, how could there be a superior?" In this way, having looked around at the four directions (*catasso disā*), the four intermediate directions (*catasso anudisā*), below, and above—ten directions—and not seeing anyone equal to himself, [he said], "This is the northern direction (*uttarā disā*)," and went northwards by the seven-stride gait. Thus, the meaning should be understood here. *"Āsabhi"* means the best (*uttamaṃ*). *"Aggo"* means the first of all in qualities (*guṇehi sabbapaṭhamo*). The other two words are synonyms for this very thing. *"This is my last birth, now there is no future existence"*—with this pair of words, he declared the state of an *arhat* to be attained in this very existence. And: *Sabbā ca disā āsabhi aggo ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo* Here, the standing on the earth with even feet is a preliminary sign of obtaining the four bases of supernormal power ( *caturiddhipāda*); the state of being facing north is a preliminary sign of going having overwhelmed and surpassed the great mass of people; the going of seven strides is a preliminary sign of obtaining the seven jewels of enlightenment factors ( *sattabojjhaṅgaratana*); the holding of the divine white umbrella is a preliminary sign of obtaining the umbrella of the best liberation ( *vimuttivarachatta*); the obtaining of the five royal emblems is a preliminary sign of being freed by the five liberations (*pañca vimutti*); the looking around in all directions is a preliminary sign of obtaining unobstructed knowledge ( *anāvaraṇañāṇa*); the speaking of the *āsabhi* speech is a preliminary sign of the turning of the wheel of the irreversible Dharma ( *appaṭivattiyadhamma cakka*); the lion's roar (*sīhanāda*) "This is my last birth" is to be known as a preliminary sign of the *parinirvāṇa* of the element of *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupādisesāya nibbānadhātu*). These turns have come in the Pāḷi, but the abundant turn has not come; it should be brought and explained. For, on the day of the Great Man's (*mahāpurisa*) birth, the ten-thousand world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*) trembled. In the ten-thousand world-system, the deities assembled in one *cakkavāḷa*. First the gods received him, afterwards men. Stringed lutes (*vīṇā*) and leather-covered drums (*bheriyo*) that were not played by anyone sounded by themselves. The bonds and so on of men were cut into pieces. All diseases were calmed; they disappeared like dirt on copper that has been washed with vinegar. Congenitally blind people saw forms (rūpāni). Congenitally deaf people heard sounds (saddaṃ). Well-fed people were endowed with swiftness (javasampannā). Mindfulness was established in even the inherently dull and mute (jātijaḷānampi eḷamūgānaṃ sati patiṭṭhāsi). Immigrant boats reached a good harbor (supaṭṭanaṃ). Jewels in the sky and on the earth shone with their own brilliance (sakatejobhāsitāni). Enemies obtained minds of loving-kindness (mettacittaṃ). Fire went out in Avīci Hell (avīcimhi aggi nibbāyi). Light arose in other worlds (lokantaresu āloko udapādi). Water did not flow in the rivers (nadīsu jalaṃ nappavattati). Sweet-tasting water existed in the great ocean (mahāsamudde madhurasaṃ udakaṃ ahosi). The wind did not blow (vāto na vāyi). Birds in the sky, on mountains, and in trees, having chirped, went to the earth (ākāsapabbatarukkhagatā sakuṇā bhassitvā pathavigatā ahesuṃ). The moon shone exceedingly (cando ativiroci). The sun was not hot, not cold, pure, and endowed with the season (sūriyo na uṇho, na sītalo, nimmalo utusampanno ahosi). Gods, standing at the doors of their own palaces (attano attano vimānadvāre ṭhatvā), played a great game with clapping, making noises, tossing up their garments, and so forth (apphoṭanaseḷanacelukkhepādīhi mahākīḷakaṃ kīḷiṃsu). A four-continent great cloud rained (cātuddīpikamahāmegho vassi). Neither hunger nor thirst afflicted the great multitude (mahājanaṃ neva khudā na pipāsā pīḷesi). The doors and gates opened by themselves (dvārakavāṭāni sayameva vivariṃsu). Trees bearing flowers and fruits took flowers and fruits (pupphūpagaphalūpagā rukkhā pupphaphalāni gaṇhiṃsu). The ten-thousand world-system was a single-banner garland (dasasahassilokadhātu ekaddhajamālā ahosi). Even there, the shaking of the ten-thousand world-system was a preliminary sign of the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa). The gathering of the gods in a single *cakravāḷa* at the time of the turning of the wheel of the Dharma, having gathered together with a single strike, was a preliminary sign of receiving the Dharma. The first reception of the gods was a preliminary sign of the attainment of the four *rūpāvacara jhānā* (catunnaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ paṭilābhassa). Afterwards, the reception of humans was a preliminary sign of the attainment of the four *arūpāvacara jhānā* (catunnaṃ arūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ paṭilābhassa). The playing of stringed lutes by themselves was a preliminary sign of the attainment of successive dwelling. The playing of leather-bound kettle drums was a preliminary sign of the proclamation of the great Dharma-kettle drum. The cutting of elephant-chains and so forth was a preliminary sign of the destruction of conceit in "I am." The disappearance of disease from the great multitude was a preliminary sign of the attainment of the four truths (catusacca). The seeing of forms by the congenitally blind was a preliminary sign of the attainment of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu). The hearing of sounds by the deaf was a preliminary sign of the attainment of the divine ear-element (dibbasotadhātu). The swiftness of well-fed people was a preliminary sign of the attainment of the four bases of miraculous power (*caturiddhipāda*). The mindfulness established in the dull was a preliminary sign of the attainment of the four establishments of mindfulness (*catusatipaṭṭhāna*). The good attainment of harbors by immigrant boats was a preliminary sign of the mastery of the four kinds of analytical knowledge (*catupaṭisambhidādhigama*). The self-shining of the jewels, which will show the light of the Dharma to the world, was a preliminary sign of that. 0441"/>

The attainment of loving-kindness ( *mettā*) is a preliminary sign of the attainment of the four Brahmā-vihāras. The extinguishing of fire in Avīci is a preliminary sign of the extinguishing of the eleven fires. The light of the world-in-between, after dispelling the darkness of ignorance, is a preliminary sign of seeing the light of knowledge (*ñāṇā*) The sweetness of the great ocean is a preliminary sign of the single taste of *nibbāna*. The blowing of the wind is a preliminary sign of shattering the sixty-two kinds of [false] views. The birds going to the earth is a preliminary sign of the multitude, having heard the advice, going for refuge with their lives. The excessive brilliance of the moon is a preliminary sign of being pleasing to many people. The agreeable seasonal comfort of the sun, devoid of heat and cold, is a preliminary sign of the attainment of bodily and mental happiness (*sukha*). The gods, standing at the doors of the mansions, playing with hand-clapping etc., having attained the state of a Buddha, the utterance [of joy] is a preliminary sign of the utterance. The raining of the great cloud in the four continents is a preliminary sign of the raining of the great Dharma cloud. The absence of suffering from hunger is a preliminary sign of the attainment of mindfulness related to the body and the immortal. The absence of suffering from thirst is a preliminary sign of the state of being happy with the bliss of liberation (*vimutti*). The spontaneous opening of the door panels is a preliminary sign of the opening of the door of the eightfold path. The trees taking flowers and fruits is a preliminary sign of being flowered with the flowers of liberation and the state of being filled with the burden of the fruits of asceticism. The ten-thousand world-system being arrayed with a single flag is to be known as a preliminary sign of being arrayed with a garland of noble flags. This is called the Discourse on a Multitude of Occurrences.

Here they ask a question - "When the great man, having stood on the earth, having gone northwards on foot, spoke the bull-like speech, then did he go on the earth, or in the sky; did he go visibly, or invisibly; did he go naked, or adorned and prepared; did he go young , or old; afterwards also was he just like that, or again a young boy?" This question, however, having arisen in the Lower Copper Palace, was solved by Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya Thera. The Elder, there, having said much about the doctrine of fate, past action, the Lord, and creation, in the end, he declared thus - "The great man went on the earth, but to the multitude, he was as if going in the sky. He went visibly, but to the multitude, he was as if invisible. He went naked, but to the multitude, he appeared as if adorned and prepared. He went young, but to the multitude, he was as if sixteen years old. Afterwards, however, he was a young boy, not like that." And his assembly was delighted, saying - "The question was spoken by the Elder, as if having become a Buddha." The discourse on the world-in-between is as already stated.

These, however, all the qualities of the Dharma spoken from the beginning, are to be known as belonging to all Bodhisattvas.

Description of the Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man

mula_pali:
32. ‘‘Dhammatā esā, bhikkhave, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, atha sadevake loke samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya appamāṇo uḷāro obhāso pātubhavati, atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Yāpi tā lokantarikā aghā asaṃvutā andhakārā andhakāratimisā, yattha pime candimasūriyā evaṃmahiddhikā evaṃmahānubhāvā ābhāya nānubhonti, tatthapi appamāṇo uḷāro obhāso pātubhavati atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Yepi tattha sattā upapannā, tepi tenobhāsena aññamaññaṃ sañjānanti – ‘aññepi kira, bho, santi sattā idhūpapannā’ti. Ayañca dasasahassī lokadhātu saṅkampati sampakampati sampavedhati appamāṇo ca uḷāro obhāso loke pātubhavati atikkammeva devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ. Ayamettha dhammatā.

Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇā
mula_english:
32. It is the rule (*dharmatā*), monks, that when a *bodhisattva* departs from his mother’s womb, then in this world with its deities (*sadevake loke*), with *Māras* (*samārake*), with *Brahmās* (*sabrahmake*), with its ascetics and Brahmins (*sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā*), with its princes and people (*sadevamanussāya*), an immeasurable, splendid light (*appamāṇo uḷāro obhāso*) appears, surpassing the glory of the gods (*devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ*).

And whatever dark spaces lie beyond the world’s end (*lokantarikā*), chaotic (*aghā*), blind and black (*asaṃvutā andhakārā andhakāratimisā*), such that they are not even reached by the moon and the sun (*candimasūriyā*) so mighty and powerful (*evaṃmahiddhikā evaṃmahānubhāvā ābhāya nānubhonti*), are yet illumined by this immeasurable splendid light (*appamāṇo uḷāro obhāso*) surpassing the glory of the gods (*devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ*).

And those beings that have been reborn there (*tatra sattā upapannā*) recognise each other by this light (*tenobhāsena aññamaññaṃ sañjānanti*) and know: “Other beings, too, have been born here (*aññepi kira, bho, santi sattā idhūpapannā*)!”

And this ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassī lokadhātu*) shakes and quakes and trembles (*saṅkampati sampakampati sampavedhati*), and there too a great immeasurable light (*appamāṇo ca uḷāro obhāso*) surpassing the splendour of the gods (*devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ*) appears in the world (*loke pātubhavati*).

This is the natural law (*ayamettha dhammatā*).

The Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man (*dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇā*)

mula_pali: 33. ‘‘Jāte kho pana, bhikkhave, vipassimhi kumāre bandhumato rañño paṭivedesuṃ – ‘putto te, deva deva te (ka.), jāto, taṃ devo passatū’ti. Addasā kho, bhikkhave, bandhumā rājā vipassiṃ kumāraṃ, disvā nemitte brāhmaṇe āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘passantu bhonto nemittā brāhmaṇā kumāra’nti. Addasaṃsu kho, bhikkhave, nemittā brāhmaṇā vipassiṃ kumāraṃ, disvā bandhumantaṃ rājānaṃ etadavocuṃ – ‘attamano, deva, hohi, mahesakkho te putto uppanno, lābhā te, mahārāja, suladdhaṃ te, mahārāja, yassa te kule evarūpo putto uppanno. Ayañhi, deva, kumāro dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato. Tassimāni sattaratanāni bhavanti. Seyyathidaṃ – cakkaratanaṃ hatthiratanaṃ assaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ itthiratanaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṃ. Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasati. Sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭacchado.
mula_english:
33. Monks, when Prince Vipassi was born, they reported to King Bandhuma: "A son is born to you, O King, may the King see him."

Then, monks, King Bandhuma saw Prince Vipassi, and having seen him, summoned the Brahmins skilled in interpreting signs and said this: "Let the honorable Brahmins skilled in signs examine the prince."

Then, monks, the Brahmins skilled in signs examined Prince Vipassi, and having seen him, said this to King Bandhuma: "Rejoice, O King, be happy, a mighty son has been born to you. It is a gain for you, Great King, a great gain for you, Great King, that such a son has been born into your family.

Indeed, O King, this prince is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man (dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato), and for a great man endowed with these, there are only two possible destinies (dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā).

If he lives the household life, he will be a king, a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī), a righteous king (dhammarājā), a conqueror of the four quarters (cāturanto), a subjugator, who has attained stability in his country and is possessed of the seven treasures (sattaratanasamannāgato).

These are the seven treasures (sattaratanāni bhavanti):

namely, the wheel treasure (cakkaratanaṃ), the elephant treasure (hatthiratanaṃ), the horse treasure (assaratanaṃ), the jewel treasure (maṇiratanaṃ), the woman treasure (itthiratanaṃ), the householder treasure (gahapatiratanaṃ), and the counselor treasure (pariṇāyakaratanameva), as the seventh.

He has more than a thousand sons, who are brave (sūrā), heroic (vīraṅgarūpā), and crush the armies of others (parasenappamaddanā).

He dwells having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean, without stick or sword, by the Dharma (dhammena).

But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness (agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati), he becomes an Arhat (arahaṃ hoti), a Fully Enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddho), one who draws back the veil in the world (loke vivaṭacchado)."
commentary_pali:
33.Addasa khoti dukūlacumbaṭake nipajjāpetvā ānītaṃ addasa. Mahāpurisassāti jātigottakulapadesādivasena mahantassa purisassa. Dve gatiyoti dve niṭṭhā, dve nipphattiyo. Ayañhi gatisaddo – ‘‘pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo’’ti (ma. ni. 1.153) ettha nirayādibhedāya sattehi gantabbagatiyā vattati. ‘‘Imesaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ kalyāṇadhammānaṃ neva jānāmi āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vā’’ti (ma. ni. 1.508) ettha ajjhāsaye. ‘‘Nibbānaṃ arahato gatī’’ti (pari. 339) ettha paṭissaraṇe. ‘‘Api ca tyāhaṃ brahme gatiñca pajānāmi, jutiñca pajānāmi evaṃmahiddhiko bako brahmā’’ti (ma. ni. 1.503) ettha nipphattiyaṃ vattati. Svāyamidhāpi nipphattiyaṃ vattatīti veditabbo. Anaññāti aññā gati nipphatti nāma natthi.

Dhammikoti dasakusaladhammasamannāgato agatigamanavirahito. Dhammarājāti idaṃ purimapadasseva vevacanaṃ. Dhammena vā laddharajjattā dhammarājā. Cāturantoti puratthimasamuddādīnaṃ catunnaṃ samuddānaṃ vasena caturantāya pathaviyā issaro. Vijitāvīti vijitasaṅgāmo. Janapado asmiṃ thāvariyaṃ thirabhāvaṃ pattoti janapadatthāvariyappatto. Caṇḍassa hi rañño balidaṇḍādīhi lokaṃ pīḷayato manussā majjhimajanapadaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbatasamuddatīrādīni nissāya paccante vāsaṃ kappenti. Atimudukassa rañño corehi sāhasikadhanavilopapīḷitā manussā paccantaṃ pahāya janapadamajjhe vāsaṃ kappenti, iti evarūpe rājini janapado thirabhāvaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Imasmiṃ pana kumāre rajjaṃ kārayamāne etassa janapado pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapetvā ayopaṭṭena parikkhitto viya thiro bhavissatīti dassento – ‘‘janapadatthāvariyappatto’’ti āhaṃsu.

Dhammiko Dhammarājā Cāturanto Vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto.

Sattaratanasamannāgatoti ettha ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Apica –

Sattaratanasamannāgato ratanaṃ.

‘‘Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccati’’.

Cakkaratanassa ca nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya aññaṃ devaṭṭhānaṃ nāma na hoti, sabbe gandhapupphādīhi tasseva pūjañca abhivādanādīni ca karontīti cittīkataṭṭhena ratanaṃ. Cakkaratanassa ca ettakaṃ nāma dhanaṃ agghatīti aggho natthi, iti mahagghaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Cakkaratanañca aññehi loke vijjamānaratanehi asadisanti atulaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Yasmā ca pana yasmiṃ kappe buddhā uppajjanti, tasmiṃyeva cakkavattino uppajjanti, buddhā ca kadāci karahaci uppajjanti, tasmā dullabhadassanaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Tadetaṃ jātirūpakulaissariyādīhi anomassa uḷārasattasseva uppajjati, na aññassāti anomasattaparibhogaṭṭhenāpi ratanaṃ. Yathā cakkaratanaṃ, evaṃ sesānipīti. Imehi sattahi ratanehi parivārabhāvena ceva sabbabhogūpakaraṇabhāvena ca samannāgatoti sattaratanasamannāgato.

Idāni tesaṃ sarūpato dassanatthaṃ tassimānītiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha cakkaratanantiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepādhippāyo – dvesahassadīpaparivārānaṃ catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ sirivibhavaṃ gahetvā dātuṃ samatthaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavati. Tathā purebhattameva sāgarapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anusaṃyāyanasamatthaṃ vehāsaṅgamaṃ hatthiratanaṃ, tādisameva assaratanaṃ, caturaṅgasamannāgate andhakāre yojanappamāṇaṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā ālokadassanasamatthaṃ maṇiratanaṃ, chabbidhadosavivajjitaṃ manāpacāri itthiratanaṃ, yojanappamāṇe antopathavigataṃ nidhiṃ dassanasamatthaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ, aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā sakalarajjamanusāsanasamatthaṃ jeṭṭhaputtasaṅkhātaṃ pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pātubhavati.

tassimānī cakkaratana hatthiratanaṃ, assaratanaṃ, maṇiratanaṃ, itthiratanaṃ, gahapatiratanaṃ, pariṇāyakaratanaṃ

Parosahassanti atirekasahassaṃ. Sūrāti abhīrukā. Vīraṅgarūpāti vīrānaṃ aṅgaṃ vīraṅgaṃ, vīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ, vīraṅgaṃ rūpametesanti vīraṅgarūpā, vīriyajātikā vīriyasabhāvā vīriyamayā akilāsuno ahesuṃ. Divasampi yujjhantā na kilamantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāgarapariyantanti cakkavāḷapabbataṃ sīmaṃ katvā ṭhitasamuddapariyantaṃ. Adaṇḍenāti ye katāparādhe satte satampi sahassampi gaṇhanti, te dhanadaṇḍena rajjaṃ kārenti. Ye chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsanti, te satthadaṇḍena. Ayaṃ pana duvidhampi daṇḍaṃ pahāya adaṇḍena ajjhāvasati. Asatthenāti ye ekatodhārādinā satthena paraṃ vihesanti, te satthena rajjaṃ kārenti nāma. Ayaṃ pana satthena khuddamakkhikāyapi pivanamattaṃ lohitaṃ kassaci anuppādetvā dhammeneva – ‘‘ehi kho mahārājā’’ti evaṃ paṭirājūhi sampaṭicchitāgamano vuttappakāraṃ pathaviṃ abhivijinitvā ajjhāvasati, abhibhavitvā sāmī hutvā vasatīti attho.

Parosahassa Sūrā Vīraṅgarūpā Sāgarapariyanta Adaṇḍenā Asatthenā

Evaṃ ekaṃ nipphattiṃ kathetvā dutiyaṃ kathetuṃ sace kho panātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhikilesataṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ chadanaṃ āvaraṇaṃ vivaṭaṃ viddhaṃsitaṃ vivaṭakaṃ etenāti vivaṭacchado. ‘‘Vivaṭṭacchadā’’tipi pāṭho, ayameva attho.

sace kho panā vivaṭacchado.
commentary_english:
33. "Addasa kho" means he saw, he saw the one brought after being laid down on a dukūla mat. "Mahāpurisassa" means of a great man (mahāpurisa), due to birth, lineage, family, place, and so forth. "Dve gatiyo" means two conclusions, two accomplishments. Now, this word *gati* [means] – "There are these five destinations, Sāriputta" (Majjhima Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.153). Here, *gati* refers to the destination to be reached by beings, for example, the various hells. "Imesaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ kalyāṇadhammānaṃ neva jānāmi āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vā" (Majjhima Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.508) refers to their inclinations. "Nibbānaṃ arahato gatī" (Pāri 339) refers to relying [on something]. "Api ca tyāhaṃ brahme gatiñca pajānāmi, jutiñca pajānāmi evaṃmahiddhiko bako Brahmā" (Majjhima Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.503) is related to the accomplishment [of something]. It should be understood that here too, it relates to accomplishment. "Anaññā" means there is no other *gati*, accomplishment is just a name. "Dhammiko" means possessing the ten wholesome qualities, free from going to bad destinations. "Dhammarājā" means this is a synonym of the preceding word. Or, because the Dharma King (dhammarājā) has obtained sovereignty through the Dharma. "Cāturanto" means the lord of the earth (pathavī) bounded by the four oceans, beginning with the eastern ocean, on account of the four oceans. "Vijitāvī" means victorious in battle (vijitasaṅgāmo). *Janapada* having attained stability in this *thāvariya* means *janapadatthāvariyappatto*: one who has achieved stability in the territory. Indeed, when a cruel king oppresses the world with forced levies and punishments, people abandon the central region (majjhimajanapada) and, relying on mountains, seashores, and the like, they establish their homes in outlying regions. When a very gentle king is oppressed by thieves who violently plunder wealth, people abandon the outlying regions and establish their homes in the central region. Thus, the territory does not attain stability in such a king's reign. However, when this prince makes the kingdom function, showing that his territory will be as stable as if it were placed on a stone slab and surrounded by an iron fence, they said, "He has achieved stability in the territory (janapadatthāvariyappatto)." *Dhammiko, Dhammarājā, Cāturanto, Vijitāvī, Janapadatthāvariyappatto.* "Sattaratanasamannāgato" means here, *ratana* [means] because of producing delight. Moreover– *Sattaratanasamannāgato ratanaṃ.* ‘‘Adorned, very valuable, incomparable, rarely seen; The non-common enjoyment of beings, therefore it is called *ratana*." And from the time of the arising of the wheel-jewel (cakkaratana), there is no other place of the gods, all make offerings and pay homage to it with fragrances, flowers, and the like. Therefore *ratana* [means] adorned. And the value of the wheel-jewel is such that... There is no price for a jewel. And the wheel-jewel is dissimilar to other jewels existing in the world, therefore it is a jewel because of its matchlessness. And since in whatever *kappa* Buddhas arise, in that very one *cakravartins* arise, and Buddhas arise only rarely, therefore it is a jewel because it is rarely seen. This arises only for an excellent being who is uncommon due to birth, appearance, family, and power, and not for another; therefore it is a jewel because an uncommon being enjoys it. Just as the wheel-jewel, so are the remaining ones. Because he is endowed with these seven jewels as retinue and as means of enjoying all possessions, [he is called] one who is endowed with the seven jewels (*sattaratnasamannāgata*).

Now, in order to show their specific forms, it is said, "These are..." There, in the [passages] beginning with "wheel-jewel," this is the abbreviated intention: the wheel jewel appears capable of taking the splendor and wealth of the four great islands that are surrounded by two thousand islands and giving it [to the *cakravartin*]. Likewise, the elephant-jewel (*hastiratna*) is capable of travelling over the earth up to the edge of the sea in time for the morning meal and moves through the sky; similarly, the horse-jewel (*aśvaratna*); the jewel-gem (*maṇiratna*) is capable of dispelling the darkness measuring a *yojana* and giving a view of light; the woman-jewel (*strīratna*) is free from six kinds of faults and behaves agreeably; the householder-jewel (*gṛhapatiratna*) is capable of showing the treasure hidden beneath the earth measuring a *yojana*; the counselor-jewel (*pariṇāyakaratna*), reckoned as the eldest son, having arisen in the womb of the chief queen, is capable of ruling the entire kingdom. These are the wheel-jewel (*cakkaratana*), elephant-jewel (*hastiratna*), horse-jewel (*aśvaratna*), jewel-gem (*maṇiratna*), woman-jewel (*strīratna*), householder-jewel (*gṛhapatiratna*), and counselor-jewel (*pariṇāyakaratna*). The phrase *parosahassanti* means more than a thousand. *Sūrā* means fearless. *Vīraṅgarūpā* means *vīrānaṃ aṅgaṃ vīraṅgaṃ*, this is a name for energy; *vīraṅgaṃ rūpametesanti vīraṅgarūpā*, they were energetic by birth, energetic by nature, made of energy, and untiring. It is said that even fighting during the day, they did not get tired. *Sāgarapariyanta* means up to the ocean which stands having made the *cakravāḷa* mountain the boundary. *Adaṇḍenā* means those who seize beings who have committed offenses, even a hundred or a thousand [lashes], they rule the kingdom with the punishment of wealth. Those who instruct what should be cut and what should be broken, [do so] with the punishment of the weapon. But this one, having abandoned even the two kinds of punishment, dwells without punishment. *Asatthenā* means those who injure others with a weapon, beginning with a single-edged sword, they rule the kingdom with the weapon. But this one, without producing even as much blood as the drinking of a small fly with a weapon, having conquered the earth in the manner described by *dharma* alone – "Come, great king!" – [and] whose arrival is welcomed by rival kings, dwells, having overcome [them], he lives as their lord, this is the meaning. *Parosahassa, sūrā, vīraṅgarūpā, sāgarapariyanta, adaṇḍenā, asatthenā* Thus, having spoken of one accomplishment, in order to speak of the second, it is said, "*Sace kho panā*, etc." There, *rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhikilesataṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ chadanaṃ āvaraṇaṃ vivaṭaṃ viddhaṃsitaṃ vivaṭakaṃ etenāti vivaṭacchado* means that with which covering, obstruction, openness, destruction, and the state of being uncovered, which are reckoned as passion, hatred, delusion, pride, [wrong] views, defilements, and craving, [are removed]. There is also a reading "*vivaṭṭacchadā*," this is the very meaning. *Sace kho panā vivaṭacchado*.

mula_pali: 34. ‘Katamehi cāyaṃ, deva, kumāro dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi samannāgato, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāpī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato. Tassimāni sattaratanāni bhavanti . Seyyathidaṃ – cakkaratanaṃ hatthiratanaṃ assaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ itthiratanaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṃ. Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasati. Sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭacchado.
mula_english:
‘And what, Sire, are these thirty-two marks with which the prince is endowed, due to which a great man has only two possible destinies?

If he lives the householder's life, he becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch ( *cakravartin*), a righteous king (*dhārmika dharmarājā*) who rules by the Dharma, master of the four quarters (*cāturanta*), all-victorious (*vijitāpī*), who has stabilised his country (*janapadatthāvariyappatto*) and possesses the seven treasures (*sattaratanasamannāgato*).

He has these seven treasures (*sattaratnāni*):

namely: the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratanaṃ*), the Elephant-Treasure (*hatthiratanaṃ*), the Horse-Treasure (*assaratanaṃ*), the Jewel-Treasure (*maṇiratanaṃ*), the Woman-Treasure (*itthiratanaṃ*), the Householder-Treasure (*gahapatiratanaṃ*), and the Counsellor-Treasure (*pariṇāyakaratanameva*) as the seventh.

His sons, who exceed a thousand (*parosahassaṃ*), are brave (*śūrā*), heroic (*vīraṅgarūpā*), and crush the armies of others (*parasenappamaddanā*).

He dwells having conquered this sea-girt land (*sāgarapariyantaṃ*) without stick (*adaṇḍena*) or sword (*asatthena*), by the Dharma (*dhammena*).

But if he goes forth from the householder's life (*agārasmā*) into homelessness (*anagāriyaṃ*), then he will become an *Arhat* (*arahaṃ*), a Fully Enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddho*), one who draws back the veil (*vivaṭacchado*) from the world.

35. Indeed, O deva, this prince has feet with level tread ( *supratiṣṭhitapāda*).

Whatever place he treads, O deva, this prince has feet with level tread ( *supratiṣṭhitapāda*).

This is, for this great man ( *mahāpurisa*), a mark of a great man ( *mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ*).

O deva, beneath this prince's feet, on the soles of his feet, wheels ( *cakka* ) have arisen, with a thousand spokes ( *sahassāra* ), with rims ( *sanemika* ), with hubs ( *sanābhika* ), complete in every way ( *sabbākāraparipūra* ).

And again, O deva, beneath this prince's feet, on the soles of his feet, wheels ( *cakka* ) have arisen, with a thousand spokes ( *sahassāra* ), with rims ( *sanemika* ), with hubs ( *sanābhika* ), complete in every way ( *sabbākāraparipūra* ), this is, for this great man ( *mahāpurisa*), a mark of a great man ( *mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ*).

commentary_pali:
35. Evaṃ dutiyaṃ nipphattiṃ kathetvā tāsaṃ nimittabhūtāni lakkhaṇāni dassetuṃ ayañhi, deva, kumārotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha suppatiṭṭhitapādoti yathā aññesaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pādaṃ ṭhapentānaṃ aggapādatalaṃ vā paṇhi vā passaṃ vā paṭhamaṃ phusati, vemajjhe vā pana chiddaṃ hoti, ukkhipantānaṃ aggatalādīsu ekakoṭṭhāsova paṭhamaṃ uṭṭhahati, na evamassa. Assa pana suvaṇṇapādukatalamiva ekappahāreneva sakalaṃ pādatalaṃ bhūmiṃ phusati, ekappahāreneva bhūmito uṭṭhahati. Tasmā ayaṃ suppatiṭṭhitapādo.

Cakkānīti dvīsu pādatalesu dve cakkāni, tesaṃ arā ca nemi ca nābhi ca pāḷiyaṃ vuttāva. Sabbākāraparipūrānīti iminā pana ayaṃ viseso veditabbo, tesaṃ kira cakkānaṃ pādatalassa majjhe nābhi dissati, nābhiparicchinnā vaṭṭalekhā dissati, nābhimukhaparikkhepapaṭṭo dissati, panāḷimukhaṃ dissati, arā dissanti, aresu vaṭṭilekhā dissanti, nemimaṇikā dissanti. Idaṃ tāva pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva. Sambahulavāro pana anāgato, so evaṃ daṭṭhabbo – satti, sirivaccho, nandi, sovattiko, vaṭaṃsako, vaḍḍhamānakaṃ, macchayugaḷaṃ, bhaddapīṭhaṃ, aṅkusako, pāsādo, toraṇaṃ, setacchattaṃ, khaggo, tālavaṇṭaṃ, morahatthako, vāḷabījanī, uṇhīsaṃ, maṇi, patto, sumanadāmaṃ, nīluppalaṃ, rattuppalaṃ, setuppalaṃ, padumaṃ, puṇḍarīkaṃ, puṇṇaghaṭo , puṇṇapāti, samuddo, cakkavāḷo, himavā, sineru, candimasūriyā, nakkhattāni, cattāro mahādīpā, dviparittadīpasahassāni, antamaso cakkavattirañño parisaṃ upādāya sabbo cakkalakkhaṇasseva parivāro.

Cakkānī Sabbākāraparipūrānī

Āyatapaṇhīti dīghapaṇhi, paripuṇṇapaṇhīti attho. Yathā hi aññesaṃ aggapādo dīgho hoti, paṇhimatthake jaṅghā patiṭṭhāti, paṇhiṃ tacchetvā ṭhapitā viya hoti, na evaṃ mahāpurisassa. Mahāpurisassa pana catūsu koṭṭhāsesu dve koṭṭhāsā aggapādo hoti, tatiye koṭṭhāse jaṅghā patiṭṭhāti, catutthakoṭṭhāse āraggena vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitā viya rattakambalageṇḍukasadisā paṇhi hoti.
