The prince, having paid homage to the Blessed One, exchanged friendly greetings.
“When did you come, Prince?” “Venerable sir, when you had entered the Fragrant Cottage.”
The monks, however – “We do not obtain [the chance] to see the Blessed One at any moment we wish” – sent me to the Elder’s presence.
The Elder, however, showed [him] with just one word.
“That Elder, venerable sir, is esteemed in your teaching.”
“Yes, Prince, that monk is esteemed in my teaching.”
“Venerable sir, having done what in the Buddhas’ teaching does one become esteemed?” “By giving a gift, by undertaking moral conduct, by performing the uposatha act, Prince.”
“Blessed One, like that Elder, I wish to be esteemed in the Buddhas’ teaching; may you consent to my rains-residence for three months!”
The Blessed One – “Is there any purpose by going there?” – having looked over and seeing that there was a purpose, said, “In an empty dwelling, Prince, the *tathāgatas* delight.”
The prince, saying, “Understood, Blessed One! Understood, Sugata!” said, “Venerable sir, I shall go first and have a *vihāra* made; may you come together with a hundred thousand monks sent by me!” Having taken the promise, having gone to his father’s presence, [he said,] “A promise has been given to me, Sire, by the Blessed One; may you send the Blessed One when [he is] sent by me!” Having paid homage to his father, and having departed, having had a *vihāra* made at each *yojana*, having gone a distance of twenty hundred *yojanas*, while seeking a site for a *vihāra* in his own city, having seen a park of a householder named Sobhana, having bought it for a hundred thousand, having spent a hundred thousand, he had a *vihāra* made.
There, having had a Fragrant Cottage made for the Blessed One, and *kuṭi* and *leṇa* and *maṇḍapa* made for the remaining monks for the purpose of a night-place and a day-place, having made an enclosure of walls, and also having finished a gate-tower, he sent [word] to his father’s presence, “My task is finished; may you send the Teacher!”

The king, having fed the Blessed One, said, “Blessed One, Sumana’s task is finished; he awaits your going.”
The Blessed One, surrounded by a hundred thousand monks, while dwelling in *vihāras* at each *yojana*, went.
The prince, having heard “The Teacher has come!” having gone forth to meet [him] for a *yojana*, while honouring [him] with garlands and so on, having led [him] into the *vihāra* –
“By a hundred thousand was it bought by me, by a hundred thousand was it built;
The park named Sobhana, receive [it], Great Sage!”
He gave the *vihāra*.
Then, on the day of entering the rains retreat, having given alms, he summoned his sons and wives and ministers and said: “This Teacher has come from afar to our presence, and Buddhas are, by nature, reverent of the Dhamma, not reverent of material things. Therefore, having worn two robes for three months, having undertaken the ten precepts, I will dwell right here. You should give alms for three months to a hundred thousand who have destroyed the āsavas with this same method."

Dwelling in a place that was in the same portion as the dwelling place of the Elder Sumanatthera, seeing all the duties that the Elder performed for the Blessed One, he thought, "In this place, this Elder is exceedingly beloved. It is fitting for me to desire this rank after him." Approaching the end of the rains retreat, having entered the village, having given a great alms for seven days, on the seventh day, having placed a triple robe at the feet of a hundred thousand bhikkhus, having worshipped the Blessed One, he said, "Venerable Sir, whatever merit I have done, starting from when I had monasteries built every yojana along the road, I did not do it desiring the wealth of Sakka, nor the wealth of Māra, nor the wealth of Brahmā, but desiring the state of being an attendant to the Buddha. Therefore, may I also, O Blessed One, in the future, be an attendant to the Buddha, like the Elder Sumanatthera." Having fallen down with the fivefold prostration, he worshipped.

The Blessed One, looking to see, "Is the mind of the clansman great? Will it succeed or not?" knowing, "In the future, after a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, he will be his attendant," said:

"May all your desired wishes be fulfilled; may all your intentions be fulfilled, like the moon on the fifteenth day."

Having heard that, the youth thought, "Buddhas speak words that are unwavering," and from the second day itself, taking the bowl and robe of that Blessed One, he was as if going behind him.

In that arising of a Buddha, having given alms for a hundred thousand years, having been reborn in heaven, even in the time of Kassapa Buddha, he gave an upper robe to the Elder who was walking for alms, for the purpose of taking his bowl, and made an offering. Again, having been reborn in heaven, having passed away from there, having become the king of Bārāṇasī, having had leaf huts made for eight Paccekabuddhas, having had jewel stands set up, he attended to them for ten thousand years with the four requisites. These are the obvious places.

However, giving alms for a hundred thousand aeons, having been reborn with our Bodhisatta in the Tusita heaven, having passed away from there, having taken rebirth in the house of Amitodana Sakka, having gradually made his renunciation, having attained perfect enlightenment, having come to Kapilavatthu on his first journey, when the Blessed One was leaving from there, when princes were ordained among the royal princes for the sake of the Blessed One's retinue, having left with Bhaddiya and others, having been ordained in the presence of the Blessed One, not long after, having heard a Dhamma talk from the venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (Saṃ. Ni. 3.83). In this way, this venerable one, endowed with prior supporting conditions, because of that attainment of prior supporting conditions, even the profound dependent origination appeared to him as if it were shallow.

Description of dwelling in a sacred place, etc.

Dwelling in a sacred place means the repeated learning, hearing, questioning, and holding in mind in the presence of teachers. That was exceedingly pure for the Elder; therefore, even the profound dependent origination appeared to him as if it were shallow.

For stream-enterers, the mode of conditionality appears as if it were shallow; and this venerable one is a stream-enterer. And for those who have heard much, the delineation of name and form is clear, like a couch or chair in a four-handed room with a lamp burning; and this venerable one is foremost among those who have heard much. Even because of the power of much learning, the profound mode of conditionality appeared to him as if it were shallow.

The Profundity of Dependent Origination

There, dependent origination is called profound in four ways: profundity of meaning (attha), profundity of the Dhamma, profundity of teaching (desanā), and profundity of realization (paṭivedha).

There, the profound meaning is that old age and death are born from the condition of birth...and the profound meaning is that volitional formations are born from the condition of ignorance.

The profound Dhamma is that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations...and birth is the condition for old age and death.

The profound teaching is that in some suttas, dependent origination is taught in forward order, in some in reverse order, in some in both forward and reverse order, in some beginning from the middle in forward or reverse or both forward and reverse order, in some three connections and four groupings, in some two connections and three groupings, in some one connection and two groupings.

Furthermore, the profound realization is that ignorance is the state of not knowing, not seeing, and not penetrating the truth; the profound volitional formations are the state of constructing, planning, being colored, and being uncolored; the profound consciousness is the state of emptiness, inactivity, non-transference, rebirth, and manifestation; the profound name and form is the state of simultaneous arising, separateness, inseparateness, naming, and forming; the profound six sense bases are the state of being a lord, world, door, field, and object; the profound contact
being in contact, collision, association, and aggregation; being the basis of feeling, which experiences the taste of the object, pleasure, pain, and neutrality; being the basis of craving, which delights in, is attached to, flows like a river, is a thirst, an ocean of craving that is difficult to fill; being the basis of grasping, which is taking, holding, clinging, adhering, and difficult to overcome; being the basis of existence, which throws [beings] into the accumulation, conditioning, womb, destiny, duration, and abodes; being the basis of birth, which is being born, completely born, descent, production, manifestation; [and] being the basis of old age and death, which is decay, decline, disintegration, and change—[all this] is profound.

Thus, the nature of ignorance, etc., by which penetration ignorance, etc., are fully penetrated in terms of their essential characteristics—this is known as *depth of penetration*.

All that appeared to the Elder like something spread out.

Therefore, the Blessed One, extolling the venerable Ānanda, said, “Do not say so, etc.!”

And here the meaning is this: Ānanda, you have great wisdom and clear knowledge; therefore, even dependent origination, which is profound, appears to you as something spread out. Therefore, do not say, “Does it appear spread out only to me, or to others as well?”

The Explanation of Depreciation

Now, what was said, “Depreciating,” there the meaning is this: Ānanda, do not say, “But it appears to me as plain as plain can be!”

If it appears to you as plain as plain can be, why have you not become a stream-enterer on your own, by means of your own nature, but you penetrate the path of stream-entry only after having stood in the method given by me?

Ānanda, this *nirvāṇa* itself is profound, but the principle of conditionality has become spread out for you. So why do you not realize the fruit of once-returning by completely uprooting these four defilements: the coarse bond of sensual lust, the bond of aversion, the underlying tendency to coarse sensual lust, [and] the underlying tendency to aversion? Why do you not realize the fruit of non-returning by completely uprooting these four defilements that are associated with subtle sensations? Why do you not realize arahantship by completely uprooting these eight defilements: the five bonds beginning with lust for form, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to conceit, [and] the underlying tendency to ignorance?

Why have you not penetrated the knowledge of a disciple, like Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable period and one hundred thousand aeons? Why have you not penetrated the knowledge of a *pratyekabuddha*, like the *pratyekabuddhas*, who fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable periods and one hundred thousand aeons? Or, if this appears to you as fully spread out in every way, then why do you not realize the omniscient knowledge of a Buddha, like the Buddhas, who fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable periods and one hundred thousand aeons? Are you indifferent to these distinguished achievements? Look how much you have done wrong! You, a disciple abiding in limited knowledge, say of the extremely deep principle of conditionality, “It appears spread out to me!” This statement of yours is contrary to the explanation of the Buddhas. It is not proper for such a bhikkhu to utter something contrary to the explanation of the Buddhas.

Indeed, Ānanda, have not four incalculable periods and one hundred thousand aeons passed by for me just while striving to penetrate this principle of conditionality? And there is no gift that has not been given by me, no perfection that has not been fulfilled, for the sake of penetrating the principle of conditionality.

When I was about to penetrate the principle of conditionality, this great earth did not tremble even by two finger-breadths when I was dispersing the army of Māra as though it were powerless, nor when I was developing the recollection of former lives in the first watch of the night, nor when I was developing the divine eye in the middle watch of the night.

But in the last watch of the night, at dawn, as soon as it was seen, “Ignorance is a condition for volitional formations through nine modes,” this ten thousandfold world-system, sounding like a brass gong beaten by an iron rod, released a hundred roars, a thousand roars, and it trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf struck by the wind.

Thus, Ānanda, this dependent origination is deep, and its appearance is deep.

It is because of not understanding this Dhamma…and not transcending [suffering].

*“Of this Dhamma”* means of this causal Dhamma.

*“Because of not understanding”* means because of not understanding by way of the full understanding of the known.

*“Because of not penetrating”* means because of not penetrating by way of decisive abandonment and full understanding.

*"Having the nature of a tangled skein"* means having the nature of a tangled skein.

Just as the yarn of weavers that has been badly kept and gnawed by mice is tangled in various places, and it is difficult to straighten it out, saying, “This is the beginning, this is the end,” from beginning to end, just so beings stumble in this principle of conditionality; they are confused and bewildered, and they are not able to straighten out that principle of conditionality.

There, it may be possible to straighten out a skein by relying on one’s own personal ability. But, except for two bodhisattas, other beings are not able to straighten out the principle of conditionality by their own nature.

Just as a tangled skein, after being dipped in lye and beaten with a comb, becomes clustered and knotted in various places, in the same way, these beings, after slipping on the conditions, being unable to straighten out the conditions, are confused and knotted in terms of the sixty-two kinds of views.

For all those who rely on views are simply unable to straighten out the principle of conditionality.

*“Of this Dhamma,”* *“because of not understanding,”* *“because of not penetrating,”* *“having the nature of a tangled skein,”*

*"Having the nature of a kulāgaṇṭhika,"* the *kulāgaṇṭhika* is said to be the weavers’ skein dipped in lye.

Kulā means a bird’s nest; some say that *kulāvaka* means that.

Just as that both are tangled, and it is difficult to straighten out from beginning to end, saying, “This is the beginning, this is the end,” so it should be interpreted by the previous simile.

*“Having the nature of a kulāgaṇṭhika,”* *"having become like *muñja* rushes and *pabbaja* rushes"* means they have become like *muñja* grass and like *pabbaja* grass.

Just as, having pounded those grasses and taken an old rope that has fallen somewhere, it is difficult to straighten out, saying, “This is the beginning, this is the end.”
However, it is possible for a person to straighten them out by relying on his own personal ability. But except for the two kinds of *bodhisattvas*, other beings are incapable of straightening out the principle of conditionality on their own.

Thus this generation, being unable to straighten out the principle of conditionality, has become like a ball of thread and does not pass beyond *saṃsāra* with its plane of misery (*apāya*), unfortunate destinations (*duggati*), and lower realms (*vinipāta*).

Being one who has attained the nature of the *muñja pabbaja*.

Therein, *apāya* refers to the realms of hell, animals, the hungry ghosts, and the *asura* beings.

All these are called the “plane of misery (*apāya*)” because of the absence of the joy consisting in progress.

Likewise, *duggati* [is so-called] because of the nature of suffering's course.

The "lower realms (*vinipāta*)" because they have fallen from the heights of happiness.

The other, however: Plane of misery (*apāya*), unfortunate destination (*duggati*), lower realms (*vinipāta*).

“The succession of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), proceeding without interruption, is called *saṃsāra*."

*Saṃsāra*: That, it does not pass beyond, it does not overcome.

But rather, it goes from death (*cuti*) to rebirth (*pratisandhi*), and from rebirth (*pratisandhi*) to death (*cuti*). Passing away and taking rebirth-linking over and over, like a ship on the ocean driven by a storm or like an ox yoked to a mill-wheel, it only revolves in the three realms of existence (*bhava*), the four modes of origin (*yoni*), the five destinations (*gati*), the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānaṭṭhiti*), and the nine abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*) .

The Exalted One, it should be understood, said all this to restrain the Venerable Ānanda.

Explanation of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

mula_pali:
96. ‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iti ce vadeyya, ‘jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā jātī’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā jātī’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘bhavapaccayā jātī’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā bhavo’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ . ‘Kiṃpaccayā bhavo’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘upādānapaccayā bhavo’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā upādāna’nti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā upādāna’nti iti ce vadeyya, ‘taṇhāpaccayā upādāna’nti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā taṇhā’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā taṇhā’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘vedanāpaccayā taṇhā’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā vedanā’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā vedanā’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘phassapaccayā vedanā’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā phasso’ti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā phasso’ti iti ce vadeyya, ‘nāmarūpapaccayā phasso’ti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā nāmarūpa’nti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā nāmarūpa’nti iti ce vadeyya, ‘viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa’nti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.

‘‘‘Atthi idappaccayā viññāṇa’nti iti puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃpaccayā viññāṇa’nti iti ce vadeyya, ‘nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇa’nti iccassa vacanīyaṃ.
mula_english:
96. “Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for aging and death? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there aging and death? ’ one should say: ‘With birth (*jāti*) as condition there is aging and death.’

“Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for birth (*jāti*)? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there birth (*jāti*)? ’ one should say: ‘With existence (*bhava*) as condition there is birth (*jāti*).’

“Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for existence (*bhava*)? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there existence (*bhava*)? ’ one should say: ‘With clinging (*upādāna*) as condition there is existence (*bhava*).’

“Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for clinging (*upādāna*)? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there clinging (*upādāna*)? ’ one should say: ‘With craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as condition there is clinging (*upādāna*).’

“Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for craving (*tṛṣṇā*)? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there craving (*tṛṣṇā*)? ’ one should say: ‘With feeling (*vedanā*) as condition there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).’

“Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for feeling (*vedanā*)? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there feeling (*vedanā*)? ’ one should say: ‘With contact (*sparśa*) as condition there is feeling (*vedanā*).’

“Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for contact (*sparśa*)? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there contact (*sparśa*)? ’ one should say: ‘With mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) as condition there is contact (*sparśa*).’

“Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*)? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*)? ’ one should say: ‘With consciousness (*vijñāna*) as condition there is mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*).’

“Ānanda, if one is asked: ‘Is there a specific condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*)? ’ one should say: ‘There is.’ If one is asked: ‘Through what condition is there consciousness (*vijñāna*)? ’ one should say: ‘With mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) as condition there is consciousness (*vijñāna*).’
commentary_pali:
96. Idāni yasmā idaṃ suttaṃ – ‘‘gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo’’ti ca ‘‘tantākulakajātā’’ti ca dvīhiyeva padehi ābaddhaṃ, tasmā – ‘‘gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo’’ti iminā tāva anusandhinā paccayākārassa gambhīrabhāvadassanatthaṃ desanaṃ ārabhanto atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇantiādimāha. Tatrāyamattho – imassa jarāmaraṇassa paccayo idappaccayo, tasmā idappaccayā atthi jarāmaraṇaṃ, atthi nu kho jarāmaraṇassa paccayo, yamhā paccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ bhaveyyāti evaṃ puṭṭhena satā, ānanda, paṇḍitena puggalena yathā – ‘‘taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra’’nti vutte ṭhapanīyattā pañhassa tuṇhī bhavitabbaṃ hoti, ‘‘abyākatametaṃ tathāgatenā’’ti vā vattabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ appaṭipajjitvā, yathā – ‘‘cakkhu sassataṃ asassata’’nti vutte asassatanti ekaṃseneva vattabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ ekaṃseneva atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. Puna kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ, ko nāma so paccayo, yato jarāmaraṇaṃ hotīti vutte jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iccassa vacanīyaṃ, evaṃ vattabbaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. Esa nayo sabbapadesu.

Nāmarūpapaccayā phassoti idaṃ pana yasmā saḷāyatanapaccayāti vutte cakkhusamphassādīnaṃ channaṃ vipākasamphassānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ hoti, idha ca ‘‘saḷāyatanapaccayā’’ti iminā padena gahitampi agahitampi paccayuppannavisesaṃ phassassa ca saḷāyatanato atirittaṃ aññampi visesapaccayaṃ dassetukāmo, tasmā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iminā pana vārena bhagavatā kiṃ kathitanti? Paccayānaṃ nidānaṃ kathitaṃ. Idañhi suttaṃ paccaye nijjaṭe niggumbe katvā kathitattā mahānidānanti vuccati.

Nāmarūpapaccayā phasso mahānidāna
commentary_english:
96. Now, because this *sutta* – "deep is this, Ānanda, dependent arising ( *paṭiccasamuppāda* )" and "tangled like a ball of string" – is bound by just two statements, therefore – "deep is this, Ānanda, dependent arising" – beginning the teaching to show the profundity of the conditionality, with this reflection, he says, "With this as condition, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)" and so on.

Here is the meaning: with this as condition, the condition for aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is this condition. Therefore, with this as condition, there is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Is there a condition for aging and death, through which condition aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) would come to be?

Thus, when asked by a wise person, Ānanda, a learned individual, as when it is said, "the soul (*jīva*) is the body (*śarīra*)," silence should be maintained because the question should be set aside, or it should be said, "This has not been explained by the Tathāgata." Without proceeding in this way, as when it is said, "The eye (*cakkhu*) is eternal (*sassataṃ*) or non-eternal (*asassata*)," it should be said unequivocally that it is non-eternal (*asassataṃ*). Thus, it should be stated unequivocally that it is.

Furthermore, through what condition [do] aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) [arise]? What is that condition called, through which aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) arise? When asked, it should be said, "With birth (*jāti*) as condition, [there is] aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)." Thus, it should be said that this is the meaning.

The same method [applies] to all the remaining cases.

With name and form (*nāmarūpa*) as condition, contact (*phassa*). Now, because when it is said, "With the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) as condition," only the six kinds of resultant contacts, namely eye-contact and so on, are included, but here, wishing to show the distinct conditionally arisen contacts, whether included or not included by this phrase "With the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*) as condition," and also another distinctive condition for contact (*phassa*) different from the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), therefore, it should be understood that [this] was said.

What has the Exalted One explained in this section? The origin (*nidāna*) of the conditions has been explained.

Because this *sutta*, having made the conditions free from knots and tangles, has been explained, it is called the Great Origin (*mahānidāna*).

With name and form (*nāmarūpa*) as condition, contact (*phassa*). Great Origin (*mahānidāna*).

mula_pali: 97. ‘‘Iti kho, ānanda, nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo, bhavapaccayā jāti , jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.
mula_english:
“Thus, Ānanda, with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as condition, there is consciousness (*vijñāṇaṃ*); with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, there is contact (*phasso*); with contact as condition, there is feeling (*vedanā*); with feeling as condition, there is craving (*taṇhā*); with craving as condition, there is clinging (*upādānaṃ*); with clinging as condition, there is existence (*bhavo*); with existence as condition, there is birth (*jāti*); and with birth as condition, there arise aging and death (*jarāmaraṇaṃ*), sorrow (*śoka*), lamentation (*parideva*), pain (*duḥkha*), despair (*daurmanassupāyāsā*).

Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering (*dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti*).

mula_pali: 98. ‘‘‘Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ. Jāti ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – devānaṃ vā devattāya, gandhabbānaṃ vā gandhabbattāya, yakkhānaṃ vā yakkhattāya, bhūtānaṃ vā bhūtattāya, manussānaṃ vā manussattāya, catuppadānaṃ vā catuppadattāya, pakkhīnaṃ vā pakkhittāya, sarīsapānaṃ vā sarīsapattāya siriṃsapānaṃ siriṃsapattāya (sī. syā.), tesaṃ tesañca hi, ānanda, sattānaṃ tadattāya jāti nābhavissa. Sabbaso jātiyā asati jātinirodhā api nu kho jarāmaraṇaṃ paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo jarāmaraṇassa, yadidaṃ jāti’’.
mula_english:
98. “‘From birth as a requisite condition come aging and death (jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṁ).’ Thus it has been said. And this is the way to understand how from birth as a requisite condition come aging and death.

If there were no birth (jāti) at all, in any way, of anything anywhere—i. e., of gods (devānaṃ) into the state of gods (devattāya), of celestials (gandhabbānaṃ) into the state of celestials (gandhabbattāya), of spirits (yakkhānaṃ) into the state of spirits (yakkhattāya), of demons (bhūtānaṃ) into the state of demons (bhūtattāya), of human beings (manussānaṃ) in the human state (manussattāya), of quadrupeds (catuppadānaṃ) into the state of quadrupeds (catuppadattāya), of birds (pakkhīnaṃ) into the state of birds (pakkhittāya), of snakes (sarīsapānaṃ) into the state of snakes (sarīsapattāya),—if there were no birth (jāti) of beings of any sort into any state,

in the utter absence of birth (jātiyā), with the cessation of birth (jātinirodhā), would aging and death (jarāmaraṇaṃ) be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (hetu), this is a reason (nidāna), this is an origination (samudayo), this is a requisite condition (paccayo) for aging and death (jarāmaraṇassa), i.e., birth (jāti).”
commentary_pali:
98. Idāni tesaṃ tesaṃ paccayānaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti kho panetaṃ vuttantiādimāha. Tattha pariyāyenāti kāraṇena. Sabbenasabbaṃ sabbathāsabbanti nipātadvayametaṃ. Tassattho – ‘‘sabbākārena sabbā sabbena sabhāvena sabbā jāti nāma yadi na bhaveyyā’’ti. Bhavādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Kassacīti aniyamavacanametaṃ, devādīsu yassa kassaci. Kimhicīti idampi aniyamavacanameva, kāmabhavādīsu navasu bhavesu yattha katthaci. Seyyathidanti aniyamitanikkhittaatthavibhajanatthe nipāto, tassattho – ‘‘yaṃ vuttaṃ ‘kassaci kimhicī’ti, tassa te atthaṃ vibhajissāmī’’ti. Atha naṃ vibhajanto – ‘‘devānaṃ vā devattāyā’’tiādimāha. Tattha devānaṃ vā devattāyāti yā ayaṃ devānaṃ devabhāvāya khandhajāti, yāya khandhajātiyā devā ‘‘devā’’ti vuccanti. Sace hi jāti sabbena sabbaṃ nābhavissāti iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Ettha ca devāti upapattidevā. Gandhabbāti mūlakhandhādīsu adhivatthadevatāva. Yakkhāti amanussā. Bhūtāti ye keci nibbattasattā. Pakkhinoti ye keci aṭṭhipakkhā vā cammapakkhā vā lomapakkhā vā. Sarīsapāti ye keci bhūmiyaṃ sarantā gacchanti. Tesaṃ tesanti tesaṃ tesaṃ devagandhabbādīnaṃ. Tadatthāyāti devagandhabbādibhāvāya. Jātinirodhāti jātivigamā, jātiabhāvāti attho.

Hetūtiādīni sabbānipi kāraṇavevacanāni eva. Kāraṇañhi yasmā attano phalatthāya hinoti pavattati, tasmā ‘‘hetū’’ti vuccati. Yasmā taṃ phalaṃ nideti – ‘‘handa, naṃ gaṇhathā’’ti appeti viya tasmā nidānaṃ. Yasmā phalaṃ tato samudeti uppajjati, tañca paṭicca eti pavattati, tasmā samudayoti ca paccayoti ca vuccati. Esa nayo sabbattha. Api ca yadidaṃ jātīti ettha yadidanti nipāto. Tassa sabbapadesu liṅgānurūpato attho veditabbo. Idha pana – ‘‘yā esā jātī’’ti ayamassa attho. Jarāmaraṇassa hi jāti upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hoti.

Hetū nidānaṃ. samudayo paccayo yadidaṃ jātī yadida
commentary_english:
Now, to show how those conditions are true, not untrue, and not otherwise, [the text] begins by saying, “*jāti* (birth) is the condition for aging and death,” and so forth.

There, "*pariyāyena*," means by way of *kāraṇa* (cause).

"*sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathāsabbaṃ*"—this is a pair of particles.

Its meaning is: "In every way, by every nature, if all *jāti* were not to exist."

In the case of *bhava* (becoming) and so on, the meaning should be understood in this way.

"*kassacī*" means this is an indefinite expression, [referring] to anyone whatsoever among the *deva*s (gods) and so forth.

"*kimhicī*" this too is an indefinite expression, [referring to] wherever whatsoever among the nine realms of existence (*kāma-bhava* etc.).

"*seyyathidaṃ*" is a particle used to divide the meaning of what has been indefinitely stated; its meaning is: "What was said, 'to anyone, anything,' I will divide its meaning for you."

Then, dividing it, [the text] says, "either for the *devatā*s (gods) or for the state of being a *deva*," and so forth.

There, "*devānaṃ vā devattāyā*" means that this *jāti* of aggregates for the *devatā*s is for the state of being a *deva*, by which *jāti* of aggregates the *devatā*s are called "*devā*s."

If *jāti* were not to exist in every way, the meaning should be understood in all instances in this way.

Here, "*devā*" means gods by rebirth (*upapattidevā*).

"*gandhabbā*" means deities dwelling in roots, tree-trunks, etc. (*mūlakhandhādīsu adhivatthadevatāva*).

"*yakkhā*" means non-humans (*amanussā*).

"*bhūtā*" means whatever beings are generated (*ye keci nibbattasattā*).

"*pakkhino*" means whatever have bone-wings (*aṭṭhipakkhā*) or skin-wings (*cammapakkhā*) or feather-wings (*lomapakkhā*).

"*sarīsapā*" means whatever crawl on the ground (*bhūmiyaṃ sarantā gacchanti*).

"*tesaṃ tesaṃ*" means of those respective *deva*s, *gandhabba*s, and so forth.

"*tadatthāyā*" means for the state of being a *deva*, *gandhabba*, and so forth.

"*jātinirodhā*" means the cessation of *jāti*, which is the non-existence of *jāti*.

*hetū* (cause), etc., are all synonyms for *kāraṇa* (cause).

For, because a *kāraṇa* diminishes and proceeds for its own fruit, therefore it is called “*hetu*”.

Since it brings forth that fruit, as if commanding, “Come, take it!” therefore it is called *nidāna*.

Since the fruit originates and arises from it, and since it proceeds in dependence on that, therefore it is called *samudaya* (origin) and *paccaya* (condition).

This method [of explanation] applies everywhere.

Moreover, "*yadidaṃ jātī*" here, "*yadidaṃ*" is a particle.

Its meaning should be understood in all instances in accordance with the gender.

Here, however, “*yā esā jātī*” this is its meaning.

For *jarāmaraṇa* (aging and death), *jāti* (birth) is a condition in the sense of decisive support (*upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hoti*).

*hetū*, *nidānaṃ*, *samudayo*, *paccayo*, *yadidaṃ jātī*, *yadidaṃ*.

mula_pali: 99. ‘‘‘Bhavapaccayā jātī’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā bhavapaccayā jāti. Bhavo ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – kāmabhavo vā rūpabhavo vā arūpabhavo vā, sabbaso bhave asati bhavanirodhā api nu kho jāti paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo jātiyā, yadidaṃ bhavo’’.
mula_english:
99. “‘With becoming as a condition, there is birth (bhavapaccayā jāti)’— thus, Ānanda, this should be understood in this way, by this explanation: ‘With becoming as a condition, there is birth.’

And if there were no becoming at all, Ānanda, in any way, of anything, anywhere—that is, sensual becoming (kāmabhavo), form becoming (rūpabhavo), or formless becoming (arūpabhavo)—in the utter absence of becoming, from the cessation of becoming, would birth be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this itself is the cause (hetu), this is the source (nidāna), this is the origin (samudayo), this is the condition (paccayo) for birth (jātiyā), namely, becoming (bhavo).”
commentary_pali: 99. Bhavapade – ‘‘kimhicī’’ti iminā okāsapariggaho kato. Tattha heṭṭhā avīcipariyantaṃ katvā upari paranimmitavasavattideve antokaritvā kāmabhavo veditabbo. Ayaṃ nayo upapattibhave. Idha pana kammabhave yujjati. So hi jātiyā upanissayakoṭiyāva paccayo hoti. Upādānapadādīsupi – ‘‘kimhicī’’ti iminā okāsapariggahova katoti veditabbo.
commentary_english:
In the context of becoming, the delimitation of space is done with "kimhicī".

Therein, having made the limit as low as the Avīci hell and including the gods who control the creations of others as the upper limit, sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhavo*) should be understood.

That is the method of interpretation in regard to rebirth-existence (*upapattibhave*).

But here existence should be interpreted as karma-existence (*kammabhave*),

for this is a condition for birth under the heading of decisive support (*upanissayakoṭiyā*).

Also in the case of the *upādāna* words, it should be understood that the delimitation of space is done with "kimhicī".

mula_pali: 100. ‘‘‘Upādānapaccayā bhavo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā upādānapaccayā bhavo. Upādānañca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici , seyyathidaṃ – kāmupādānaṃ vā diṭṭhupādānaṃ vā sīlabbatupādānaṃ vā attavādupādānaṃ vā, sabbaso upādāne asati upādānanirodhā api nu kho bhavo paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo bhavassa, yadidaṃ upādānaṃ’’.
mula_english:
100. “'From clinging (*upādāna*) as a requisite condition comes becoming (*bhava*).' Thus it has been said. And this, Ānanda, is the way to understand how from clinging (*upādāna*) as a requisite condition comes becoming (*bhava*).

If there were no clinging (*upādāna*) at all, in any way, of anything anywhere—that is, clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), clinging to precepts and practices (*sīlabbatupādāna*), or clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*)—in the utter absence of clinging (*upādāna*), from the cessation of clinging (*upādānanirodha*), would becoming (*bhava*) be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is a cause (*hetu*), this is a reason (*nidāna*), this is an origination (*samudaya*), this is a requisite condition (*paccaya*) for becoming (*bhava*), i. e. , clinging (*upādāna*).
commentary_pali: 100.Upādānapaccayābhavoti ettha kāmupādānaṃ tiṇṇampi kammabhavānaṃ tiṇṇañca upapattibhavānaṃ paccayo, tathā sesānipīti upādānapaccayā catuvīsatibhavā veditabbā. Nippariyāyenettha dvādasa kammabhavā labbhanti. Tesaṃ upādānāni sahajātakoṭiyāpi upanissayakoṭiyāpi paccayo.
commentary_english: 100. upādānapaccayā (Due to grasping) bhavo (becoming) , here *kāmupādānaṃ* ( grasping of desires) is the condition for three *kammabhavānaṃ* ( karma-existences), and also the condition for three *upapattibhavānaṃ* (rebirth-existences). Thus, due to grasping as condition, twenty-four *bhavā* (existences) should be known. But literally, twelve kinds of *kammabhavā* (karma-existences) obtain here. The graspings are a condition for these under the heading of conascence (*sahajātakoṭiyāpi*) as well as under the heading of decisive support (*upanissayakoṭiyāpi*).

mula_pali: 101. ‘‘‘Taṇhāpaccayā upādāna’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ. Taṇhā ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – rūpataṇhā saddataṇhā gandhataṇhā rasataṇhā phoṭṭhabbataṇhā dhammataṇhā, sabbaso taṇhāya asati taṇhānirodhā api nu kho upādānaṃ paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo upādānassa, yadidaṃ taṇhā’’.
mula_english:
“‘With craving (*taṇhā*) as condition there is clinging (*upādāna*)’ Thus it was said, Ānanda, and this is how it should be understood, namely that with craving (*taṇhā*) as condition, there is clinging (*upādāna*).

If there were no craving (*taṇhā*) at all, Ānanda, in any way, of anything, anywhere—that is, no craving for visible forms (*rūpa-taṇhā*), craving for sounds (*śabda-taṇhā*), craving for smells (*gandha-taṇhā*), craving for tastes (*rasa-taṇhā*), craving for tangibles (*sparśa-taṇhā*), or craving for mental objects (*dharma-taṇhā*)—then, in the complete absence of craving (*taṇhā*), with the cessation of craving (*taṇhā-nirodha*), would clinging (*upādāna*) be discerned?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (*hetu*), this is the source (*nidāna*), this is the origin (*samudaya*), this is the condition (*pratyaya*) for clinging (*upādāna*), namely, craving (*taṇhā*).”
commentary_pali: 101.Rūpataṇhāti rūpārammaṇe taṇhā. Esa nayo saddataṇhādīsu. Sā panesā taṇhā upādānassa sahajātakoṭiyāpi upanissayakoṭiyāpi paccayo hoti.
commentary_english: 101. rūpataṇhā: *rūpa*-craving is craving in relation to a *rūpa* object. Similarly with *sadda*-craving and the rest. Craving is a condition for clinging under the heading of conascence as well as under the heading of decisive support.

mula_pali: 102. ‘‘‘Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Vedanā ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – cakkhusamphassajā vedanā sotasamphassajā vedanā ghānasamphassajā vedanā jivhāsamphassajā vedanā kāyasamphassajā vedanā manosamphassajā vedanā, sabbaso vedanāya asati vedanānirodhā api nu kho taṇhā paññāyethā’’ti ? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo taṇhāya, yadidaṃ vedanā’’.
mula_english:
“It was said: ‘*taṇhā* (craving) comes from *vedanā* (feeling) as a requisite condition.’ Thus it has been said. And this is the way to understand how *taṇhā* (craving) comes from *vedanā* (feeling) as a requisite condition.

If there were absolutely and utterly no *vedanā* (feeling) of any kind anywhere—that is, no *vedanā* (feeling) born of eye-contact (*cakṣusamphassajā vedanā*), *vedanā* (feeling) born of ear-contact (*sotasamphassajā vedanā*), *vedanā* (feeling) born of nose-contact (*ghānasamphassajā vedanā*), *vedanā* (feeling) born of tongue-contact (*jivhāsamphassajā vedanā*), *vedanā* (feeling) born of body-contact (*kāyasamphassajā vedanā*), or *vedanā* (feeling) born of mind-contact (*manosamphassajā vedanā*)—then, in the complete absence of *vedanā* (feeling), with the cessation of *vedanā* (feeling), would *taṇhā* (craving) be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is a cause, this is a reason, this is an origination, this is a requisite condition for *taṇhā* (craving), i. e. , *vedanā* (feeling)."
commentary_pali: 102.Esa paccayo taṇhāya, yadidaṃvedanāti ettha vipākavedanā taṇhāya upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hoti, aññā aññathāpīti.
commentary_english: This is the condition for thirst, namely, sensation ( *vedanā*). Here, resultant sensation is the condition for thirst through the condition of decisive support, while other [sensations] are otherwise.

mula_pali: 103. ‘‘Iti kho panetaṃ, ānanda, vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā, taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā, pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho, lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo, vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo, chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosānaṃ, ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho, pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariyaṃ, macchariyaṃ paṭicca ārakkho. Ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti.
mula_english: “Thus, Ānanda, in dependence upon feeling (*vedanā*) there is craving (*taṇhā*); in dependence upon craving there is pursuit (*pariyesanā*); in dependence upon pursuit there is gain (*lābho*); in dependence upon gain there is decision-making (*vinicchayo*); in dependence upon decision-making there is desire and lust (*chandarāgo*); in dependence upon desire and lust there is attachment (*ajjhosānaṃ*); in dependence upon attachment there is possessiveness (*pariggaho*); in dependence upon possessiveness there is stinginess (*macchariyaṃ*); in dependence upon stinginess there is safeguarding (*ārakkho*). Because of safeguarding, various evil, unskillful (*akusalā dhammā*) phenomena originate—the taking up of clubs and weapons (*daṇḍādānasatthādāna*), conflicts (*kalahaviggaha*), quarrels, and disputes (*vivādatuvaṃtuvaṃ*), insulting speech, slander (*pesuññamusāvādā*), and falsehoods.
commentary_pali:
103. Ettāvatā pana bhagavā vaṭṭamūlabhūtaṃ purimataṇhaṃ dassetvā idāni desanaṃ, piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā kesesu vā gahetvā viravantaṃ viravantaṃ maggato okkamento viya navahi padehi samudācārataṇhaṃ dassento – ‘‘iti kho panetaṃ, ānanda, vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā’’tiādimāha. Tattha taṇhāti dve taṇhā esanataṇhā ca, esitataṇhā ca. Yāya taṇhāya ajapathasaṅkupathādīni paṭipajjitvā bhoge esati gavesati, ayaṃ esanataṇhā nāma. Yā tesu esitesu gavesitesu paṭiladdhesu taṇhā, ayaṃ esitataṇhā nāma. Tadubhayampi samudācārataṇhāya eva adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā duvidhāpesā vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā nāma. Pariyesanā nāma rūpādiārammaṇapariyesanā, sā hi taṇhāya sati hoti. Lābhoti rūpādiārammaṇapaṭilābho, so hi pariyesanāya sati hoti. Vinicchayo pana ñāṇataṇhādiṭṭhivitakkavasena catubbidho. Tattha – ‘‘sukhavinicchayaṃ jaññā, sukhavinicchayaṃ ñatvā ajjhattaṃ sukhamanuyuñjeyyā’’ti (ma. ni. 3.323) ayaṃ ñāṇavinicchayo. ‘‘Vinicchayoti dve vinicchayā – taṇhāvinicchayo ca diṭṭhivinicchayo cā’’ti (mahāni. 102). Evaṃ āgatāni aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni taṇhāvinicchayo. Dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhivinicchayo. ‘‘Chando kho, devānaminda, vitakkanidāno’’ti (dī. ni. 2.358) imasmiṃ pana sutte idha vinicchayoti vutto vitakkoyeva āgato. Lābhaṃ labhitvā hi iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ sundarāsundarañca vitakkeneva vinicchināti – ‘‘ettakaṃ me rūpārammaṇatthāya bhavissati, ettakaṃ saddādiārammaṇatthāya, ettakaṃ mayhaṃ bhavissati, ettakaṃ parassa, ettakaṃ paribhuñjissāmi, ettakaṃ nidahissāmī’’ti. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo’’ti.

Chandarāgoti evaṃ akusalavitakkena vitakkitavatthusmiṃ dubbalarāgo ca balavarāgo ca uppajjati, idañhi idha taṇhā. Chandoti dubbalarāgassādhivacanaṃ. Ajjhosānanti ahaṃ mamanti balavasanniṭṭhānaṃ. Pariggahoti taṇhādiṭṭhavasena pariggahaṇakaraṇaṃ. Macchariyanti parehi sādhāraṇabhāvassa asahanatā. Tenevassa porāṇā evaṃ vacanatthaṃ vadanti – ‘‘idaṃ acchariyaṃ mayhameva hotu, mā aññesaṃ acchariyaṃ hotūti pavattattā macchariyanti vuccatī’’ti. Ārakkhoti dvārapidahanamañjūsagopanādivasena suṭṭhu rakkhaṇaṃ. Adhikarotīti adhikaraṇaṃ, kāraṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ārakkhādhikaraṇanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, ārakkhahetūti attho. Daṇḍādānādīsu paranisedhanatthaṃ daṇḍassa ādānaṃ daṇḍādānaṃ. Ekato dhārādino satthassa ādānaṃ satthādānaṃ. Kalahoti kāyakalahopi vācākalahopi. Purimo purimo virodho viggaho. Pacchimo pacchimo vivādo. Tuvaṃtuvanti agāravavacanaṃ tuvaṃtuvaṃ.

Chandarāgo Chando Ajjhosāna Pariggaho Macchariya Ārakkho adhikaraṇaṃ, Ārakkhādhikaraṇa daṇḍādānaṃ. satthādānaṃ. Kalaho viggaho. vivādo. tuvaṃtuvaṃ.
commentary_english:
103. To this extent, the Blessed One, having shown the previous craving that is the root of the round [of rebirths] ( *vaṭṭamūlabhūtaṃ purimataṇhaṃ*), now, as if striking [someone] on the back or grabbing [him] by the hair and pulling [him] away while he wails, the Blessed One pulls the teaching down from its usual sequence and speaks the present passage to show, by way of nine terms, obsessional craving (*samudācārataṇhaṃ*): "Thus indeed, Ānanda, craving ( *taṇhā*) is in dependence upon feeling ( *vedanaṃ paṭicca*)," and so forth.

Therein, craving (*taṇhā*): There are two kinds of craving ( *taṇhā*): acquisitive craving ( *esanataṇhā*) and possessive craving ( *esitataṇhā*).

Acquisitive craving (*esanataṇhā*): Acquisitive craving is the craving ( *taṇhā*) because of which one travels along rough and rugged paths (*ajapathasaṅkupathādīni paṭipajjitvā*) seeking wealth (*bhoge esati gavesati*).

Possessive craving (*esitataṇhā*): Possessive craving ( *esitataṇhā*) is the craving ( *taṇhā*) for those things which have been sought after and obtained (*esu esitesu gavesitesu paṭiladdhesu*).

Both of these are designations for obsessional craving (*samudācārataṇhā*).

Therefore, this twofold craving (*duvidhāpesā*) arises in dependence upon feeling (*vedanaṃ paṭicca taṇhā*).

Pursuit (*pariyesanā*): “Pursuit” (*pariyesanā*) is the pursuit of objects such as visible forms (*rūpādiārammaṇa*), etc., and it exists when there is craving ( *taṇhāya sati hoti*).

Gain (*lābho*): “Gain” (*lābho*) is the obtaining of objects such as visible forms (*rūpādiārammaṇa paṭilābho*), etc., and it exists when there is pursuit ( *pariyesanāya sati hoti*).

Decision-making (*vinicchayo*): Decision-making (*vinicchayo*), however, is fourfold by way of knowledge ( *ñāṇa*), craving ( *taṇhā*), views ( *diṭṭhi*) and thought ( *vitakka*).

Therein, “One should know how to decide on happiness. Knowing how to decide on happiness, one should be devoted to inner happiness” ( *sukhavinicchayaṃ jaññā, sukhavinicchayaṃ ñatvā ajjhattaṃ sukhamanuyuñjeyyā*): This is decision-making as knowledge ( *ñāṇavinicchayo*).

“Decision-making” ( *vinicchayo*): There are two kinds of decision-making ( *vinicchayā*): decision-making as craving ( *taṇhāvinicchayo*) and decision-making as views ( *diṭṭhivinicchayo*).

Eight hundred craving-related wanderings that have thus come are decision-making as craving (*taṇhāvinicchayo*). Sixty-two views are decision-making as views (*diṭṭhivinicchayo*).

“Desire, lord of gods, has its source in thought” ( *chando kho, devānaminda, vitakkanidāno*): Since it is said “Desire, lord of gods, has its source in thought”, in this sutta here “decision-making” ( *vinicchayo*) is intended as thought ( *vitakkoyeva āgato*).

For having gained something ( *lābhaṃ labhitvā*), one thinks of it as desirable or undesirable ( *iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ*), beautiful or ugly ( *sundarāsundarañca*), and then decides ( *vinicchināti*): "This much will be for visible forms ( *rūpārammaṇatthāya*), this much for sounds, etc. ( *saddādiārammaṇatthāya*). This is for me ( *mayhaṃ*), this for others ( *parassa*). This I will use ( *paribhuñjissāmi*), this I will keep ( *nidahissāmī*)."

Thus it is said: “In dependence upon gain there is decision-making” ( *lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo*).

Desire and lust (*chandarāgo*): Because of unwholesome thoughts ( *akusalavitakkena*), weak lust (*dubbalarāgo*) and strong lust ( *balavarāgo*) arise towards the object thought about ( *vitakkitavatthusmiṃ*). This here is craving (*taṇhā*).

Desire (*chando*): “Desire” ( *chando*) is a designation for weak lust (*dubbalarāgassa adhivacanaṃ*).

Attachment (*ajjhosāna*): “Attachment” (*ajjhosāna*) is strong conviction of “I” ( *ahaṃ*) and “mine” ( *mamanti balavasanniṭṭhānaṃ*).

Grasping (*pariggaho*): “Grasping” (*pariggaho*) is the act of grasping by way of craving ( *taṇhā*) and views ( *diṭṭhi*) (*pariggahaṇakaraṇaṃ*).

Avarice (*macchariya*): “Avarice” (*macchariya*) is intolerance of others sharing in prosperity (*parehi sādhāraṇabhāvassa asahanatā*).

Therefore, the ancients say the following about its meaning ( *vacanatthaṃ vadanti*): "Let this wonder be for me alone ( *idaṃ acchariyaṃ mayhameva hotu*), may this wonder not be for others ( *mā aññesaṃ acchariyaṃ hotūti pavattattā*)." Because it is so inclined, it is called avarice ( *macchariyanti vuccatī*).

Protection (*ārakkho*): "Protection" (*ārakkho*) is guarding ( *rakkhaṇaṃ*) well by way of closing doors, covering containers, hiding treasures, and so forth ( *dvārapidahanamañjūsagopanādivasena suṭṭhu*).

Because it superintends, it is superintendence (*adhikaraṇaṃ*): this is a name for cause (*kāraṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ*).

Superintendence of protection ( *ārakkhādhikaraṇa*): this is a neuter verbal noun ( *bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ*); its meaning ( *attho*) is the cause of protection ( *ārakkhahetūti*).

The taking up of clubs ( *daṇḍassa ādānaṃ*) to restrain others ( *paranisedhanatthaṃ*) in cases of using clubs and so forth ( *daṇḍādānādīsu*) is the taking up of clubs ( *daṇḍādānaṃ*).

The taking up of weapons ( *satthassa ādānaṃ*) such as swords ( *dhārādino*) is the taking up of weapons ( *satthādānaṃ*).

Quarrel (*kalaho*): "Quarrel" (*kalaho*) is either a bodily quarrel ( *kāyakalahopi*) or a verbal quarrel ( *vācākalahopi*).

A prior opposition is strife (*viggaho*).
The final, the final dispute.

"You, you" is a disrespectful expression, "you, you."

*Chandarāga*, *chando*, *ajjhosāna*, *pariggaho*, *macchariya*, *ārakkho adhikaraṇaṃ*, *ārakkhādhikaraṇa daṇḍādānaṃ*, *satthādānaṃ*, *kalaho*, *viggaho*, *vivādo*, *tuvaṃtuvaṃ*.

mula_pali: 104. ‘‘‘Ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ ārakkhaṃ paṭicca ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ (syā.) daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavantī’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhavanti. Ārakkho ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso ārakkhe asati ārakkhanirodhā api nu kho daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā sambhaveyyu’’nti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādatuvaṃtuvaṃpesuññamusāvādānaṃ anekesaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ sambhavāya yadidaṃ ārakkho.
mula_english:
104. “Because of safeguarding (*ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ*), various evil unwholesome phenomena originate—the taking up of clubs (*daṇḍa*) and weapons (*sattha*), conflicts (*kalaha*), quarrels (*viggaha*), and disputes (*vivāda*), insulting speech (*tuvaṃtuvaṃ*), slander (*pesuñña*), and falsehoods (*musāvāda*).’ Thus was it said.

And this is the way, Ānanda, to understand how it is that because of defensiveness (*ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ*) various evil, unskillful phenomena come into play: the taking up of sticks (*daṇḍa*) and knives (*sattha*); conflicts (*kalaha*), quarrels (*viggaha*), and disputes (*vivāda*); accusations (*tuvaṃtuvaṃ*), divisive speech (*pesuñña*), and lies (*musāvāda*).

If there were absolutely and utterly no safeguarding (*ārakkho*) of any kind anywhere, then, in the complete absence of safeguarding (*ārakkhe*), with the cessation of safeguarding (*ārakkhanirodhā*), would those various evil unwholesome phenomena originate?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is a cause (*hetu*), this is a reason (*nidānaṃ*), this is an origination (*samudayo*), this is a requisite condition (*paccayo*) for the coming-into-play of various evil, unskillful phenomena — the taking up of sticks (*daṇḍa*) and knives (*sattha*); conflicts (*kalaha*), quarrels (*viggaha*), and disputes (*vivāda*); accusations (*tuvaṃtuvaṃ*), divisive speech (*pesuñña*), and lies (*musāvādānaṃ*) — i. e. , defensiveness (*ārakkho*).

mula_pali: 105. ‘‘‘Macchariyaṃ paṭicca ārakkho’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā macchariyaṃ paṭicca ārakkho. Macchariyañca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici , sabbaso macchariye asati macchariyanirodhā api nu kho ārakkho paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo ārakkhassa, yadidaṃ macchariyaṃ’’.
mula_english:
105. “'In dependence upon stinginess (*mātsarya*) there is safeguarding (*ārakṣa*).' Thus it has been said. And this, Ānanda, is the way to understand how safeguarding is dependent on stinginess (*mātsarya*).

If, Ānanda, there were no stinginess (*mātsarya*) in any way, in every respect, in every way, for anyone, in anything, could safeguarding be discerned when stinginess (*mātsarya*) does not exist, when stinginess (*mātsarya*) ceases?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (*hetu*), this is the source (*nidāna*), this is the origin (*samudaya*), this is the condition (*pratyaya*) for safeguarding (*ārakṣa*), namely, stinginess (*mātsarya*).”

mula_pali: 106. ‘‘‘Pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariya’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā pariggahaṃ paṭicca macchariyaṃ. Pariggaho ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso pariggahe asati pariggahanirodhā api nu kho macchariyaṃ paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo macchariyassa, yadidaṃ pariggaho’’.
mula_english:
“'Stinginess arises in dependence upon possessiveness (parigraha).' Thus it was said. Ānanda, this should be understood in this way: stinginess arises in dependence upon possessiveness (parigraha).

And Ānanda, if possessiveness (parigraha) were completely and totally absent, in every way, for anyone, in anything, would stinginess be evident when possessiveness (parigraha) ceases?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (hetu), this is the source (nidāna), this is the origin (samudaya), this is the condition (paccayo) for stinginess (macchariya), namely, possessiveness (parigraha).”

mula_pali: 107. ‘‘‘Ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā ajjhosānaṃ paṭicca pariggaho. Ajjhosānañca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso ajjhosāne asati ajjhosānanirodhā api nu kho pariggaho paññāyethā’’ti ? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo pariggahassa – yadidaṃ ajjhosānaṃ’’.
mula_english:
107. “'In dependence upon attachment there is possessiveness ( *parigraha*)'— it was said. How that is so, Ānanda, should be understood in this way: in dependence upon attachment, there is possessiveness ( *parigraha*).

If there were absolutely and utterly no attachment (*ajjhosānaṃ*) of any kind anywhere, then, in the complete absence of attachment (*ajjhosānaṃ*), with the cessation of attachment (*ajjhosāna-nirodha*), would possessiveness (*parigraha*) be discerned?”

“No, venerable sir ( *bhante*).”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause ( *hetu*), source ( *nidānaṃ*), origin ( *samudayo*), and condition ( *paccayo*) for possessiveness (*pariggahassa*), namely, attachment (*ajjhosānaṃ*).”

mula_pali: 108. ‘‘‘Chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosāna’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā chandarāgaṃ paṭicca ajjhosānaṃ. Chandarāgo ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso chandarāge asati chandarāganirodhā api nu kho ajjhosānaṃ paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo ajjhosānassa, yadidaṃ chandarāgo’’.
mula_english:
108. “It was said: ‘In dependence upon desire and lust there is attachment (ajjhosāna).’ How that is so, Ānanda, should be understood in this way: in dependence upon desire and lust there is attachment (ajjhosāna).
If there were absolutely and utterly no desire and lust of any kind anywhere for anyone in anything, then, in the complete absence of desire and lust, with the cessation of desire and lust, would attachment (ajjhosāna) be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”
“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (hetu), source (nidāna), origin (samudayo), and condition (paccayo) for attachment (ajjhosānassa), namely, desire and lust (chandarāgo).”

mula_pali: 109. ‘‘‘Vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā vinicchayaṃ paṭicca chandarāgo. Vinicchayo ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso vinicchaye asati vinicchayanirodhā api nu kho chandarāgo paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ , bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo chandarāgassa, yadidaṃ vinicchayo’’.
mula_english:
109. "‘In dependence upon decision-making there is desire and lust (chandarāga).’" It was said thus, Ānanda. This should be understood in this way, namely, in dependence upon decision-making there is desire and lust (chandarāga).

If decision-making (vinicchaya), Ānanda, did not exist in any way, in every way, for anyone, in anything, if decision-making (vinicchaya) were completely absent, through the cessation of decision-making (vinicchayanirodha), would desire and lust (chandarāga) be evident?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this itself is the cause (hetu), this the source (nidāna), this the origin (samudaya), this the condition (paccayo) for desire and lust (chandarāgassa), namely, decision-making (vinicchayo).”

mula_pali: 110. ‘‘‘Lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo. Lābho ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso lābhe asati lābhanirodhā api nu kho vinicchayo paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo vinicchayassa, yadidaṃ lābho’’.
mula_english: “'Decision-making is dependent on gain (lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo).' Thus it has been said. And this is the way to understand how decision-making is dependent on gain (lābhaṃ paṭicca vinicchayo), Ānanda. If there were absolutely and utterly no gain of any kind anywhere, then, in the complete absence of gain, with the cessation of gain, would decision-making be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, source, origin, and condition for decision-making, namely, gain (lābho).”

mula_pali: 111. ‘‘‘Pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā pariyesanaṃ paṭicca lābho. Pariyesanā ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, sabbaso pariyesanāya asati pariyesanānirodhā api nu kho lābho paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo lābhassa, yadidaṃ pariyesanā’’.
mula_english:
111. “‘In dependence upon pursuit there is gain (lābha).’ Thus it has been said. And this is the way to understand how pursuit is dependent on gain, Ānanda.

If there were absolutely and utterly no pursuit of any kind anywhere by anyone in anything, then, in the complete absence of pursuit, with the cessation of pursuit, would gain be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (hetu), this is a reason (nidāna), this is an origination (samudaya), this is a requisite condition (paccayo) for gain (lābha), namely, pursuit (pariyesanā).

mula_pali: 112. ‘‘‘Taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā. Taṇhā ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhā, sabbaso taṇhāya asati taṇhānirodhā api nu kho pariyesanā paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo pariyesanāya, yadidaṃ taṇhā. Iti kho, ānanda, ime dve dhammā ime dhammā (ka.) dvayena vedanāya ekasamosaraṇā bhavanti’’.
mula_english:
112. “‘Seeking is dependent on craving’—thus it was said. Ānanda, this should be understood in this way, namely, that seeking is dependent on craving.

If there were no craving at all, in any way, of anything anywhere—that is, no craving for sense pleasures (*kāma-taṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*), or craving for non-existence (*vibhava-taṇhā*)—then, in the utter absence of craving, with the cessation of craving, would seeking be discerned?” "No, venerable sir."

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is a cause, this is a source, this is an origin, this is a requisite condition for seeking, namely, craving (*taṇhā*).

Thus, Ānanda, these two phenomena—(these two *dharmas*)—converge into a unity through feeling (*vedanā*)."
commentary_pali: 112. Idāni paṭilomanayenāpi taṃsamudācārataṇhaṃ dassetuṃ puna – ‘‘ārakkhādhikaraṇa’’nti ārabhanto desanaṃ nivattesi. Tattha kāmataṇhāti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgavasena uppannā rūpāditaṇhā. Bhavataṇhāti sassatadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo. Vibhavataṇhāti ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato rāgo. Ime dve dhammāti vaṭṭamūlataṇhā ca samudācārataṇhā cāti ime dve dhammā. Dvayenāti taṇhālakkhaṇavasena ekabhāvaṃ gatāpi vaṭṭamūlasamudācāravasena dvīhi koṭṭhāsehi vedanāya ekasamosaraṇā bhavanti, vedanāpaccayena ekapaccayāti attho. Tividhañhi samosaraṇaṃ osaraṇasamosaraṇaṃ, sahajātasamosaraṇaṃ, paccayasamosaraṇañca. Tattha – ‘‘atha kho sabbāni tāni kāmasamosaraṇāni bhavantī’’ti idaṃ osaraṇasamosaraṇaṃ nāma. ‘‘Chandamūlakā, āvuso, ete dhammā phassasamudayā vedanāsamosaraṇā’’ti (a. ni. 8.83) idaṃ sahajātasamosaraṇaṃ nāma. ‘‘Dvayena vedanāya ekasamosaraṇā’’ti idaṃ pana paccayasamosaraṇanti veditabbaṃ.
commentary_english:
112. Now to show obsessional craving (*taṇhā*) in reverse order, the Buddha, beginning with the section on "grounds for defense," traces back the teaching.

There, *kāma-taṇhā* means craving for forms (rūpa) and so forth, which arises through attachment (*rāga*) to the qualities of the five sense objects.

*Bhava-taṇhā* means attachment (*rāga*) associated with the eternalist view (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).

*Vibhava-taṇhā* means attachment (*rāga*) associated with the annihilationist view (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

"These two phenomena" (*ime dve dhammā*) means craving that is the root of the round (*vaṭṭamūlataṇhā*) and obsessional craving (*samudācārataṇhā*); these are the two phenomena.

“Being a duality” (*dvayenā*) means although having reached a state of unity by way of the characteristic of craving (*taṇhā-lakkhaṇa*), due to the round root (*vaṭṭamūla*) and habitual craving (*samudācāra*), through two parts, in feeling (*vedanā*) there is a single convergence (*ekasamosaraṇā*); the meaning is a single condition through the condition of feeling (*vedanāpaccayena ekapaccayāti attho*).

"Convergence" (*samosaraṇa*) is threefold: convergence by descent (*osaraṇasamosaraṇaṃ*), convergence by co-nascence (*sahajātasamosaraṇaṃ*), and convergence by condition (*paccayasamosaraṇañca*).

There – “then all of those are convergences of desire (*kāmasamosaraṇāni bhavantī*)” – this is called “convergence by descent” (*osaraṇasamosaraṇaṃ nāma*).

“These phenomena, friend, are rooted in desire (*chandamūlakā*), originate from contact (*phassasamudayā*), and converge upon feeling (*vedanāsamosaraṇā*)” (A.Ni. 8.83) this is called “convergence by co-nascence” (*sahajātasamosaraṇaṃ nāma*).

“Being a duality, converge into a unity in feeling” (*dvayena vedanāya ekasamosaraṇā*) this, however, is known as "convergence by condition" (*paccayasamosaraṇa*).

mula_pali: 113. ‘‘‘Phassapaccayā vedanā’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā ‘phassapaccayā vedanā. Phasso ca hi, ānanda, nābhavissa sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ kassaci kimhici, seyyathidaṃ – cakkhusamphasso sotasamphasso ghānasamphasso jivhāsamphasso kāyasamphasso manosamphasso, sabbaso phasse asati phassanirodhā api nu kho vedanā paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda , eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo vedanāya, yadidaṃ phasso’’.
mula_english:
“‘From contact (*sparśa*) as a requisite condition comes feeling (vedanā).’ Thus it has been said. And this is the way to understand how from contact as a requisite condition comes feeling (vedanā).

If there were absolutely and utterly no contact (*sparśa*) of any kind anywhere—that is, no eye-contact (*cakṣu-samphassa*), ear-contact (*sota-samphassa*), nose-contact (*ghāna-samphassa*), tongue-contact (*jihvā-samphassa*), body-contact (*kāya-samphassa*), or mind-contact (*mano-samphassa*)—then, in the complete absence of contact (*sparśa*), with the cessation of contact (*sparśa-nirodha*), would feeling (vedanā) be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (hetu), source (nidāna), origin (samudaya), and condition (pratyaya) for feeling (vedanā), namely, contact (*sparśa*).
commentary_pali: 113.Cakkhusamphassoti ādayo sabbe vipākaphassāyeva. Tesu ṭhapetvā cattāro lokuttaravipākaphasse avasesā dvattiṃsa phassā honti. Yadidaṃ phassoti ettha pana phasso bahudhā vedanāya paccayo hoti.
commentary_english: " *Cakkhusamphasso* ti (eye-contact) etc. are all resultant contacts only. Excepting the four supramundane resultant contacts *lokuttaravipākaphasse*, the remainder number thirty-two. Moreover, here, *yadidaṃ phasso* ti (namely contact), contact is in many ways the condition for feeling *vedanāya*.

mula_pali: 114. ‘‘‘Nāmarūpapaccayā phasso’ti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā nāmarūpapaccayā phasso. Yehi, ānanda, ākārehi yehi liṅgehi yehi nimittehi yehi uddesehi nāmakāyassa paññatti hoti, tesu ākāresu tesu liṅgesu tesu nimittesu tesu uddesesu asati api nu kho rūpakāye adhivacanasamphasso paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yehi, ānanda, ākārehi yehi liṅgehi yehi nimittehi yehi uddesehi rūpakāyassa paññatti hoti, tesu ākāresu…pe… tesu uddesesu asati api nu kho nāmakāye paṭighasamphasso paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yehi, ānanda, ākārehi…pe… yehi uddesehi nāmakāyassa ca rūpakāyassa ca paññatti hoti , tesu ākāresu…pe… tesu uddesesu asati api nu kho adhivacanasamphasso vā paṭighasamphasso vā paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Yehi, ānanda, ākārehi…pe… yehi uddesehi nāmarūpassa paññatti hoti, tesu ākāresu …pe… tesu uddesesu asati api nu kho phasso paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo phassassa, yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ’’.
mula_english:
“'From name-and-form as a requisite condition comes contact.' Thus it has been said. And this is the way to understand how, Ānanda, from name-and-form as a requisite condition comes contact.

If those qualities, traits, signs, and indicators through which there is a description of the *nāmakāya* (mental body) were all absent, would designation-contact (*adhivacanasamphassa*) be discerned in the *rūpakāya* (material body)?” “No, venerable sir.”

“If those qualities, traits, signs, and indicators through which there is a description of the *rūpakāya* (material body) were all absent, would impingement-contact (*paṭighasamphassa*) be discerned in the *nāmakāya* (mental body)?” “No, venerable sir.”

“If those qualities, traits, signs, and indicators through which there is a description of the *nāmakāya* (mental body) and the *rūpakāya* (material body) were all absent, would either designation-contact (*adhivacanasamphassa*) or impingement-contact (*paṭighasamphassa*) be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“If those qualities, traits, signs, and indicators through which there is a description of *nāmarūpa* (mentality-materiality) were all absent, would contact (*phassa*) be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (*hetu*), this is the source (*nidānaṃ*), this is the origin (*samudayo*), and this is the condition (*paccayo*) for contact (*phassa*), namely, *nāmarūpa* (mentality-materiality).”
commentary_pali:
114.Yehi, ānanda, ākārehītiādīsu ākārā vuccanti vedanādīnaṃ aññamaññaṃ asadisasabhāvā. Teyeva sādhukaṃ dassiyamānā taṃ taṃ līnamatthaṃ gamentīti liṅgāni. Tassa tassa sañjānanahetuto nimittāni. Tathā tathā uddisitabbato uddesā. Tasmā ayamettha attho – ‘‘ānanda, yehi ākārehi…pe… yehi uddesehi nāmakāyassa nāmasamūhassa paññatti hoti, yā esā ca vedanāya vedayitākāre vedayitaliṅge vedayitanimitte vedanāti uddese sati, saññāya sañjānanākāre sañjānanaliṅge sañjānananimitte saññāti uddese sati, saṅkhārānaṃ cetanākāre cetanāliṅge cetanānimitte cetanāti uddese sati, viññāṇassa vijānanākāre vijānanaliṅge vijānananimitte viññāṇanti uddese sati – ‘ayaṃ nāmakāyo’ti nāmakāyassa paññatti hoti. Tesu nāmakāyappaññattihetūsu vedanādīsu ākārādīsu asati api nu kho rūpakāye adhivacanasamphasso paññāyetha? Yvāyaṃ cattāro khandhe vatthuṃ katvā manodvāre adhivacanasamphassavevacano manosamphasso uppajjati, api nu kho so rūpakāye paññāyetha, pañca pasāde vatthuṃ katvā katvā uppajjeyyā’’ti. Atha āyasmā ānando ambarukkhe asati jamburukkhato ambapakkassa uppattiṃ viya rūpakāyato tassa uppattiṃ asampaṭicchanto no hetaṃ bhanteti āha.

Dutiyapañhe ruppanākāraruppanaliṅgaruppananimittavasena rūpanti uddesavasena ca ākārādīnaṃ attho veditabbo. Paṭighasamphassoti sappaṭighaṃ rūpakkhandhaṃ vatthuṃ katvā uppajjanakasamphasso. Idhāpi thero jamburukkhe asati ambarukkhato jambupakkassa uppattiṃ viya nāmakāyato tassa uppattiṃ asampaṭicchanto ‘‘no hetaṃ bhante’’ti āha.

Paṭighasamphasso

Tatiyapañho ubhayavaseneva vutto. Tatra thero ākāse ambajambupakkānaṃ uppattiṃ viya nāmarūpābhāve dvinnampi phassānaṃ uppattiṃ asampaṭicchanto ‘‘no hetaṃ bhante’’ti āha.

Evaṃ dvinnaṃ phassānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ paccayaṃ dassetvā idāni dvinnampi tesaṃ avisesato nāmarūpapaccayataṃ dassetuṃ – ‘‘yehi ānanda ākārehī’’ti catutthaṃ pañhaṃ ārabhi. Yadidaṃ nāmarūpanti yaṃ idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, yaṃ idaṃ chasupi dvāresu nāmarūpaṃ, eseva hetu eseva paccayoti attho. Cakkhudvārādīsu hi cakkhādīni ceva rūpārammaṇādīni ca rūpaṃ, sampayuttakā khandhā nāmanti evaṃ pañcavidhopi so phasso nāmarūpapaccayāva phasso. Manodvārepi hadayavatthuñceva yañca rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti, idaṃ rūpaṃ. Sampayuttadhammā ceva yañca arūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti, idaṃ arūpaṃ nāma. Evaṃ manosamphassopi nāmarūpapaccayā phassoti veditabbo. Nāmarūpaṃ panassa bahudhā paccayo hoti.

Yadidaṃ nāmarūpa
commentary_english:
114. “Ānanda, by which qualities (yehi ākārehi)” and so forth, the qualities (ākārā) are said to be the mutually dissimilar characteristics of feeling and so forth.

They are also called “traits” (liṅgāni) because, when carefully looked at, they betray the concealed meanings.

“Indicators” (nimittāni) because of being the cause of recognizing that and that.

“Designations” (uddesā) because of what should be designated in that and that way.

Therefore, this is the meaning here: “Ānanda, when there are present those qualities, traits, signs, and indicators through which there is a description of the ‘mental body,’ the mental group; that is, when there is present feeling’s quality, trait, and sign of being what is felt, and its indicator ‘feeling’; when there is present perception’s quality, trait, and sign of perceiving, and its indicator ‘perception’; when there is present the mental formations’ quality, trait, and sign of volition, and their indicator ‘volition’; when there is present consciousness’s quality, trait, and sign of cognizing, and its indicator ‘consciousness’—the description of the ‘mental body’ occurs as ‘this is the mental body.’

When feeling and so forth, and qualities and so forth, the causes for the description of the mental body are not present, would designation-contact be discerned in the material body? The mind-contact, which is synonymous with designation-contact and which arises in the mind-door taking as its basis the four aggregates, would that be discerned in the material body? Would it arise taking as its basis one or another of the five kinds of sensitive matter?”

Then the Venerable Ānanda, rejecting the arising of that origination from the material body just as one would the arising of a mango fruit from a rose-apple tree when mango trees are absent, said: “Certainly not, venerable sir (no hetaṃ bhante).”

In the second question, the meaning of form (rūpa) should be understood in terms of the mode of disintegration, the trait of disintegration, the indicator of disintegration, and by way of designation, and the meaning of qualities, etc.

“Impaction-contact (paṭighasamphasso)” is contact that arises by taking as its basis the material aggregate that is with impaction (sappaṭighaṃ rūpakkhandhaṃ vatthuṃ katvā uppajjanakasamphasso).

Here also, the Elder, rejecting the arising of the origination of a rose-apple from a mango tree when rose-apple trees are absent, just as he would the arising of the mental body from the material body, said: “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

Impaction-contact (paṭighasamphasso). The third question is stated in terms of both.

There the Elder, rejecting the arising of the origination of mangoes and rose-apples in space, just as he would the arising of the contact of the two in the absence of name and form (nāmarūpa), said: “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

Thus, having shown the conditions for the two kinds of contact separately, now, in order to show without making distinctions, that name and form (nāmarūpa) is the condition for both of them, he began the fourth question: “By which qualities, Ānanda…”

That is, this name and form (yadidaṃ nāmarūpa): that name and form (nāmarūpa) which is in the six doors, this itself is the cause, this itself is the condition, is the meaning.

For in the eye-door, the eye and the rest as well as visible form objects and the rest are form, and the aggregates associated [with contact] are name (nāma). Thus that fivefold contact is still “contact with name and form (nāmarūpa) as condition."

In the mind-door, too, the heart-basis and any material object are form (rūpa).

The phenomena associated with contact and any immaterial object are name (nāma).

Thus mind-contact, too, is “contact with name and form (nāmarūpa) as condition.”

But name and form (nāmarūpa) is a condition in many ways.

mula_pali: 115. ‘‘‘Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ. Viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, mātukucchismiṃ na okkamissatha, api nu kho nāmarūpaṃ mātukucchismiṃ samuccissathā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, mātukucchismiṃ okkamitvā vokkamissatha, api nu kho nāmarūpaṃ itthattāya abhinibbattissathā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, daharasseva sato vocchijjissatha kumārakassa vā kumārikāya vā, api nu kho nāmarūpaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjissathā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo nāmarūpassa – yadidaṃ viññāṇaṃ’’.
mula_english:
115. “‘With consciousness as condition, there is name and form (nāmarūpa).’ Thus it has been said. And this, Ānanda, should be understood in this way: that with consciousness as condition, there is name and form.

If consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, Ānanda, would name and form take shape in the womb?” “No, venerable sir.”

“If, after descending into the womb, consciousness were to depart, Ānanda, would name and form be generated into this present state of being?” “No, venerable sir.”

“If the consciousness of a young boy or girl were to be cut off, Ānanda, would name and form grow up, develop, and reach maturity?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (hetu), source (nidāna), origin (samudaya), and condition (paccaya) for name and form (nāmarūpa), namely, consciousness (vijñāṇa).”
commentary_pali:
115.Na okkamissathāti pavisitvā pavattamānaṃ viya paṭisandhivasena na vattissatha. Samuccissathāti paṭisandhiviññāṇe asati api nu kho suddhaṃ avasesaṃ nāmarūpaṃ antomātukucchismiṃ kalalādibhāvena samuccitaṃ missakabhūtaṃ hutvā vattissatha. Okkamitvā vokkamissathāti paṭisandhivasena okkamitvā cutivasena vokkamissatha, nirujjhissathāti attho. So panassa nirodho na tasseva cittassa nirodhena, na tato dutiyatatiyānaṃ nirodhena hoti. Paṭisandhicittena hi saddhiṃ samuṭṭhitāni samatiṃsa kammajarūpāni nibbattanti. Tesu pana ṭhitesuyeva soḷasa bhavaṅgacittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti. Etasmiṃ antare gahitapaṭisandhikassa dārakassa vā mātuyā vā panassa antarāyo natthi. Ayañhi anokāso nāma. Sace pana paṭisandhicittena saddhiṃ samuṭṭhitarūpāni sattarasamassa bhavaṅgassa paccayaṃ dātuṃ sakkonti, pavatti pavattati, paveṇī ghaṭiyati. Sace pana na sakkonti, pavatti nappavattati, paveṇī na ghaṭiyati, vokkamati nāma hoti. Taṃ sandhāya ‘‘okkamitvā vokkamissathā’’ti vuttaṃ.

Itthattāyāti itthabhāvāya, evaṃ paripuṇṇapañcakkhandhabhāvāyāti attho. Daharasseva satoti mandassa bālasseva santassa. Vocchijjissathāti upacchijjissatha vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullanti viññāṇe upacchinne suddhaṃ nāmarūpameva uṭṭhahitvā paṭhamavayavasena vuḍḍhiṃ, majjhimavayavasena virūḷhiṃ, pacchimavayavasena vepullaṃ api nu kho āpajjissathāti. Dasavassavīsativassavassasatavassasahassasampāpanena vā api nu kho vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjissathāti attho.

Itthattāyā Daharasseva sato Vocchijjissathā vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepulla

Tasmātihānandāti yasmā mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇepi kucchivāsepi kucchito nikkhamanepi, pavattiyaṃ dasavassādikālepi viññāṇamevassa paccayo, tasmā eseva hetu esa paccayo nāmarūpassa, yadidaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Yathā hi rājā attano parisaṃ niggaṇhanto evaṃ vadeyya – ‘‘tvaṃ uparājā, tvaṃ senāpatīti kena kato nanu mayā kato, sace hi mayi akaronte tvaṃ attano dhammatāya uparājā vā senāpati vā bhaveyyāsi, jāneyyāma vo bala’’nti; evameva viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpassa paccayo hoti. Atthato evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ vadati viya ‘‘tvaṃ nāmaṃ, tvaṃ rūpaṃ, tvaṃ nāmarūpaṃ nāmāti kena kataṃ, nanu mayā kataṃ, sace hi mayi purecārike hutvā mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ agaṇhante tvaṃ nāmaṃ vā rūpaṃ vā nāmarūpaṃ vā bhaveyyāsi, jāneyyāma vo bala’’nti. Taṃ panetaṃ viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpassa bahudhā paccayo hoti.

Tasmātihānandā
commentary_english:
115. "You will not descend" means that you will not continue in rebirth due to rebirth-linking.

"You will accumulate" means that in the absence of rebirth-linking consciousness, will merely pure, unseparated mentality-materiality accumulate in the mother's womb, in the state of the embryo, and continue as a mixed entity?

"Having descended, you will depart" means that having descended by way of rebirth-linking, you will depart by way of death-consciousness, and cease. This is the meaning.
