But this cessation does not come about through the ceasing of that consciousness itself, nor through the subsequent ceasing of the second and third [moments of consciousness].

For thirty *karma*-born material phenomena are produced originating along with the rebirth-linking consciousness.

While they endure, sixteen moments of life-continuum consciousness arise and cease.

During this time there is no obstacle to the child who has taken rebirth-linking or to the mother.

This is called "the period of safety" (*anokāso*).

If the material phenomena originating along with the rebirth-linking consciousness can provide a condition for the seventeenth life-continuum consciousness, the course of existence occurs and the current continues.

But if they cannot provide a condition, the course of existence does not occur and the current does not continue. This is called "departing" (*vokkamati*).

It was in reference to this that the Buddha said: "If, after descending, consciousness were to depart."

"For the state of suchness" means for the state of being thus, thus for the state of having complete five aggregates. This is the meaning.

"While still young" means for one who is slow-witted and childish.

"You will be cut off" means you will be terminated. Growth, development, and abundance means when consciousness is cut off, will merely pure mentality-materiality arise and undergo growth according to the initial stage of life, development according to the middle stage of life, and abundance according to the final stage of life?

Or will you attain growth, development, and abundance through the accomplishment of ten years, twenty years, one hundred years, or one thousand years? This is the meaning.

For the state of suchness, while still young, you will be cut off. Growth, development, and abundance.

"Therefore, Ānanda," because at the moment of grasping rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, during the stay in the womb, and at the time of exiting the womb, consciousness itself is the condition. Therefore, this itself is the cause, this is the condition for mentality-materiality, namely, consciousness.

Just as a king, restraining his retinue, might say: "Who was it that made you viceroy and you general? Didn't I do so? For if you could become a viceroy or general by yourself, without my making you such, then we would know your power." In the same way, consciousness is a condition for mentality-materiality.

In essence, consciousness might say to mentality-materiality: "Who is it that made you mentality, you materiality, you mentality-materiality? Didn't I do so? For if you could become mentality, materiality, or mentality-materiality without myself having become a forerunner and taken rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, then we would know your power."

Consciousness is a condition for mentality-materiality in many ways.

Therefore, Ānanda.

mula_pali:
116. ‘‘‘Nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇa’nti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, tadānanda, imināpetaṃ pariyāyena veditabbaṃ, yathā nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ. Viññāṇañca hi, ānanda, nāmarūpe patiṭṭhaṃ na labhissatha, api nu kho āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇaṃ dukkhasamudayasambhavo jātijarāmaraṇadukkhasamudayasambhavo (sī. syā. pī.) paññāyethā’’ti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu etaṃ nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo viññāṇassa yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ. Ettāvatā kho, ānanda, jāyetha vā jīyetha jiyyetha (ka.) vā mīyetha miyyetha (ka.) vā cavetha vā upapajjetha vā. Ettāvatā adhivacanapatho, ettāvatā niruttipatho, ettāvatā paññattipatho, ettāvatā paññāvacaraṃ, ettāvatā vaṭṭaṃ vattati itthattaṃ paññāpanāya yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇena aññamaññapaccayatā pavattati.

Attapaññatti
mula_english:
“It was said: ‘With name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as condition there is consciousness (*vijñāṇa*).’ How that is so, Ānanda, should be understood in this way: namely, with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as condition, there is consciousness (*vijñāṇa*).

If consciousness (*vijñāṇa*) were not to gain a footing in name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), would an origination of the mass of suffering—of future birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), and death (*maraṇa*)—be discerned?" "No, venerable sir." "Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause (*hetu*), this is the source (*nidāna*), this is the origin (*samudaya*), and this is the condition (*paccayo*) for consciousness (*vijñāṇassa*), namely, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). To this extent, Ānanda, there is arising (*jāyetha*), decaying (*jīyetha*), dying (*mīyetha*), passing away (*cavetha*), or reappearing (*upapajjetha*). To this extent there is a pathway for designation, to this extent there is a pathway for language, to this extent there is a pathway for description, to this extent there is a sphere for wisdom, to this extent the round turns for describing this state of being, that is, when there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) together with consciousness (*vijñāṇena*) due to their conditionality.

Self-designation
commentary_pali:
116.Dukkhasamudayasambhavoti dukkharāsisambhavo. Yadidaṃ nāmarūpanti yaṃ idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, eseva hetu esa paccayo. Yathā hi rājapurisā rājānaṃ niggaṇhanto evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘‘tvaṃ rājāti kena kato, nanu mayā kato, sace hi mayi uparājaṭṭhāne, mayi senāpatiṭṭhāne atiṭṭhante tvaṃ ekakova rājā bhaveyyāsi, passeyyāma te rājabhāva’’nti; evameva nāmarūpampi atthato evaṃ viññāṇaṃ vadati viya ‘‘tvaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇanti kena kataṃ, nanu amhehi kataṃ, sace hi tvaṃ tayo khandhe hadayavatthuñca anissāya paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ nāma bhaveyyāsi, passeyyāma te paṭisandhiviññāṇabhāva’’nti. Tañca panetaṃ nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇassa bahudhā paccayo hoti.

Ettāvatā khoti viññāṇe nāmarūpassa paccaye honte, nāmarūpe viññāṇassa paccaye honte, dvīsu aññamaññapaccayavasena pavattesu ettakena jāyetha vā…pe… upapajjetha vā, jātiādayo paññāyeyyuṃ aparāparaṃ vā cutipaṭisandhiyoti.

Ettāvatā kho

Adhivacanapathoti ‘‘sirivaḍḍhako dhanavaḍḍhako’’tiādikassa atthaṃ adisvā vacanamattameva adhikicca pavattassa vohārassa patho. Niruttipathoti saratīti sato, sampajānātīti sampajānotiādikassa kāraṇāpadesavasena pavattassa vohārassa patho. Paññattipathoti – ‘‘paṇḍito byatto medhāvī nipuṇo kataparappavādo’’tiādikassa nānappakārato ñāpanavasena pavattassa vohārassa patho. Iti tīhi padehi adhivacanādīnaṃ vatthubhūtā khandhāva kathitā. Paññāvacaranti paññāya avacaritabbaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Vaṭṭaṃ vattatīti saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ vattati. Itthattanti itthaṃbhāvo, khandhapañcakassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Paññāpanāyāti nāmapaññattatthāya. ‘‘Vedanā saññā’’tiādinā nāmapaññattatthāya, khandhapañcakampi ettāvatā paññāyatīti attho. Yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇenāti yaṃ idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇena aññamaññapaccayatāya pavattati, ettāvatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañhettha niyyātitavacanaṃ.

Adhivacanapatho Niruttipatho Paññattipatho Paññāvacara Vaṭṭaṃ vattatī Itthatta Paññāpanāyā Yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇenā

Attapaññattivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
116. *Dukkhasamudayasambhavo* means the arising of the mass of suffering.

*Yadidaṃ nāmarūpa* means whatever this mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) is, this itself is the cause, this is the condition.

For example, just as the king's officers, restraining the king, might say: "Who was it that made you king? Didn't we do so? If you could become king alone, without one of us occupying the position of viceroy, another the position of general, then we would see what kind of king you are." In the same way, as it were, mentality-materiality might say to consciousness: “Who is it that made you the rebirth-linking consciousness? Didn’t we do so? If you could become a rebirth-linking consciousness without the three aggregates and the heart-basis, then we would see what kind of rebirth-linking consciousness you are.”

Mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) is a condition for consciousness in many ways.

*Ettāvatā kho* means when consciousness is a condition for mentality-materiality, when mentality-materiality is a condition for consciousness, when the two occur as conditions for one another, it is by this much that one can be born … pass away and re-arise, that birth, etc., or repeated death and rebirth-linking, can be discerned.

*Ettāvatā kho*

*Adhivacanapatho* means “a pathway for designation”: a pathway for an expression used through the application of a mere word regardless of meaning, as in the case of names such as “Sirivaḍḍhaka,” “Dhanavaḍḍhaka,” etc.

*Niruttipatho* means a pathway for an expression used to communicate through diverse aspects; thus “mindful” (*sato*), “fully understanding” (*sampajāno*), etc., because of causal designation.

*Paññattipatho* means “a pathway for description”: a pathway for an expression used to communicate through diverse aspects; thus “wise, clever, intelligent, subtle, proficient,” etc.

These three terms refer to the aggregates which become the basis for designation, language, and description.

*Paññāvacara* means that which should be investigated and known by wisdom (*paññā*).

*Vaṭṭaṃ vattatī* means the round of *saṃsāra* turns.

*Itthatta* means suchness (*itthaṃbhāvo*), this is a name for the five aggregates (*khandha*).

*Paññāpanāya* means for the description by names.

"Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*)," etc., are for the description by names. The meaning is: the five aggregates (*khandha*) too are discerned to this extent.

*Yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇenā* means whatever this mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) is together with consciousness (*viññāṇa*), occurs as conditions for one another; what is meant is, to this extent.

This statement refers back.

*Adhivacanapatho* *niruttipatho* *paññattipatho* *paññāvacara* *vaṭṭaṃ vattatī* *itthatta* *paññāpanāya* *yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saha viññāṇenā*

Explanation of the designation of self.

mula_pali: 117. ‘‘Kittāvatā ca, ānanda, attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti? Rūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti – ‘‘rūpī me paritto attā’’ti. Rūpiṃ vā hi , ānanda, anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti – ‘rūpī me ananto attā’ti. Arūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti – ‘arūpī me paritto attā’ti. Arūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti – ‘arūpī me ananto attā’ti.
mula_english:
117. How far, Ānanda, does one who delineates a self delineate it?

Either, Ānanda, delineating a self possessed of form and finite, one delineates that ‘My self is possessed of form and finite.’

Or, Ānanda, delineating a self possessed of form and infinite, one delineates that ‘My self is possessed of form and infinite.’

Or, Ānanda, delineating a self formless and finite, one delineates that ‘My self is formless and finite.’

Or, Ānanda, delineating a self formless and infinite, one delineates that ‘My self is formless and infinite.’
commentary_pali: 117. Iti bhagavā – ‘‘gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo, gambhīrāvabhāso cā’’ti padassa anusandhiṃ dassetvā idāni ‘‘tantākulakajātā’’ti padassa anusandhiṃ dassento ‘‘kittāvatā cā’’tiādikaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha rūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānantiādīsu yo avaḍḍhitaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ attāti gaṇhāti, so rūpiṃ parittaṃ paññapeti. Yo pana nānākasiṇalābhī hoti, so taṃ kadāci nīlo, kadāci pītakoti paññapeti. Yo vaḍḍhitaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ attāti gaṇhāti, so rūpiṃ anantaṃ paññapeti. Yo vā pana avaḍḍhitaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ ugghāṭetvā nimittaphuṭṭhokāsaṃ vā tattha pavatte cattāro khandhe vā tesu viññāṇamattameva vā attāti gaṇhāti, so arūpiṃ parittaṃ paññapeti. Yo vaḍḍhitaṃ nimittaṃ ugghāṭetvā nimittaphuṭṭhokāsaṃ vā tattha pavatte cattāro khandhe vā tesu viññāṇamattameva vā attāti gaṇhāti, so arūpiṃ anantaṃ paññapeti.
commentary_english:
117. Thus said the Blessed One: "This dependent arising, Ānanda, is deep and appears deep." Having shown the connection to that statement, he now began the following teaching, starting with "To what extent?" showing the connection to the statement, "This generation has become like a tangled skein."

Therein, one who apprehends the unextended *kasiṇa*-sign as self, in statements beginning with "<hi rend="bold">Having material form or, Ānanda, limited self</hi>," describes self as having material form and as limited (*rūpiṃ parittaṃ paññāpeti*).

One who gains different *kasiṇas* sometimes describes it as blue (*nīlo*), sometimes as yellow (*pītako*), etc.

One who apprehends the extended *kasiṇa*-sign as self describes self as having material form and as infinite (*rūpiṃ anantaṃ paññāpeti*).

One who removes the unextended *kasiṇa*-sign and apprehends as self either the area that had been covered by the sign or the four aggregates (*khandha*) occurring there, or, from among these, mere consciousness (*vijñāṇamattameva*) describes self as immaterial and limited (*arūpiṃ parittaṃ paññāpeti*).

One who removes the extended sign and apprehends as self either the area that had been covered by the sign or the four aggregates occurring there, or, from among these, mere consciousness describes self as immaterial and infinite (*arūpiṃ anantaṃ paññāpeti*).

mula_pali:
118. ‘‘Tatrānanda, yo so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti. Etarahi vā so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, rūpiṃ rūpī (ka.) parittattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

‘‘Tatrānanda, yo so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti. Etarahi vā so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, rūpiṃ rūpī (ka.) anantattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

‘‘Tatrānanda, yo so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti. Etarahi vā so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, arūpiṃ arūpī (ka.) parittattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

arūpī (ka.)

‘‘Tatrānanda, yo so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti. Etarahi vā so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, arūpiṃ arūpī (ka.) anantattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya. Ettāvatā kho, ānanda, attānaṃ paññapento paññapeti.

arūpī (ka.)

Naattapaññatti
mula_english:
118. “Therein, Ānanda, one who describes self describes it as having material form and as limited.

Either he describes self as having material form and as limited in the present, or he describes self as having material form and as limited in the future, or he thinks, ‘Although it is not that way now, I will make it that way.’

This being so, Ānanda, it is fitting to say that a settled view of self as having material form and as limited underlies this.

“Therein, Ānanda, one who describes self describes it as having material form and as infinite.

Either he describes self as having material form and as infinite in the present, or he describes self as having material form and as infinite in the future, or he thinks, ‘Although it is not that way now, I will make it that way.’

This being so, Ānanda, it is fitting to say that a settled view of self as having material form and as infinite underlies this.

“Therein, Ānanda, one who describes self describes it as immaterial and as limited.

Either he describes self as immaterial and as limited in the present, or he describes self as immaterial and as limited in the future, or he thinks, ‘Although it is not that way now, I will make it that way.’

This being so, Ānanda, it is fitting to say that a settled view of self as immaterial and as limited underlies this.

“Therein, Ānanda, one who describes self describes it as immaterial and as infinite.

Either he describes self as immaterial and as infinite in the present, or he describes self as immaterial and as infinite in the future, or he thinks, ‘Although it is not that way now, I will make it that way.’

This being so, Ānanda, it is fitting to say that a settled view of self as immaterial and as infinite underlies this.

It is in these ways, Ānanda, that one describing self describes it.

Non-self-designation
commentary_pali:
118.Tatrānandāti ettha tatrāti tesu catūsu diṭṭhigatikesu. Etarahi vāti idāneva, na ito paraṃ. Ucchedavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatthabhāviṃ vāti tattha vā paraloke bhāviṃ. Sassatavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Atathaṃ vā pana santanti atathasabhāvaṃ samānaṃ. Tathattāyāti tathabhāvāya. Upakappessāmīti sampādessāmi. Iminā vivādaṃ dasseti. Ucchedavādī hi ‘‘sassatavādino attānaṃ atathaṃ anucchedasabhāvampi samānaṃ tathatthāya ucchedasabhāvāya upakappessāmi, sassatavādañca jānāpetvā ucchedavādameva naṃ gāhessāmī’’ti cinteti. Sassatavādīpi ‘‘ucchedavādino attānaṃ atathaṃ asassatasabhāvampi samānaṃ tathatthāya sassatabhāvāya upakappessāmi, ucchedavādañca jānāpetvā sassatavādameva naṃ gāhessāmī’’ti cinteti.

Evaṃsantaṃ khoti evaṃ samānaṃ rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ paññapentanti attho. Rūpinti rūpakasiṇalābhiṃ. Parittattānudiṭṭhi anusetīti paritto attāti ayaṃ diṭṭhi anuseti, sā pana na valli viya ca latā viya ca anuseti. Appahīnaṭṭhena anusetīti veditabbo. Iccālaṃ vacanāyāti taṃ puggalaṃ evarūpā diṭṭhi anusetīti vattuṃ yuttaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Evaṃ santaṃ kho Rūpi Parittattānudiṭṭhi anusetī Iccālaṃ vacanāyā

Arūpinti ettha pana arūpakasiṇalābhiṃ, arūpakkhandhagocaraṃ vāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Ettāvatā lābhino cattāro, tesaṃ antevāsikā cattāro, takkikā cattāro, tesaṃ antevāsikā cattāroti attato soḷasa diṭṭhigatikā dassitā honti.

Arūpi

Naattapaññattivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
118.
"Tatrānandā" (in that delight) is in these four kinds of theorists.

"Etarahi vā" (in the present) means now only, not afterwards.

This is said by way of annihilationism ( *ucchedavāda*).

"Tatthabhāviṃ vā" (existing there) means existing there or in another world.

This is said by way of eternalism ( *sassatavāda*).

"Atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ" (or not real, but existent) means having an unreal nature, [yet] existing.

"Tathattāyā" (for the sake of suchness) means for the sake of that state.

"Upakappessāmī" (I will bring about) means I will accomplish.

The third position shows their dispute.

For the annihilationist thinks: "The self, which the eternalist posits as not subject to annihilation, is not thus. I will convert him to the way it really is—subject to annihilation. I will make him understand his eternalism and cause him to accept annihilationism."

The eternalist, too, thinks: "The self, which the annihilationist posits as non-eternal, is not thus. I will convert him to the way it really is—eternal. I will make him understand his annihilationism and cause him to accept eternalism."

"Evaṃ santaṃ kho" (thus, existent indeed) means thus, the meaning is that they describe the self as having material form, limited.

"Rūpi" (having material form) means having attained the form *kasiṇa*.

"Parittattānudiṭṭhi anusetī" (a settled view as having material form and limited underlies this) means this view underlies this, [thinking] "the self is limited," but it does not underlie this like a vine or creeper.

It should be understood that it underlies this in the sense that it has not been abandoned.

"Iccālaṃ vacanāyā" (it is enough to say) means it is proper to say that such a view underlies that person.

This method applies to all the other cases.

"Evaṃ...arūpi" (thus...formless) means here, *arūpakasiṇalābhiṃ*, *arūpakkhandhagocaraṃ vāti*, this is how the meaning should be understood.

To this extent sixteen kinds of theorists have been shown: four who gain meditative attainments, their respective disciples, four rationalists, and their respective disciples.

*Arūpi*.

A description of the non-self designation.

mula_pali: 119. ‘‘Kittāvatā ca, ānanda, attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti? Rūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti – ‘rūpī me paritto attā’ti. Rūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti – ‘rūpī me ananto attā’ti. Arūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti – ‘arūpī me paritto attā’ti. Arūpiṃ vā hi, ānanda, anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti – ‘arūpī me ananto attā’ti.
mula_english: 119. Now, Ānanda, in what way does one not describe the self? Either, Ānanda, not describing self as having material form (rūpim) and as limited (paritta), one does not describe it thus: ‘My self has material form and is limited (rūpī me paritto attā).’ Or, Ānanda, not describing self as having material form (rūpim) and as infinite (ananta), one does not describe it thus: ‘My self has material form and is infinite (rūpī me ananto attā).’ Or, Ānanda, not describing self as immaterial (arūpim) and as limited (paritta), one does not describe it thus: ‘My self is immaterial and limited (arūpī me paritto attā).’ Or, Ānanda, not describing self as immaterial (arūpim) and as infinite (ananta), one does not describe it thus: ‘My self is immaterial and infinite (arūpī me ananto attā).’
commentary_pali:
119. Evaṃ ye attānaṃ paññapenti, te dassetvā idāni ye na paññapenti, te dassetuṃ – ‘‘kittāvatā ca ānandā’’tiādimāha. Ke pana na paññapenti? Sabbe tāva ariyapuggalā na paññapenti. Ye ca bahussutā tipiṭakadharā dvipiṭakadharā ekapiṭakadharā, antamaso ekanikāyampi sādhukaṃ vinicchinitvā uggahitadhammakathikopi āraddhavipassakopi puggalo, te na paññapentiyeva. Etesañhi paṭibhāgakasiṇe paṭibhāgakasiṇamicceva ñāṇaṃ hoti. Arūpakkhandhesu ca arūpakkhandhā icceva.

Attasamanupassanāvaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
Having thus shown those who describe self, the Buddha speaks the present section to show those who do not describe self.
Who do not describe self? All noble individuals, firstly, do not describe self.
Then those who are highly learned—one who is a master of three *Piṭakas* (tipiṭakadhara), two *Piṭakas* (dvipiṭakadhara), one *Piṭaka* (ekapiṭakadhara), or even the studious expounder of the *Dharma* who has thoroughly discriminated one *Nikāya* (ekanikāyampi), as well as one who has undertaken insight—they do not describe self.
They know that the counterpart sign of the *kasiṇa* is only a counterpart sign (paṭibhāgakasiṇe paṭibhāgakasiṇamicceva ñāṇaṃ hoti).
And that the immaterial aggregates are only immaterial aggregates (arūpakkhandhesu ca arūpakkhandhā icceva).

Explanation of Considering Self. (attasamanupassanāvaṇṇanā)

mula_pali:
120. ‘‘Tatrānanda, yo so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti. Etarahi vā so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so rūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa na hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, rūpiṃ parittattānudiṭṭhi nānusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

‘‘Tatrānanda , yo so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti. Etarahi vā so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so rūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa na hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, rūpiṃ anantattānudiṭṭhi nānusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

‘‘Tatrānanda, yo so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti. Etarahi vā so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so arūpiṃ parittaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa na hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, arūpiṃ parittattānudiṭṭhi nānusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya.

‘‘Tatrānanda, yo so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti. Etarahi vā so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, tattha bhāviṃ vā so arūpiṃ anantaṃ attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti, ‘atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ tathattāya upakappessāmī’ti iti vā panassa na hoti. Evaṃ santaṃ kho, ānanda, arūpiṃ anantattānudiṭṭhi nānusetīti iccālaṃ vacanāya. Ettāvatā kho, ānanda, attānaṃ na paññapento na paññapeti.

Attasamanupassanā
mula_english:
“Therein, Ānanda, one who does not delineate a self, does not delineate it as possessed of form (rūpiṃ) and finite (parittaṃ). He does not delineate it as possessed of form and finite in the present, nor does he delineate it as of such a nature that it will naturally become possessed of form and finite in the future/after death, nor does he believe that ‘Although it is not yet that way, I will convert it into being that way.’ This being so, it can aptly be said that a settled view as having material form and as limited does not underlie this.

“Therein, Ānanda, one who does not delineate a self, does not delineate it as possessed of form (rūpiṃ) and infinite (anantaṃ). He does not delineate it as possessed of form and infinite in the present, nor does he delineate it as of such a nature that it will naturally become possessed of form and infinite in the future/after death, nor does he believe that ‘Although it is not yet that way, I will convert it into being that way.’ This being so, it can aptly be said that a settled view as having material form and as infinite does not underlie this.

“Therein, Ānanda, one who does not delineate a self, does not delineate it as formless (arūpiṃ) and finite (parittaṃ). He does not delineate it as formless and finite in the present, nor does he delineate it as of such a nature that it will naturally become formless and finite in the future/after death, nor does he believe that ‘Although it is not yet that way, I will convert it into being that way.’ This being so, it can aptly be said that a settled view as immaterial and limited does not underlie this.

“Therein, Ānanda, one who does not delineate a self, does not delineate it as formless (arūpiṃ) and infinite (anantaṃ). He does not delineate it as formless and infinite in the present, nor does he delineate it as of such a nature that it will naturally become formless and infinite in the future/after death, nor does he believe that ‘Although it is not yet that way, I will convert it into being that way.’ This being so, it can aptly be said that a settled view as immaterial and infinite does not underlie this. It is in these ways, Ānanda, that one not describing self does not describe it.

Observation of Self

mula_pali: 121. ‘‘Kittāvatā ca, ānanda, attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati? Vedanaṃ vā hi, ānanda, attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati – ‘vedanā me attā’ti. ‘Na heva kho me vedanā attā, appaṭisaṃvedano me attā’ti iti vā hi, ānanda, attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati. ‘Na heva kho me vedanā attā, nopi appaṭisaṃvedano me attā, attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti iti vā hi, ānanda, attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati.
mula_english:
121. And to what extent, Ānanda, does one considering self consider self? Either one considering self considers feeling (*vedanā*) as self, saying: ‘Feeling is my self’ (*vedanā me attā*).

Or he considers: ‘Feeling is not my self; my self is without experience of feeling’ (*na heva kho me vedanā attā, appaṭisaṃvedano me attā’ti*).

Or he considers: ‘Feeling is not my self, nor is my self oblivious to feeling, but rather my self feels, in that my self is subject to feeling’ (*na heva kho me vedanā attā, nopi appaṭisaṃvedano me attā, attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti*).
commentary_pali:
121. Evaṃ ye na paññapenti, te dassetvā idāni ye te paññapenti, te yasmā diṭṭhivasena samanupassitvā paññapenti, sā ca nesaṃ samanupassanā vīsativatthukāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā appahīnattā hoti, tasmā taṃ vīsativatthukaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiṃ dassetuṃ puna kittāvatā ca ānandātiādimāha.

Tattha vedanaṃ vā hīti iminā vedanākkhandhavatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi kathitā. Appaṭisaṃvedano me attāti iminā rūpakkhandhavatthukā. Attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attāti iminā saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇakkhandhavatthukā . Idañhi khandhattayaṃ vedanāsampayuttattā vediyati. Etassa ca vedanādhammo avippayuttasabhāvo.

vedanaṃ vā hī Appaṭisaṃvedano me attā Attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā
commentary_english:
121. Thus, those who do not describe self, having shown them, now those who describe self, because they describe self after considering it by way of views, and their consideration comes about because they have not abandoned personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) with its twenty cases. Therefore the Exalted One speaks the present section to show personality view with its twenty cases, beginning with "<hi rend="bold">How far, Ānanda?</hi>"

Therein, “Considers Feeling as Self (vedanaṃ vā hī)” By this, personality view based on the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) is explained.

“My self is without feeling (appaṭisaṃvedano me attā)” By this, [personality view] based on the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) [is explained].

“My self feels; for my self is subject to feeling (attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā).” This is personality view based on the aggregates of perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa).

For these three aggregates (khandhattayaṃ) feel (vediyati) because they are associated with feeling (vedanāsampayuttattā).

The phenomenon of feeling (vedanādhammo) belongs to them and cannot be dissociated from them (avippayuttasabhāvo).

Considers Feeling as Self (vedanaṃ vā hī). My self is without feeling (appaṭisaṃvedano me attā). My self feels; for my self is subject to feeling (attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā).

mula_pali: 122. ‘‘Tatrānanda, yo so evamāha – ‘vedanā me attā’ti, so evamassa vacanīyo – ‘tisso kho imā, āvuso, vedanā – sukhā vedanā dukkhā vedanā adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Imāsaṃ kho tvaṃ tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ katamaṃ attato samanupassasī’ti? Yasmiṃ, ānanda, samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; sukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ, ānanda, samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; dukkhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ, ānanda, samaye adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti; adukkhamasukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti.
mula_english:
122.
Therein, Ānanda, the one who says ‘Feeling (vedanā) is my self (attā)’ should be asked: ‘Friend (āvuso), there are these three kinds of feeling (vedanā)—pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*), painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhā vedanā*).

Of these three feelings, which do you regard as the self (attato)? Ānanda, at a moment when a pleasant feeling (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃ*) is sensed, no feeling of pain (*dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ*) or of neither pleasure nor pain (*adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ*) is sensed. Only a pleasant feeling (*sukhaṃyeva vedanaṃ*) is sensed at that moment.

Ānanda, at a moment when a feeling of pain (*dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ*) is sensed, no feeling of pleasure (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃ*) or of neither pleasure nor pain (*adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ*) is sensed. Only a feeling of pain (*dukkhaṃyeva vedanaṃ*) is sensed at that moment.

Ānanda, at a moment when a feeling of neither pleasure nor pain (*adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ*) is sensed, no feeling of pleasure (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃ*) or of pain (*dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ*) is sensed. Only a feeling of neither pleasure nor pain (*adukkhamasukhaṃyeva vedanaṃ*) is sensed at that moment.
commentary_pali: 122. Idāni tattha dosaṃ dassento – ‘‘tatrānandā’’tiādimāha. Tattha tatrāti tesu tīsu diṭṭhigatikesu. Yasmiṃ, ānanda, samayetiādi yo yo yaṃ yaṃ vedanaṃ attāti samanupassati, tassa tassa attano kadāci bhāvaṃ, kadāci abhāvanti evamādidosadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.
commentary_english:
Now, showing the fault therein, [the Blessed One] speaks the passage beginning "There, Ānanda..."

There, *tatra*, refers to those three viewpoints (*dṛṣṭigatikeṣu*).

"On the occasion when, Ānanda..." etc., is stated to show the fault, namely, that whatever feeling (*vedanāṃ*) one considers as self (*ātmā*), for that self, there is sometimes existence (*bhāvaṃ*), sometimes non-existence (*abhāvanti*), and so forth.

mula_pali: 123. ‘‘Sukhāpi kho, ānanda, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Dukkhāpi kho, ānanda, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Adukkhamasukhāpi kho, ānanda, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Tassa sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamānassa ‘eso me attā’ti hoti. Tassāyeva sukhāya vedanāya nirodhā ‘byagā byaggā (sī. ka.) me attā’ti hoti. Dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamānassa ‘eso me attā’ti hoti. Tassāyeva dukkhāya vedanāya nirodhā ‘byagā me attā’ti hoti. Adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamānassa ‘eso me attā’ti hoti. Tassāyeva adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya nirodhā ‘byagā me attā’ti hoti. Iti so diṭṭheva dhamme aniccasukhadukkhavokiṇṇaṃ uppādavayadhammaṃ attānaṃ samanupassamāno samanupassati, yo so evamāha – ‘vedanā me attā’ti. Tasmātihānanda, etena petaṃ nakkhamati – ‘vedanā me attā’ti samanupassituṃ.
mula_english:
123.
“Ānanda, pleasant feeling (sukhā vedanā) is impermanent (aniccā), conditioned (saṅkhatā), dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppannā), subject to destruction (khayadhammā), subject to falling away (vayadhammā), subject to fading out (virāgadhammā), and subject to ceasing (nirodhadhammā).
Ānanda, painful feeling ( dukkhā vedanā) is impermanent (aniccā), conditioned (saṅkhatā), dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppannā), subject to destruction (khayadhammā), subject to falling away (vayadhammā), subject to fading out (virāgadhammā), and subject to ceasing (nirodhadhammā).
Ānanda, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukhā vedanā) is impermanent (aniccā), conditioned (saṅkhatā), dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppannā), subject to destruction (khayadhammā), subject to falling away (vayadhammā), subject to fading out (virāgadhammā), and subject to ceasing (nirodhadhammā).
When experiencing a pleasant feeling (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ), one thinks: ‘This is my self’ (‘eso me attā’ti hoti).
Then with the cessation (nirodhā) of that very pleasant feeling (sukhāya vedanāya), one thinks: ‘My self has perished’ (‘byagā me attā’ti hoti).
When experiencing a painful feeling (dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ), one thinks: ‘This is my self’ (‘eso me attā’ti hoti).
Then with the cessation (nirodhā) of that very painful feeling ( dukkhāya vedanāya), one thinks: ‘My self has perished’ (‘byagā me attā’ti hoti).
When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ), one thinks: ‘This is my self’ (‘eso me attā’ti hoti).
Then with the cessation (nirodhā) of that very neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya), one thinks: ‘My self has perished’ (‘byagā me attā’ti hoti).
Thus, he assumes, assuming in the immediate present (diṭṭheva dhamme) a self (attānaṃ) inconstant (anicca), entangled in pleasure and pain (sukhadukkhavokiṇṇaṃ), subject to arising and passing away (uppādavayadhammaṃ), he who says, ‘Feeling (vedanā) is my self’ (‘vedanā me attā’ti).
Therefore, Ānanda, because of this it is not acceptable to consider: ‘Feeling (vedanā) is my self’ (‘vedanā me attā’ti samanupassituṃ).
commentary_pali:
123. Aniccādīsu hutvā abhāvato aniccā. Tehi tehi kāraṇehi saṅgamma samāgamma katāti saṅkhatā. Taṃ taṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca sammā kāraṇeneva uppannāti paṭiccasamuppannā. Khayotiādi sabbaṃ bhaṅgassa vevacanaṃ. Yañhi bhijjati, taṃ khiyatipi vayatipi virajjhatipi nirujjhatipi, tasmā khayadhammātiādi vuttaṃ.

Byagā meti viagāti byagā, vigato niruddho me attāti attho. Kiṃ pana ekasseva tīsupi kālesu – ‘‘eso me attā’’ti hotīti, kiṃ pana na bhavissati? Diṭṭhigatikassa hi thusarāsimhi nikkhittakhāṇukasseva niccalatā nāma natthi, vanamakkaṭo viya aññaṃ gaṇhāti, aññaṃ muñcati. Aniccasukhadukkhavokiṇṇanti visesena taṃ taṃ vedanaṃ attāti samanupassanto aniccañceva sukhañca dukkhañca attānaṃ samanupassati avisesena vedanaṃ attāti samanupassanto vokiṇṇaṃ uppādavayadhammaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati. Vedanā hi tividhā ceva uppādavayadhammā ca, tañcesa attāti samanupassati. Iccassa anicco ceva attā āpajjati, ekakkhaṇe ca bahūnaṃ vedanānaṃ uppādo. Taṃ kho panesa aniccaṃ attānaṃ anujānāti, na ekakkhaṇe bahūnaṃ vedanānaṃ uppatti atthi. Imamatthaṃ sandhāya – ‘‘tasmātihānanda, etenapetaṃ nakkhamati ‘vedanā me attā’ti samanupassitu’’nti vuttaṃ.

Byagā me Aniccasukhadukkhavokiṇṇa
commentary_english:
123.
Having been in impermanence, etc., due to non-existence, [it is] impermanent (*anitya*).
Having come together and assembled from those various causes, [it is] compounded (*saṃkhata*).
Because it has arisen from that particular condition (*pratyaya*) depending on right causes, [it is] dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
*Khayo'tiādi* all of that is a synonym for dissolution (*bhaṅga*).
For whatever breaks up also decays, wastes away, fades away, and ceases; therefore, it is said to be subject to decay (*khayadhammā*).

"My Self has disappeared" means: "My self has departed, my self has ceased." (*vigato niruddho me ātmāti arthaḥ*).
What then? Does it happen that there is one single self in all three times, saying, "This is my self?" What then, will it not be? For the one attached to views has no stability, like a stake stuck in a heap of chaff. Like a forest monkey, he grasps one thing and lets go of another.
"Impermanent, a mixture of pleasure and pain" means, specifically, when observing each feeling as the self, he observes as the self something that is impermanent, pleasant, and painful. Without distinguishing, when observing feeling as the self, he observes as the self something mixed, subject to arising and passing away.
He observes the self.
For feeling is threefold and subject to arising and falling away, and the theorist considers that threefold feeling collectively to be self.
Thus, he commits the error of accepting an impermanent self, and the arising of many feelings at a single moment.
But he allows that an impermanent self exists? There is no arising of many feelings at a single moment.
With this meaning in mind, it was said: "Therefore, Ānanda, in this manner, one does not see fit to assume feeling to be the self."

My Self. Impermanent, a mixture of pleasure and pain.

mula_pali: 124. ‘‘Tatrānanda , yo so evamāha – ‘na heva kho me vedanā attā, appaṭisaṃvedano me attā’ti, so evamassa vacanīyo – ‘yattha panāvuso, sabbaso vedayitaṃ natthi api nu kho, tattha ‘‘ayamahamasmī’’ti siyā’’’ti ? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, etena petaṃ nakkhamati – ‘na heva kho me vedanā attā, appaṭisaṃvedano me attā’ti samanupassituṃ.
mula_english: “Ānanda, if someone says, ‘Feeling is not my self, and my self is without experience of feeling,’ he should be told, ‘But, friend, where there is absolutely no experience, could there be [the thought], “I am this”?’” “No, venerable sir.” “Therefore, Ānanda, because of this it is not acceptable to consider: ‘Feeling is not my self; my self is without experience of feeling.’
commentary_pali:
124.Yattha panāvusoti yattha suddharūpakkhandhe sabbaso vedayitaṃ natthi. Api nu kho tatthāti api nu kho tasmiṃ vedanāvirahite tālavaṇṭe vā vātapāne vā asmīti evaṃ ahaṃkāro uppajjeyyāti attho. Tasmātihānandāti yasmā suddharūpakkhandho uṭṭhāya ahamasmīti na vadati, tasmā etenapi etaṃ nakkhamatīti attho. Api nu kho tattha ayamahamasmīti siyāti api nu kho tesu vedanādhammesu tīsu khandhesu ekadhammopi ayaṃ nāma ahamasmīti evaṃ vattabbo siyā. Atha vā vedanānirodhā saheva vedanāya niruddhesu tesu tīsu khandhesu api nu kho ayamahamasmīti vā ahamasmīti vā uppajjeyyāti attho. Athāyasmā ānando sasavisāṇassa tikhiṇabhāvaṃ viya taṃ asampaṭicchanto no hetaṃ bhanteti āha.

Ettāvatā kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Vaṭṭakathā kathitā hoti. Bhagavā hi vaṭṭakathaṃ kathento katthaci avijjāsīsena kathesi, katthaci taṇhāsīsena, katthaci diṭṭhisīsena. Tattha ‘‘purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi nappaññāyati avijjāya, ‘ito pubbe avijjā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti. Evañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati. Atha ca pana paññāyati idappaccayā avijjā’’ti (a. ni. 10.61) evaṃ avijjāsīsena kathitā. ‘‘Purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi nappaññāyati bhavataṇhāya, ‘ito pubbe bhavataṇhā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti. Evañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati. Atha ca pana paññāyati idappaccayā bhavataṇhā’’ti (a. ni. 10.62) evaṃ taṇhāsīsena kathitā. ‘‘Purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi nappaññāyati bhavadiṭṭhiyā, ‘ito pubbe bhavadiṭṭhi nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti, evañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati. Atha ca pana paññāyati idappaccayā bhavadiṭṭhī’’ti evaṃ diṭṭhisīsena kathitā. Idhāpi diṭṭhisīseneva kathitā.

Diṭṭhigatiko hi sukhādivedanaṃ attāti gahetvā ahaṅkāramamaṅkāraparāmāsavasena sabbabhavayonigati – viññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu tato tato cavitvā tattha tattha upapajjanto mahāsamudde vātukkhittanāvā viya satataṃ samitaṃ paribbhamati, vaṭṭato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃyeva na sakkoti.
commentary_english:
124. "Where, friend," means where there is absolutely no feeling in the bare aggregate of material form.

"Could it be there?" means, could the ego-conception "I am" arise in that which is devoid of feeling, such as a palm-leaf fan or a window panel? That is the meaning.

"Therefore, Ananda," means, since the bare aggregate of material form does not rise up and say "I am," therefore this is not acceptable. That is the meaning.

"Could 'I am this' occur there?" means, among those three aggregates subject to feeling, would there be even one phenomenon which could be spoken of thus: ‘I am this’?

Or else: When, through the cessation of feeling, those three aggregates have ceased along with feeling, could ‘I am’ or ‘I am this’ arise? That is the meaning.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, not accepting that, as if it were the sharp point of a rabbit's horn, said, "No, venerable sir."

To this extent, what has been spoken? The exposition of the round has been spoken.

For the Blessed One, when giving an exposition of the round, sometimes explained it under the heading of ignorance (*avidyā*), sometimes under the heading of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and sometimes under the heading of views (*dṛṣṭi*).

Therein, in the passage: “No first point of ignorance (*avidyā*) can be discerned, bhikkhus, before which there was no ignorance (*avidyā*) and after which it arose."

Of which it could be said, "Thus it is, monastics."

Nevertheless, it can be discerned that ignorance (*avidyā*) has a specific condition" (A.

N.

10.
61)—thus the round is explained under the heading of ignorance (*avidyā*).

“No first point of the craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) can be discerned, bhikkhus, before which there was no craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) and after which it arose."

Of which it could be said, "Thus it is, monastics."

Nevertheless, it can be discerned that the craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) has a specific condition" (A.

N.

10.
62)—thus the round is explained under the heading of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

“No first point of the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*) can be discerned, bhikkhus, before which there was no view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*) and after which it arose." Of which it could be said, "Thus it is, monastics."

Nevertheless, the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*) has a specific condition”—thus the round is explained under the heading of views (*dṛṣṭi*).

Here, too, the round is explained under the heading of views (*dṛṣṭi*).

For the theorist, having taken pleasant feeling, etc. to be self (*ātman*), misapprehends them through ego-conceptions (*ahaṃkāra*) and conceptions of “mine”; because of this, passing away and re-arising from one state to another in all the realms of existence, modes of origin, destinations, stations for consciousness (*vijñāna*), and abodes of beings, he continually and constantly revolves like a ship on the ocean driven by a storm, unable to lift his head out from the round.

mula_pali: 125. ‘‘Tatrānanda , yo so evamāha – ‘na heva kho me vedanā attā, nopi appaṭisaṃvedano me attā, attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti. So evamassa vacanīyo – vedanā ca hi, āvuso, sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ aparisesā nirujjheyyuṃ. Sabbaso vedanāya asati vedanānirodhā api nu kho tattha ‘ayamahamasmī’ti siyā’’ti? ‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tasmātihānanda, etena petaṃ nakkhamati – ‘‘na heva kho me vedanā attā, nopi appaṭisaṃvedano me attā, attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti samanupassituṃ.
mula_english:
“125. Ānanda, the one who says ‘Feeling (*vedanā*) is not my self (*ātmā*), but my self (*ātmā*) is not without experience of feeling (*vedanā*). My self (*ātmā*) feels (*vedayati*); for my self (*ātmā*) is subject to feeling (*vedanā-dharma*)’—

he should be addressed as follows: ‘My friend, should feelings (*vedanā*) altogether and every way stop without remainder,

then, in the complete absence of feeling (*vedanā*), with the cessation of feeling (*vedanā-nirodha*), could “I am this” occur there? ’.” ‘No, venerable sir.’

“Therefore, Ānanda, because of this it is not acceptable to consider: ‘Feeling (*vedanā*) is not my self (*ātmā*), but my self (*ātmā*) is not without experience of feeling (*vedanā*). My self (*ātmā*) feels (*vedayati*); for my self (*ātmā*) is subject to feeling (*vedanā-dharma*).’

mula_pali:
126. ‘‘Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu neva vedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, nopi appaṭisaṃvedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, nopi ‘attā me vediyati, vedanādhammo hi me attā’ti samanupassati. So evaṃ na samanupassanto na ca kiñci loke upādiyati, anupādiyaṃ na paritassati, aparitassaṃ aparitassanaṃ (ka.) paccattaññeva parinibbāyati, ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Evaṃ vimuttacittaṃ kho, ānanda, bhikkhuṃ yo evaṃ vadeyya – ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa iti sā (aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pāṭhantaraṃ) diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ. ‘Na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ. ‘Hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ. ‘Neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā itissa diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yāvatā, ānanda, adhivacanaṃ yāvatā adhivacanapatho, yāvatā nirutti yāvatā niruttipatho, yāvatā paññatti yāvatā paññattipatho, yāvatā paññā yāvatā paññāvacaraṃ, yāvatā vaṭṭaṃ yāvatā vaṭṭaṃ vaṭṭati (ka. sī.), yāvatā vaṭṭati yāvatā vaṭṭaṃ vaṭṭati (ka. sī.), tadabhiññāvimutto bhikkhu, tadabhiññāvimuttaṃ bhikkhuṃ ‘na jānāti na passati itissa diṭṭhī’ti, tadakallaṃ.

Satta viññāṇaṭṭhiti
mula_english:
126. “Now, Ānanda, in as far as a *bhikkhu* does not assume feeling (*vedanā*) to be the self (*ātmā*), nor the self as without experience of feeling, nor that ‘My self feels, in that my self is subject to feeling.’

Then, not assuming in this way, he does not cling to anything in the world (*loka*). Not clinging, he is not agitated. Not being agitated, he personally attains *parinirvāṇa*. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth (*jāti*), the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’

Ānanda, if someone were to say this of a *bhikkhu* whose mind is thus liberated: ‘The *Tathāgata* exists after death (*maraṇa*)’—that would not be proper.

‘The *Tathāgata* does not exist after death’—that would not be proper.

‘The *Tathāgata* both exists and does not exist after death’—that would not be proper.

‘The *Tathāgata* neither exists nor does not exist after death’—that would not be proper.

What is the reason for that? Ānanda, because that *bhikkhu* is liberated by directly knowing this: the extent of designation (*adhivacana*) and the extent of the pathway for designation (*adhivacana-patha*), the extent of language (*nirutti*) and the extent of the pathway for language (*nirutti-patha*), the extent of description (*paññatti*) and the extent of the pathway for description (*paññatti-patha*), the extent of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the extent of the sphere for wisdom (*prajñāvacara*), the extent of the round (*vaṭṭa*) and the extent to which the round turns. To say of a *bhikkhu* who is liberated by directly knowing this that he holds the view ‘One does not know, one does not see’ is not correct.

Seven abodes of consciousness (*satta viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).
commentary_pali:
126. Iti bhagavā paccayākāramūḷhassa diṭṭhigatikassa ettakena kathāmaggena vaṭṭaṃ kathetvā idāni vivaṭṭaṃ kathento yato kho pana, ānanda, bhikkhūtiādimāha.

Tañca pana vivaṭṭakathaṃ bhagavā desanāsu kusalattā vissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhānaṃ navakammādivasena vikkhittapuggalaṃ anāmasitvā kārakassa satipaṭṭhānavihārino puggalassa vasena ārabhanto neva vedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassatītiādimāha. Evarūpo hi bhikkhu – ‘‘yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre vā santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Dukkhato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Anattato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasana’’ntiādinā nayena vuttassa sammasanañāṇassa vasena sabbadhammesu pavattattā neva vedanaṃ attāti samanupassati, na aññaṃ, so evaṃ asamanupassanto na kiñci loke upādiyatīti khandhalokādibhede loke rūpādīsu dhammesu kiñci ekadhammampi attāti vā attaniyanti vā na upādiyati.

neva vedanaṃ attānaṃ samanupassatī

Anupādiyaṃna paritassatīti anupādiyanto taṇhādiṭṭhimānaparitassanāyāpi na paritassati. Aparitassanti aparitassamāno. Paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyatīti attanāva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyati. Evaṃ parinibbutassa panassa paccavekkhaṇāpavattidassanatthaṃ khīṇā jātītiādi vuttaṃ.

Anupādiyaṃ na paritassatī Aparitassa Paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyatī khīṇā jātī

Iti sā diṭṭhīti yā tathāvimuttassa arahato diṭṭhi, sā evaṃ diṭṭhi. ‘‘Itissa diṭṭhī’’tipi pāṭho. Yo tathāvimutto arahā, evamassa diṭṭhīti attho. Tadakallanti taṃ na yuttaṃ. Kasmā? Evañhi sati – ‘‘arahā na kiñci jānātī’’ti vuttaṃ bhaveyya, evaṃ ñatvā vimuttañca arahantaṃ ‘‘na kiñci jānātī’’ti vattuṃ na yuttaṃ. Teneva catunnampi nayānaṃ avasāne – ‘‘taṃ kissa hetū’’tiādimāha.

Iti sā diṭṭhī Tadakalla

Tattha yāvatā ānanda adhivacananti yattako adhivacanasaṅkhāto vohāro atthi. Yāvatā adhivacanapathoti yattako adhivacanassa patho, khandhā āyatanāni dhātuyo vā atthi. Esa nayo sabbattha. Paññāvacaranti paññāya avacaritabbaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Tadabhiññāti taṃ abhijānitvā. Ettakena bhagavatā kiṃ dassitaṃ? Tantākulapadasseva anusandhi dassito.

yāvatā ānanda adhivacana Yāvatā adhivacanapatho Paññāvacara Tadabhiññā

Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitivaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
126. Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken about the round of conditioned arising to those bewildered by it, to those whose course [is determined by] views, with this much of a talk that is [like] a raft, now, while speaking about release, said, "From the fact that, Ānanda, a monk..." and so on.

Moreover, the Blessed One, skillful in discourses, not touching upon scattered individuals who have relinquished their meditation subject through reasons such as new work, beginning with new work, but commencing on the basis of the individual who dwells in mindfulness of the body, said, "He does not regard feeling as self," and so on.

Such a *bhikṣu*—"Whatever form (rūpa) there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, base or excellent, far or near, he defines all form as impermanent; this is one kind of comprehension.

He defines it as suffering; this is one kind of comprehension.

He defines it as not-self; this is one kind of comprehension," etc. Because he proceeds among all phenomena by means of the exploration knowledge that was described in this way, he does not consider feeling as self, nor anything else. Not considering in such a way, “he does not cling to anything in the world”; that is, among the phenomena such as material form, etc. belonging to the world of the aggregates, etc., he does not cling to even one thing as self or as belonging to self.

He does not regard feeling as self.

Not clinging, he is not tormented; not being tormented, he is without agitation; **having attained what is individually realized, he is extinguished;** destroyed is birth," etc., was said for the purpose of showing the course of reviewing the consciousness of such a one who is extinguished.

Not clinging, he is not tormented; without agitation, having attained what is individually realized, he is extinguished; destroyed is birth—"Thus is his view," that is, the view of an *arhat* who is thus liberated, that is his view.

There is also the reading, "Thus is *his* view."

The meaning is: he who is thus liberated is an *arhat*; thus is his view.

“*Tadakalla*” means that is not suitable.

Why? Because if it were thus, it would be said, “An *arhat* knows nothing.” And having known and liberated the *arhat*, it is not suitable to say, “He knows nothing.”

Therefore, at the end of the four alternatives, he said, “For what reason?” etc.

Thus is his view, *tadakalla*.

There, “As far as, Ānanda, there is designation” means as much as there is a usage called designation.

"As far as is the path of designation," is as much as is the path of designation: the aggregates (skandha), the sense bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), or whatever there is.

This method applies everywhere.

"*Prajñāvacara*" means the five aggregates (*skandhapañcaka*) that should be roamed about by wisdom (*prajñā*).

"*Tadabhiññā*" means having directly known that.

What has been shown by the Blessed One with so much? The connection of just that statement which was tangled with [wrong] meaning has been shown.

As far as, Ānanda, there is designation, as far as is the path of designation, *prajñāvacara*, *tadabhiññā*: the description of the abiding of the seven consciousnesses (*sattaviññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

mula_pali: 127. ‘‘Satta kho, ānanda satta kho imā ānanda (ka. sī. syā.), viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, dve āyatanāni. Katamā satta? Santānanda, sattā nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā , ekacce ca devā, ekacce ca vinipātikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā paṭhamābhinibbattā. Ayaṃ dutiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā ekattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā. Ayaṃ tatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā. Ayaṃ catutthī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ pañcamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti . Santānanda, sattā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ chaṭṭhī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Santānanda, sattā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ sattamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Asaññasattāyatanaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanameva dutiyaṃ.
mula_english:
127. "Ānanda, there are these seven stations for consciousness ( *viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) and two bases (*āyatana*). What are the seven?

“Ānanda, there are beings with diversity of body and diversity of perception, such as humans, some gods, and some beings in states of loss. This is the first station for consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

“Ānanda, there are beings with diversity of body and singularity of perception, such as the gods of the Brahma hosts generated by the first *jhāna*. This is the second station for consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

“Ānanda, there are beings with singularity of body and diversity of perception, such as the Radiant Devas (*ābhassarā*). This is the third station for consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

“Ānanda, there are beings with singularity of body and singularity of perception, such as the Beautifully Lustrous Devas (*subhakiṇhā*). This is the fourth station for consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

“Ānanda, there are beings who, through the complete surmounting of perceptions of material form (*rūpasaññānaṃ*), the passing away of perceptions of resistance (*paṭighasaññānaṃ*), and non-attention to perceptions of diversity (*nānattasaññānaṃ*), perceiving, ‘Space is infinite’ (*ananto ākāso*), arrive at the base of the infinity of space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*). This is the fifth station for consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

“Ānanda, there are beings who, having completely surmounted the base of the infinity of space (*ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ*), perceiving, ‘Consciousness is infinite’ (*anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ*), arrive at the base of the infinity of consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*). This is the sixth station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

“Ānanda, there are beings who, having completely surmounted the base of the infinity of consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ*), perceiving, ‘There is nothing’ (*natthi kiñcī*), arrive at the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). This is the seventh station for consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

“The base of non-percipient beings (*asaññasattāyatanaṃ*) and, second, the base of neither perception nor non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*).
commentary_pali:
127. Idāni yo – ‘‘na paññapetī’’ti vutto, so yasmā gacchanto gacchanto ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma hoti. Yo ca – ‘‘na samanupassatī’’ti vutto, so yasmā gacchanto gacchanto paññāvimutto nāma hoti. Tasmā tesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ dvinnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nigamanañca nāmañca dassetuṃ satta kho imānanda viññāṇaṭṭhitiyotiādimāha.

Tattha sattāti paṭisandhivasena vuttā, ārammaṇavasena saṅgītisutte (dī. ni. 3.311) vuttā catasso āgamissanti. Viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhati etthāti viññāṇaṭṭhiti, viññāṇapatiṭṭhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Dve ca āyatanānīti dve nivāsaṭṭhānāni. Nivāsaṭṭhānañhi idhāyatananti adhippetaṃ. Teneva vakkhati – ‘‘asaññasattāyatanaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanameva dutiya’’nti. Kasmā panetaṃ sabbaṃ gahitanti? Vaṭṭapariyādānatthaṃ. Vaṭṭañhi na suddhaviññāṇaṭṭhitivasena suddhāyatanavasena vā pariyādānaṃ gacchati, bhavayonigatisattāvāsavasena pana gacchati, tasmā sabbametaṃ gahitaṃ.

sattā viññāṇaṭṭhiti, Dve ca āyatanānī

Idāni anukkamena tamatthaṃ vibhajanto katamā sattātiādimāha. Tattha seyyathāpīti nidassanatthe nipāto, yathā manussāti attho. Aparimāṇesu hi cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇānaṃ manussānaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena dvepi ekasadisā natthi. Yepi hi katthaci yamakabhātaro vaṇṇena vā saṇṭhānena vā ekasadisā honti, tesampi ālokitavilokitakathitahasitagamanaṭhānādīhi viseso hotiyeva. Tasmā nānattakāyāti vuttā. Paṭisandhisaññā pana nesaṃ tihetukāpi dvihetukāpi ahetukāpi honti, tasmā nānattasaññinoti vuttā. Ekacce ca devāti cha kāmāvacaradevā. Tesu hi kesañci kāyo nīlo hoti, kesañci pītakādivaṇṇo. Saññā pana nesaṃ dvihetukāpi tihetukāpi honti, ahetukā natthi. Ekacce ca vinipātikāti catuapāyavinimuttā uttaramātā yakkhinī, piyaṅkaramātā, phussamittā, dhammaguttāti evamādikā aññe ca vemānikā petā. Etesañhi pītaodātakāḷamaṅguracchavisāmavaṇṇādivasena ceva kisathūlarassadīghavasena ca kāyo nānā hoti, manussānaṃ viya dvihetukatihetukaahetukavasena saññāpi. Te pana devā viya na mahesakkhā, kapaṇamanussā viya appesakkhā, dullabhaghāsacchādanā dukkhapīḷitā viharanti. Ekacce kāḷapakkhe dukkhitā juṇhapakkhe sukhitā honti, tasmā sukhasamussayato vinipatitattā vinipātikāti vuttā. Ye panettha tihetukā tesaṃ dhammābhisamayopi hoti, piyaṅkaramātā hi yakkhinī paccūsasamaye anuruddhattherassa dhammaṃ sajjhāyato sutvā –

katamā sattā seyyathāpī nānattakāyā nānattasaññino Ekacce ca devā Ekacce ca vinipātikā vinipātikā

‘‘Mā saddamakari piyaṅkara, bhikkhu dhammapadāni bhāsati;

Api dhammapadaṃ vijāniya, paṭipajjema hitāya no siyā;

Pāṇesu ca saṃyamāmase, sampajānamusā na bhaṇāmase;

Sikkhema susīlyamattano, api muccema pisācayoniyā’’ti. (saṃ. ni. 2.40);

Evaṃ puttakaṃ saññāpetvā taṃ divasaṃ sotāpattiphalaṃ pattā. Uttaramātā pana bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvāva sotāpannā jātā.

Brahmakāyikāti brahmapārisajjabrahmapurohitamahābrahmāno. Paṭhamābhinibbattāti te sabbepi paṭhamena jhānena abhinibbattā. Tesu brahmapārisajjā pana parittena abhinibbattā, tesaṃ kappassa tatiyo bhāgo āyuppamāṇaṃ. Brahmapurohitā majjhimena, tesaṃ upaḍḍhakappo āyuppamāṇaṃ, kāyo ca tesaṃ vipphārikataro hoti. Mahābrahmāno paṇītena, tesaṃ kappo āyuppamāṇaṃ, kāyo pana tesaṃ ativipphāriko hoti. Iti te kāyassa nānattā, paṭhamajjhānavasena saññāya ekattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññinoti veditabbā.

Brahmakāyikā Paṭhamābhinibbattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino

Yathā ca te, evaṃ catūsu apāyesu sattā. Nirayesu hi kesañci gāvutaṃ, kesañci aḍḍhayojanaṃ, kesañci yojanaṃ attabhāvo hoti, devadattassa pana yojanasatiko jāto. Tiracchānesupi keci khuddakā, keci mahantā. Pettivisayepi keci saṭṭhihatthā, keci sattatihatthā, keci asītihatthā honti, keci suvaṇṇā, keci dubbaṇṇā honti. Tathā kālakañjikā asurā. Api cettha dīghapiṭṭhikapetā nāma saṭṭhiyojanikāpi honti. Saññā pana sabbesampi akusalavipākaahetukāva honti. Iti āpāyikāpi nānattakāyā ekattasaññinotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti.

Ābhassarāti daṇḍaukkāya acci viya etesaṃ sarīrato ābhā chijjitvā chijjitvā patantī viya sarati vissaratīti ābhassarā. Tesu pañcakanayena dutiyatatiyajjhānadvayaṃ parittaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā parittābhā nāma honti, tesaṃ dve kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Majjhimaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā appamāṇābhā nāma honti, tesaṃ cattāro kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Paṇītaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā ābhassarā nāma honti, tesaṃ aṭṭha kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Idha pana ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena sabbepi te gahitā. Sabbesañhi tesaṃ kāyo ekavipphārova hoti, saññā pana avitakkavicāramattā vā avitakkaavicārā vāti nānā.

Ābhassarā parittābhā appamāṇābhā

Subhakiṇhāti subhena okiṇṇā vikiṇṇā, subhena sarīrappabhāvaṇṇena ekagghanāti attho. Etesañhi ābhassarānaṃ viya na chijjitvā chijjitvā pabhā gacchati. Pañcakanaye pana parittamajjhimapaṇītassa catutthajjhānassa vasena soḷasadvattiṃsacatusaṭṭhikappāyukā parittasubhaappamāṇasubhasubhakiṇhā nāma hutvā nibbattanti. Iti sabbepi te ekattakāyā ceva catutthajjhānasaññāya ekattasaññino cāti veditabbā. Vehapphalāpi catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitimeva bhajanti. Asaññasattā viññāṇābhāvā ettha saṅgahaṃ na gacchanti, sattāvāsesu gacchanti.

Subhakiṇhā parittasubhaappamāṇasubhasubhakiṇhā ekattakāyā ceva Vehapphalāpi Asaññasattā

Suddhāvāsā vivaṭṭapakkhe ṭhitā na sabbakālikā, kappasatasahassampi asaṅkhyeyyampi buddhasuññe loke nuppajjanti. Soḷasakappasahassabbhantare buddhesu uppannesuyeva uppajjanti, dhammacakkappavattassa bhagavato khandhavāraṭṭhānasadisā honti. Tasmā neva viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ na sattāvāsaṃ bhajanti. Mahāsīvatthero pana – ‘‘na kho pana so sāriputta sattāvāso sulabharūpo yo mayā anivutthapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehī’’ti (ma. ni. 1.160) iminā suttena suddhāvāsāpi catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ catutthasattāvāsaṃyeva bhajantīti vadati, taṃ appaṭibāhiyattā suttassa anuññātaṃ.

Suddhāvāsā

Sabbaso rūpasaññānantiādīnaṃ attho visuddhimagge vutto. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pana yatheva saññāya, evaṃ viññāṇassapi sukhumattā neva viññāṇaṃ nāviññāṇaṃ. Tasmā viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu avatvā āyatanesu vuttaṃ.

Sabbaso rūpasaññāna
commentary_english:
127. Now the person spoken of as “not describing self,” as he goes along, eventually becomes one “liberated in both ways” ( *ubhatobhāgavimutto*).

And the person spoken of as “not considering self,” as he goes along, eventually becomes one “liberated by wisdom” (*paññāvimutto*).

Therefore, to show both the conclusion and the name of the two *bhikkhus* mentioned below, he said, “Seven, Ānanda, are the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) ,” and so forth.

There, "sentient beings (*sattā*)" are spoken of in terms of rebirth (*paṭisandhi*), and four will come, spoken of in the *Saṅgīti Sutta* in terms of object (*ārammaṇa*).

Because consciousness stands here, therefore, it is a station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), this term is an epithet of the foundation of consciousness (*viññāṇapatiṭṭhāna*).

“And two bases (*āyatanānī*)” means two dwelling places (*nivāsaṭṭhānāni*).

For the word “base” here means a dwelling place (*nivāsaṭṭhāna*).

He will say just that: “The realm of beings without perception (*asaññasattāyatanaṃ*) and the realm of neither perception nor non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*) are the second."

Why is all this included? For the purpose of exhaustively surveying the round (*vaṭṭapariyādāna*).

For the round is not exhaustively surveyed either by the stations for consciousness alone or by the bases alone, as it is by way of the realms of existence, modes of origin, destinations, and abodes of beings. Therefore all this is included.

Sentient beings (*sattā*) , the station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and two bases (*āyatanānī*). Now, dividing that meaning in sequence, he said, “Which are the sentient beings (*sattā*)?” and so forth.

There, "just as (*seyyathāpī*)" is an indeclinable in the sense of illustration, the meaning is, just as humans.

For among the countless world systems there are not even two of countless humans who are exactly the same in complexion, figure, etc.

Sometimes twins might have the same complexion or figure, but they can still be distinguished by the way they look ahead, look aside, speak, smile, walk, stand, etc.

Therefore, they are called "diverse in body (*nānattakāyā*)."

Their perception associated with rebirth (*paṭisandhi*) may be triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless, therefore they are called "diverse in perception (*nānattasaññino*)."

"Some gods (*devā*)" means the six gods of the desire realm (*kāmāvacaradeva*).

For these may have bodies that are blue, yellow, etc.

and their perception may be triple-rooted or double-rooted, though not rootless.

"Some beings in the lower realms (*vinipātikā*)" means those liberated from the four woeful states, such as Uttarā's mother, the *yakkhinī*, Piyaṅkara's mother, Phussamittā, and Dhammaguttā and other aerial ghosts (*vemānika peta*).

For their bodies are diverse in terms of yellow, white, black, reddish, skin-colored, and uniform colors, and also in terms of being thin, stout, short, and long, and like humans their perception may be double-rooted, triple-rooted, or rootless.

But unlike the gods they are not powerful; they are powerless like low-class humans. They have trouble finding food and clothing and live oppressed by pain.

Some are afflicted during the dark fortnight and happy during the bright fortnight. Therefore, because they have fallen from the heights of happiness, they are called “beings in the lower realms (*vinipātikā*)."

But those who are triple-rooted here also have the understanding of the *dharma*; for Piyaṅkara's mother, the *yakkhinī*, having heard the *dharma* recited by the Elder Anuruddha at dawn...

Which are the sentient beings (*sattā*)? Just as (*seyyathāpī*)... Diverse in body (*nānattakāyā*), diverse in perception (*nānattasaññino*), some gods (*devā*), some beings in the lower realms (*vinipātikā*), beings in the lower realms (*vinipātikā*).

"Piyaṅkara, do not make a sound; the *bhikkhu* is speaking the verses of the Dharma (*dhamma*).

Even knowing the verses of the Dharma (*dhamma*), may we practice for our welfare;

And we will restrain ourselves regarding living beings, we will not speak deliberate lies;

May we train ourselves in our own good morality, may we be freed from the womb of a demon (*pisāca*)".

(Saṃ. Ni. 2.40);

Having convinced her son in this way, she attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*) that day.
Uttaramátá, indeed, having heard the Dhamma from the Exalted One, became a stream-enterer.

*Brahmakāyikā* means the Brahmā’s retinue, Brahmā’s ministers, and the Great Brahmās.

*Pathamābhinibbattā* means all of them are generated through the first *jhāna*.

Among them, the gods of Brahmā’s retinue are generated through a limited . Their life-span is a third of an aeon.

The Brahmā’s ministers are generated through a middling . Their life-span is half an aeon, and their bodies are more pervasive.

The Great Brahmās are generated through a superior . Their life-span is an aeon, and their bodies are extremely pervasive.

Thus, owing to the diversity of their bodies, but oneness of their perception due to the first *jhāna*, they are to be understood as *nānattakāyā ekattasaññino* – "diverse in body, identical in perception."

*Brahmakāyikā*, *pathamābhinibbattā*, *nānattakāyā ekattasaññino* just as beings in the four woeful courses ( *apāya*).

In hells, the individual existence (*attabhāva*) of some is a *gāvuta*, of some half a *yojana*, of some a *yojana*, but that of Devadatta is a hundred *yojanas*.

Among animals too, some are small, some are large.

Even in the realm of ghosts (*pettivisaya*), some are sixty *hatthas* tall, some seventy *hatthas*, some eighty *hatthas*; some are golden-colored, some are of bad complexion.

Likewise, are the Kālakañjika demons (*asurā*).

Furthermore, even here, there are ghosts called Long-Backed (*dīghapiṭṭhika*), who are sixty *yojanas* in size.

Yet for all, perception is a rootless unwholesome resultant.

Thus, beings in the planes of misery are also reckoned as "diverse in body but identical in perception."

*Ābhassarā* means that from their bodies, radiance streams out, flying out after flickering again and again like the flame of a torch.

Those who are reborn as *Parittābhā* – "gods of limited radiance" – are generated as a result of developing the second and third *jhānas* of the fivefold system to a limited extent; their life-span is two aeons.

Those who are reborn as *Appamāṇābhā* – "gods of immeasurable radiance" – are generated as a result of developing to a middling extent; their life-span is four aeons.

Those who are reborn as *Ābhassarā* – "gods of streaming radiance" – are generated as a result of developing to a superior extent; their life-span is eight aeons.

By mentioning the most excellent, all three are included here.

For all these gods have bodies that are identical in pervasion; but their perception is diverse in that some have applied thought but with sustained thought, while some have without either applied thought or sustained thought.

*Ābhassarā*, *Parittābhā*, *Appamāṇābhā*.

*Subhakiṇhā* means crowded and filled with beauty; their bodies are a single mass of beautiful radiance.

Unlike the gods of streaming radiance, their aura is emitted without flickering.

The gods of limited beauty (*parittasubha*), of immeasurable beauty (*appamāṇasubha*), and of refulgent beauty (*subhakiṇhā*) are generated into these states by developing the fourth *jhāna* of the fivefold system to a limited, middling, and superior extent, respectively; their respective life-spans are sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four aeons.

Thus, they are all to be understood as "identical in body" (*ekattakāyā ca*), and also, through the perception pertaining to the fourth *jhāna*, "identical in perception" (*ekattasaññino*).

The *Vehapphalā* gods too resort to the fourth consciousness-sphere (*catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitimeva*).

The non-percipient beings (*asaññasattā*), not having consciousness, are not included here, but they are included among the abodes of beings (*sattāvāsesu*).

*Subhakiṇhā*, *parittasubhaappamāṇasubhasubhakiṇhā*, *ekattakāyā ceva*, *vehapphalāpi*, *asaññasattā*.

The *Suddhāvāsā* gods, standing on the side of the evolved, are not perpetual; they do not arise in a world devoid of Buddhas, even for hundreds of thousands of aeons, even for incalculable aeons.

They arise only when Buddhas have arisen, during a period of 16,000 aeons. These planes are like a special camp-ground of the Exalted One, after he has set in motion the wheel of Dhamma.

Therefore, they resort neither to a consciousness-sphere (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) nor to an abode of beings (*sattāvāsaṃ*).

The Elder Mahāsīva, however, said: "That abode of beings, Sāriputta, is not easy to obtain, which I have not inhabited before during this long journey, apart from the gods of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*)."
1.  160) By this *sutta*, it is said that even the *Śuddhāvāsas* resort to the fourth foundation of consciousness, namely the fourth abode of beings; this is permitted by the *sutta* because it cannot be refuted.

**Śuddhāvāsas**

The meaning of "when there is complete cessation of the perception of form (*sabbaso rūpasaññāna*)," etc., has been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

However, the base of neither perception nor non-perception, like perception, has consciousness that is so subtle that it is called "neither consciousness nor non-consciousness."

Therefore, not being included among the foundations of consciousness, it is stated among the bases.

**When there is complete cessation of the perception of form (*sabbaso rūpasaññāna*)**

mula_pali:
128. ‘‘Tatrānanda, yāyaṃ paṭhamā viññāṇaṭṭhiti nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā, ekacce ca devā, ekacce ca vinipātikā. Yo nu kho, ānanda, tañca pajānāti, tassā ca samudayaṃ pajānāti, tassā ca atthaṅgamaṃ pajānāti, tassā ca assādaṃ pajānāti, tassā ca ādīnavaṃ pajānāti, tassā ca nissaraṇaṃ pajānāti, kallaṃ nu tena tadabhinanditu’’nti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’…pe… ‘‘tatrānanda, yamidaṃ asaññasattāyatanaṃ. Yo nu kho, ānanda, tañca pajānāti, tassa ca samudayaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca atthaṅgamaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca assādaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca ādīnavaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca nissaraṇaṃ pajānāti, kallaṃ nu tena tadabhinanditu’’nti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. ‘‘Tatrānanda, yamidaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ. Yo nu kho, ānanda, tañca pajānāti, tassa ca samudayaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca atthaṅgamaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca assādaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca ādīnavaṃ pajānāti, tassa ca nissaraṇaṃ pajānāti, kallaṃ nu tena tadabhinanditu’’nti? ‘‘No hetaṃ, bhante’’. Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu imāsañca sattannaṃ viññāṇaṭṭhitīnaṃ imesañca dvinnaṃ āyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādā vimutto hoti, ayaṃ vuccatānanda, bhikkhu paññāvimutto.

Aṭṭha vimokkhā
mula_english:
128. “Therein, Ānanda, the first station for consciousness ( *viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) is that of beings who are diverse in body (*nānattakāyā*) and diverse in perception (*nānattasaññino*), such as human beings (*manussā*), some devas, and some beings in the lower realms.

If one discerns that station of consciousness, discerns its origination (*samudayaṃ*), discerns its passing away (*atthaṅgamaṃ*), discerns its allure (*assādaṃ*), discerns its drawbacks (*ādīnavaṃ*), discerns the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from it, would it be proper, by means of that discernment to take delight there?”

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“…If one understands the remaining stations for consciousness… the base of non-percipient beings (*asaññasattāyatanaṃ*).

and if one understands its origin (*samudayaṃ*), its passing away (*atthaṅgamaṃ*), its satisfaction (*assādaṃ*), its unsatisfactoriness (*ādīnavaṃ*), and the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from it, is it proper for one to seek enjoyment in it?”

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Therein, Ānanda, the base of neither perception nor non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ*).

and if one understands its origin (*samudayaṃ*), its passing away (*atthaṅgamaṃ*),

its satisfaction (*assādaṃ*), its unsatisfactoriness (*ādīnavaṃ*), and the escape (*nissaraṇaṃ*) from it, is it proper for one to seek enjoyment in it?”

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Ānanda, when a *bhikkhu*—having understood as they really are the origin (*samudayañca*), passing away (*atthaṅgamañca*), satisfaction (*assādañca*), unsatisfactoriness (*ādīnavañca*), and escape (*nissaraṇañca*) in regard to these seven stations for consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhitīnaṃ*) and two bases (*āyatanānaṃ*)—is liberated through non-clinging (*anupādā vimutto*), then he is called a *bhikkhu* liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutto*).

Eight liberations (*aṭṭha vimokkhā*)
commentary_pali:
128.Tatrāti tāsu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu. Tañca pajānātīti tañca viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ pajānāti. Tassā ca samudayanti ‘‘avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo’’tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.49) nayena tassā samudayañca pajānāti. Tassā ca atthaṅgamanti – ‘‘avijjānirodhā rūpanirodho’’tiādinā nayena tassā atthaṅgamañca pajānāti. Assādanti yaṃ rūpaṃ paṭicca…pe… yaṃ viññāṇaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ viññāṇassa assādoti, evaṃ tassā assādañca pajānāti. Ādīnavanti yaṃ rūpaṃ…pe… yaṃ viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, ayaṃ viññāṇassa ādīnavoti, evaṃ tassā ādīnavañca pajānāti. Nissaraṇanti yo rūpasmiṃ…pe… yo viññāṇe chandarāgavinayo, chandarāgappahānaṃ, idaṃ viññāṇassa nissaraṇanti (saṃ. ni. 2.26) evaṃ tassā nissaraṇañca pajānāti. Kallaṃ nu tenāti yuttaṃ nu tena bhikkhunā taṃ viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena ahanti vā mamanti vā abhinanditunti. Etenupāyena sabbattha veditabbo. Yattha pana rūpaṃ natthi, tattha catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ vasena, yattha viññāṇaṃ natthi, tattha ekassa khandhassa vasena samudayo yojetabbo. Āhārasamudayā āhāranirodhāti idañcettha padaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhūti yadā kho ānanda, bhikkhu. Anupādā vimuttoti catūhi upādānehi aggahetvā vimutto. Paññāvimuttoti paññāya vimutto. Aṭṭha vimokkhe asacchikatvā paññābaleneva nāmakāyassa ca rūpakāyassa ca appavattiṃ katvā vimuttoti attho. So sukkhavipassako ca paṭhamajjhānādīsu aññatarasmiṃ ṭhatvā arahattaṃ patto cāti pañcavidho. Vuttampi cetaṃ – ‘‘katamo ca puggalo paññāvimutto? Idhekacco puggalo na heva kho aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo paññāvimutto’’ti (pu. pa. 15).

Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhū Anupādā vimutto Paññāvimutto

Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
128. *Tatrā* means in those stations of consciousness (*vijñānaṭṭhiti*).

*Tañca pajānāti* means he understands that station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

*Tassā ca samudaya* means, "from the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*) arises form (*rūpa*)," and so forth, by this method, he understands its arising.

*Tassā ca atthaṅgama* means, "from the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases form (*rūpa*)," and so forth, by this method, he understands its passing away.

*Assāda* means, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on form (*rūpa*)…pe… whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on consciousness (*vijñāṇa*), this is the satisfaction in consciousness (*vijñāṇassa assāda*). Thus, he understands its satisfaction.

*Ādīnava* means, whatever form (*rūpa*)…pe… whatever consciousness (*vijñāṇa*) is impermanent (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and subject to change (*vipariṇāmadhamma*), this is the unsatisfactoriness in consciousness (*vijñāṇassa ādīnava*). Thus he understands its unsatisfactoriness.

*Nissaraṇa* means, whatever removal of desire and lust for form (*rūpa*)…pe… whatever removal of desire and lust for consciousness (*vijñāṇa*), the abandoning of desire and lust, this is the escape from consciousness (*vijñāṇassa nissaraṇa*). Thus, he understands its escape.

*Kallaṃ nu tenā* means, is it proper for one to seek enjoyment in it? Is it right for that *bhikkhu* to seek enjoyment in that station for consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) as "I" or "mine" by way of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), or views (*diṭṭhi*)?

This method of interpretation should be applied to all the other stations for consciousness.

But where there is no form (*rūpa*), the origin (*samudaya*) should be interpreted by way of the four aggregates (*khandha*) only; and where there is no consciousness (*vijñāṇa*) it should be interpreted by way of the one aggregate (*khandha*).

“through the origination of nutriment (*āhāra*)” and “through the cessation of nutriment (*āhāra*),” thus here the passage should be interpreted with these phrases.

*Yato kho, Ānanda, bhikkhū* means, when, Ānanda, a *bhikkhu*.

*Anupādā vimutto* means, released through lack of clinging (*upādāna*) to the four clingings.

*Paññāvimutto* means, liberated by wisdom (*prajñā*).

Having brought about the future non-occurrence of the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the material body (*rūpakāya*), he is liberated solely by the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) without realizing the eight emancipations (*vimokkha*). This is the meaning.

This type is fivefold: the dry-insight meditator (*sukkhavipassako*) and those who attain *arhattva* after having become established in one or another of the first *dhyāna* and so forth.

It was also said: “What individual is liberated through wisdom (*paññāvimutto*)? Herein, some individual does not dwell suffusing the eight emancipations (*vimokkha*) with the body (*kāya*); but having seen with wisdom (*prajñā*), his cankers (*āsava*) are destroyed. This individual is called ‘one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutto*)’ ”.

*Yato kho, Ānanda, bhikkhū*
*Anupādā vimutto*
*Paññāvimutto*
Explanation of the Eight Liberations (*aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā*)
