He, having had the *yakkha* attendants summoned, having had a *bali-kamma* performed, even not seeing the end or the boundary, worshipping the deities – “I, having taken these relics, having deposited (them) in eighty-four thousand monasteries, will make *sakkāra*; may the deities not cause any obstruction for me,” he said.

Sakka, the deva-king, while wandering on tour, seeing him, addressed Vissakamma – “Dear Tata, Asoka, the *dhamma* king, ‘I will extract the relics,’ has descended into the enclosure; having gone, remove the wood-figures.”
He, in the guise of a boy from five *cūḷa* villages, having gone in front of the king, standing with a bow in his hand – “I will carry (them) off, great king,” he said.

“Carry (them) off, Tata,” having taken an arrow, he pierced (it) right at the joint, he scattered everything.
Then the king, in the *āviñchana*, took a binding, a key-seal, he saw a jewel aggregate.
“In the future, a poor king, having taken this jewel, may make *sakkāra* for the relics,” again seeing the letters, becoming angry – “For such as me, to say ‘a poor king’ is not proper,” having repeatedly arranged (things), having had the door opened, he entered the inner chamber.

Lamps placed above two hundred and eighteen years continue to blaze just so.
Blue lotus flowers, having been brought and placed at that very moment, as it were; a scattering of flowers, arranged at that very moment, as it were; fragrances, ground and placed at that moment, as it were; the king, having taken a golden plate – “In the future, a youth named Piyadassa, having raised a parasol, will become a *dhamma* king named Asoka; he will expand these relics,” having had (this) read – “O venerable sir, I was seen by the venerable Mahākassapa Thera,” having said (this), having bent his left hand, he clapped with his right hand.

He, in that place, having placed only the *paricaraṇa-dhātu*, having taken the remaining relics, having closed the relic-house with the very same method as before, having done everything just as before, having established a stone *cetiya* above, in eighty-four thousand monasteries, relics, having established (them), having worshipped the great *thera*, he asked – “Am I an heir, venerable sir, in the Buddha’s Dispensation?”
“Whose heir are you, great king? You are an outsider to the Dispensation.”
“Venerable sir, having given away ninety-six *koṭi*s of wealth, having had eighty-four thousand monasteries built, am I not an heir? Who else is an heir?” “You, great king, are a giver of requisites; but whoever ordains his own son and daughter, he is said to be an heir in the Dispensation.”
He ordained his son and daughter.
Then the *thera*s said to him – “Now, great king, you are an heir in the Dispensation.”

Thus it was; having been in the past; thus, this deposit of relics was also in the past on the surface of Jambudīpa.
The reciters of the Third Council also established this saying.

Thus it was; having been in the past; “Eight *doṇa*s, the body of the one with eyes,” etc., these verses, however, were spoken by the *thera*s on Tambapaṇṇidīpa.

“Eight *doṇa*s, the body of the one with eyes”
Thus ends the *Mahāparinibbānasuttavaṇṇanā* in the *Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathā* by Sumaṅgalavilāsinī.

mula_pali: 241. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kusinārāyaṃ viharati upavattane mallānaṃ sālavane antarena yamakasālānaṃ parinibbānasamaye. Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘‘mā, bhante, bhagavā imasmiṃ khuddakanagarake ujjaṅgalanagarake sākhānagarake parinibbāyi. Santi, bhante, aññāni mahānagarāni. Seyyathidaṃ – campā, rājagahaṃ, sāvatthi, sāketaṃ, kosambī, bārāṇasī; ettha bhagavā parinibbāyatu. Ettha bahū khattiyamahāsālā brāhmaṇamahāsālā gahapatimahāsālā tathāgate abhippasannā, te tathāgatassa sarīrapūjaṃ karissantī’’ti.
mula_english:
241. Thus have I heard: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Kusinārā in the Upavattana, the Sāl grove of the Mallas, between the twin Sāl trees, at the time of his *parinirvāṇa*.

Then venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, and having approached, bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Do not, venerable sir (*bhante*), let the Blessed One attain *parinirvāṇa* in this small town, this town of wattle and daub, this branch town.

There are, venerable sir (*bhante*), other great cities.

Namely: Campā, Rājagaha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, Bārāṇasī; let the Blessed One attain *parinirvāṇa* there.

For in those places there are many wealthy nobles (*khattiyamahāsālā*), wealthy Brahmins (*brāhmaṇamahāsālā*), and wealthy householders (*gahapatimahāsālā*) who are devoted to the *tathāgata*. They will perform the funeral rites (*sarīrapūjā*) for the *tathāgata*.”
commentary_pali:
241.Evaṃme sutanti mahāsudassanasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – sabbaratanamayoti ettha ekā iṭṭhakā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā, ekā lohitaṅkamayā, ekā masāragallamayā, ekā sabbaratanamayā, ayaṃ pākāro sabbapākārānaṃ anto ubbedhena saṭṭhihattho ahosi. Eke pana therā – ‘‘nagaraṃ nāma anto ṭhatvā olokentānaṃ dassanīyaṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā sabbabāhiro saṭṭhihattho, sesā anupubbanīcā’’ti vadanti. Eke – ‘‘bahi ṭhatvā olokentānaṃ dassanīyaṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā sabbaabbhantarimo saṭṭhihattho, sesā anupubbanīcā’’ti. Eke – ‘‘anto ca bahi ca ṭhatvā olokentānaṃ dassanīyaṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā majjhe pākāro saṭṭhihattho, anto ca bahi ca tayo tayo anupubbanīcā’’ti.

Esikāti esikatthambho. Tiporisaṅgāti ekaṃ porisaṃ majjhimapurisassa attano hatthena pañcahatthaṃ, tena tiporisaparikkhepā pannarasahatthaparimāṇāti attho. Te pana kathaṃ ṭhitāti? Nagarassa bāhirapasse ekekaṃ mahādvārabāhaṃ nissāya ekeko, ekekaṃ khuddakadvārabāhaṃ nissāya ekeko, mahādvārakhuddakadvārānaṃ antarā tayo tayoti. Tālapantīsu sabbaratanamayānaṃ tālānaṃ ekaṃ sovaṇṇamayanti pākāre vuttalakkhaṇameva veditabbaṃ, paṇṇaphalesupi eseva nayo. Tā pana tālapantiyo asītihatthā ubbedhena, vippakiṇṇavāluke samatale bhūmibhāge pākārantare ekekā hutvā ṭhitā.

Esikā Tiporisaṅgā

Vaggūti cheko sundaro. Rajanīyoti rañjetuṃ samattho. Khamanīyoti divasampi suyyamāno khamateva, na bībhaccheti. Madanīyoti mānamadapurisamadajanano. Pañcaṅgikassāti ātataṃ vitataṃ ātatavitataṃ susiraṃ ghananti imehi pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatassa. Tattha ātataṃ nāma cammapariyonaddhesu bherīādīsu ekatalaṃ tūriyaṃ. Vitataṃ nāma ubhayatalaṃ. Ātatavitataṃ nāma sabbato pariyonaddhaṃ. Susiraṃ nāma vaṃsādi. Ghanaṃ nāma sammādi. Suvinītassāti ākaḍḍhanasithilakaraṇādīhi sumucchitassa. Suppaṭitāḷitassāti pamāṇe ṭhitabhāvajānanatthaṃ suṭṭhu paṭitāḷitassa. Sukusalehi samannāhatassāti ye vādituṃ chekā kusalā, tehi vāditassa. Dhuttāti akkhadhuttā,. Soṇḍāti surāsoṇḍā. Teyeva punappunaṃ pātukāmatāvasena pipāsā. Paricāresunti (dī. ni. 2.132) hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā cāletvā naccantā kīḷiṃsu.

Vaggū Rajanīyo Khamanīyo Madanīyo Pañcaṅgikassā ātataṃ Vitataṃ Ātatavitataṃ Susiraṃ Ghanaṃ Suvinītassā Suppaṭitāḷitassā Sukusalehi samannāhatassā Dhuttā Soṇḍā pipāsā. Paricāresu

Cakkaratanavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
241. Thus have I heard: the Mahāsudassana Sutta.

Here, the description of the words that did not occur before [is as follows]: In "**sabbaratanamayo**" (made of all jewels), one brick was made of gold (*sovaṇṇamayā*), one of silver (*rūpiyamayā*), one of beryl (*veḷuriyamayā*), one of crystal (*phalikamayā*), one of red stone (*lohitaṅkamayā*), one of agate (*masāragallamayā*), and one of all jewels (*sabbaratanamayā*). This wall (*pākāro*), inside all the walls, was sixty cubits in height (*saṭṭhihattho*).

But some elders say, "A city is suitable to be seen by those who stand inside and look around, therefore, the entire outer wall was sixty cubits, the rest were successively lower."

Some [say], "It is suitable to be seen by those who stand outside and look around, therefore, the entire innermost [wall] was sixty cubits, the rest were successively lower."

Some [say], "It is suitable to be seen by those who stand both inside and outside and look around, therefore, the middle wall was sixty cubits, and inside and outside [of that wall], there were three [walls] each that were successively lower."

**Esikā** means a gate pillar.

**Tiporisaṅgā** means one *porisa*, which is five cubits (*hatthaṃ*) according to the cubit (*hattha*) of a man (*purisaṃ*) of middle stature (*majjhimapurisassa*); therefore, *tiporisaparikkhepā* means a circumference of fifteen cubits (*pannarasahatthaparimāṇāti attho*).

How were they situated? On the outer side (*bāhirapasse*) of the city (*nagarassa*), there was one [pillar] relying on each large gate wing (*mahādvārabāhaṃ nissāya ekeko*), one [pillar] relying on each small gate wing (*khuddakadvārabāhaṃ nissāya ekeko*), [and] three [pillars] between the large and small gates (*mahādvārakhuddakadvārānaṃ antarā tayo tayoti*).

Among the rows of palm trees (*tālapantīsu*) made of all jewels (*sabbaratanamayānaṃ tālānaṃ*), one was made of gold (*sovaṇṇamayanti*); it should be understood that the characteristic described for the wall (*pākāre vuttalakkhaṇameva*) is the same [here]. This same method (*eseva nayo*) [applies] to the leaves and fruits (*paṇṇaphalesupi*).

Those rows of palm trees (*tā pana tālapantiyo*) were eighty cubits in height (*asītihatthā ubbedhena*), standing as single [trees] (*ekekā hutvā ṭhitā*) in the space between the walls (*pākārantare*) on a level (*samatale*) ground area with scattered sand (*vippakiṇṇavāluke bhūmibhāge*).

**Esikā**, **tiporisaṅgā**

**Vaggū** means clever, beautiful.

**Rajanīyo** means capable of delighting.

**Khamanīyo** means it is bearable even when being heard for a day; it is not disgusting.

**Madanīyo** means generating the intoxication and pride of men (*mānamadapurisamadajanano*).

**Pañcaṅgikassā** means endowed with these five parts (*imehi pañcahaṅgehi samannāgatassa*): *ātataṃ* (covered), *vitataṃ* (stretched), *ātatavitataṃ* (covered and stretched), *susiraṃ* (hollow), *ghanaṃ* (solid).

There, **ātataṃ** is a single-faced drum (*ekatalaṃ tūriyaṃ*) among drums and so on (*bherīādīsu*) covered with skin (*cammapariyonaddhesu*).

**Vitataṃ** means double-faced.

**Ātatavitataṃ** means covered all around.

**Susiraṃ** means flute and so on (*vaṃsādi*).

**Ghanaṃ** means cymbals and so on (*sammādi*).

**Suvinītassā** means well-composed (*sumucchitassa*) through actions such as tightening and loosening (*ākaḍḍhanasithilakaraṇādīhi*).

**Suppaṭitāḷitassā** means well-struck (*suṭṭhu paṭitāḷitassa*) to know the state of being established in measure (*pamāṇe ṭhitabhāvajānanatthaṃ*).

**Sukusalehi samannāhatassā** means played by those who are clever and skilled (*ye vādituṃ chekā kusalā, tehi vāditassa*) at playing [instruments].

**Dhuttā** means dice players (*akkhadhuttā*).

**Soṇḍā** means spirituous liquor drinkers (*surāsoṇḍā*).

They, through the desire to appear again and again (*punappunaṃ pātukāmatāvasena*), [experience] **thirst** (*pipāsā*).

In performances (*paricāresu*), (D. II, 132) they danced and played (*naccantā kīḷiṃsu*) moving their hands or feet (*hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā cāletvā*).

**Vaggū**, **rajanīyo**, **khamanīyo**, **madanīyo**, **pañcaṅgikassā**, **ātataṃ**, **vitataṃ**, **ātatavitataṃ**, **susiraṃ**.
Dense, well-disciplined, well-trained, well-controlled by skillful means, thirst is dispelled, O Soṇḍā.

Description of the Cakka-ratana in attendance.

mula_pali:
242. ‘‘Mā hevaṃ, ānanda, avaca; mā hevaṃ, ānanda, avaca – khuddakanagarakaṃ ujjaṅgalanagarakaṃ sākhānagaraka’’nti.

Kusāvatīrājadhānī

‘‘Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano nāma ahosi khattiyo muddhāvasitto khattiyo muddhābhisitto (ka.), cakkavattīdhammiko dhammarājā (mahāparinibbānasutta) cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto . Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa ayaṃ kusinārā kusāvatī nāma rājadhānī ahosi. Puratthimena ca pacchimena ca dvādasayojanāni āyāmena, uttarena ca dakkhiṇena ca sattayojanāni vitthārena. Kusāvatī, ānanda, rājadhānī iddhā ceva ahosi phītā ca bahujanā ca ākiṇṇamanussā ca subhikkhā ca. Seyyathāpi, ānanda , devānaṃ āḷakamandā nāma rājadhānī iddhā ceva hoti phītā ca iddhā ceva ahosi phītā ca (syā.) bahujanā ca ākiṇṇayakkhā ca subhikkhā ca; evameva kho, ānanda, kusāvatī rājadhānī iddhā ceva ahosi phītā ca bahujanā ca ākiṇṇamanussā ca subhikkhā ca. Kusāvatī, ānanda , rājadhānī dasahi saddehi avivittā ahosi divā ceva rattiñca, seyyathidaṃ – hatthisaddena assasaddena rathasaddena bherisaddena mudiṅgasaddena vīṇāsaddena gītasaddena saṅkhasaddena sammasaddena pāṇitāḷasaddena ‘asnātha pivatha khādathā’ti dasamena saddena.

khattiyo muddhābhisitto (ka.), cakkavattīdhammiko dhammarājā (mahāparinibbānasutta) iddhā ceva ahosi phītā ca (syā.)

‘‘Kusāvatī, ānanda, rājadhānī sattahi pākārehi parikkhittā ahosi. Eko pākāro sovaṇṇamayo, eko rūpiyamayo, eko veḷuriyamayo, eko phalikamayo, eko lohitaṅkamayo lohitaṅgamayo (ka.), lohitakamayo (byākaraṇesu), eko masāragallamayo, eko sabbaratanamayo. Kusāvatiyā, ānanda, rājadhāniyā catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ dvārāni ahesuṃ. Ekaṃ dvāraṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ, ekaṃ rūpiyamayaṃ, ekaṃ veḷuriyamayaṃ, ekaṃ phalikamayaṃ . Ekekasmiṃ dvāre satta satta esikā nikhātā ahesuṃ tiporisaṅgā tiporisanikhātā dvādasaporisā ubbedhena. Ekā esikā sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā, ekā lohitaṅkamayā, ekā masāragallamayā, ekā sabbaratanamayā. Kusāvatī, ānanda, rājadhānī sattahi tālapantīhi parikkhittā ahosi. Ekā tālapanti sovaṇṇamayā, ekā rūpiyamayā, ekā veḷuriyamayā, ekā phalikamayā, ekā lohitaṅkamayā, ekā masāragallamayā, ekā sabbaratanamayā. Sovaṇṇamayassa tālassa sovaṇṇamayo khandho ahosi, rūpiyamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Rūpiyamayassa tālassa rūpiyamayo khandho ahosi, sovaṇṇamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Veḷuriyamayassa tālassa veḷuriyamayo khandho ahosi, phalikamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Phalikamayassa tālassa phalikamayo khandho ahosi, veḷuriyamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Lohitaṅkamayassa tālassa lohitaṅkamayo khandho ahosi, masāragallamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Masāragallamayassa tālassa masāragallamayo khandho ahosi, lohitaṅkamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Sabbaratanamayassa tālassa sabbaratanamayo khandho ahosi, sabbaratanamayāni pattāni ca phalāni ca. Tāsaṃ kho panānanda, tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo ahosi vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo kamanīyo (sī. syā. pī.) ca madanīyo ca. Seyyathāpi, ānanda, pañcaṅgikassa tūriyassa suvinītassa suppaṭitāḷitassa sukusalehi samannāhatassa saddo hoti vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca , evameva kho, ānanda, tāsaṃ tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo ahosi vaggu ca rajanīyo ca khamanīyo ca madanīyo ca. Ye kho panānanda, tena samayena kusāvatiyā rājadhāniyā dhuttā ahesuṃ soṇḍā pipāsā, te tāsaṃ tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddena paricāresuṃ.

lohitaṅgamayo (ka.), lohitakamayo (byākaraṇesu) kamanīyo (sī. syā. pī.)

Cakkaratanaṃ
mula_english:
242.
‘Ānanda, don’t speak like that! Ānanda, don’t speak like that – [calling it] a miserable little town, a town right in the jungle, a branch town!’

Kusāvatī, the Royal Capital

Once upon a time, Ānanda, there was a king named Mahāsudassana, a Kṣatriya, anointed to rule (khattiyo muddhābhisitto), a wheel-turning monarch, righteous and following the Dharma (chakravartin dharmiko dhammarājā (Mahāparinibbānasutta), victorious in the four directions, who had achieved stability in his realm.

And this Kusinārā, Ānanda, was the capital city of King Mahāsudassana, named Kusāvatī. It extended twelve *yojanas* from east to west, and seven *yojanas* from north to south.

Kusāvatī, Ānanda, the capital city, was powerful, rich, prosperous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food.

Just as, Ānanda, the city of the gods, Āḷakamandā, is powerful, rich, and prosperous, crowded with *yakṣas*, and well-supplied with food, so too, Ānanda, was the capital city of Kusāvatī powerful, rich, prosperous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food.

Kusāvatī, Ānanda, the capital city, was never silent with ten sounds day or night, that is to say: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of kettle drums, the sound of side drums, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of cymbals, the sound of gongs, and as the tenth, the sound of, "Eat, drink, and be merry!"

Kusāvatī, Ānanda, the capital city, was surrounded by seven encircling walls (sattahi pākārehi parikkhittā ahosi). One wall was made of gold (sovaṇṇamayo), one of silver (rūpiyamayo), one of beryl (veḷuriyamayo), one of crystal (phalikamayo), one of ruby (lohitaṅkamayo), one of emerald (masāragallamayo), and one of all sorts of gems (sabbaratanamayo).

In Kusāvatī, Ānanda, the royal capital, the gates were of four colors. One gate was made of gold (sovaṇṇamayaṃ), one of silver (rūpiyamayaṃ), one of beryl (veḷuriyamayaṃ), and one of crystal (phalikamayaṃ).

At each gate, seven pillars (satta esikā) were set, sunk three or four *purisas* deep, and twelve *purisas* in height. One pillar (ekā esikā) was made of gold (sovaṇṇamayā), one of silver (rūpiyamayā), one of beryl (veḷuriyamayā), one of crystal (phalikamayā), one of ruby (lohitaṅkamayā), one of emerald (masāragallamayā), and one of all sorts of gems (sabbaratanamayā).

Kusāvatī, Ānanda, the capital city, was surrounded by seven rows of palm trees (sattahi tālapantīhi parikkhittā ahosi). One row of palm trees (ekā tālapanti) was made of gold (sovaṇṇamayā), one of silver (rūpiyamayā), one of beryl (veḷuriyamayā), one of crystal (phalikamayā), one of ruby (lohitaṅkamayā), one of emerald (masāragallamayā), and one of all sorts of gems (sabbaratanamayā).

The gold palm trees (sovaṇṇamayassa tālassa) had trunks of gold (sovaṇṇamayo khandho ahosi), and leaves (pattāni) and fruits (phalāni) of silver (rūpiyamayāni).

The silver palm trees (rūpiyamayassa tālassa) had trunks of silver (rūpiyamayo khandho ahosi), and leaves (pattāni) and fruits (phalāni) of gold (sovaṇṇamayāni).

The beryl palm trees (veḷuriyamayassa tālassa) had trunks of beryl (veḷuriyamayo khandho ahosi), and leaves (pattāni) and fruits (phalāni) of crystal (phalikamayāni).

The crystal palm trees (phalikamayassa tālassa) had trunks of crystal (phalikamayo khandho ahosi), and leaves (pattāni) and fruits (phalāni) of beryl (veḷuriyamayāni).

The ruby palm trees (lohitaṅkamayassa tālassa) had trunks of ruby (lohitaṅkamayo khandho ahosi), and leaves (pattāni) and fruits (phalāni) of emerald (masāragallamayāni).

The emerald palm trees (masāragallamayassa tālassa) had trunks of emerald (masāragallamayo khandho ahosi), and leaves (pattāni) and fruits (phalāni) of ruby (lohitaṅkamayāni).

The palm trees of all sorts of gems (sabbaratanamayassa tālassa) had trunks of all sorts of gems (sabbaratanamayo khandho ahosi), and leaves (pattāni) and fruits (phalāni) of all sorts of gems (sabbaratanamayāni).

The sound of those palm trees, Ānanda, when stirred by the wind (tāsaṃ kho panānanda, tālapantīnaṃ vāteritānaṃ saddo ahosi), was delightful (vaggu), pleasing (rajanīyo), and agreeable (khamanīyo).
And intoxicating.

Just as, Ānanda, the sound of a five-piece orchestra, well-tuned, well-beaten, and played by skilled musicians, is delightful, pleasing, agreeable, and intoxicating, so too, Ānanda, was the sound of those palm leaves stirred by the wind delightful, pleasing, agreeable, and intoxicating.

And, Ānanda, those libertines and drunkards in the capital city of Kuśāvatī at that time, were refreshed by the sound of those palm leaves stirred by the wind.

Cakkaratanaṃ (Wheel Jewel).

mula_pali: 243. ‘‘Rājā , ānanda, mahāsudassano sattahi ratanehi samannāgato ahosi catūhi ca iddhīhi. Katamehi sattahi? Idhānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa tadahuposathe pannarase sīsaṃnhātassa uposathikassa uparipāsādavaragatassa dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosi sahassāraṃ sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ. Disvā rañño mahāsudassanassa etadahosi – ‘sutaṃ kho panetaṃ – ‘‘yassa rañño khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa tadahuposathe pannarase sīsaṃnhātassa uposathikassa uparipāsādavaragatassa dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavati sahassāraṃ sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ, so hoti rājā cakkavattī’’ti. Assaṃ nu kho ahaṃ rājā cakkavattī’ti.
mula_english:
‘Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was endowed with the seven treasures (sapta ratnāṇi) and the four powers (catūhi iddhi).

What are the seven? Here, Ānanda, on the fifteenth day, the *uposatha* day, when King Mahāsudassana had washed his head and gone up to the excellent upper terrace of the palace to observe the *uposatha*, a divine wheel-treasure (divyaṃ cakraratanaṃ) appeared to him, with a thousand spokes (sahasrāraṃ), with a felly (sanemikaṃ), with a hub (sanābhikaṃ), complete in every way (sabbākāraparipūraṃ).

On seeing it, King Mahāsudassana thought: “I have heard that when a head-anointed noble king (khattiyassa muddhāvasittassa) sees such a wheel on the *uposatha* day of the fifteenth, having washed his head and ascended to the upper palace chamber for the *uposatha*, there appears to him the divine wheel-treasure (divyaṃ cakkaratanaṃ) with its thousand spokes (sahasrāraṃ), its tire (sanemikaṃ), and its nave (sanābhikaṃ), complete in every aspect (sabbākāraparipūraṃ), then that king becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch (rājā cakkavattī).”

May I become such a Wheel-turning Monarch (rājā cakkavattī)!”
commentary_pali:
243.Sīsaṃ nhātassāti sīsena saddhiṃ gandhodakena nahātassa. Uposathikassāti samādinnauposathaṅgassa. Uparipāsādavaragatassāti pāsādavarassa upari gatassa, subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā pāsādavarassa uparimahātale sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sīlāni āvajjantassa. Tadā kira rājā pātova satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ datvā soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi sīsaṃ nahāyitvā katapātarāso suddhaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā uparipāsādassa sirisayane pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno attano dānādimayaṃ puññasamudāyaṃ āvajjanto nisīdi. Ayaṃ sabbacakkavattīnaṃ dhammatā.

Tesaṃ taṃ āvajjantānaṃyeva vuttappakārapuññakammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nīlamaṇisaṅghātasadisaṃ pācīnasamuddajalatalaṃ bhindamānaṃ viya, ākāsaṃ alaṅkurumānaṃ viya dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavati. Taṃ mahāsudassanassāpi tatheva pāturahosi. Tayidaṃ dibbānubhāvayuttattā dibbanti vuttaṃ. Sahassaṃ assa arānanti sahassāraṃ. Saha nemiyā, saha nābhiyā cāti sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ. Sabbehi ākārehi paripuṇṇanti sabbākāraparipūraṃ.

sahassāraṃ. sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ. sabbākāraparipūraṃ.

Tattha cakkañca taṃ ratijananaṭṭhena ratanañcāti cakkaratanaṃ. Yāya pana taṃ nābhiyā ‘‘sanābhika’’nti vuttaṃ, sā indanīlamayā hoti, majjhe panassā sārarajatamayā panāḷi, yāya suddhasiniddhadantapantiyā hasamānā viya virocati, majjhe chiddena viya candamaṇḍalena, ubhosupi bāhirantesu rajatapaṭṭena kataparikkhepā hoti. Tesu panassa nābhipanāḷiparikkhepapaṭṭesu yuttayuttaṭṭhānesu paricchedalekhā suvibhattāva hutvā paññāyanti. Ayaṃ tāva assa nābhiyā sabbākāraparipūratā.

cakkaratanaṃ.

Yehi pana taṃ – ‘‘arehi sahassāra’’nti vuttaṃ, te sattaratanamayā sūriyarasmiyo viya pabhāsampannā honti, tesampi ghaṭakamaṇikaparicchedalekhādīni suvibhattāneva hutvā paññāyanti. Ayamassa arānaṃ sabbākāraparipūratā.

Yāya pana taṃ nemiyā – ‘‘sanemika’’nti vuttaṃ, sā bālasūriyarasmikalāpasiriṃ avahasamānā viya surattasuddhasiniddhapavāḷamayā hoti. Sandhīsu panassā sañjhārāgasassirikā rattajambunadapaṭṭā vaṭṭaparicchedalekhā suvibhattā hutvā paññāyanti. Ayamassa nemiyā sabbākāraparipūratā.

Nemimaṇḍalapiṭṭhiyaṃ panassa dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānaṃ antare dhamanavaṃso viya anto susiro chiddamaṇḍalakhacito vātagāhī pavāḷadaṇḍo hoti, yassa vāteritassa sukusalasamannāhatassa pañcaṅgikatūriyassa viya saddo vaggu ca rajanīyo ca kamanīyo ca madanīyo ca hoti. Tassa kho pana pavāḷadaṇḍassa upari setacchattaṃ ubhosu passesu samosaritakusumadāmānaṃ dve pantiyoti evaṃ samosaritakusumadāmapantisatadvayaparivārasetacchattasatadhārinā pavāḷadaṇḍasatena samupasobhitanemiparikkhepassa dvinnampi nābhipanāḷīnaṃ anto dve sīhamukhāni honti, yehi tālakkhandhappamāṇā puṇṇacandakiraṇakalāpasassirīkā taruṇaravisamānarattakambalageṇḍukapariyantā ākāsagaṅgāgatisobhaṃ avahasamānā viya dve muttakalāpā olambanti. Yehi cakkaratanena saddhiṃ ākāse samparivattamānehi tīṇi cakkāni ekato parivattantāni viya khāyanti. Ayamassa sabbaso sabbākāraparipūratā.

Taṃ panetaṃ evaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ pakatiyā sāyamāsabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā attano attano gharadvāre paññattāsanesu nisīditvā pavattakathāsallāpesu manussesu vīthicatukkādīsu kīḷamāne dārakajane nātiuccena nātinīcena vanasaṇḍamatthakāsannena ākāsappadesena upasobhayamānaṃ viya, rukkhasākhaggāni dvādasayojanato paṭṭhāya suyyamānena madhurassarena sattānaṃ sotāni odhāpayamānaṃ yojanato paṭṭhāya nānappabhāsamudayasamujjalena vaṇṇena nayanāni samākaḍḍhantaṃ viya, rañño cakkavattissa puññānubhāvaṃ ugghosayantaṃ viya, rājadhāniyā abhimukhaṃ āgacchati.

Athassa cakkaratanassa saddasavaneneva – ‘‘kuto nu kho, kassa nu kho ayaṃ saddo’’ti āvajjitahadayānaṃ puratthimadisaṃ ālokayamānānaṃ tesaṃ manussānaṃ aññataro aññataraṃ evamāha – ‘‘passatha, bho, acchariyaṃ, ayaṃ puṇṇacando pubbe eko uggacchati, ajjeva pana attadutiyo uggato, etañhi rājahaṃsamithunamiva puṇṇacandamithunaṃ pubbāpariyena gaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghatī’’ti. Tamañño āha – ‘‘kiṃ kathesi, samma, kuhiṃ nāma tayā dve puṇṇacandā ekato uggacchantā diṭṭhapubbā, nanu esa tapanīyaraṃsidhāro piñcharakiraṇo divākaro uggato’’ti, tamañño hasitaṃ katvā evamāha – ‘‘kiṃ ummattosi, nanu idāneva divākaro atthaṅgato, so kathaṃ imaṃ puṇṇacandaṃ anubandhamāno uggacchissati? Addhā panetaṃ anekaratanappabhāsamudayujjalaṃ ekassāpi puññavato vimānaṃ bhavissatī’’ti. Te sabbepi apasārayantā aññe evamāhaṃsu – ‘‘bho, kiṃ bahuṃ vilapatha, nevāyaṃ puṇṇacando, na sūriyo na devavimānaṃ. Na hetesaṃ evarūpā sirisampatti atthi, cakkaratanena pana etena bhavitabba’’nti.

Evaṃ pavattasallāpasseva tassa janassa candamaṇḍalaṃ ohāya taṃ cakkaratanaṃ abhimukhaṃ hoti. Tato tehi – ‘‘kassa nu kho idaṃ nibbatta’’nti vutte bhavanti vattāro – ‘‘na kassaci aññassa, nanu amhākaṃ mahārājā pūritacakkavattivatto, tassetaṃ nibbatta’’nti. Atha so ca mahājano, yo ca añño passati, sabbo cakkaratanameva anugacchati. Taṃ cāpi cakkaratanaṃ raññoyeva atthāya attano āgatabhāvaṃ ñāpetukāmaṃ viya sattakkhattuṃ pākāramatthakeneva nagaraṃ anusaṃyāyitvā, atha rañño antepuraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, antepurassa ca uttarasīhapañjarasadise ṭhāne yathā gandhapupphādīhi sukhena sakkā hoti pūjetuṃ, evaṃ akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati.

Evaṃ ṭhitassa panassa vātapānachiddādīhi pavisitvā nānāvirāgaratanappabhāsamujjalaṃ antopāsādaṃ alaṅkurumānaṃ pabhāsamūhaṃ disvā dassanatthāya sañjātābhilāso rājā hoti. Parijanopissa piyavacanapābhatena āgantvā tamatthaṃ nivedeti. Atha rājā balavapītipāmojjaphuṭasarīro pallaṅkaṃ mocetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā sīhapañjarasamīpaṃ gantvā taṃ cakkaratanaṃ disvā ‘‘sutaṃ kho pana meta’’ntiādikaṃ cintanaṃ cintayati. Mahāsudassanassāpi sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘disvā rañño mahāsudassanassa…pe… assaṃ nu kho ahaṃ rājā cakkavattī’’ti. Tattha so hoti rājā cakkavattīti kittāvatā cakkavattī hotīti? Ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattampi cakkaratane ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pavatte idāni tassa pavattāpanatthaṃ yaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ dassento atha kho ānandātiādimāha.

so hoti rājā cakkavattī atha kho ānandā
commentary_english:
243. sīsaṃ nhātassāti: "[Regarding] one who has bathed the head," [this means] one who has bathed with fragrant water along with [bathing] the head. uposathikassāti: "[Regarding] one observing the *uposatha*," [this means] one who has undertaken the elements of the *uposatha*. uparipāsādavaragatassāti: "[Regarding] one who has gone to the upper part of the excellent palace," [this means] one who has gone to the upper part of the excellent palace, and after enjoying fine food, having entered the auspicious chamber on the upper main floor of the excellent palace, reflects on moral conduct (*śīlāni*). Then, it is said that the king, early in the morning, after disbursing a hundred thousand [coins] and giving a great offering (mahādāna), bathing his head with sixteen pitchers of fragrant water, having taken his morning meal, putting on a pure upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*) arranging it over one shoulder, sat having crossed his legs in the *pallaṅka* posture on the auspicious bed in the *śrī* chamber of the upper palace, reflecting on the accumulation of merit (*puṇya*) consisting of his giving, and so forth. This is the nature of all universal monarchs (*sabbacakravattīnaṃ dhammatā*).

For those reflecting in that way, just as from the power of merit (*puṇya*) and action (*karma*) of the previously described kind, a mass resembling a heap of blue sapphires, breaking through the surface of the eastern ocean, as if adorning the sky, the divine wheel-jewel (*cakkaratana*) appears. That appeared to Mahāsudassana in just that way. Thus, it is said to be divine because it is endowed with divine power (*dibbānubhāva*). "It has a thousand spokes" [is equivalent to] sahassāraṃ (thousand-spoked). "Together with its rim, together with its hub" [is equivalent to] sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ (with rim and hub). "Complete in all its aspects" [is equivalent to] sabbākāraparipūraṃ (complete in every way).

sahassāraṃ. sanemikaṃ sanābhikaṃ. sabbākāraparipūraṃ.

There, the wheel (*cakra*) and the jewel (*ratana*) because of its nature of generating delight (*rati*) [is called] cakkaratanaṃ (wheel-jewel). Moreover, that hub (*nābhi*) by which it is called “*sanābhika*” is made of sapphire (*indanīla*); in the middle of it, however, is a pipe (*panāḷi*) made of quintessential silver, by which it shines as if laughing with a row of pure smooth teeth, like a moon-circle with a hole in the middle; on both the outer and inner sides, it has a circumference made of a silver plate (*rajatapaṭṭa*). On those hub-pipe-circumference-plates, the lines of demarcation in appropriate places appear very clearly divided. This, to be sure, is the completeness in every way (*sabbākāraparipūratā*) of its hub (*nābhiyā*).

cakkaratanaṃ.

Those spokes by which it is said, “thousand-spoked" are made of the seven jewels (*sattaratana*), possess splendor like the sun's rays (*sūriyarasmī*); also those lines of demarcation consisting of knobs, jewels, and so forth, appear very clearly divided. This is the completeness in every way (*sabbākāraparipūratā*) of its spokes (*arānaṃ*).

Moreover, that rim (*nemi*) by which it is called "*sanemika*," is made of very red, pure, smooth coral (*pavāḷa*), as if mocking the splendor of a collection of the rays of the young sun. At its joints (*sandhi*), however, the lines of demarcation of round circumferences, possessing the loveliness of twilight (*sañjhārāga*), with red jambu-gold plates (*rattajambunadapaṭṭa*), appear clearly divided. This is the completeness in every way (*sabbākāraparipūratā*) of its rim (*nemiyā*).

On the surface of the rim-circle (*nemimaṇḍala*), however, between each set of ten spokes, like a reed shaft (*dhamanavaṃsa*), on the inside, a coral stick (*pavāḷadaṇḍa*) that is hollow, studded with circles of holes, and wind-catching, exists, of which, when moved by the wind and well-struck by a skillful [player], the sound is pleasing, delightful, lovely, and charming, like that of a five-piece orchestra (*pañcaṅgikatūriya*). Above that coral stick (*pavāḷadaṇḍa*), moreover, is a white umbrella (*setacchatta*); on both sides, two rows of garlands of jasmine flowers that are closely set exist; thus, with that hundredfold coral stick (*pavāḷadaṇḍa*) bearing a hundred white umbrellas (*setacchatta*) surrounded by two sets of rows of closely set jasmine flower garlands, on the inside of both the hub-pipes, are two lion faces, from which two pearl strands (*muttakalāpa*), of the size of palm trunks, possessing the splendor of a collection of full moon rays (*puṇṇacandakiraṇa*), with ends like young red sun-blanket balls, hang down, as if mocking the beauty of the flow of the *ākāśa* Ganges. With that wheel-jewel (*cakkaratana*), as they whirl around in the sky, the three wheels appear as if whirling together. This is its total completeness in every way (*sabbākāraparipūratā*).

That, moreover, being thus complete in every way (*sabbākāraparipūraṃ*), after naturally enjoying the evening meal of rice and curry, as people sit at their own house doors on designated seats, engaging in pleasant conversation, in the intersections of streets and so forth, among the crowds of playing children, not too high, not too low, near the tops of the wooded groves, as if adorning the expanse of sky, with a sweet sound that is heard from twelve leagues (*yojana*) away from the tree branch tips captivating the ears of beings, from a league away, with a color brilliant from the rising of various splendors, as if attracting the eyes, as if proclaiming the power of the merit (*puṇyānubhāva*) of the universal monarch (*cakkavattissa*), it comes toward the capital (*rājadhāniyā*).

Then, upon hearing the sound of that wheel-treasure (cakraratna), as those men, their hearts drawn in, looked toward the eastern direction, one of them said to another: 0189"/> – “Look, sirs, a wonder! This full moon (pūrṇacandra) usually rises alone, but today another has risen along with it! Indeed, a pair of royal swans (rājahaṃsamithuna) seems to be crossing the sky (gaganatala) together with a pair of full moons (pūrṇacandramithuna)!” Another said, “What are you saying, friend? Where have you ever seen two full moons (pūrṇacandā) rising together? Surely, this is the sun (divākara), with its stream of golden rays (tapanīyaraṃsidhāra) and speckled light (piñcharakiraṇa)!” Another, laughing, said, “Are you mad? Just now the sun (divākara) has set. How could it rise again, chasing after this full moon (pūrṇacandra)? Truly, this must be a celestial mansion (vimāna) of some meritorious being (puṇyavato), shining with a multitude of jewel-like lights (anekaratanaprabhāsamudayujjala)!” Pushing them all aside, others said, “Sirs, why do you babble so much? This is not the full moon (pūrṇacandra), nor the sun (sūriya), nor a celestial mansion (devavimāna). Such glorious prosperity (sirisampatti) does not belong to them; it must be due to the wheel-treasure (cakraratnena)!” 0189"/> Thus, as that crowd was engaged in conversation, the moon’s orb (candamaṇḍala) faded away, and that wheel-treasure (cakraratna) appeared before them. Then they said, “To whom does this belong?” And the speakers replied, “It belongs to no one else; surely it belongs to our great king (mahārājā), who fulfills the duty of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin); it belongs to him!” Then that great multitude (mahājano), and whoever else saw it, all followed the wheel-treasure (cakkaratanameva). And that wheel-treasure (cakraratna), as if wishing to make known its arrival for the sake of the king (rañño), circled the city (nagaraṃ) seven times just along the ramparts (pākāramatthakeneva), then, having circumambulated the king’s inner palace (antepuraṃ), it stood in a place similar to the northern lion-window (uttarasīhapañjarasadise), where it could easily be honored with incense, flowers (gandhapupphādīhi), and so on, as if it were fixed in place. 0620"/> Thus, as it stood there, having entered through openings such as the lattice windows (vātapānachiddādīhi), and having adorned the inner palace (antopāsādaṃ) with a collection of rays (pabhāsamūhaṃ), shining with various exquisite jewel-like lights (nānāvirāgaratanappabhāsamujjalaṃ), the king (rājā) became filled with longing to see it. His attendant, approaching with pleasant words (piyavacanapābhatena), informed him of the matter (tamatthaṃ nivedeti). Then the king (rājā), his body thrilled with powerful joy and delight (balavapītipāmojjaphuṭasarīro), having released his couch (pallaṅkaṃ mocetvā), arose from his seat (utthāyāsanā), went near the lion-window (sīhapañjarasamīpaṃ gantvā), and, seeing that wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ disvā), pondered thoughts such as, “I have heard of this.” Everything was just like that for Mahāsudassana as well. Therefore, it was said – “Having seen the king (rañño) Mahāsudassana…pe… would that I were a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartī)!” There, what does it mean to say, “He becomes a wheel-turning monarch (rājā cakkavattī)”? Even if the wheel-treasure (cakkaratane) were to rise into the sky (ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā) only one or two finger-widths (ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattampi), now, in order to show what should be done to set it in motion (pavattāpanatthaṃ), he said, “Then, Ānanda (atha kho ānandā),” and so on. so hoti rājā cakkavattī atha kho ānandā

mula_pali: 244. ‘‘Atha kho, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā vāmena hatthena suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇena hatthena cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkiri – ‘pavattatu bhavaṃ cakkaratanaṃ, abhivijinātu bhavaṃ cakkaratana’nti. Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimaṃ disaṃ pavatti pavattati (syā. ka.), anvadeva anudeva (syā.) rājā mahāsudassano saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya, yasmiṃ kho panānanda, padese cakkaratanaṃ patiṭṭhāsi, tattha rājā mahāsudassano vāsaṃ upagacchi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Ye kho panānanda, puratthimāya disāya paṭirājāno, te rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘ehi kho mahārāja, svāgataṃ te mahārāja, sakaṃ te mahārāja, anusāsa mahārājā’ti. Rājā mahāsudassano evamāha – ‘pāṇo na hantabbo, adinnaṃ na ādātabbaṃ, kāmesu micchā na caritabbā, musā na bhaṇitabbā, majjaṃ na pātabbaṃ, yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā’ti . Ye kho panānanda, puratthimāya disāya paṭirājāno, te rañño mahāsudassanassa anuyantā ahesuṃ. Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pavatti…pe… dakkhiṇaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā pacchimaṃ disaṃ pavatti…pe… pacchimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā uttaraṃ disaṃ pavatti, anvadeva rājā mahāsudassano saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Yasmiṃ kho panānanda, padese cakkaratanaṃ patiṭṭhāsi, tattha rājā mahāsudassano vāsaṃ upagacchi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Ye kho panānanda, uttarāya disāya paṭirājāno, te rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘ehi kho mahārāja, svāgataṃ te mahārāja, sakaṃ te mahārāja, anusāsa mahārājā’ti. Rājā mahāsudassano evamāha – ‘pāṇo na hantabbo, adinnaṃ na ādātabbaṃ, kāmesu micchā na caritabbā, musā na bhaṇitabbā, majjaṃ na pātabbaṃ , yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā’ti. Ye kho panānanda, uttarāya disāya paṭirājāno , te rañño mahāsudassanassa anuyantā ahesuṃ.
mula_english:
244. Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, rising from his seat, covering one shoulder with his upper robe, and taking a golden vessel (suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ) in his left hand and sprinkling the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ) with his right hand, said: ‘May the noble Wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ) turn, may the noble Wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ) conquer!’

Then, Ānanda, the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ) turned towards the eastern direction, and King Mahāsudassana followed with his four-constituent army (caturaṅginiyā senāya). And in whatever region, Ānanda, the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ) paused, there King Mahāsudassana took up his abode with his four-constituent army (caturaṅginiyā senāya).

And those opposing kings (paṭirājāno) in the eastern direction, Ānanda, approached King Mahāsudassana and said thus: ‘Come, Great King (mahārāja), welcome to you, Great King (mahārāja), we are yours, Great King (mahārāja), rule us, Great King (mahārāja)!’

King Mahāsudassana said thus: ‘Life should not be taken (pāṇo na hantabbo), what is not given should not be taken (adinnaṃ na ādātabbaṃ), one should not misconduct oneself in sensual pleasures (kāmesu micchā na caritabbā), one should not speak falsely (musā na bhaṇitabbā), intoxicants should not be drunk (majjaṃ na pātabbaṃ), and you should eat according to what is customary (yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā)’.

And those opposing kings (paṭirājāno) in the eastern direction, Ānanda, became followers of King Mahāsudassana.

Then, Ānanda, the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ), plunging into the eastern ocean and emerging again, turned towards the southern direction…pe… plunging into the southern ocean and emerging again, it turned towards the western direction…pe… plunging into the western ocean and emerging again, it turned towards the northern direction, and King Mahāsudassana followed with his four-constituent army (caturaṅginiyā senāya).

And in whatever region, Ānanda, the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ) paused, there King Mahāsudassana took up his abode with his four-constituent army (caturaṅginiyā senāya).

And those opposing kings (paṭirājāno) in the northern direction, Ānanda, approached King Mahāsudassana and said thus: ‘Come, Great King (mahārāja), welcome to you, Great King (mahārāja), we are yours, Great King (mahārāja), rule us, Great King (mahārāja)!’

King Mahāsudassana said thus: ‘Life should not be taken (pāṇo na hantabbo), what is not given should not be taken (adinnaṃ na ādātabbaṃ), one should not misconduct oneself in sensual pleasures (kāmesu micchā na caritabbā), one should not speak falsely (musā na bhaṇitabbā), intoxicants should not be drunk (majjaṃ na pātabbaṃ), and you should eat according to what is customary (yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā)’.

And those opposing kings (paṭirājāno) in the northern direction, Ānanda, became followers of King Mahāsudassana.
commentary_pali:
244. Tattha uṭṭhāyāsanāti nisinnāsanato uṭṭhahitvā cakkaratanasamīpaṃ āgantvā. Suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ gahetvāti hatthisoṇḍasadisapanāḷiṃ suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ ukkhipitvā. Anvadeva rājā mahāsudassano saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyāti sabbacakkavattīnañhi udakena abbhukkiritvā – ‘‘abhivijinātu bhavaṃ cakkaratana’’nti vacanasamanantarameva vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā cakkaratanaṃ pavattati. Yassa pavatti samakālameva so rājā cakkavattī nāma hoti. Pavatte pana cakkaratane taṃ anubandhamānova rājā cakkavattiyānavaraṃ āruyha vehāsaṃ abbhuggacchati. Athassa chattacāmarādihattho parijano ceva antepurajano ca tato nānākārakañcukakavacādisannāhavibhūsitena vividhābharaṇappabhāsamujjalena samussitaddhajapaṭākapaṭimaṇḍitena attano attano balakāyena saddhiṃ uparājasenāpatipabhutayopi vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rājānameva parivārenti.

Rājayuttā pana janasaṅgahatthaṃ nagaravīthīsu bheriyo carāpenti – ‘‘tātā, amhākaṃ rañño cakkaratanaṃ nibbattaṃ, attano vibhavānurūpena maṇḍitapasādhikā sannipatathā’’ti. Mahājano pana pakatiyā cakkaratanasaddeneva sabbakiccāni pahāya gandhapupphādīni ādāya sannipatitova sopi sabbo vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rājānameva parivāreti. Yassa yassa hi raññā saddhiṃ gantukāmatācittaṃ uppajjati, so so ākāsagatova hoti. Evaṃ dvādasayojanāyāmavitthārā parisā hoti. Tattha ekapurisopi chinnabhinnasarīro vā kiliṭṭhavattho vā natthi. Suciparivāro hi rājā cakkavattī. Cakkavattiparisā nāma vijjādharapurisā viya ākāse gacchamānā indanīlamaṇitale vippakiṇṇaratanasadisā hoti. Mahāsudassanassāpi tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘anvadeva rājā mahāsudassano saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyā’’ti.

Taṃ pana cakkaratanaṃ rukkhaggānaṃ uparūpari nātiuccena nātinīcena gaganappadesena pavattati. Yathā rukkhānaṃ pupphaphalapallavehi atthikā, tāni sukhena gahetuṃ sakkonti. Yathā ca bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitā ‘‘esa rājā, esa uparājā, esa senāpatī’’ti sallakkhetuṃ sakkonti. Ṭhānādīsu ca iriyāpathesu yo yena icchati, so teneva gacchati. Cittakammādisippapasutā cettha attano attano kiccaṃ karontāyeva gacchanti. Yatheva hi bhūmiyaṃ, tathā tesaṃ sabbakiccāni ākāseva ijjhanti. Evaṃ cakkavattiparisaṃ gahetvā taṃ cakkaratanaṃ vāmapassena sineruṃ pahāya mahāsamuddassa uparibhāgena sattasahassayojanappamāṇaṃ pubbavidehaṃ gacchati.

Tattha yo vinibbedhena dvādasayojanāya, parikkhepato chattiṃsayojanāya parisāya sannivesakkhamo sulabhāhārūpakaraṇo chāyudakasampanno sucisamatalo ramaṇīyo bhūmibhāgo, tassa uparibhāge taṃ cakkaratanaṃ akkhāhataṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Atha tena saññāṇena so mahājano otaritvā yathāruci nahānabhojanādīni sabbakiccāni karonto vāsaṃ kappeti. Mahāsudassanassāpi sabbaṃ tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘yasmiṃ kho panānanda, padese cakkaratanaṃ patiṭṭhāti, tattha so rājā mahāsudassano vāsaṃ upagacchi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāyā’’ti.

Evaṃ vāsaṃ upagate cakkavattimhi ye tattha rājāno, te ‘‘paracakkaṃ āgata’’nti sutvāpi na balakāyaṃ sannipātetvā yuddhasajjā honti. Cakkaratanassa hi uppattisamanantarameva natthi so satto nāma, yo paccatthikasaññāya taṃ rājānaṃ ārabbha āvudhaṃ ukkhipituṃ visaheyya. Ayamānubhāvo cakkaratanassa.

Cakkānubhāvena hi tassa rañño,

Arī asesā damathaṃ upenti;

Arindamaṃ nāma narādhipassa,

Arindamaṃ

Teneva taṃ vuccati tassa cakkanti.

Tasmā sabbepi te rājāno attano attano rajjasirivibhavānurūpaṃ pābhataṃ gahetvā taṃ rājānaṃ upagamma onatasirā attano moḷimaṇippabhābhisekena tassa pādapūjaṃ karontā – ‘‘ehi kho, mahārājā’’tiādīhi vacanehi tassa kiṃkārapaṭisāvitaṃ āpajjanti. Mahāsudassanassāpi tatheva akaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘ye kho, panānanda, puratthimāya disāya…pe… anusāsa, mahārājā’’ti.

Tattha svāgatanti su āgataṃ. Ekasmiñhi āgate socanti, gate nandanti. Ekasmiṃ āgate nandanti, gate socanti, tādiso tvaṃ āgamananandano, gamanasocano. Tasmā tava āgamanaṃ suāgamananti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ vutte pana rājā cakkavattī nāpi – ‘‘ettakaṃ nāma me anuvassaṃ baliṃ upakappethā’’ti vadati, nāpi aññassa bhogaṃ acchinditvā aññassa deti. Attano pana dhammarājabhāvassa anurūpāya paññāya pāṇātipātādīni upaparikkhitvā pemanīyena mañjunā sarena – ‘‘passatha tātā, pāṇātipāto nāmesa āsevito bhāvito bahulīkato nirayasaṃvattaniko hotī’’tiādinā nayena dhammaṃ desetvā ‘‘pāṇo na hantabbo’’tiādikaṃ ovādaṃ deti. Mahāsudassanopi tatheva akāsi, tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘rājā mahāsudassano evamāha – ‘pāṇo na hantabbo…pe… yathābhuttañca bhuñjathā’ti’’. Kiṃ pana sabbepi rañño imaṃ ovādaṃ gaṇhantīti? Buddhassāpi tāva sabbe na gaṇhanti, rañño kiṃ gaṇhissantīti. Tasmā ye paṇḍitā vibhāvino, te gaṇhanti. Sabbe pana anuyantā bhavanti. Tasmā ye kho panānandātiādimāha.

svāgata ye kho panānandā

Atha taṃ cakkaratanaṃ evaṃ pubbavidehavāsīnaṃ ovāde dinne katapātarāse cakkavattibalena vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā puratthimasamuddaṃ ajjhogāhati. Yathā yathā ca taṃ ajjhogāhati, tathā tathā agadagandhaṃ ghāyitvā saṅkhittaphaṇo nāgarājā viya, saṅkhittaūmivipphāraṃ hutvā ogacchamānaṃ mahāsamuddasalilaṃ yojanamattaṃ ogantvā antosamudde veḷuriyabhitti viya tiṭṭhati. Taṅkhaṇaññeva ca tassa rañño puññasiriṃ daṭṭhukāmāni viya mahāsamuddatale vippakiṇṇāni nānāratanāni tato tato āgantvā taṃ padesaṃ pūrayanti. Atha sā rājaparisā taṃ nānāratanaparipūraṃ mahāsamuddatalaṃ disvā yathāruci ucchaṅgādīhi ādiyati, yathāruci ādinnaratanāya pana parisāya taṃ cakkaratanaṃ paṭinivattati. Paṭinivattamāne ca tasmiṃ parisā aggato hoti, majjhe rājā, ante cakkaratanaṃ. Tampi jalanidhijalaṃ palobhiyamānamiva cakkaratanasiriyā, asahamānamiva ca tena viyogaṃ nemimaṇḍalapariyantaṃ abhihanantaṃ nirantarameva upagacchati. Evaṃ rājā cakkavattī puratthimamahāsamuddapariyantaṃ pubbavidehaṃ abhivijinitvā dakkhiṇasamuddapariyantaṃ jambudīpaṃ vijetukāmo cakkaratanadesitena maggena dakkhiṇasamuddābhimukho gacchati. Mahāsudassanopi tatheva agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘atha kho, ānanda, cakkaratanaṃ puratthimaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā paccuttaritvā dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pavattī’’ti.

Evaṃ pavattamānassa pana tassa pavattanavidhānaṃ, senāsanniveso, paṭirājāgamanaṃ, tesaṃ anusāsanippadānaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddaajjhogāhanaṃ samuddasalilassa ogacchamānaṃ ratanānaṃ ādānanti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Vijinitvā pana taṃ dasasahassayojanappamāṇaṃ jambudīpaṃ dakkhiṇasamuddatopi paccuttaritvā sattayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ aparagoyānaṃ vijetuṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva gantvā tampi samuddapariyantaṃ tatheva abhivijinitvā pacchimasamuddatopi uttaritvā aṭṭhayojanasahassappamāṇaṃ uttarakuruṃ vijetuṃ tatheva gantvā tampi samuddapariyantaṃ tatheva abhivijiya uttarasamuddato paccuttarati.

Ettāvatā raññā cakkavattinā cāturantāya pathaviyā ādhipaccaṃ adhigataṃ hoti. So evaṃ vijitavijayo attano rajjasirisampattidassanatthaṃ sapariso uddhaṃ gaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghitvā suvikasitapadumakumudapuṇḍarīkavanavicitte cattāro jātassare viya pañcasatapañcasataparittadīpaparivāre cattāro mahādīpe oloketvā cakkaratanadesiteneva maggena yathānukkamaṃ attano rājadhāniṃ paccāgacchati. Atha taṃ cakkaratanaṃ antepuradvāraṃ sobhayamānaṃ viya hutvā tiṭṭhati.

Evaṃ patiṭṭhite pana tasmiṃ cakkaratane rājantepure ukkāhi vā dīpikāhi vā kiñci karaṇīyaṃ na hoti, cakkaratanobhāsoyeva rattiṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamatiyeva. Ye pana andhakāratthikā honti, tesaṃ andhakārameva hoti. Mahāsudassanassāpi sabbametaṃ tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘dakkhiṇaṃ samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā…pe… evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosī’’ti.

Hatthiratanavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
244. Then, "having risen from the seat" means having risen from the seat where [he was] sitting and having come near to the wheel treasure.

"Having taken the golden pitcher" means having raised the golden pitcher with a spout like an elephant's trunk.

"Then, King Mahāsudarsana followed with the fourfold army" means that all the wheel-turning monarchs, having sprinkled with water and saying, "May the wheel treasure conquer," immediately rose into the sky and the wheel treasure turned.

That king is called a wheel-turning monarch when its turning occurs at the same time.

When the wheel treasure has started turning, then, following it, the king, mounting the excellent wheel-turning vehicle, rises into the sky.

Then his retinue, with umbrellas, chowries, and so forth in their hands, and the women of the inner apartments, and then, together with their own armies, adorned with various kinds of mail coats, armor, and so forth, radiant with various ornaments and jewels, decorated with raised flags and banners, the viceroy, the commander-in-chief, and others also rise into the sky and surround the king.

Then the royal officers cause drums to be sounded in the city streets for the purpose of gathering the people: "Fathers, a wheel treasure has arisen for our king; gather together, adorned and embellished according to your means."

The great multitude, giving up all their affairs at the mere sound of the wheel treasure, taking perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and gathering together, also all rise into the sky and surround the king.

Whoever has the intention to go with the king, that person goes into the sky.

Thus, the assembly is twelve yojanas in breadth.

There, not even one person is mutilated or has soiled clothes.

The wheel-turning monarch, indeed, has a pure retinue.

The wheel-turning monarch's assembly, going in the sky like *vidyādhara* men, is like jewels scattered on a ground of dark blue sapphires.

So it was also with Mahāsudarsana.

Therefore, it was said: "Then, King Mahāsudarsana followed with the fourfold army."

That wheel treasure turns in the sky not too high, not too low, above the tops of the trees.

Just as the fruits, flowers, and shoots of trees are easily taken.

And just as those standing on the ground are able to recognize, "This is the king, this is the viceroy, this is the commander-in-chief."

And in places and paths, whoever wishes [to go] by whatever [path], goes by that very [path].

Those skilled in painting and other arts, doing their own work, go along.

Just as, indeed, on the earth, so all their affairs succeed in the sky.

Thus, taking the wheel-turning monarch's assembly, that wheel treasure, leaving Mount Meru on its left side, goes to Pūrvavideha, a distance of seven thousand yojanas above the great ocean.

There, that ground area, capable of accommodating an assembly of twelve yojanas in extent and thirty-six yojanas in circumference, is easily provided with food and equipment, is endowed with shade and water, is very level, delightful, and pleasing; on that upper part, that wheel treasure stands as if fixed to an axle.

Then, by that sign, that great multitude, descending and doing all their affairs, such as bathing, eating, and so forth, arranges their dwelling.

Everything was just like that for Mahāsudarsana.

Therefore, it was said: "Wherever, Ānanda, the wheel treasure stops, there King Mahāsudarsana took up residence with the fourfold army."

Thus, when the wheel-turning monarch had taken up residence, those kings there, even having heard that "a foreign wheel has come," do not mobilize their armies and prepare for battle.

For, immediately after the arising of the wheel treasure, there is no being who would dare to raise a weapon, thinking hostility against that king.

This is the power of the wheel treasure.

Because of that king, all the enemies submit to taming; the king of men [is] named *arindama*, *arindama*; therefore, it is called his wheel.

Therefore, all those kings, taking tribute appropriate to their own royal glory and power, approaching that king, with bowed heads, performing reverence at his feet with the shining gems of their diadems, with words beginning with "Come here, great king!", submit to being at his command.

Mahāsudassana also did the same.

Therefore it was said: "Those, Ānanda, from the eastern direction...pe...he instructs, great king!"

There, "*svāgata*" means "well come."

For when one comes, they grieve; when one goes, they rejoice.

When one comes, they rejoice; when one goes, they grieve; you are such a one, bringing joy in coming, causing sorrow in going.

Therefore, it is said that your coming is a *suāgamana* (welcome).

When this was said, the universal monarch neither says, "May you provide me with so much tribute annually," nor does he take away the property of one person and give it to another.

But, in accordance with the wisdom appropriate to his state as a righteous king, having examined the prohibition of killing and so on, with a lovely, sweet voice, teaching the Dharma in a way beginning with, "See, fathers, killing, if practiced, developed, and made abundant, leads to hell," he gives the instruction ending with "Life should not be taken."

Mahāsudassana also did the same; therefore it was said: "King Mahāsudassana said thus: 'Life should not be taken...pe...and you should eat according to what you have received.'"

Do all the kings accept this instruction of the king? Even all of the Buddha's [instructions] are not accepted; how much less will they accept the king's?

Therefore, those who are wise and discerning accept [it].

But all become followers.

Therefore, he said, "Those, Ānanda..." and so on.

*Svāgata*

Those, Ānanda

Then that wheel-treasure, having given instruction in this way to those living in Pūrbavideha, when breakfast was done, by the power of the universal monarch, rising up into the sky, plunges into the eastern sea.

And as it plunges, so the water of the great ocean, smelling the fragrance of immortality, contracting its hood like a Nāga king, becoming a contracted wave, receding, receding for the space of a *yojana*, stands like a wall of *vaiḍūrya* within the sea.

And at that very moment, as if wishing to see the meritorious glory of that king, various jewels, scattered on the surface of the great ocean, coming from here and there, fill that place.

Then that royal retinue, seeing that surface of the great ocean filled with various jewels, take [them] according to their pleasure with their laps and so on; but to the retinue with the jewels taken according to their pleasure, that wheel-treasure turns back.

And as it turns back, the retinue is in front, the king in the middle, the wheel-treasure at the rear.

And that water of the ocean, as if being enticed by the glory of the wheel-treasure, and as if unable to bear separation from it, constantly approaches, striking the perimeter of the felly.

In this way, King Cakkavattī, having completely conquered Pūrbavideha as far as the eastern great ocean, wishing to conquer Jambudvīpa as far as the southern ocean, goes towards the southern ocean by the path shown by the wheel-treasure.

Mahāsudassana also went in the same way.

Therefore it was said: "Then, Ānanda, the wheel-treasure, having plunged into the eastern sea, having come out again, turns towards the southern direction."

Thus, the way of proceeding of one proceeding in this way, the arrangement of the army, the arrival of opposing kings, the giving of instruction to them, the plunging into the southern sea, the receding of the water of the ocean, the taking of the jewels—all this should be understood in the same way as before.

But having conquered Jambudvīpa, which is ten thousand *yojanas* in extent, having crossed back from the southern ocean, in order to conquer Aparagoyāna, which is seven thousand *yojanas* in extent, having gone in the same way as previously said, having completely conquered that also as far as the ocean, and having crossed over from the western ocean, in order to conquer Uttarakuru, which is eight thousand *yojanas* in extent, having gone in the same way, having completely conquered that also as far as the ocean, he crosses back from the northern ocean.

Thus, by the king, the universal monarch, sovereignty over the four-cornered earth has been attained.

He, having thus won the victory, in order to show the prosperity and glory of his own kingdom, together with his retinue, having leaped up into the sky, having looked upon the four great islands, variegated with forests of well-opened lotuses, water lilies, and white lotuses, with the four hundred and five hundred surrounding lesser islands, like golden-born [beings], by the very path shown by the wheel-treasure, he returns to his own capital in due order.

Then that wheel-treasure, having become like one beautifying the gate of the inner palace, stands [there].
Thus, when that wheel-treasure (cakkaratane) was established in the royal palace, nothing needed to be done with torches (ukkāhi) or lamps (dīpikāhi). The light of the wheel-treasure (cakkaratanobhāso) dispelled the darkness (andhakāraṃ) at night.

But those who are intent on darkness (andhakāratthikā), for them, there is only darkness (andhakārameva).

All this happened to Mahāsudassana in the same way (tatheva).

Therefore it was said: "Having plunged into the southern sea... an such like wheel-treasure (cakkaratanaṃ) appeared."

Description of the elephant-treasure (hatthiratanavaṇṇanā).

mula_pali:
245. ‘‘Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, cakkaratanaṃ samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ abhivijinitvā kusāvatiṃ rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā rañño mahāsudassanassa antepuradvāre atthakaraṇapamukhe akkhāhataṃ maññe aṭṭhāsi rañño mahāsudassanassa antepuraṃ upasobhayamānaṃ. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosi.

Hatthiratanaṃ
mula_english:
“Then, Ānanda, that Wheel-Jewel, having conquered the earth to the sea limits, returned to the royal capital Kusāvatī, and it seems it stopped at the palace gate of King Mahāsudassana, at the head of the place for deciding matters, as if adorning the inner palace of King Mahāsudassana. And this is how the Wheel-Treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana (rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosi.).

Elephant-Jewel

mula_pali:
246. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa hatthiratanaṃ pāturahosi sabbaseto sattappatiṭṭho iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo uposatho nāma nāgarājā. Taṃ disvā rañño mahāsudassanassa cittaṃ pasīdi – ‘bhaddakaṃ vata bho hatthiyānaṃ, sace damathaṃ upeyyā’ti. Atha kho taṃ, ānanda, hatthiratanaṃ – seyyathāpi nāma gandhahatthājāniyo dīgharattaṃ suparidanto, evameva damathaṃ upagacchi. Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tameva hatthiratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno pubbaṇhasamayaṃ abhiruhitvā samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anuyāyitvā kusāvatiṃ rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā pātarāsamakāsi. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ hatthiratanaṃ pāturahosi.

Assaratanaṃ
mula_english:
246. Furthermore, Ānanda, the elephant-treasure ( *hastiratanaṃ*) appeared to King Mahāsudassana, perfectly white, with sevenfold strength, possessing psychic power, traversing the sky, a Nāga king named Uposatha.

Seeing him, the mind of King Mahāsudassana was pleased: "What a wonderful riding-elephant (*hatthiyānaṃ*), if only he could be brought under control!"

Then, Ānanda, that elephant-treasure (*hastiratanaṃ*) submitted to control just like a thoroughbred elephant (*gandhahatthājāniyo*) that had been well trained for a long time, even so he underwent taming (*damathaṃ upagacchi*).

Formerly, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, testing that very elephant-treasure (*hastiratanaṃ*), mounted him at daybreak, and after traversing the earth to the edge of the sea, returned to the capital Kusāvatī in time for his morning meal.

To King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda, such an elephant-treasure (*hastiratanaṃ*) appeared.

Horse-treasure (*assaratanaṃ*)
commentary_pali:
246. Evaṃ pātubhūtacakkaratanasseva cakkavattino amaccā pakatimaṅgalahatthiṭṭhānaṃ samaṃ sucibhūmibhāgaṃ kāretvā haricandanādīhi surabhigandhehi upalimpāpetvā heṭṭhā vicittavaṇṇasurabhikusumasamokiṇṇaṃ upari suvaṇṇatārakānaṃ antarantarā samosaritamanuññakusumadāmapaṭimaṇḍitavitānaṃ devavimānaṃ viya abhisaṅkharitvā – ‘‘evarūpassa nāma deva hatthiratanassa āgamanaṃ cintethā’’ti vadanti. So pubbe vuttanayeneva mahādānaṃ datvā sīlāni ca samādāya taṃ puññasampattiṃ āvajjanto nisīdi. Athassa puññānubhāvacodito chaddantakulā vā uposathakulā vā taṃ sakkāravisesaṃ anubhavitukāmo taruṇaravimaṇḍalābhirattacaraṇagīvāmukhapaṭimaṇḍitavisuddhasetasarīro sattapatiṭṭho susaṇṭhitaaṅgapaccaṅgasanniveso vikasitarattapadumacārupokkharo iddhimā yogī viya vehāsagamanasamattho manosilācuṇṇarañjitapariyanto viya rajatapabbato hatthiseṭṭho āgantvā tasmiṃ padese tiṭṭhati. So chaddantakulā āgacchanto sabbakaniṭṭho āgacchati. Uposathakulā āgacchanto sabbajeṭṭho. Pāḷiyaṃ pana uposatho nāgarājā icceva āgataṃ. Nāgarājā nāma kassaci aparibhogo, sabbakaniṭṭho āgacchatīti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Svāyaṃ pūritacakkavattivattānaṃ cakkavattīnaṃ vuttanayeneva cintayantānaṃ āgacchati. Mahāsudassanassa pana sayameva pakatimaṅgalahatthiṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā taṃ hatthiṃ apanetvā tattha aṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘puna caparaṃ ānanda…pe… nāgarājā’’ti.

Evaṃ pātubhūtaṃ pana taṃ hatthiratanaṃ disvā hatthigopakādayo haṭṭhatuṭṭhā vegena gantvā rañño ārocenti. Rājā turitaturito āgantvā taṃ disvā pasannacitto – ‘‘bhaddakaṃ vata bho hatthiyānaṃ, sace damathaṃ upeyyā’’ti cintayanto hatthaṃ pasāreti. Atha so gharadhenuvacchako viya kaṇṇe olambitvā sūratabhāvaṃ dassento rājānaṃ upasaṅkamati. Rājā taṃ ārohitukāmo hoti. Athassa parijanā adhippāyaṃ ñatvā taṃ hatthiratanaṃ suvaṇṇaddhajaṃ suvaṇṇālaṅkāraṃ hemajālapaṭicchannaṃ katvā upanenti. Rājā taṃ anisīdāpetvāva sattaratanamayāya nisseṇiyā āruyha ākāsagamananinnacitto hoti. Tassa saha cittuppādeneva so nāgarājā rājahaṃso viya indanīlamaṇippabhājālaṃ nīlagaganatalaṃ abhilaṅghati. Tato cakkacārikāya vuttanayeneva sakalarājaparisā. Iti sapariso rājā antopātarāseyeva sakalapathaviṃ anusaṃyāyitvā rājadhāniṃ paccāgacchati. Evaṃ mahiddhikaṃ cakkavattino hatthiratanaṃ hoti. Mahāsudassanassāpi tādisameva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘disvā rañño…pe… pāturahosī’’ti.

Assaratanavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
246. Thus, just as the manifested wheel-gem appeared, the advisors of the wheel-turning monarch, after having a level, pure ground area prepared for the customary auspicious elephant-station, and after having it smeared with fragrant scents such as yellow sandalwood, etc., and after constructing a pavilion adorned with various colored fragrant flowers scattered below, and above, a canopy decorated with interwoven gold stars and with delightful flower garlands placed at intervals, like a celestial abode, say, "Imagine the arrival of the elephant-gem, oh god, in such a form."

He, having given a great gift in just the way previously described, and also having undertaken the precepts, sat reflecting on that meritorious accomplishment.

Then, impelled by the power of merit, whether from the Chaddanta clan or the Uposatha clan, with the desire to experience that special honor, his body being adorned with a pure white color, his feet, neck, and face being delighted by the orb of the fresh sun, firmly established in mindfulness, with a well-arranged assemblage of major and minor limbs, with lovely lotus-like petals having blossomed, like a powerful yogi, capable of traveling through the sky, like a silver mountain with its borders painted with realgar powder, the best of elephants, having come, stands in that place.

That one, coming from the Chaddanta clan, comes as the youngest of all.

Coming from the Uposatha clan, [he is] the eldest of all.

In the Pāli [text], however, the Uposatha nāga-king is said to have arrived.

The nāga-king, namely, is unshared by anyone; it is said in the commentaries that he comes as the youngest of all.

He comes thinking in just the way described before, for the wheel-turning monarchs whose observances of the wheel-turning [monarch] have been fulfilled.

But Mahāsudassana himself, having come to the customary auspicious elephant-station, having removed that elephant, stood there.

Therefore, it was said, "Again, moreover, Ānanda…pe… nāga-king."

Thus, having seen that manifested elephant-gem, the elephant-keepers and others, delighted and joyous, quickly go and announce it to the king.

The king, hurrying quickly, having come, his mind being pleased, thinking, "Excellent indeed, oh, is the elephant-vehicle, if it would approach control," extends his hand.

Then he, like a calf of a domestic cow, drooping his ear, showing a friendly disposition, approaches the king.

The king wants to mount him.

Then his attendants, knowing his intention, having made that elephant-gem golden-bannered, golden-ornamented, and covered with a net of gold, bring it near.

The king, without making him sit down, having ascended by a ladder made of the seven precious things, becomes one whose mind is inclined to traveling in the sky.

For him, with the arising of thought itself, that nāga-king, like a royal swan, crosses over the blue surface of the sky, a web of light from an sapphire jewel.

Then, the entire royal assembly [follows] in the way described for the wheel-journey.

Thus, the king, together with his retinue, having roamed over the entire earth, as easily as crossing a courtyard, returns to the capital.

Thus, the elephant-gem of the wheel-turning monarch is greatly powerful.

Even Mahāsudassana's was just like that.

Therefore, it was said, "Having seen the king…pe… appeared."

assaratanavaṇṇanā (Description of the horse-gem)

mula_pali:
247. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa assaratanaṃ pāturahosi sabbaseto kāḷasīso muñjakeso iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo valāhako nāma assarājā. Taṃ disvā rañño mahāsudassanassa cittaṃ pasīdi – ‘bhaddakaṃ vata bho assayānaṃ sace damathaṃ upeyyā’ti. Atha kho taṃ , ānanda, assaratanaṃ seyyathāpi nāma bhaddo assājāniyo dīgharattaṃ suparidanto, evameva damathaṃ upagacchi. Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tameva assaratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno pubbaṇhasamayaṃ abhiruhitvā samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anuyāyitvā kusāvatiṃ rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā pātarāsamakāsi. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ assaratanaṃ pāturahosi.

Maṇiratanaṃ
mula_english:
247. Furthermore, Ānanda, the horse-treasure (*aśvaratna*) appeared to King Mahāsudassana, all white, with a crow's head (kāḷasīsa), with mane like *muñja* grass (muñjakeso), powerful (iddhimā), travelling through the air (vehāsaṅgamo), a royal stallion called Valāhaka (*assarājā*).

Seeing him, the King Mahāsudassana’s mind was pleased: "What a wonderful mount (*assayānaṃ*), if only he could be brought under control (damathaṃ upeyyā)!"

Then, Ānanda, that horse-treasure (*assaratanaṃ*) submitted to control just like a thoroughbred (bhaddo assājāniyo) that had been trained for a long time (dīgharattaṃ suparidanto); just so (*evameva*) it came under control (damathaṃ upagacchi).

Once, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, when testing that very horse-treasure (*assaratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno*), mounted it in the morning (pubbaṇhasamayaṃ abhiruhitvā), and after traversing the whole earth (samuddapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ anuyāyitvā) to the edge of the ocean, he returned to Kusāvatī, the royal capital (*rājadhāniṃ paccāgantvā*), to take his morning meal (*pātarāsamakāsi*).

That is how such a horse-treasure (*evarūpaṃ assaratanaṃ*) appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

Gem-treasure (*maṇiratanaṃ*)
commentary_pali:
247. Evaṃ pātubhūtahatthiratanassa pana cakkavattino amaccā pakatimaṅgalaassaṭṭhānaṃ sucisamatalaṃ kāretvā alaṅkaritvā ca purimanayeneva rañño tassa āgamanacintanatthaṃ ussāhaṃ janenti. So purimanayeneva katadānamānanasakkāro samādinnasīlabbato pāsādatale sukhanisinno puññasampattiṃ samanussarati. Athassa puññānubhāvacodito sindhavakulato vijjulatāvinaddhasaradakālasetavalāhakarāsisassirīko rattapādo rattatuṇḍo candappabhāpuñjasadisasuddhasiniddhaghanasaṃhatasarīro kākagīvā viya indanīlamaṇi viya ca kāḷavaṇṇena sīsena samannāgatattā kāḷasīsoti suṭṭhu kappetvā ṭhapitehi viya muñjasadisehi saṇhavaṭṭaujugatehi kesehi samannāgatattā muñjakeso vehāsaṅgamo valāhako nāma assarājā āgantvā tasmiṃ ṭhāne patiṭṭhāti. Mahāsudassanassa panesa hatthiratanaṃ viya āgato. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ hatthiratane vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Evarūpaṃ assaratanaṃ sandhāya bhagavā – ‘‘puna ca para’’ntiādimāha.

Maṇiratanavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
247. Thus, when the elephant-treasure has appeared, the advisors of the Wheel-turning Monarch, having had the site for the customary auspicious horse prepared, made clean and level, and adorned, generate enthusiasm for the king's reflection on its arrival, just as before.

He, having performed acts of giving, honoring, and respect as before, having undertaken the precepts and observances, happily seated on the palace terrace, reflects on the accomplishment of merit.

Then, impelled by the power of his merit, there comes a horse-king named Valāhaka, who travels in the sky, is Kālasīsa because he has a head with black coloring like a crow's neck, like an indigo gem, and Muñjakesa because he has hair that is smooth, round, straight, and like muñja grass, whose body is compact and solid, resembling a mass of lightning-like clouds, whose feet are red, whose beak is red, whose color is like a heap of moonlight, from the Sindhava breed, and who establishes himself in that place.

This elephant-treasure has come like the elephant-treasure of Mahāsudassana.

The rest should be understood in the way already described in the section on the elephant-treasure.

Referring to such a horse-treasure, the Blessed One said, "Furthermore..." etc.

Description of the Jewel-Treasure.

mula_pali:
248. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa maṇiratanaṃ pāturahosi. So ahosi maṇi veḷuriyo subho jātimā aṭṭhaṃso suparikammakato accho vippasanno anāvilo sabbākārasampanno. Tassa kho panānanda, maṇiratanassa ābhā samantā yojanaṃ phuṭā ahosi. Bhūtapubbaṃ, ānanda, rājā mahāsudassano tameva maṇiratanaṃ vīmaṃsamāno caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā maṇiṃ dhajaggaṃ āropetvā rattandhakāratimisāya pāyāsi. Ye kho panānanda, samantā gāmā ahesuṃ, te tenobhāsena kammante payojesuṃ divāti maññamānā. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ maṇiratanaṃ pāturahosi.

Itthiratanaṃ
mula_english:
248. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Jewel-Treasure (**maṇiratanaṃ**) appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

It was a beryl gem (**maṇi veḷuriyo**), pure (**subho**), excellent (**jātimā**), well-cut into eight facets (**aṭṭhaṃso**), well-crafted (**suparikammakato**), clear (**accho**), bright (**vippasanno**), unflawed (**anāvilo**), perfect in every respect (**sabbākārasampanno**).

Now, Ānanda, the radiance (**ābhā**) of this Jewel-Treasure (**maṇiratanaṃ**) spread around for a whole *yojana*.

And it so happened that once King Mahāsudassana, testing that very Jewel-Treasure (**maṇiratanaṃ**), drew up his four-constituent army (**caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ**) in array (**sannayhitvā**), and mounting the jewel (**maṇiṃ**) on top of his banner (**dhajaggaṃ āropetvā**), he set forth in the darkness and gloom of the night (**rattandhakāratimisāya pāyāsi**).

Then all the inhabitants of the villages nearby (**samantā gāmā ahesuṃ**) began their work by its light (**tenobhāsena**), thinking that it was day (**divāti maññamānā**).

Ānanda, that is how such a Jewel-Treasure (**maṇiratanaṃ**) appeared to King Mahāsudassana.

Woman-Treasure (**itthiratanaṃ**)
commentary_pali:
248. Evaṃ pātubhūtaassaratanassa pana rañño cakkavattino catuhatthāyāmaṃ sakaṭanābhisamapariṇāhaṃ ubhosu antesu kaṇṇikapariyantato viniggatehi suparisuddhamuttākalāpehi dvīhi kañcanapadumehi alaṅkataṃ caturāsītimaṇisahassaparivāraṃ tārāgaṇaparivutassa puṇṇacandasassiriṃ pharamānaṃ viya vepullapabbatato maṇiratanaṃ āgacchati. Tassevaṃ āgatassa muttājālake ṭhapetvā veḷuparamparāya saṭṭhihatthappamāṇaṃ ākāsaṃ āropitassa rattibhāge samantā yojanappamāṇaṃ okāsaṃ ābhā pharati, yāya sabbo so okāso aruṇuggamanavelā viya sañjātāloko hoti. Tato kassakā kasikammaṃ vāṇijā āpaṇugghāṭanaṃ te te sippino taṃ taṃ kammantaṃ payojenti ‘‘divā’’ti maññamānā. Mahāsudassanassāpi sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘puna ca paraṃ ānanda,…pe… maṇiratanaṃ pāturahosī’’ti.

Itthiratanavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
Thus, when the horse-jewel had appeared to the king, the wheel-turner, it was adorned with two golden lotuses, with very pure pearl clusters emerging from the *kaṇṇika* limits on both ends, with a compass of four cubits in length and equal to the nave of a cart, surrounded by a retinue of eighty-four thousand jewels, covered with a host of stars, radiating the splendor of the full moon, like the jewel-treasure coming from Mount Vepulla. When it had thus arrived, having placed it in a pearl net and raised it into the sky to a height of sixty cubits by means of a bamboo ladder, during the night its light pervades a space of one *yojana* all around, by which all that space becomes like the time of sunrise. Then the farmers apply themselves to farming, the merchants to opening shops, and those skilled artisans apply themselves to their respective crafts, thinking, "It is day." All that happened thus to Mahāsudassana as well. Therefore it was said – "Again, further, Ānanda,...pe...the jewel-treasure appeared."

Description of the woman-jewel.

mula_pali:
249. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa itthiratanaṃ pāturahosi abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā nātidīghā nātirassā nātikisā nātithūlā nātikāḷikā nāccodātā atikkantā mānusivaṇṇaṃ mānussivaṇṇaṃ (syā.) appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ. Tassa kho panānanda, itthiratanassa evarūpo kāyasamphasso hoti, seyyathāpi nāma tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vā. Tassa kho panānanda, itthiratanassa sīte uṇhāni gattāni honti, uṇhe sītāni. Tassa kho panānanda, itthiratanassa kāyato candanagandho vāyati, mukhato uppalagandho. Taṃ kho panānanda, itthiratanaṃ rañño mahāsudassanassa pubbuṭṭhāyinī ahosi pacchānipātinī kiṅkārapaṭissāvinī manāpacārinī piyavādinī. Taṃ kho panānanda, itthiratanaṃ rājānaṃ mahāsudassanaṃ manasāpi no aticari aticarī (ka.), aticārī (sī. syā. pī.), kuto pana kāyena. Rañño, ānanda, mahāsudassanassa evarūpaṃ itthiratanaṃ pāturahosi.

Gahapatiratanaṃ
mula_english:
‘Then again, Ānanda, the Woman-Treasure (itthiratanaṃ) appeared to King Mahāsudassana, lovely, fair to see, charming, possessing the utmost beauty of complexion, not too tall or too short, not too thin or too fat, not too dark or too fair, surpassing human beauty, yet not attaining divine beauty.

The touch of the Woman-Treasure, Ānanda, was such that it was like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of cotton-wool.

When it was cool, the limbs of the Woman-Treasure, Ānanda, were warm; when it was warm, they were cool.

From her body, Ānanda, the scent of sandalwood (candanagandho) came forth, and from her mouth the scent of lotuses (uppalagandho).

And the Woman-Treasure, Ānanda, was the first to rise and the last to retire, willing to do his pleasure, pleasant of demeanour, and pleasant of speech.

And this Woman-Treasure, Ānanda, was not unfaithful to the King Mahāsudassana even in thought, much less in deed.

And that is how the Woman-Treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana, Ānanda.

The Householder-Treasure (gahapatiratanaṃ)
commentary_pali:
249. Evaṃ pātubhūtamaṇiratanassa pana cakkavattino visayasukhavisesassa visesakāraṇaṃ itthiratanaṃ pātubhavati. Maddarājakulato vā hissa aggamahesiṃ ānenti, uttarakuruto vā puññānubhāvena sayaṃ āgacchati. Avasesā panassā sampatti – ‘‘puna ca paraṃ, ānanda, rañño mahāsudassanassa itthiratanaṃ pāturahosi, abhirūpā dassanīyā’’tiādinā nayena pāḷiyaṃyeva āgatā.

Tattha saṇṭhānapāripūriyā adhikaṃ rūpaṃ assāti abhirūpā. Dissamānāva cakkhūni piṇayati, tasmā aññaṃ kiccavikkhepaṃ hitvāpi daṭṭhabbāti dassanīyā. Dissamānāva somanassavasena cittaṃ pasādetīti pāsādikā. Paramāyāti evaṃ pasādāvahattā uttamāya. Vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti vaṇṇasundaratāya. Samannāgatāti upetā. Abhirūpā vā yasmā nātidīghā nātirassā. Dassanīyā yasmā nātikisā nātithūlā. Pāsādikā yasmā nātikāḷikā nāccodātā. Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā yasmā abhikkantā mānusivaṇṇaṃ appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ. Manussānañhi vaṇṇābhā bahi na niccharati. Devānaṃ pana atidūrampi niccharati.

abhirūpā. dassanīyā. pāsādikā. Paramāyā Vaṇṇapokkharatāyā Samannāgatā Abhirūpā Dassanīyā Pāsādikā Paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā

Tassā pana dvādasahatthappamāṇaṃ padesaṃ sarīrābhā obhāseti. Nātidīghādīsu cassā paṭhamayugaḷena ārohasampatti, dutiyayugaḷena pariṇāhasampatti, tatiyayugaḷena vaṇṇasampatti vuttā. Chahi vāpi etehi kāyavipattiyā abhāvo, atikkantā mānusivaṇṇanti iminā kāyasampatti vuttā. Tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vāti sappimaṇḍe pakkhipitvā ṭhapitassa satavāravihatassa tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno vā. Sīteti rañño sītakāle. Uṇheti rañño uṇhakāle. Candanagandhoti niccakālameva supisitassa abhinavassa catujjātisamāyojitassa haricandanassa gandho kāyato vāyati. Uppalagandho vāyatīti hasitakathitakālesu mukhato taṅkhaṇaṃ vikasitasseva nīluppalassa atisurabhigandho vāyati.

atikkantā mānusivaṇṇa Tūlapicuno vā kappāsapicuno Sīte Uṇhe Candanagandho Uppalagandho vāyatī

Evaṃ rūpasamphassagandhasampattiyuttāya panassā sarīrasampattiyā anurūpaṃ ācāraṃ dassetuṃ taṃ kho panātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha rājānaṃ disvā nisinnāsanato aggidaḍḍhā viya paṭhamameva uṭṭhātīti pubbuṭṭhāyinī. Tasmiṃ nisinne tassa tālavaṇṭena bījanādikiccaṃ katvā pacchā nipatati nisīdatīti pacchānipātinī. Kiṃ karomi, te devāti vācāya kiṃ-kāraṃ paṭisāvetīti kiṃ kārapaṭissāvinī. Rañño manāpameva carati karotīti manāpacārinī. Yaṃ rañño piyaṃ tadeva vadatīti piyavādinī.

taṃ kho panā pubbuṭṭhāyinī. pacchānipātinī. kiṃ kārapaṭissāvinī. manāpacārinī. piyavādinī.

Idāni – ‘‘svāssā ācāro bhāvavisuddhiyāva, na sāṭheyyanā’’ti dassetuṃ taṃ kho panātiādimāha. Tattha no aticarīti na atikkamitvā cari, ṭhapetvā rājānaṃ aññaṃ purisaṃ cittenapi na patthesīti vuttaṃ hoti.

taṃ kho panā no aticarī

Tattha ye tassā ādimhi ‘‘abhirūpā’’tiādayo, ante ‘‘pubbuṭṭhāyinī’’tiādayo guṇā vuttā, te pakatiguṇā eva. ‘‘Atikkantā mānusivaṇṇa’’ntiādayo pana cakkavattino puññaṃ upanissāya cakkaratanapātubhāvato paṭṭhāya purimakammānubhāvena nibbattāti veditabbā.

Abhirūpatādikāpi vā cakkaratanapātubhāvato paṭṭhāya sabbākāraparipūrā jātā. Tenāha – ‘‘evarūpaṃ itthiratanaṃ pāturahosī’’ti.

Gahapatiratanavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
249. Thus, the *itthiratana* (woman-jewel), a special cause for the special pleasure and enjoyment of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), appears, once the merit-produced gem-jewel has appeared.

Either they bring his chief queen (*aggamahesiṃ*) from the Madda royal family, or by the power of merit, she comes of her own accord from Uttarakuru. But the remainder of her accomplishments come in the *Pāḷi* itself in the way beginning, "Again, Ānanda, the *itthiratana* appeared to the king Mahāsudassana, beautiful, lovely," etc.
