That mindfulness *sati*, recollection *anussati*, memory *paṭissati sati*, remembering *saraṇatā*, retention *dhāraṇatā*, non-confusion *apilāpanatā*, non-forgetfulness *asammusanatā sati*, faculty of mindfulness *satindriyaṃ*, power of mindfulness *satibalaṃ*, right mindfulness *sammāsati*, this is called mindfulness *sati*. By this mindfulness *imāya satiyā* he is furnished with *upeto hoti*... he is endowed with *samannāgato*, therefore he is called mindful *satimāti*. Contemplating *anupassī*, abiding *viharatī*, ardent *ātāpī*, clearly comprehending *sampajāno*, mindful *satimā*. Eliminating covetousness and grief in the world *vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassa* means there, what is the world *loko*? Just the body *kāyo* is the world *loko*. Even the five aggregates of clinging *pañcapi upādānakkhandhā* are the world *loko*, this is called the world *loko*. There, what is covetousness *abhijjhā*? That desire *rāgo*, intense desire *sārāgo*, compliance *anunayo*, fondness *anurodho*, delight *nandī*, delight in desire *nandirāgo*, intense desire of the mind *cittassa sārāgo*, this is called covetousness *abhijjhā*. There, what is grief *domanassaṃ*? That mental *cetasikaṃ* discomfort *asātaṃ*, mental *cetasikaṃ* pain *dukkhaṃ*, discomfort *asātā* and painful * dukkhā* feeling *vedanā* born of mind-contact *cetosamphassajā*, this is called grief *domanassaṃ*. Thus, in this world, both covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and displeasure (*domanassaṃ*) are abandoned, completely abandoned, calmed, pacified, have ceased, are caused to cease, are applied, are purified, are dried up, are thoroughly dried up, and are eradicated. Therefore, it is said, "having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world" (Vibha. 357-362). **Having Removed Covetousness and Displeasure in the World**: The meaning of these words has been stated in this way. In accordance with this, this method of the commentary corresponds; thus, it should be understood. This much is the explanation of the meaning of the section on the Mindfulness of the Body (*kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*). Now, concerning feelings (*vedanāsu*)... ...concerning the mind (*citte*)... ...concerning mental objects (*dhammesu*), he dwells contemplating mental objects, etc., "having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world." Here, the purpose of repeating *vedanāsu vedanānupassī* ("contemplating feeling in feelings"), and so forth, should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the Mindfulness of the Body (*kāyānupassanā*). Contemplating feeling in feelings (*vedanāsu vedanānupassī*). Contemplating mind in mind (*citte cittānupassī*). Concerning mental objects, he dwells contemplating mental objects. Here, *vedanā* ("feeling") refers to the three feelings; these are only mundane (*lokiyā eva*). Consciousness (*citta*) is also only mundane (*lokiyaṃ*), and so too are mental objects (*dhammā*). Their distinction will be evident in the section on analysis (*niddesavāre*). However, here, just as feeling is to be contemplated, so too, contemplating them, he should be understood as "contemplating feeling in feelings" (*vedanāsu vedanānupassī*). This is the method regarding the mind and mental objects. And how is feeling to be contemplated? Pleasant feeling is suffering (*dukkhato*), painful feeling is a dart (*sallato*), and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling is impermanent (*aniccato*). As it was said: Contemplating feeling in feelings (*vedanāsu vedanānupassī*): Feeling (*vedanā*): "Whoever has seen happiness as suffering (*dukkhato*), and seen pain as a dart (*sallato*), Whoever has seen the peaceful that is neither-pleasant-nor-painful as impermanent (*aniccato*); He, indeed, is a bhikkhu of right view (*sammaddaso bhikkhu*), who dwells calmed." (Saṃ. Ni. 4.253); Moreover, all these should be contemplated as "suffering" (*dukkhā*). It was said, "Whatever is experienced, that I call suffering" (*taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī*) (Saṃ. Ni. 4.259). And, they should also be contemplated as happiness and suffering (*sukhadukkhato*). As it was said, "Pleasant feeling is agreeable while it lasts and is disagreeable when it changes" (*sukhā vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā*) (Ma. Ni. 1.465). All of it should be explained in detail. Moreover, they should also be contemplated in terms of impermanence (*aniccādi*) and non-self (*anatta*). The remainder will be evident in the section on analysis (*niddesavāre*). Concerning the mind and mental objects, the mind, in particular, should be contemplated by way of its various distinctions of object (*ārammaṇa*), dominance (*adhipati*), co-nascence (*sahajāta*), plane (*bhūmi*), action (*kamma*), result (*vipāka*), and activity (*kiriyā*), and by way of the contemplations of impermanence, etc., and by way of the distinctions of attachment (*sarāga*), etc., that are presented in the section on analysis (*niddesavāre*). Mental objects (*dhammā*) should be contemplated by way of their own characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), general characteristics (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), the emptiness of phenomena (*suññatadhamma*), and the contemplations of impermanence (*aniccādi*) and non-self (*anatta*), and by way of the distinctions of peace (*santa*), etc., that are presented in the section on analysis (*niddesavāre*). The rest is as already stated. If, in the meditator’s body, called the world ( *kāyasaṅkhāte loke*), covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and grief (*domanassaṃ*) are abandoned, in the worlds of his feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth too, these are abandoned. Still, everywhere, the abandoning has been stated by way of the different types of persons and by way of the diversity of the thought-unit, in which the development of the different subjects of the Arousing of Mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna bhāvanā*) takes place. Since what is abandoned in one place is abandoned in the remaining places, therefore it should be understood that this was said to show the abandonment there as well.

The exposition of the sections is finished.

Explanation of Mindfulness of the Body: The Section on Mindfulness of Breathing

374. ‘‘Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā. So satova assasati, satova passasati. Dīghaṃ vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, dīghaṃ vā passasanto ‘dīghaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti. Rassaṃ vā assasanto ‘rassaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā passasanto ‘rassaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati , ‘sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. ‘Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati.

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho bhamakāro vā bhamakārantevāsī vā dīghaṃ vā añchanto ‘dīghaṃ añchāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā añchanto ‘rassaṃ añchāmī’ti pajānāti evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dīghaṃ vā assasanto ‘dīghaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, dīghaṃ vā passasanto ‘dīghaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā assasanto ‘rassaṃ assasāmī’ti pajānāti, rassaṃ vā passasanto ‘rassaṃ passasāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati. ‘Atthi kāyo’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho evampi (sī. syā. pī.), bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

evampi (sī. syā. pī.)

Ānāpānapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Kāyānupassanā iriyāpathapabbaṃ
mula_english:
374. But how, monks, does a monk abide contemplating the body as a body? Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty place, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him.

Mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out.

Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short.’

He trains himself, thinking: “I will breathe in, conscious of the whole body." He trains himself, thinking: “I will breathe out, conscious of the whole body.

He trains himself, thinking: “I will breathe in, calming the whole bodily process.’ He trains himself, thinking: “I will breathe out, calming the whole bodily process.

“ Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, understands: ‘I make a long turn’; or, when making a short turn, understands: ‘I make a short turn’; so too, breathing in long, a *bhikkhu* understands: ‘I breathe in long’… breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short.’

He trains himself, thinking: “I will breathe in, conscious of the whole body." He trains himself, thinking: “I will breathe out, conscious of the whole body. He trains himself, thinking: “I will breathe in, calming the whole bodily process.’ He trains himself, thinking: “I will breathe out, calming the whole bodily process.’

So he abides contemplating body as body internally, contemplating body as body externally, abides contemplating body as body both internally and externally.

He abides contemplating arising phenomena in the body, contemplating vanishing phenomena in the body, he abides contemplating both arising and vanishing phenomena in the body.

Or his mindfulness that ‘There is a body’ is maintained to the extent of knowledge & remembrance. And he remains independent, unsustained by not clinging to anything in the world.

And that, monks, is how a monk abides contemplating body as body.

The Ānāpāna Section is finished.

The Kāyānupassanā Iriyāpatha Section
commentary_pali:
374. Idāni seyyathāpi nāma cheko vilīvakārako thūlakilañjasaṇhakilañjacaṅkoṭakapeḷāpuṭādīni upakaraṇāni kattukāmo ekaṃ mahāveṇuṃ labhitvā catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ veṇukhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā phāletvā taṃ taṃ upakaraṇaṃ kareyya, evameva bhagavā satipaṭṭhānadesanāya sattānaṃ anekappakāraṃ visesādhigamaṃ kattukāmo ekameva sammāsatiṃ ‘‘cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatī’’tiādinā nayena ārammaṇavasena catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā kāyaṃ vibhajanto ‘‘kathañca bhikkhave’’tiādinā nayena niddesavāraṃ vattumāraddho.

Tattha kathañcātiādi vitthāretukamyatāpucchā. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – bhikkhave, kena ca pakārena bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatīti? Esa nayo sabbapucchāvāresu. Idha bhikkhave bhikkhūti bhikkhave imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Ayañhettha idhasaddo sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano ca. Vuttañhetaṃ ‘‘idheva bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī’’ti (ma. ni. 1.139). Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū’’ti.

kathañcā Idha bhikkhave bhikkhū

Araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vāti idamassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpanaṃ. Imassa hi bhikkhuno dīgharattaṃ rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu anuvisaṭaṃ cittaṃ kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ otarituṃ na icchati, kūṭagoṇayuttaratho viya uppathameva dhāvati. Tasmā seyyathāpi nāma gopo kūṭadhenuyā sabbaṃ khīraṃ pivitvā vaḍḍhitaṃ kūṭavacchaṃ dametukāmo dhenuto apanetvā ekamante mahantaṃ thambhaṃ nikhaṇitvā tattha yottena bandheyya. Athassa so vaccho ito cito ca vipphanditvā palāyituṃ asakkonto tameva thambhaṃ upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā, evameva imināpi bhikkhunā dīgharattaṃ rūpārammaṇādirasapānavaḍḍhitaṃ duṭṭhacittaṃ dametukāmena rūpādiārammaṇato apanetvā araññaṃ vā rukkhamūlaṃ vā suññāgāraṃ vā pavisitvā tattha satipaṭṭhānārammaṇatthambhe satiyottena bandhitabbaṃ. Evamassa taṃ cittaṃ ito cito ca vipphanditvāpi pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇaṃ alabhamānaṃ satiyottaṃ chinditvā palāyituṃ asakkontaṃ tamevārammaṇaṃ upacārappanāvasena upanisīdati ceva upanipajjati ca. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā

‘‘Yathā thambhe nibandheyya, vacchaṃ damaṃ naro idha;

Bandheyyevaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ, satiyārammaṇe daḷha’’nti.

Evamassetaṃ senāsanaṃ bhāvanānurūpaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘idamassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpana’’nti.

Apica yasmā idaṃ kāyānupassanāya muddhabhūtaṃ sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ itthipurisahatthiassādisaddasamākulaṃ gāmantaṃ apariccajitvā na sukaraṃ sampādetuṃ, saddakaṇḍakattā jhānassa. Agāmake pana araññe sukaraṃ yogāvacarena idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasitvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ, tasmāssa anurūpasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā, ‘‘araññagato vā’’tiādimāha.

Vatthuvijjācariyo viya hi bhagavā. So yathā vatthuvijjācariyo nagarabhūmiṃ passitvā suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā ‘‘ettha nagaraṃ māpethā’’ti upadisati, sotthinā ca nagare niṭṭhite rājakulato mahāsakkāraṃ labhati, evameva yogāvacarassa anurūpasenāsanaṃ upaparikkhitvā ‘‘ettha kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjitabba’’nti upadisati, tato tattha kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjantena yoginā anukkamena arahatte patte ‘‘sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā’’ti mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ labhati.

Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu dīpisadisoti vuccati. Yathā hi mahādīpirājā araññe tiṇagahanaṃ vā vanagahanaṃ vā pabbatagahanaṃ vā nissāya nilīyitvā vanamahiṃsagokaṇṇasūkarādayo mige gaṇhāti, evameva ayaṃ araññādīsu kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto bhikkhu yathākkamena cattāro magge ceva cattāri ariyaphalāni ca gaṇhāti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

‘‘Yathāpi dīpiko nāma, nilīyitvā gaṇhatī mige;

Tathevāyaṃ buddhaputto, yuttayogo vipassako;

Araññaṃ pavisitvāna, gaṇhāti phalamuttama’’nti.

Tenassa parakkamajavayoggabhūmiṃ araññasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā ‘‘araññagato vā’’tiādimāha. Ito paraṃ imasmiṃ ānāpānapabbe yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ visuddhimagge vuttameva. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho bhamakāro vāti idañhi upamāmattameva iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāyeti idaṃ appanāmattameva ca tattha anāgataṃ, sesaṃ āgatameva.

Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho bhamakāro vā iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye

Yaṃ pana anāgataṃ, tattha dakkhoti cheko. Dīghaṃ vā añchantoti mahantānaṃ bherīpokkharādīnaṃ likhanakāle hatthe ca pāde ca pasāretvā dīghaṃ kaḍḍhanto. Rassaṃ vā añchantoti khuddakānaṃ dantasūcivedhakādīnaṃ likhanakāle mandamandaṃ rassaṃ kaḍḍhanto. Evameva khoti evaṃ ayampi bhikkhu addhānavasena ittaravasena ca pavattānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ vasena dīghaṃ vā assasanto dīghaṃ assasāmīti pajānāti…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhatīti. Tassevaṃ sikkhato assāsapassāsanimitte cattāri jhānāni uppajjanti, so jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā assāsapassāse vā pariggaṇhāti jhānaṅgāni vā.

dakkho Dīghaṃ vā añchanto Rassaṃ vā añchanto Evameva kho

Tattha assāsapassāsakammiko ‘‘ime assāsapassāsā kiṃ nissitā? Vatthunissitā. Vatthu nāma karajakāyo, karajakāyo nāma cattāri mahābhūtāni upādārūpañce’’ti evaṃ rūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti. Tato tadārammaṇe phassapañcamake nāmanti. Evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pariggahetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjādipaṭiccasamuppādaṃ disvā ‘‘paccayapaccayuppannadhammamattamevetaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthī’’ti vitiṇṇakaṅkho sappaccayanāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Idaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhaṃ.

Jhānakammikopi ‘‘imāni jhānaṅgāni kiṃ nissitāni, vatthunissitāni, vatthu nāma karajakāyo jhānaṅgāni nāmaṃ, karajakāyo rūpa’’nti nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjādipaccayākāraṃ disvā ‘‘paccayapaccayuppannadhammamattamevetaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthī’’ti vitiṇṇakaṅkho sappaccayanāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Idamekassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhaṃ.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā assāsapassāsakāye kāyānupassī viharati. Bahiddhā vāti parassa vā assāsapassāsakāye. Ajjhattabahiddhā vāti kālena attano, kālena parassa assāsapassāsakāye. Etenassa paguṇakammaṭṭhānaṃ aṭṭhapetvā aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakālo kathito. Ekasmiṃ kāle panidaṃ ubhayaṃ na labbhati.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā Bahiddhā vā Ajjhattabahiddhā vā

Samudayadhammānupassīvāti yathā nāma kammārassa bhastañca gaggaranāḷiñca tajjañca vāyāmaṃ paṭicca vāto aparāparaṃ sañcarati, evaṃ bhikkhuno karajakāyañca nāsapuṭañca cittañca paṭicca assāsapassāsakāyo aparāparaṃ sañcarati. Kāyādayo dhammā samudayadhammā, te passanto ‘‘samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharatī’’ti vuccati. Vayadhammānupassī vāti yathā bhastāya apanītāya gaggaranāḷiyā bhinnāya tajje ca vāyāme asati so vāto nappavattati, evameva kāye bhinne nāsapuṭe viddhaste citte ca niruddhe assāsapassāsakāyo nāma nappavattatīti kāyādinirodhā assāsapassāsanirodhoti evaṃ passanto ‘‘vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharatī’’ti vuccati. Samudayavayadhammānupassī vāti kālena samudayaṃ kālena vayaṃ anupassanto. Atthi kāyoti vā panassāti kāyova atthi, na satto, na puggalo, na itthī, na puriso, na attā, na attaniyaṃ, nāhaṃ, na mama, na koci, na kassacīti evamassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti.

Samudayadhammānupassī vā Vayadhammānupassī vā Samudayavayadhammānupassī vā Atthi kāyoti vā panassā

Yāvadevāti payojanaparicchedavavatthāpanametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā sā sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti, sā na aññadatthāya. Atha kho yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya aparāparaṃ uttaruttari ñāṇapamāṇatthāya ceva satipamāṇatthāya ca, satisampajaññānaṃ vuḍḍhatthāyāti attho. Anissito ca viharatīti taṇhānissayadiṭṭhinissayānaṃ vasena anissitova viharati. Na ca kiñci loke upādiyatīti lokasmiṃ kiñci rūpaṃ vā…pe… viññāṇaṃ vā ‘‘ayaṃ me attā vā attaniyaṃ vā’’ti na gaṇhāti. Evampīti upari atthaṃ upādāya sampiṇḍanattho pi-kāro. Iminā pana padena bhagavā ānāpānapabbadesanaṃ niyyātetvā dasseti.

Yāvadevā Anissito ca viharatī Na ca kiñci loke upādiyatī Evampī

Tattha assāsapassāsapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa assāsapassāsavasena abhiniviṭṭhassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Ānāpānapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
374. Now, just as a clever worker in mat and basket weaving, wishing to make coarse and fine mats, *caṅkoṭaka* boxes, cases, and the like, should get a mammoth bamboo, split it into four, and then take each bamboo section, split it further, and make that particular implement, just so, the Blessed One, wishing to enable beings to attain various kinds of special knowledge by way of the exposition of the Arousing of Mindfulness, divided into four the one mindfulness that is right (*sammāsatiṃ*) by way of the four arousings of mindfulness (*cattāro satipaṭṭhānā*).

What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body (*kāye kāyānupassī viharati*), and so on. In this way, having divided [mindfulness] into four according to the object, then taking each arousing of mindfulness, and analyzing the body, he began to state the section on exposition by way of the method beginning with "And how, monks?" (*kathañca bhikkhave*).

There, the question beginning with "And how?" is a desire for detailed explanation.

Here, in brief, is the meaning: Monks, by what means does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? This is the method in all sections of questioning.

"Here, monks, a monk (*idha bhikkhave bhikkhū*)" means, monks, a monk in this Dispensation (*imasmiṃ sāsane*).

For in this context, the word "here" (*idha*) signifies the Dispensation of the Buddha as the basis for the person producing body-contemplation in all modes, and it denies that such a state exists in any other dispensation.

For it was said, "Only here, monks, is there an ascetic… empty are the other, opposing ways of thought with ascetics" (M.i.139).

Therefore, it was said, "Monks in this Dispensation (*imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū*)."

And how? "Gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty place (*araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā*)," this signifies that he has found an abode appropriate to the meditator for the culture of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpanaṃ*).

For the mind of this monk has long been dissipated among visible data, etc., as its object, and it does not want to enter the road of meditation; it runs off the track like a chariot harnessed to a wild ox.

Therefore, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a wild calf reared on the milk of a wild cow, after leading it away from the cow, ties it with a rope to a stout post dug into the ground in a secluded spot, so too, when a monk wants to tame his own wicked mind which has long been nourished on the taste of visible data, etc., as object for its food and drink, he should lead it away from visible and other objects and, having entered a forest or the foot of a tree or an empty place, tie it there with the rope of mindfulness to the post of the object of mindfulness-arousing.

And so his mind, even though it may dash to and fro, no longer getting the objects it was formerly used to, and finding it impossible to break the rope of mindfulness and get away, sits down, lies down, by that very object under the influence of access and absorption.

Therefore, the ancients said:

"Just as to a post one should tether a calf for taming,
So should one bind one's own mind firmly to the object of mindfulness."

In this way, this abode becomes appropriate in the meditator.

Therefore, it was said, "This signifies that he has found an abode favorable to the development of mindfulness."

Moreover, since it is not easy to bring to perfection this mindfulness of breathing meditation subject (*ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ*), which is the chief thing in contemplation of the body, the basis for the attainment of special knowledge and a pleasant abiding in the here and now for all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples, without abandoning a village boundary crowded with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, etc., because sound is a thorn to absorption.

But in a non-village forest it is easy for the yogin, having taken up this meditation subject, to produce the fourth *jhāna* of mindfulness of breathing, and having made that very *jhāna* a foundation, to comprehend the *saṃkhāras* and attain the supreme fruit, Arahantship; therefore, the Blessed One, in pointing out an abode appropriate to him, said, "Gone to the forest," and so on.

For the Blessed One is like a master of the art of building sites. Just as a master of the art of building sites, having seen the proposed site for a town, thoroughly examines it, and directs, "Build the town here," and when the town is safely finished, he receives great honor from the royal family, so the Blessed One examines an abode as to its suitability for the meditator, and directs, "Devote yourself to the meditation subject here," and later on, when the meditator has devoted himself to the meditation subject there and has attained Arahantship in due course, he receives great honor, [thinking,] "Verily, the Blessed One was a *sammāsambuddho*."

This monk, however, is called like a leopard.

Just as a great leopard king lurks in a grass wilderness or a jungle wilderness or a rock wilderness in the forest and seizes wild beasts—the wild buffalo, wild ox, boar, etc.—so too, the monk who devotes himself to his meditation subject in the forest, etc., gains successively the four paths and the four noble fruits.

Therefore, the ancients said:

"Just as a leopard, lurking, seizes wild beasts,
So too, this son of the Buddha, yoked to yoga, an observer,
Having entered the forest, gains the supreme fruit."

Therefore, the Blessed One, in pointing out a forest abode as a place likely to hasten his advancement toward effort, swiftness, and fitness, said "Gone to the forest," and so on.
Hereafter in this section on mindfulness of breathing, what should be said has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Just as, monks, a clever turner or... This is just a simile. "...either internally in the body," this is just an application. And there, the future is not discussed; only the past is.

Just as, monks, a clever turner or... "...either internally in the body..." What is not discussed is the future; there, "clever" means skilled.

"When drawing a long [line]," that means at the time of drawing large kettle drums etc., stretching out the hands and feet, he draws a long [line].

"When drawing a short [line]," that means at the time of drawing small toothpicks, needles, etc., slowly he draws a short [line].

"Just so, indeed," that means in this way also, the monk, knowing, "When breathing in long, I am breathing in long," because of the duration and because of the limited nature of the breaths that are occurring... He trains, "...I will breathe out"....

To him thus training, with regard to the sign of the in-breath and the out-breath, the four *jhānas* arise. Then, having emerged from those *jhānas*, he either examines the in-breath and the out-breath, or the factors of *jhāna*.

There, the practitioner of mindfulness of breathing [thinks]: "Supported by what are these in-breaths and out-breaths? Supported by a basis."

*Vatthu* means the coarse body (*karajakāya*). The coarse body means the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived materiality (*upādārūpa*). Thus he cognizes form (*rūpa*).

Then, with regard to that object, he names the pentad of sense-impression (*phassa*).

Thus, having grasped name and form (*nāmarūpa*), seeking its cause, seeing dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), [and realizing] "This is merely a mass of phenomena arisen from causes and conditions; there is no other being or person," having dispelled doubt, establishing the three characteristics on name and form together with their conditions, developing insight (*vipassanā*), in due course, he attains arahantship.

This is the portal to emancipation up to arahantship for a certain monk.

The practitioner of *jhāna* also [thinks]: "Supported by what are these factors of *jhāna*? Supported by a basis. *Vatthu* means the coarse body (*karajakāya*). The factors of *jhāna* are name (*nāma*), the coarse body is form (*rūpa*)." Having determined name and form in this way, seeking its cause, seeing the causal pattern beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), [and realizing] "This is merely a mass of phenomena arisen from causes and conditions; there is no other being or person," having dispelled doubt, establishing the three characteristics on name and form together with their conditions, developing insight (*vipassanā*), in due course, he attains arahantship.

This is the portal to emancipation up to arahantship for a certain monk.

"...either internally," that is, in this way, one dwells contemplating the body in the body of one's own in-breath and out-breath.

"...or externally," that is, in the body of the in-breath and out-breath of another.

"...or both internally and externally," that is, at one time in one's own, at another time in the body of the in-breath and out-breath of another.

By this, the occasion for the arising of skill in the practice has been explained, and the time for wandering has been spoken of.

But at one time, both are not obtained.

"...either internally," "...or externally," "...or both internally and externally," "...contemplating origination-phenomena:" Just as, namely, dependent on the bellows of a smith, and the leathern tube, and appropriate effort, the wind moves back and forth, so likewise, dependent on the coarse body of the monk, and the nostrils, and the mind, the body of the in-breath and out-breath moves back and forth.

The things beginning with the body are origination-phenomena. Seeing them, it is said, "He dwells contemplating origination-phenomena in the body."

"...contemplating dissolution-phenomena:" Just as when the skin of the bellows has been removed, and the leathern tube is broken, and appropriate effort is lacking, that wind does not proceed, just so, when the body is broken, and the nostrils are destroyed, and the mind has ceased, the body of the in-breath and out-breath does not proceed. Thus, seeing the cessation of the in-breath and out-breath as [resulting] from the cessation of the body etc., it is said, "He dwells contemplating dissolution-phenomena in the body."

"...contemplating origination-and-dissolution phenomena," that means contemplating origination at one time, and dissolution at another time.

"...'there is a body'," or indeed, for him, there is just a body, not a being, not a person, not a woman, not a man, not a self (*ātmā*), not something belonging to a self, not "I," not "mine," not anyone, not belonging to anyone. Thus mindfulness is present to him.

"...contemplating origination-phenomena," "...either contemplating dissolution-phenomena," "...contemplating origination-and-dissolution phenomena," "...'there is a body'," "to the extent necessary," this establishes the demarcation of purpose.

This is said: That mindfulness that is present is not for another purpose.

But rather, just for a measure of knowledge, for a greater and greater, higher and higher measure of knowledge, and for a measure of mindfulness, that is, for the increase of mindfulness and clear comprehension, is the meaning.

"And he dwells unattached," that is, he dwells unattached by way of attachment to craving (*taṇhā*) and attachment to views (*diṭṭhi*).

"And he clings to nothing in the world," that is, in the world, he does not grasp any form (*rūpa*) or...or consciousness (*vijñāṇa*) [thinking], "This is my self (*ātmā*) or something belonging to a self."

"Even so," that means the *pi*-sound is for collecting together the meaning based on the foregoing.
However, with this passage, the Blessed One, having brought forth the teaching on the ānāpāna section, shows it.

“As long as one dwells without relying [on anything] and does not cling to anything in the world," even in this way...

There, mindfulness that takes hold of the in-breath and out-breath is the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya). The former craving that gives rise to it is the truth of origination (samudayasatya). The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya). The noble path (āryamārga) whose object is cessation, abandoning origination, understanding suffering, is the truth of the path (mārgasatya).

Thus, having striven by way of the Four Truths (catursatya), a person arrives at peace (nirvṛti). This is the portal to emancipation (niyyānamukha) up to arahantship of the bhikkhu devoted to meditation on breathing.

The Ānāpāna Section is finished.

Explanation of the Iriyāpatha Section

mula_pali:
375. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gacchanto vā ‘gacchāmī’ti pajānāti, ṭhito vā ‘ṭhitomhī’ti pajānāti, nisinno vā ‘nisinnomhī’ti pajānāti, sayāno vā ‘sayānomhī’ti pajānāti, yathā yathā vā panassa kāyo paṇihito hoti, tathā tathā naṃ pajānāti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati. ‘Atthi kāyo’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Iriyāpathapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Kāyānupassanā sampajānapabbaṃ
mula_english:
“Furthermore, *bhikkhus*, when walking, a *bhikkhu* understands, ‘I am walking’; when standing, he understands, ‘I am standing’; when sitting, he understands, ‘I am sitting’; when lying down, he understands, ‘I am lying down’; or he understands accordingly however his body (*kāya*) is disposed.

In this way, he abides contemplating the body (*kāya*) as a body (*kāya*) internally (*ajjhattaṃ*), or he abides contemplating the body (*kāya*) as a body (*kāya*) externally (*bahiddhā*), or he abides contemplating the body (*kāya*) as a body (*kāya*) both internally and externally (*ajjhattabahiddhā*).

Or he abides contemplating arising phenomena (*samudayadhamma*) in the body (*kāyasmiṃ*), contemplating vanishing phenomena (*vayadhamma*) in the body (*kāyasmiṃ*), he abides contemplating both arising and vanishing phenomena (*samudayavayadhamma*) in the body (*kāyasmiṃ*).

Or else, mindfulness that “there is body (*kāyo*)” is present to him just to the extent necessary for knowledge (*ñāṇamattāya*) and awareness (*paṭissatimattāya*). And he abides independent (*anissito*), not clinging to anything in the world (*loke upādiyati*).

That is how a *bhikkhu*, abides contemplating the body (*kāya*) as a body (*kāya*).

The section on deportment is concluded.

The section on mindfulness of the body (*kāyānupassanā sampajānapabbaṃ*).
commentary_pali:
375. Evaṃ assāsapassāsavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni iriyāpathavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha kāmaṃ soṇasiṅgālādayopi gacchantā ‘‘gacchāmā’’ti jānanti, na panetaṃ evarūpaṃ jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evarūpañhi jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ na pajahati, attasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hoti. Imassa pana bhikkhuno jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ pajahati, attasaññaṃ ugghāṭeti kammaṭṭhānañceva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca hoti. Idañhi ‘‘ko gacchati, kassa gamanaṃ, kiṃ kāraṇā gacchatī’’ti evaṃ sampajānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo.

Tattha ko gacchatīti? Na koci satto vā puggalo vā gacchati. Kassa gamananti? Na kassaci sattassa vā puggalassa vā gamanaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇā gacchatīti ? Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena gacchati. Tasmā esa evaṃ pajānāti – ‘‘gacchāmī’’ti cittaṃ uppajjati , taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalakāyassa purato abhinīhāro gamananti vuccati. Ṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo.

Tatrāpi hi ‘‘tiṭṭhāmī’’ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalakāyassa koṭito paṭṭhāya ussitabhāvo ṭhānanti vuccati. ‘‘Nisīdāmī’’ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena heṭṭhimakāyassa samiñjanaṃ uparimakāyassa ussitabhāvo nisajjāti vuccati. ‘‘Sayāmī’’ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalasarīrassa tiriyato pasāraṇaṃ sayananti vuccatīti.

Tassa evaṃ pajānato evaṃ hoti ‘‘satto gacchati, satto tiṭṭhatī’’ti vuccati, atthato pana koci satto gacchanto vā ṭhito vā natthi. Yathā pana ‘‘sakaṭaṃ gacchati, sakaṭaṃ tiṭṭhatī’’ti vuccati, na ca kiñci sakaṭaṃ nāma gacchantaṃ vā ṭhitaṃ vā atthi, cattāro pana goṇe yojetvā chekamhi sārathimhi pājente ‘‘sakaṭaṃ gacchati, sakaṭaṃ tiṭṭhatī’’ti vohāramattameva hoti, evameva ajānanaṭṭhena sakaṭaṃ viya kāyo, goṇā viya cittajavātā, sārathi viya cittaṃ. ‘‘Gacchāmi tiṭṭhāmī’’ti citte uppanne vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena gamanādīni pavattanti, tato ‘‘satto gacchati, satto tiṭṭhati, ahaṃ gacchāmi, ahaṃ tiṭṭhāmī’’ti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Tenāha –

‘‘Nāvā mālutavegena, jiyāvegena tejanaṃ;

Yathā yāti tathā kāyo, yāti vātāhato ayaṃ.

Yantaṃ suttavaseneva, cittasuttavasenidaṃ;

Payuttaṃ kāyayantampi, yāti ṭhāti nisīdati.

Ko nāma ettha so satto, yo vinā hetupaccaye;

Attano ānubhāvena, tiṭṭhe vā yadi vā vaje’’ti.

Tasmā evaṃ hetupaccayavaseneva pavattāni gamanādīni sallakkhento esa ‘‘gacchanto vā gacchāmīti pajānāti, ṭhito vā, nisinno vā, sayāno vā sayānomhīti pajānātī’’ti veditabbo.

Yathā yathā vā panassa kāyo paṇihito hoti, tathā tathā naṃ pajānātīti sabbasaṅgāhikavacanametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yena yena vā ākārenassa kāyo ṭhito hoti, tena tena naṃ pajānāti. Gamanākārena ṭhitaṃ gacchatīti pajānāti. Ṭhānanisajjasayanākārena ṭhitaṃ sayānoti pajānātīti.

Yathā yathā vā panassa kāyo paṇihito hoti, tathā tathā naṃ pajānātī

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Bahiddhā vāti parassa vā catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena. Ajjhattabahiddhā vāti kālena attano, kālena parassa catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vātiādīsu pana avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayotiādinā nayena pañcahākārehi rūpakkhandhassa samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Tañhi sandhāya idha ‘‘samudayadhammānupassī vā’’tiādi vuttaṃ. Atthi kāyoti vā panassātiādi vuttasadisameva.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā Bahiddhā vā Ajjhattabahiddhā vā Samudayadhammānupassī vā Atthi kāyoti vā panassā

Idhāpi catuiriyāpathapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa catuiriyāpathapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Iriyāpathapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
375. Thus, having divided the contemplation of the body as a body by way of inhalation and exhalation, now to divide it by way of the deportment, he says, beginning with, "Again, moreover."

There, though dogs, jackals, and so on, while going, know "we are going," this is not said referring to that kind of awareness.

Indeed, awareness of that sort does not relinquish belief in a being, does not knock out the perception of a soul, and neither becomes a subject of meditation nor the development of the Arousing of Mindfulness.

But the knowledge of this *bhikkhu* casts out the belief in a being, uproots the perception of a being, is a subject of meditation and is the cultivation of the Arousing of Mindfulness.

Indeed, these words, "Who goes? Whose going is it? On account of what does the going take place?" are said referring to the knowledge of the going of the meditating *bhikkhu*.

The same is the method of exposition as regards the other postures: standing and so forth.

There, who goes? No living being or person whatsoever goes.

Whose going is it? Not the going of any living being or person.

On account of what does the going take place? On account of the diffusion of the process of oscillation born of mental activity.

Therefore, this yogi knows thus: If there arises the thought, "I shall go," that thought produces the process of oscillation; the process of oscillation produces expression. The moving on of the whole body through the diffusion of the process of oscillation is called going.

The same is the method of exposition as regards the other postures: standing and so forth.

There, too, if there arises the thought, "I shall stand," that thought produces the process of oscillation. The process of oscillation produces bodily expression. The raising upright of the whole body from below owing to the diffusion of the process of oscillation is called standing.

If there arises the thought "I shall sit," that thought produces the process of oscillation. The process of oscillation produces bodily expression. The bending of the lower part of the body and the raising upright of the upper part of the body owing to the diffusion of the process of oscillation is called sitting.

If there arises the thought, "I shall lie down," that thought produces the process of oscillation. The process of oscillation produces bodily expression. The straightening or the spreading of the whole body horizontally or across, owing to the diffusion of the process of oscillation, is called lying down.

To him who thus knows, it occurs thus: “A being goes, a being stands,” is said, but in reality, no being whatsoever goes or stands.

Just as it is said, "A cart goes, a cart stands," and there is no such thing as a cart that goes or stands, but when four oxen are yoked and a clever driver is driving, it is merely a verbal convention that "A cart goes, a cart stands." Just so, owing to not knowing, the body is like a cart, the winds born of mental activity are like oxen, and the mind is like a driver.

When there arises the thought, "I shall go, I shall stand," the wind element arises generating expression. Through the diffusion of the process of oscillation born of mental activity, going and so forth occur; therefore, "A being goes, a being stands, I go, I stand" is merely a verbal convention.

Therefore, he said:

"As a ship with the force of the wind, propelled by the force of a bowstring,

so the body goes, struck by the wind."

"Just as a machine goes by the power of string, this is by the power of mental string;

the body-machine, being applied, goes, stands, sits."

"Who is that being here, who, without causes and conditions,

would stand or would go by the power of himself?"

Accordingly this yogi, who considers by way of causes and conditions, the states of going, standing and so forth, knows well that he is going, when he is in the state of going, that he is standing when he stands, that he is sitting when he sits, and that he is lying down when he lies down, as it is told in the passage in the discourse beginning with the words: "When he is going, a *bhikkhu* understands: 'I am going.'"

Or, in whatever way his body is disposed, he knows it is (disposed) in that way—this is a comprehensive statement.

This is what is said: In whatever way his body is disposed, in that way he knows it.

He knows it is going—the body is disposed in the mode of going.

He knows it is lying down—the body is disposed in the mode of standing, sitting or lying down.

Or, in whatever way his body is disposed, he knows it is (disposed) in that way, that is, either internally, thus examining his own four modes of deportment, he dwells contemplating the body as a body;

or externally, that is, examining the four modes of deportment of another;

or both internally and externally, that is, at one time examining his own, at another time another's four modes of deportment, he dwells contemplating the body as a body.
But in "<hi rend="bold">samudayadhammānupassī vā</hi>tiādi," the arising of the form aggregate and its passing away should be determined in five ways by the method beginning with "with the arising of ignorance, the arising of form."
Here, "<hi rend="bold">samudayadhammānupassī vā</hi>tiādi" is stated with that in mind.

"<hi rend="bold">atthi kāyoti vā panassā</hi>" is just like what was stated.

"<hi rend="bold">iti ajjhattaṃ vā</hi> <hi rend="bold">bahiddhā vā</hi> <hi rend="bold">ajjhattabahiddhā vā</hi> <hi rend="bold">samudayadhammānupassī vā</hi> <hi rend="bold">atthi kāyoti vā panassā</hi>

Here also, the mindfulness which examines the four modes of deportment is the *duḥkhasatya* (duḥkhasaccaṃ), the truth of suffering; the pre-craving which brings about that mindfulness is the *samudayasatya* (samudayasaccaṃ), the truth of origination; the non-occurrence of both is the *nirodhasatya* (nirodhasaccaṃ), the truth of cessation; the *āryamārga* (ariyamaggo), the Noble Path, which understands suffering, abandons origination, and takes cessation as its object, is the *mārgasatya* (maggasaccaṃ), the truth of the path.

Thus, the *bhikṣu* (bhikkhuno) having endeavored by way of the Four Truths (*catusaccavasena*), reaches *nirvāṇa* (nibbutiṃ). This is indeed the means of deliverance (*niyyānamukhanti*) up to *arhatship* (*arahattā*) of one who lays hold of the four modes of deportment (*catuiriyāpathapariggāhakassa*).

The section on deportment is finished.

Explanation of the section on the fourfold clear comprehension (*catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
376. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hoti, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī hoti, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī hoti, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hoti, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī hoti, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Sampajānapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Kāyānupassanā paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ
mula_english:
“Again, *bhikkhus*, a *bhikkhu* acts with full awareness (*sampajānakārī*) when going forward and returning; acts with full awareness when looking ahead and looking away; acts with full awareness when flexing and extending his limbs; acts with full awareness when wearing his robes and carrying his outer robe and bowl (*saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe*); acts with full awareness when eating (*asite*), drinking (*pīte*), consuming food (*khāyite*), and tasting (*sāyite*); acts with full awareness when defecating (*uccāra*) or urinating (*passāvakamme*); acts with full awareness when walking (*gate*), standing (*ṭhite*), sitting (*nisinne*), sleeping (*sutte*), waking up (*jāgarite*), talking (*bhāsite*), and remaining silent (*tuṇhībhāve*).

In this way, internally… and so forth… Thus, *bhikkhus*, a *bhikkhu* abides contemplating the body as body.

The section on full awareness is finished.

The section on contemplating the body through repulsiveness.
commentary_pali:
376. Evaṃ iriyāpathavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni catusampajaññavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha . Tattha abhikkantetiādīni sāmaññaphale vaṇṇitāni. Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ catusampajaññapariggaṇhanena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Idhāpi samudayavayadhammānupassītiādīsu rūpakkhandhasseva samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Sesaṃ vuttasadisameva.

Idha catusampajaññapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, vuttappakāro ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa catusampajaññapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno vasena yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Catusampajaññapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
376.
Thus, having analyzed body contemplation by way of the modes of deportment, now, in order to analyze it by way of the four kinds of clear comprehension ( *catu sampajañña*), [the text] begins with, "And further."
There, "In going forwards" and so forth have been described in the section on the fruit of ordinary life.
"Thus internally": Thus, by way of laying hold of the fourfold comprehension, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body or in another's body, or at one time in one's own body and at another time in another's body.
Here also, in "contemplating the arising and passing away of phenomena" and so forth, the arising and passing away of the aggregate of form should be brought out.
The remainder is just like what has been stated.

Here, the mindfulness which lays hold of the fourfold clear comprehension is the truth of suffering ( *duḥkha-satya*); the prior craving which originates that mindfulness is the truth of origination ( *samudaya-satya*); the non-occurrence of either is the truth of cessation ( *nirodha-satya*); the Noble Path already stated is the truth of the path ( *mārga-satya*).
Thus, having striven by way of the Four Truths ( *catusatya*), one reaches peace. This is indeed the means of deliverance up to *arhat*-ship of one who lays hold of the fourfold clear comprehension.

The chapter on the fourfold clear comprehension is finished.

Explanation of the chapter on attention to repulsiveness.

mula_pali:
377. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā nakhā dantā taco, maṃsaṃ nhāru aṭṭhi aṭṭhimiñjaṃ vakkaṃ, hadayaṃ yakanaṃ kilomakaṃ pihakaṃ papphāsaṃ, antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariyaṃ karīsaṃ karīsaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ (ka.), pittaṃ semhaṃ pubbo lohitaṃ sedo medo, assu vasā kheḷo siṅghāṇikā lasikā mutta’nti.

‘‘Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ubhatomukhā putoḷi mūtoḷī (syā.), mutoli (pī.) pūrā nānāvihitassa dhaññassa, seyyathidaṃ sālīnaṃ vīhīnaṃ muggānaṃ māsānaṃ tilānaṃ taṇḍulānaṃ. Tamenaṃ cakkhumā puriso muñcitvā paccavekkheyya – ‘ime sālī, ime vīhī ime muggā ime māsā ime tilā ime taṇḍulā’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā…pe… mutta’nti.

mūtoḷī (syā.), mutoli (pī.)

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Kāyānupassanā dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ
mula_english:
Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurity thus: ‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, contents of the stomach, feces ( *karīsaṃ* means filth), bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine.’

Just as though there were a bag with an opening at both ends full of many sorts of grain, such as hill rice (*sālīnaṃ*), red rice (*vīhīnaṃ*), mung beans (*muggānaṃ*), kidney beans (*māsānaṃ*), sesame seeds (*tilānaṃ*), and husked rice (*taṇḍulānaṃ*), and a man with good eyesight were to open it and review it thus: ‘This is hill rice, this is red rice, these are mung beans, these are kidney beans, these are sesame seeds, this is husked rice’; so too, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair, bounded by skin, as full of many kinds of impurity thus: ‘In this body there are head-hairs…and urine.’

In this way he remains focused internally…and that is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating body as body.

The section on reflection on repulsiveness is finished.

The section on contemplation of the body: reflection on the elements.
commentary_pali:
377. Evaṃ catusampajaññavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni paṭikūlamanasikāravasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha imameva kāyantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ sabbākārena vitthārato visuddhimagge kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhāne vuttaṃ. Ubhatomukhāti heṭṭhā ca upari cāti dvīhi mukhehi yuttā. Nānāvihitassāti nānāvidhassa.

Idaṃ panettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ – ubhatomukhā putoḷi viya hi cātumahābhūtiko kāyo, tattha missetvā pakkhittanānāvidhadhaññaṃ viya kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā, cakkhumā puriso viya yogāvacaro, tassa taṃ putoḷiṃ muñcitvā paccavekkhato nānāvidhadhaññassa pākaṭakālo viya yogino dvattiṃsākārassa vibhūtakālo veditabbo. Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ kesādipariggaṇhanena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha dvattiṃsākārapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
377. Thus, having analyzed body contemplation (kāyānupassanā) by way of the four clear comprehensions (catu-sampajañña), now, in order to analyze it by way of contemplating repulsiveness (*paṭikūla-manasikāra*), he begins with "And further" (*puna capara*).

There, whatever should be stated in the beginning with "Indeed, this body" (*imameva kāya*), all that has been stated in every way, in detail, in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the section on mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati-kammaṭṭhāna).

"*Ubhatomukhā* means being joined by two openings, both below and above.

"*Nānāvihitassā*" means of various kinds (*nānāvidhassa*).

Here, moreover, is the application of the simile: Like a bag with two openings (*ubhatomukhā putoḷi*) is the body (kāyo) made of the four great elements (cātumahābhūtiko). There, like various grains (*nānāvidhadhaññaṃ*) thrown in after mixing, are the thirty-two parts (dvattiṃsākārā) beginning with the hair (*kesādayo*). Like a man with sight (*cakkhumā puriso*) is the yogi (yogāvacaro). Like the time when the various grains (*nānāvidhadhaññassa*) become visible to one reflecting after releasing that bag (*putoḷiṃ muñcitvā paccavekkhato*), is the time when the yogi should understand the clear manifestation (*vibhūtakālo veditabbo*) of the thirty-two parts (dvattiṃsākārassa).

"*Iti ajjhattaṃ vā* means thus, by laying hold of things beginning with hair etc. (*kesādi-pariggaṇhanena*), one dwells contemplating the body in the body (kāyānupassī viharati), either in one's own body (*attano vā kāye*), or in another's body (*parassa vā kāye*), or at one time in one's own (*kālena vā attano*), at another time in another's (*kālena vā parassa kāye*).

From here on, the exposition is just according to the method already stated (*vuttanayama eva*).

"The mindfulness (sati) which lays hold of the thirty-two parts (dvattiṃsākāra-pariggāhikā) is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasaccaṃ)." Thus, having made the connection (evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā), the portal to deliverance (*niyyānamukhaṃ*) should be understood (*veditabbaṃ*).

The rest is just the same as before (sesaṃ purimasadisameva).

*Iti ajjhattaṃ vā*

The section on contemplating repulsiveness (*paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ*) is finished (*niṭṭhitaṃ*).

Explanation of the section on contemplating the elements (*dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
378. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātū’ti.

‘‘Seyyathāpi , bhikkhave, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā gāviṃ vadhitvā catumahāpathe bilaso vibhajitvā nisinno assa, evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātū’ti.

‘‘Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Kāyānupassanā navasivathikapabbaṃ
mula_english:
Again, monks, a monk reviews this same body, however it is placed, however disposed, as consisting of elements thus: ‘In this body there are the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), the water element (*āpodhātu*), the fire element (*tejodhātu*), and the air element (*vāyodhātu*).’

Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice, having killed a cow, would sit at a crossroads cutting it up into pieces, so too, monks, a monk reviews this same body however it is placed, however disposed, as consisting of elements thus: ‘In this body there are the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*), the water element (*āpodhātu*), the fire element (*tejodhātu*), and the air element (*vāyodhātu*).’

Thus, he abides contemplating the body as body internally… And so, monks, a monk abides contemplating body as body.

The section on reflection on the elements is finished.

Section on contemplation of the body: the nine charnel grounds.
commentary_pali:
378. Evaṃ paṭikūlamanasikāravasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni dhātumanasikāravasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tatthāyaṃ opammasaṃsandanena saddhiṃ atthavaṇṇanā – yathā koci goghātako vā tasseva vā bhattavetanabhato antevāsiko gāviṃ vadhitvā vinivijjhitvā catasso disā gatānaṃ mahāpathānaṃ vemajjhaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte catumahāpathe koṭṭhāsaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā nisinno assa, evameva bhikkhu catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena ṭhitattā yathāṭhitaṃ, yathāṭhitattā ca yathāpaṇihitaṃ kāyaṃ ‘‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu…pe… vāyodhātū’’ti evaṃ paccavekkhati.

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā goghātakassa gāviṃ posentassāpi āghātanaṃ āharantassāpi āharitvā tattha bandhitvā ṭhapentassapi vadhentassāpi vadhitaṃ mataṃ passantassāpi tāvadeva gāvīti saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva naṃ padāletvā bilaso na vibhajati. Vibhajitvā nisinnassa panassa gāvīti saññā antaradhāyati, maṃsasaññā pavattati. Nāssa evaṃ hoti – ‘‘ahaṃ gāviṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime gāviṃ harantī’’ti. Atha khvassa ‘‘ahaṃ maṃsaṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime maṃsaṃ haranti’’ cceva hoti; evameva imassāpi bhikkhuno pubbe bālaputhujjanakāle gihibhūtassāpi pabbajitassāpi tāvadeva sattoti vā puggaloti vā saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā dhātuso na paccavekkhati. Dhātuso paccavekkhato panassa sattasaññā antaradhāyati, dhātuvaseneva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati. Tenāha bhagavā – ‘‘‘imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātū’ti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho goghātako vā…pe… vāyodhātū’’ti. Goghātako viya hi yogī, gāvīti saññā viya sattasaññā, catumahāpatho viya catuiriyāpatho, bilaso vibhajitvā nisinnabhāvo viya dhātuso paccavekkhaṇanti ayamettha pāḷivaṇṇanā. Kammaṭṭhānakathā pana visuddhimagge vitthāritā.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ catudhātupariggaṇhanena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha catudhātupariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ, sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
378. Thus, having divided the contemplation of the body as unattractive by way of unpleasantness, now, in order to divide by way of contemplation on the elements, he says, "Again, further" and so on.

In this connection, the meaning is elaborated together with the application of a simile: Just as if some cow-butcher, or an apprentice of that very butcher who works for his keep, having killed a cow, and having thoroughly cut it up, were sitting having made portions, portion by portion, at a four-way crossroads, known as the intersection of the main roads going in the four directions; just so, a *bhikṣu* reviews the body, however it stands because of some posture among the four postures, just as it is, and just as it is disposed, thinking thus: "There are, in this body, the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*)... and so on... the air element (*vāyodhātu*)."

What is said is this: just as the perception "cow" does not disappear from a cow-butcher while he is feeding the cow, while he is bringing it to the slaughtering place, while he is tying it there, while he is killing it, while he is seeing the killed, dead cow, just so, until he cuts it open and divides it into portions.

But for him sitting having divided it up, the perception "cow" disappears, and the perception "meat" comes into being.

He does not think, "I am selling the cow, these people are carrying away the cow."

But rather, it occurs to him, "I am selling meat; these people are carrying away meat." Just so, for this *bhikṣu* also, formerly in his time as a foolish ordinary person, even as a householder, even as one gone forth [into homelessness], just so long the perception of a being (*sattva*) or a person (*pudgala*) does not disappear, until, having made this very body, just as it stands, just as it is disposed, into a non-compact aggregate, he reviews it by way of the elements (*dhātu*).

But for him who reviews by way of the elements (*dhātu*), the perception of a being (*sattva-saṃjñā*) disappears, and the mind gets established by way of the elements (*dhātu*).

Therefore, the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) said: “'He reviews this very body, just as it stands, just as it is disposed, by way of the elements (*dhātu*), [thinking,] “There are in this body the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), the water element (*āpodhātu*), the fire element (*tejodhātu*), and the air element (*vāyodhātu*)’”.

Just as, *bhikṣus*, a skilled cow-butcher... and so on... the air element (*vāyodhātu*)’."

Indeed, the *yogī* is like a cow-butcher, the perception "cow" is like the perception "being" (*sattva-saṃjñā*), the four-way crossroads is like the four postures, the state of sitting having divided it into portions is like reviewing by way of the elements (*dhātu*). This is the explanation of the passage here.

The talk about the meditation subject (*karmaṭṭhāna-kathā*), however, is extensively explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Thus, internally. Thus, by means of the fourfold laying hold of the elements (*dhātu*), the *kāyānupassī* abides contemplating the body either in his own body (*kāya*) or in another’s body (*kāya*), or at one time in his own, and at another time in another’s body.

From here on, the exposition is just according to the method already stated.

Indeed, here, mindfulness (*smṛti*) which lays hold of the four elements (*dhātu*) is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). Thus, having made the connection, the portal to deliverance (*niryyāṇamukha*) should be known. The rest is just similar to what has already been said.

Thus, internally.

The section on contemplation on the elements (*dhātumanasikārapabba*) is finished.

Explanation of the section on the nine charnel grounds (*navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
379. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ ekāhamataṃ vā dvīhamataṃ vā tīhamataṃ vā uddhumātakaṃ vinīlakaṃ vipubbakajātaṃ. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti.

‘‘Iti ajjhattaṃ vā …pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ kākehi vā khajjamānaṃ kulalehi vā khajjamānaṃ gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ kaṅkehi vā khajjamānaṃ sunakhehi vā khajjamānaṃ byagghehi vā khajjamānaṃ dīpīhi vā khajjamānaṃ siṅgālehi vā gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, suvānehi vā khajjamānaṃ, sigālehi vā khajjamānaṃ, (syā. pī.) khajjamānaṃ vividhehi vā pāṇakajātehi khajjamānaṃ. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti.

gijjhehi vā khajjamānaṃ, suvānehi vā khajjamānaṃ, sigālehi vā khajjamānaṃ, (syā. pī.)

‘‘Iti ajjhattaṃ vā…pe… evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ…pe… aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ…pe… aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhaṃ…pe… aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhāni apagatanhārusambandhāni (syā.) disā vidisā vikkhittāni, aññena hatthaṭṭhikaṃ aññena pādaṭṭhikaṃ aññena gopphakaṭṭhikaṃ ‘‘aññena gopphakaṭṭhika’’nti idaṃ sī. syā. pī. potthakesu natthi aññena jaṅghaṭṭhikaṃ aññena ūruṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṭiṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṭaṭṭhikaṃ aññena piṭṭhaṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṇḍakaṭṭhikaṃ aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena uraṭṭhikaṃ aññena aṃsaṭṭhikaṃ aññena bāhuṭṭhikaṃ (syā.) aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena piṭṭhiṭṭhikaṃ aññena khandhaṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṭaṭṭhikaṃ aññena piṭṭhaṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṇḍakaṭṭhikaṃ aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena uraṭṭhikaṃ aññena aṃsaṭṭhikaṃ aññena bāhuṭṭhikaṃ (syā.) aññena gīvaṭṭhikaṃ aññena hanukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena dantaṭṭhikaṃ aññena sīsakaṭāhaṃ. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti.

apagatanhārusambandhāni (syā.) ‘‘aññena gopphakaṭṭhika’’nti idaṃ sī. syā. pī. potthakesu natthi aññena kaṭaṭṭhikaṃ aññena piṭṭhaṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṇḍakaṭṭhikaṃ aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena uraṭṭhikaṃ aññena aṃsaṭṭhikaṃ aññena bāhuṭṭhikaṃ (syā.) aññena kaṭaṭṭhikaṃ aññena piṭṭhaṭṭhikaṃ aññena kaṇḍakaṭṭhikaṃ aññena phāsukaṭṭhikaṃ aññena uraṭṭhikaṃ aññena aṃsaṭṭhikaṃ aññena bāhuṭṭhikaṃ (syā.)

‘‘Iti ajjhattaṃ vā …pe… viharati.

‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgāni…pe… aṭṭhikāni puñjakitāni terovassikāni …pe… aṭṭhikāni pūtīni cuṇṇakajātāni. So imameva kāyaṃ upasaṃharati – ‘ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto’ti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharati. ‘Atthi kāyo’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Navasivathikapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Cuddasa kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

Vedanānupassanā
mula_english:
379. “Again, monks, as if a monk were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground—one day dead, two days dead, three days dead—bloated, livid, and festering. He compares this body with that, thinking: ‘This body is of the same nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that fate.’

“Thus, either internally… and so forth… That too, monks, is how a monk abides contemplating the body as a body.

“Again, monks, as if a monk were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, being devoured by hawks, being devoured by vultures, being devoured by dogs, being devoured by hyenas, being devoured by jackals, or being devoured by various kinds of creatures. He compares this body with that, thinking: ‘This body is of the same nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that fate.’

“Thus, either internally… and so forth… That too, monks, is how a monk abides contemplating the body as a body.

“Again, monks, as if a monk were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, connected by tendons… and so forth… a skeleton smeared with blood, devoid of flesh, connected by tendons… and so forth… a skeleton without flesh or blood, connected by tendons… and so forth… bones disconnected, scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle-bone, here a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, here a hip-bone, here a rib, here a back-bone, here a shoulder-bone, here a neck-bone, here a jaw-bone, here a tooth, here a skull. He compares this body with that, thinking: ‘This body is of the same nature, it will become like that, it is not exempt from that fate.’

“Thus, either internally… and so forth… he abides.

“Again, monks, as if a monk were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, bones bleached white, the color of shells… and so forth… bones heaped up, more than a year old… and so forth… bones rotten and crumbled to dust.
He compares this very body with that, thinking: “This body too is of such a nature (evaṃdhammo), it will become like that (evaṃbhāvī), it is not exempt from that fate (evaṃanatīto)."

In this way, he abides contemplating the body as a body internally, or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally, or he abides contemplating the body as a body both internally and externally.

Or he abides contemplating the arising nature (samudayadhammānupassī) in the body, or he abides contemplating the dissolving nature (vayadhammānupassī) in the body, or he abides contemplating the arising and dissolving nature (samudayavayadhammānupassī) in the body.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is a body (atthi kāyo)’ is present to him just to the extent necessary for knowledge (ñāṇamattāya) and remembrance (paṭissatimattāya). And he abides independent (anissito), not clinging to anything in the world (na ca kiñci loke upādiyati).

That is how, monks (bhikkhave), a monk (bhikkhu) abides contemplating the body as a body (kāye kāyānupassī viharati).

The chapter on the nine charnel grounds is finished.

The fourteen contemplations of the body are finished.

Contemplation of feeling.
commentary_pali:
379. Evaṃ dhātumanasikāravasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni navahi sivathikapabbehi vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha seyyathāpi passeyyāti yathā passeyya. Sarīranti matasarīraṃ. Sivathikāya chaḍḍitanti susāne apaviddhaṃ. Ekāhaṃ matassa assāti ekāhamataṃ. Dvīhaṃ matassa assāti dvīhamataṃ. Tīhaṃ matassa assāti tīhamataṃ. Kammārabhastā viya vāyunā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathānukkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena uddhumātattā uddhumātaṃ, uddhumātameva uddhumātakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ uddhumātanti uddhumātakaṃ. Vinīlaṃ vuccati viparibhinnavaṇṇaṃ, vinīlameva vinīlakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ. Maṃsussadaṭṭhānesu rattavaṇṇassa pubbasannicayaṭṭhānesu setavaṇṇassa yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇassa nīlaṭṭhānesu nīlasāṭakapārutasseva chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paribhinnaṭṭhānehi navahi vā vaṇamukhehi vissandamānapubbaṃ vipubbaṃ, vipubbameva vipubbakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vipubbanti vipubbakaṃ. Vipubbakaṃ jātaṃ tathābhāvaṃ gatanti vipubbakajātaṃ.

So imameva kāyanti so bhikkhu imaṃ attano kāyaṃ tena kāyena saddhiṃ ñāṇena upasaṃharati upaneti. Kathaṃ? Ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatītoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – āyu, usmā, viññāṇanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ atthitāya ayaṃ kāyo ṭhānagamanādikhamo hoti, imesaṃ pana vigamā ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃ pūtikasabhāvoyeva, evaṃbhāvī evaṃ uddhumātādibhedo bhavissati, evaṃanatīto evaṃ uddhumātādibhāvaṃ anatikkantoti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ uddhumātādipariggaṇhanena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

So imameva kāya Ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Khajjamānanti udarādīsu nisīditvā udaramaṃsaoṭṭhamaṃsaakkhikūṭādīni luñcitvā luñcitvā khādiyamānaṃ. Samaṃsalohitanti sāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttaṃ. Nimaṃsalohitamakkhitanti maṃse khīṇepi lohitaṃ na sussati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ ‘‘nimaṃsalohitamakkhita’’nti. Aññenāti aññena disābhāgena. Hatthaṭṭhikanti catusaṭṭhibhedampi hatthaṭṭhikaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vippakiṇṇaṃ. Pādaṭṭhikādīsupi eseva nayo.

Khajjamāna Samaṃsalohita Nimaṃsalohitamakkhita Aññenā Hatthaṭṭhika Pādaṭṭhikā

Terovassikānīti atikkantasaṃvaccharāni. Pūtīnīti abbhokāse ṭhitāni vātātapavuṭṭhisamphassena terovassikāneva pūtīni honti, antobhūmigatāni pana cirataraṃ tiṭṭhanti. Cuṇṇakajātānīti cuṇṇaṃ cuṇṇaṃ hutvā vippakiṇṇāni. Sabbattha so imamevāti vuttanayena khajjamānādīnaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbā. Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ khajjamānādipariggaṇhanena yāva cuṇṇakabhāvā attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Terovassikānī Pūtīnī Cuṇṇakajātānī Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Idha pana ṭhatvā navasivathikā samodhānetabbā. Ekāhamataṃ vāti hi ādinā nayena vuttā sabbāpi ekā, kākehi vā khajjamānantiādikā ekā, aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhanti ekā, nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ nhārusambandhanti ekā, apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandhanti ekā, aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhānītiādikā ekā aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgānīti ekā, puñjakitāni terovassikānīti ekā, pūtīni cuṇṇakajātānīti ekāti.

Evaṃ kho, bhikkhaveti idaṃ navasivathikā dassetvā kāyānupassanaṃ niṭṭhapento āha. Tattha navasivathikapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idaṃ navasivathikapariggāhakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave

Navasivathikapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Ettāvatā ca ānāpānapabbaṃ, iriyāpathapabbaṃ, catusampajaññapabbaṃ, paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ, dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ, navasivathikapabbānīti cuddasapabbā kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā hoti. Tattha ānāpānapabbaṃ, paṭikūlamanasikārapabbanti imāneva dve appanākammaṭṭhānāni, sivathikānaṃ pana ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā sesāni dvādasāpi upacārakammaṭṭhānānevāti.

Kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

Vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
379. Thus, having distinguished the contemplation of the body by way of the element (*dhātu*) and attention (*manasikāra*), now, to distinguish [it] by the nine charnel ground contemplations (*sivathika*), he says, "Again, furthermore" (*puna capara*), and so on.

There, "Just as he might see" (*seyyathāpi passeyyā*) means just as he might see.

"Body" (*śarīra*) means a dead body (*matasarīraṃ*).

"Thrown in the charnel ground" (*śivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ*) means thrown away in the cemetery (*susāne apaviddhaṃ*).

"One day dead" (*ekāhaṃ matassa assāti*) means one day dead (*ekāhamataṃ*).

"Two days dead" (*dvīhaṃ matassa assāti*) means two days dead (*dvīhamataṃ*).

"Three days dead" (*tīhaṃ matassa assāti*) means three days dead (*tīhamataṃ*).

Like a blacksmith's bellows, inflated by the wind, from which life has departed, having the nature of swelling arisen gradually and in due order, is the bloated [corpse]. The bloated itself is "the bloated corpse" (*uddhumātakaṃ*).

Alternatively, what is bloated is vile because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the bloated” (*uddhumātakaṃ*).

"The livid" (*vinīlaṃ*) is said to be of altered color, the livid itself is "the livid corpse" (*vinīlakaṃ*).

Or alternatively, what is livid is vile because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the livid” (*vinīlakaṃ*).

This is a term for a corpse that is reddish-coloured in places where flesh is prominent, whitish-coloured in places where pus has collected, but mostly blue-black, as if draped with blue-black cloth in the blue-black places.

What is festering with pus oozing out from nine or various wound openings is the festering, the festering itself is "the festering corpse" (*vipubbakaṃ*).

Or alternatively, what is festering is vile because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the festering” (*vipubbakaṃ*).

What has become a festering corpse, having gone to that state, is "become a festering corpse" (*vipubbakajātaṃ*).

"He applies this to this very body" (*so imameva kāyaṃ*) means that monk applies, brings near, with wisdom, this his own body, to that body.

How? "[Thinking,] this body too is of such a nature, of such a character, not deviating from this [law of nature]" (*ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto*).

This is what is said: Because of the existence of these three things – life (*āyu*), heat (*usmā*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*) – this body is capable of standing and moving, and so on. But, from the disappearance of these, this body, too, is of such a nature, of just a stinking nature, "having such a condition" (*evaṃbhāvī*) i.e., will be of just such a condition, of the nature of being bloated, and so on, "not deviating from this" (*evaṃanatīto*), i.e., not transcending the condition of being bloated, and so on.

"Thus internally" (*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*) means thus, by laying hold of the state of swelling and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in the body in regard to one's own body or another's, or at one time in regard to one's own and at another time in regard to another's.

He applies this to this very body. [Thinking,] this body too is of such a nature, of such a character, not deviating from this [law of nature].

Having such a condition, not deviating from this. Thus internally. "Being eaten" (*khajjamānaṃ*) means being eaten, being torn off and torn off again, by sitting on the stomach and so on, the flesh of the stomach, the flesh of the lips, the sockets of the eyes, and so on.

"With flesh and blood" (*samaṃsalohitaṃ*) means connected with remaining flesh and blood.

"Without flesh, smeared with blood" (*nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ*) means even though the flesh is gone, the blood does not dry up; with reference to that it was said, "without flesh, smeared with blood" (*nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ*).

"By another" (*aññena*) means by another directional part.

"Bone of the hand" (*hatthaṭṭhikaṃ*) means the sixty-four kinds of bones of the hand, each one separate, scattered apart.

The same method applies also to "bones of the foot" (*pādaṭṭhikā*), and so on.

Being eaten, with flesh and blood, without flesh, smeared with blood, by another, bone of the hand, bones of the foot. "Of three years" (*terovassikānī*) means having passed through the years.

"Rotten" (*pūtīnī*) means placed in the open air, by contact with wind, heat and rain, the bones themselves become rotten, but those gone into the interior of the earth remain for a long time.

"Turned to powder" (*cuṇṇakajātānī*) means having become powder, powder, they are scattered apart.

Everywhere, by the method stated, the connection should be made on the basis of being eaten, and so on, with "He applies this to this very body" (*so imameva*).

"Thus internally" (*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*) means thus, by laying hold of the state of being eaten and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in the body from the state when it is being eaten by crows and other creatures to the state when it is dust, in one's own body or in another's, or at one time in one's own body and at another time in another's body.

Having passed through the years, rotten. Turned to powder, thus internally.

Here, having stopped, one should put together the nine charnel ground contemplations.

One day dead is just one in the method beginning with "or" (*vā*), all those stated by way of principle; being eaten by crows, and so on, is one; a skeleton, with flesh and blood, connected with sinews, is one; without flesh, smeared with blood, connected with sinews, is one; with flesh and blood gone, connected with sinews, is one; the bones with the connections gone, and so on, is one; the bones white, having the appearance of shell color, is one; heaped up, of three years, is one; rotten, turned to powder, is one.
Thus indeed, monks,” he said, concluding the contemplation of the body by showing the nine cemetery contemplations.

There, the mindfulness which lays hold of the nine cemetery contemplations is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); the previous craving which originates that mindfulness is the Truth of Origin (*samudayasatya*); the non-occurrence of both that mindfulness and the craving is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). The Noble Eightfold Path (*āryamārga*) that understands suffering, casts out the origin, and has cessation for its object is the Truth of the Way (*mārgasatya*).

Endeavoring in this way by means of the Four Truths (*catusatya*) one arrives at peace (*nirvāṇa*). This is for the *bhikkhu* who lays hold of the nine cemetery contemplations the portal of deliverance up to *arhatship*.

Thus indeed, monks."

The section on the nine cemetery contemplations is finished.

Now, these are the fourteen sections which comprise body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā*): The section on breathing in and breathing out (*ānāpānapabba*), on the postures (*iriyāpathapabba*), on the four kinds of clear comprehension (*catusampajaññapabba*), of reflection on repulsiveness (*paṭikūlamanasikārapabba*), on the modes of materiality (*dhātumanasikārapabba*), and on the nine cemetery contemplations (*navasivathikapabba*).

There, the section on breathing in and breathing out, and the section on reflection on repulsiveness - these two alone are attainment meditation (*appanākammaṭṭhāna*), but the remaining twelve are only access meditation (*upacārakammaṭṭhāna*) since the cemeteries are spoken of by way of contemplation of disadvantages (*ādīnavānupassanā*).

Body-contemplation is finished.

Explanation of contemplation of feeling (*vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
380. ‘‘Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhaṃ vā vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti . Dukkhaṃ vā vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Adukkhamasukhaṃ vā vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Sāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, nirāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Sāmisaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sāmisaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, nirāmisaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘nirāmisaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Sāmisaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘sāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, nirāmisaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati.
