Samudayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati. ‘Atthi vedanā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati.

Vedanānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

Cittānupassanā
mula_english:
“And how, monks, does a monk abide contemplating feelings as feelings? Here, monks, when a monk feels a pleasant feeling (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel a pleasant feeling (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī)’; when feeling a painful feeling (dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel a painful feeling (dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī)’; when feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī).’ When feeling a worldly pleasant feeling (sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel a worldly pleasant feeling (sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī)’; when feeling an unworldly pleasant feeling (nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel an unworldly pleasant feeling (nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī).’ When feeling a worldly painful feeling (sāmisaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel a worldly painful feeling (sāmisaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī)’; when feeling an unworldly painful feeling (nirāmisaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel an unworldly painful feeling (nirāmisaṃ dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī).’ When feeling a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (sāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (sāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī)’; when feeling an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ), he understands: ‘I feel an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī).’

In this way, he abides contemplating feelings as feelings internally (ajjhattaṃ vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati), or he abides contemplating feelings as feelings externally (bahiddhā vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati), or he abides contemplating feelings as feelings both internally and externally (ajjhattabahiddhā vā vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati). Or else he abides contemplating in feelings their arising factors (samudayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati), or he abides contemplating in feelings their vanishing factors (vayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati), or he abides contemplating in feelings both their arising and vanishing factors (samudayavayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati).

Or else mindfulness that ‘there is feeling (atthi vedanā)’ is simply established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge (ñāṇamattāya) and mindfulness (paṭissatimattāya). And he abides independent (anissito), not clinging (anupādiyati) to anything in the world (loke).

That is how a monk abides contemplating feelings as feelings (vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati)."

End of contemplation of feelings.

Contemplation of the Mind
commentary_pali:
380. Evaṃ bhagavā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha sukhaṃ vedananti kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘‘ahaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’’ti pajānātīti attho. Tattha kāmaṃ uttānaseyyakāpi dārakā thaññapivanādikāle sukhaṃ vedayamānā ‘‘sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmā’’ti pajānanti, na panetaṃ evarūpaṃ jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evarūpañhi jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ na jahati, attasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hoti. Imassa pana bhikkhuno jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ jahati, attasaññaṃ ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānañceva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca hoti. Idañhi ‘‘ko vedayati, kassa vedanā, kiṃ kāraṇā vedanā’’ti evaṃ sampajānavediyanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Tattha ko vedayatīti na koci satto vā puggalo vā vedayati. Kassa vedanāti na kassaci sattassa vā puggalassa vā vedanā. Kiṃ kāraṇā vedanāti vatthuārammaṇāva panassa vedanā, tasmā esa evaṃ pajānāti ‘‘taṃ taṃ sukhādīnaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayati taṃ pana vedanāya pavattiṃ upādāya’ahaṃ vedayāmī’ti vohāramattaṃ hotī’’ti. Evaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatīti sallakkhento esa ‘‘sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānātī’’ti veditabbo cittalapabbate aññataratthero viya.

Thero kira aphāsukakāle balavavedanāya nitthunanto aparāparaṃ parivattati, tameko daharo āha – ‘‘kataraṃ vo, bhante, ṭhānaṃ rujjatī’’ti. Āvuso, pāṭiyekkaṃ rujjanaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatīti. Evaṃ jānanakālato paṭṭhāya adhivāsetuṃ vaṭṭati no, bhante,ti. Adhivāsemi, āvusoti. Adhivāsanā, bhante, seyyoti. Thero adhivāsesi. Vāto yāva hadayā phālesi, mañcake antāni rāsikatāni ahesuṃ. Thero daharassa dassesi ‘‘vaṭṭatāvuso, ettakā adhivāsanā’’ti. Daharo tuṇhī ahosi. Thero vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyi.

samasīsī

Yathā ca sukhaṃ, evaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘‘nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’’ti pajānāti. Iti bhagavā rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento yasmā phassavasena cittavasena vā kathiyamānaṃ pākaṭaṃ na hoti , andhakāraṃ viya khāyati, vedanānaṃ pana uppattipākaṭatāya vedanāvasena pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmā sakkapañhe viya idhāpi vedanāvasena arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Tattha ‘‘duvidhañhi kammaṭṭhānaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ arūpakammaṭṭhānañcā’’tiādi kathāmaggo sakkapañhe vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

sakkapañhe

Tattha sukhaṃ vedanantiādīsu ayaṃ aparopi pajānanapariyāyo, sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānātīti sukhavedanākkhaṇe dukkhavedanāya abhāvato sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘‘sukhaṃ vedanaṃyeva vedayāmī’’ti pajānāti. Tena yā pubbe bhūtapubbā dukkhavedanā, tassa idāni abhāvato imissā ca sukhāya vedanāya ito paṭhamaṃ abhāvato vedanā nāma aniccā adhuvā vipariṇāmadhammā, itiha tattha sampajāno hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

‘‘Yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, sukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samaye dukkhaṃ…pe… adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, adukkhamasukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Sukhāpi, kho, aggivessana, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Dukkhāpi, kho…pe… adukkhamasukhāpi kho, aggivessana, vedanā aniccā…pe… nirodhadhammā. Evaṃ passaṃ, aggivessana, sutavā ariyasāvako sukhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, dukkhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, adukkhamasukhāyapi vedanāya nibbindati, nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati, vimuttasmiṃ ‘vimuttamī’ti ñāṇaṃ hoti, ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī’’ti (ma. ni. 2.205).

Sāmisaṃ vā sukhantiādīsu sāmisā sukhā nāma pañcakāmaguṇāmisasannissitā cha gehasitasomanassavedanā. Nirāmisā sukhā nāma cha nekkhammasitasomanassavedanā. Sāmisā dukkhā nāma cha gehasitadomanassavedanā. Nirāmisā dukkhā nāma cha nekkhammasitadomanassavedanā. Sāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma cha gehasitaupekkhāvedanā. Nirāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma cha nekkhammasitaupekkhāvedanā. Tāsaṃ vibhāgo sakkapañhe vuttoyeva.

Sāmisaṃ vā sukha sāmisā sukhā Nirāmisā sukhā Sāmisā dukkhā Nirāmisā dukkhā Sāmisā adukkhamasukhā Nirāmisā adukkhamasukhā sakkapañhe

Itiajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ sukhavedanādipariggaṇhanena attano vā vedanāsu, parassa vā vedanāsu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati. Samudayavayadhammānupassī vāti ettha pana avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayotiādīhi pañcahi pañcahi ākārehi vedanānaṃ samudayañca vayañca passanto ‘‘samudayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati, kālena samudayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu, kālena vayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharatī’’ti veditabbo. Ito paraṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha vedanāpariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā vedanāpariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ, sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā Samudayavayadhammānupassī vā

Vedanānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

Cittānupassanāvaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
380. Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the fourteenfold Arousing of Mindfulness in regard to the body, now, in order to explain the ninefold contemplation of feeling, began with the words, "And how, O bhikkhus."

There, the meaning of "pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedana*) is: The bhikkhu, when experiencing a bodily or mental pleasant feeling, knows, "I experience a pleasant feeling" (*ahaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī*).

There, certainly, even infants lying on their backs know that they experience pleasure while they experience a pleasant feeling in sucking the breast and on similar occasions, [thinking] "We experience a pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmā*), but this knowledge is not meant here.

Because awareness of that sort does not shed the belief in a living being, does not knock out the percept of a self (*ātman*), and neither becomes a subject of meditation nor the development of the Arousing of Mindfulness.

But the knowledge of this *bhikkhu* sheds the belief in a living being, knocks out the idea of a self (*ātman*), and is both a subject of meditation and the development of the Arousing of Mindfulness.

Indeed, the knowledge meant here is concerned with experience that is wisely understood through inquiry: "Who feels? Whose is the feeling? What is the cause of feeling?"

There, "Who feels?" No being (*sattva*) or person (*pudgala*) feels.

"Whose is the feeling?" Not of any being (*sattva*) or person (*pudgala*).

"What is the cause of feeling?" Feeling is simply due to a property or basis. Therefore, this one understands thus: "Having made that property the object, feeling itself feels; but appropriating that tendency of feeling, [one says] 'I feel' (*ahaṃ vedayāmī*)," that is mere conventional usage.

Thus, recognizing that feeling itself feels, having made a property its object, this one knows "I experience a pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī*)," as the Elder of Cittala Mountain [did].

The Elder, during an uncomfortable time, was groaning with intense feeling and turning over and over. A certain young bhikkhu said to him, "What place of yours, venerable sir, is hurting?"

"Friend, there is no place that is specifically painful. Feeling itself feels, having made a property its object," [replied the Elder.]

"Venerable sir, from the time one knows that, is bearing up befitting?"

"I am bearing up, friend," said the Elder.

"Bearing up is excellent, venerable sir," said the young bhikkhu.

The Elder bore up.

The wind was piercing even to the heart, and the ends of the couch were like a heap [of bones].

The Elder pointed that out to the young bhikkhu and said: "Friend, is bearing up so far befitting?"

The young bhikkhu remained silent.

The Elder, having applied concentration with energy, attained *arhatship* with Analytical Knowledge and, his life span having come to an end (*samasiisi*), passed away into *parinirvana*.

His lifespan having come to an end (*samasiisi*). Just as with pleasant feeling, so too with painful feeling...and so on... Experiencing a non-attached neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, one understands, "I experience a non-attached neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling."

Thus, the Blessed One, having explained the subject of meditation regarding form (*rūpa*), and in explaining the subject of meditation apart from form (*arūpa*), because what is said in terms of contact (*sparśa*) or in terms of consciousness is not clear, but seems like darkness, [and] since, however, feeling is clear by way of its arising, it is clear by way of feeling; therefore, as in the Question of Śakra (*sakkapañha*), so also here, he explained the subject of meditation apart from form (*arūpa*) in terms of feeling.

There, "Indeed, meditation is twofold: meditation regarding form (*rūpa*) and meditation apart from form (*arūpa*)," and so forth. The course of the teaching should be understood just as it was said in the Question of Śakra (*sakkapañha*).

In the Question of Śakra (*sakkapañha*). There, in "Pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedana*), etc., this is another way of understanding: One knows "I experience a pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī*). Because of the absence of painful feeling at the moment of pleasant feeling, experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows "I experience only a pleasant feeling" (*sukhaṃ vedanaṃyeva vedayāmī*).

Therefore, owing to the absence now of whatsoever painful feeling that existed before, and owing to the absence of this pleasant feeling before this time, feeling is called an impermanent, unstable, and changeable thing. Thus there is clear comprehension.

This was also said by the Blessed One:

"Aggivessana, at the time when one experiences pleasant feeling, one does not experience painful feeling; one does not experience neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one experiences only pleasant feeling.

Aggivessana, at the time when one experiences painful feeling...and so on...[at the time when one experiences] neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not experience pleasant feeling; one does not experience painful feeling; at that time one experiences only neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Aggivessana, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.

Aggivessana, painful feeling...and so on...Aggivessana, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is impermanent...and so on...subject to cessation."
Thus seeing, Aggivessana, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, becomes disenchanted with painful feeling, becomes disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. As he is disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge that he is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further for this state of being.’

Among "pleasant worldly feeling (sāmisaṃ vā sukha)," pleasant worldly feelings (sāmisā sukhā) are the six kinds of joyful feelings connected with the senses, dependent on the five strands of sense pleasure.

"Unworldly pleasure (nirāmisā sukhā)" refers to the six kinds of joyful feeling connected with renunciation.

"Pleasant worldly feeling (sāmisā dukkhā)" refers to the six kinds of unpleasant worldly feeling.

"Unworldly painful feeling (nirāmisā dukkhā)" refers to the six kinds of unpleasant feeling connected with renunciation.

"Pleasant worldly feeling (sāmisā adukkhamasukhā)" refers to the six kinds of neutral worldly feeling.

"Unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (nirāmisā adukkhamasukhā)" refers to the six kinds of neutral feeling connected with renunciation.

Their classification has already been mentioned in the *Sakkapañha*.

"Internally (ajjhattaṃ vā)": Thus, by laying hold of pleasant feeling etc., the *bhikkhu* dwells contemplating feelings in his own feelings or in the feelings of others, or at one time in his own feelings and at another time in the feelings of others.

"Or contemplating origination-things (samudayavayadhammānupassī vā)": Here, seeing the origination and dissolution of feelings in five ways—"with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling (avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo)," etc.—the *bhikkhu* should be understood as "dwelling contemplating origination-things in feelings, dwelling contemplating dissolution-things in feelings, at one time dwelling contemplating origination-things, and at one time dwelling contemplating dissolution-things in feelings."

From here on, the exposition is just according to the method already followed in the explanation of body-contemplation.

Indeed, here, mindfulness that lays hold of feeling is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca). Thus, the portal of deliverance for the *bhikkhu* who lays hold of feeling should be understood, and the rest is similar.

The contemplation of feeling is finished.

Explanation of the contemplation of the mind.

mula_pali:
381. ‘‘Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu citte cittānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sadosaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, vītadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītadosaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Samohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samohaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītamohaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Saṅkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘saṅkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vikkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Mahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘mahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānāti, amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘amahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sauttaraṃ citta’nti pajānāti, anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘anuttaraṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānāti, asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘asamāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘avimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāti. Iti ajjhattaṃ vā citte cittānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā citte cittānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā citte cittānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati, ‘atthi citta’nti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati . Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu citte cittānupassī viharati.

Cittānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

Dhammānupassanā nīvaraṇapabbaṃ
mula_english:
381. How, monks, does a monk abide contemplating mind as mind? Here, monks, a monk understands a lustful mind as 'a lustful mind' (sarāgaṃ cittaṃ ‘sarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānāti), or a mind free from lust as 'a mind free from lust' (vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītarāgaṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

He understands a hateful mind as 'a hateful mind' (sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sadosaṃ citta’nti pajānāti), or a mind free from hate as 'a mind free from hate' (vītadosaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītadosaṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

He understands a deluded mind as 'a deluded mind' (samohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samohaṃ citta’nti pajānāti), or a mind free from delusion as 'a mind free from delusion' (vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vītamohaṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

He understands a constricted mind as 'a constricted mind' (saṅkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘saṅkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānāti), or a scattered mind as 'a scattered mind' (vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vikkhittaṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

He understands an exalted mind as 'an exalted mind' (mahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘mahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānāti), or an unexalted mind as 'an unexalted mind' (amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ ‘amahaggataṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

He understands a surpassed mind as 'a surpassed mind' (sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘sauttaraṃ citta’nti pajānāti), or an unsurpassed mind as 'an unsurpassed mind' (anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ ‘anuttaraṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

He understands a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind' (samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘samāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānāti), or an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind' (asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘asamāhitaṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

He understands a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind' (vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘vimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

He understands an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind' (avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ ‘avimuttaṃ citta’nti pajānāti).

Thus, he abides contemplating mind as mind internally, or he abides contemplating mind as mind externally, or he abides contemplating mind as mind both internally and externally.

Or he abides contemplating the arising nature in the mind (samudayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati), or he abides contemplating the vanishing nature in the mind (vayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati), or he abides contemplating both the arising and vanishing nature in the mind (samudayavayadhammānupassī vā cittasmiṃ viharati). Or mindfulness that ‘there is mind’ (atthi citta’nti vā) is simply established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.

That is how, monks, a monk abides contemplating mind as mind.

The contemplation of the mind is finished.

The section on the hindrances in the contemplation of phenomena.
commentary_pali:
381. Evaṃ navavidhena vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha sarāganti aṭṭhavidhalobhasahagataṃ. Vītarāganti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Idaṃ pana yasmā sammasanaṃ na dhammasamodhānaṃ tasmā idha ekapadepi lokuttaraṃ na labbhati. Sesāni cattāri akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Sadosanti duvidhadomanassasahagataṃ. Vītadosanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Sesāni dasa akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ, na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Samohanti vicikicchāsahagatañceva, uddhaccasahagatañcāti duvidhaṃ. Yasmā pana moho sabbākusalesu uppajjati, tasmā sesānipi idha vaṭṭantiyeva. Imasmiññeva hi duke dvādasākusalacittāni pariyādinnānīti. Vītamohanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Saṅkhittanti thinamiddhānupatitaṃ. Etañhi saṅkuṭitacittaṃ nāma. Vikkhittanti uddhaccasahagataṃ, etañhi pasaṭacittaṃ nāma.

Mahaggatanti rūpārūpāvacaraṃ. Amahaggatanti kāmāvacaraṃ. Sauttaranti kāmāvacaraṃ. Anuttaranti rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacarañca. Tatrāpi sauttaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ, anuttaraṃ arūpāvacarameva. Samāhitanti yassa appanāsamādhi upacārasamādhi vā atthi. Asamāhitanti ubhayasamādhivirahitaṃ . Vimuttanti tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttīhi vimuttaṃ. Avimuttanti ubhayavimuttivirahitaṃ. Samucchedapaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavimuttīnaṃ pana idha okāsova natthi.

Mahaggata Amahaggata Sauttara Anuttara Samāhita Asamāhita Vimutta Avimutta

Itiajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ sarāgādipariggaṇhanena yasmiṃ yasmiṃ khaṇe yaṃ yaṃ cittaṃ pavattati, taṃ taṃ sallakkhento attano vā citte, parassa vā citte, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa citte cittānupassī viharati. Samudayavayadhammānupassīti ettha pana avijjāsamudayā viññāṇasamudayoti evaṃ pañcahi pañcahi ākārehi viññāṇassa samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha cittapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ padayojanaṃ katvā cittapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā Samudayavayadhammānupassī

Cittānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

Dhammānupassanā nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
381. Thus, having explained the ninefold Arousing of Mindfulness in regard to feeling, now, to explain the contemplation of consciousness in the sixteenfold way, [the Master] began with the words, "And, how, O *bhikkhus*?"

There, *sarāga* means associated with the eightfold greed.

*vītarāga* means worldly wholesome and inexpressible.

But since this is a summary and not an integration of the Dhamma, therefore, even in a single word here, the supramundane is not obtained.

The remaining four karmically bad consciousnesses do not partake of either the former state or the latter state.

*sadosa* means accompanied by twofold dejection.

*vītadosa* means worldly wholesome and inexpressible.

The remaining ten karmically bad consciousnesses do not partake of either the former state or the latter state.

*samoha* means twofold, associated with doubt and also associated with agitation.

Because, indeed, ignorance arises in all karmically bad states, therefore the other karmically bad states too should be mentioned here.

In just this division all the twelve karmically bad, unwholesome or unskillful conscious states are included.

*vītamoha* means worldly wholesome and inexpressible.

*saṅkhitta* means fallen into sloth and torpor.

This is called the shrunken state of consciousness.

*vikkhitta* means associated with agitation; this is called the dissipated mind.

*mahaggata* means the realm of form and the formless realm.

*amahaggata* means the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

*sauttara* means the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

*anuttara* means the realm of form and the formless realm.

There also, *sauttara* is the *rūpadhātu* (form realm), *anuttara* is only the *arūpadhātu* (formless realm).

*samāhita* means he who has full absorption (*appanāsamādhi*) or proximate absorption (*upacārasamādhi*).

*asamāhita* means devoid of both absorptions.

*vimutta* means liberated by liberation through the parts and suppression.

*avimutta* means devoid of both liberations.

But here there is no opportunity for eradication, tranquility, or release.

*mahaggata*
*amahaggata*
*sauttara*
*anuttara*
*samāhita*
*asamāhita*
*vimutta*
*avimutta*

Thus, "internally," the bhikkhu lives contemplating consciousness in consciousness by laying hold on the consciousness with lust and so forth when these states of consciousness proceed in his own flux or in another’s flux or by laying hold of these conscious states at one time as they proceed in his own flux and at another time as they proceed in another’s flux.

"*samudayavayadhammānupassī*" means here, ignorance is the origin, consciousness is the origin; thus, in these five ways, the origin and decay of consciousness should be inferred.

From here on the exposition should be known just by the method already mentioned.

The mindfulness which lays hold of consciousness is the Truth of Suffering. Thus, the portal of deliverance up to arahantship of the *bhikkhu* who lays hold of consciousness as a subject of meditation ought to be understood.

The rest is as before.

Thus, "internally," "*samudayavayadhammānupassī*."

The contemplation of consciousness is finished.

Explanation of the section on the hindrances in the contemplation of the Dhamma.

mula_pali:
382. ‘‘Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu?

‘‘Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ kāmacchandaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ kāmacchandaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa kāmacchandassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa kāmacchandassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ byāpādaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ byāpādaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa byāpādassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa byāpādassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa byāpādassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ thinamiddhaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ thinamiddha’nti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ thinamiddhaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ thinamiddha’nti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa thinamiddhassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa thinamiddhassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ uddhaccakukkucca’nti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ uddhaccakukkuccaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ uddhaccakukkucca’nti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa uddhaccakukkuccassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ vicikicchaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ vicikicchaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannāya vicikicchāya uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannāya vicikicchāya pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnāya vicikicchāya āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati ‘atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu.

Nīvaraṇapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Dhammānupassanā khandhapabbaṃ
mula_english:
382. “And how, monks, does a monk abide contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects? Here, monks, a monk abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in terms of the five hindrances. And how, monks, does a monk abide contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in terms of the five hindrances?

“Here, monks, if sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is present in himself, a monk understands: ‘There is sensual desire in me (atthi me ajjhattaṃ kāmacchando)’; or if sensual desire is absent in himself, a monk understands: ‘There is no sensual desire in me (natthi me ajjhattaṃ kāmacchando)’; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen sensual desire, and how there comes to be the future non-arising of abandoned sensual desire.

“If ill-will (byāpāda) is present in himself, a monk knows that it is present; or if ill-will is absent in himself, he knows that it is absent; and he knows how unarisen ill-will comes to arise, and he knows how the abandonment of arisen ill-will comes about, and he knows how the non-arising of the abandoned ill-will in the future will come about.

“If sloth and torpor (thinamiddha) is present in himself, a monk knows that it is present; or if sloth and torpor is absent in himself, he knows that it is absent; and he knows how unarisen sloth and torpor comes to arise, and he knows how the abandonment of arisen sloth and torpor comes about, and he knows how the non-arising of the abandoned sloth and torpor in the future will come about.

“If restlessness and remorse (uddhaccakukkucca) is present in himself, a monk knows that it is present; or if restlessness and remorse is absent in himself, he knows that it is absent; and he knows how unarisen restlessness and remorse comes to arise, and he knows how the abandonment of arisen restlessness and remorse comes about, and he knows how the non-arising of the abandoned restlessness and remorse in the future will come about.

“If doubt (vicikicchā) is present in himself, a monk understands: ‘There is doubt in me’; or if doubt is absent in himself, he understands: ‘There is no doubt in me’; and he understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen doubt, and how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen doubt, and how there comes to be the future non-arising of abandoned doubt.

“In this way, he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects internally, or he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects externally, or he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects both internally and externally. Or else, he abides contemplating in mind-objects their arising factors, or he abides contemplating in mind-objects their vanishing factors, or he abides contemplating in mind-objects both their arising and vanishing factors. Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are mind-objects (atthi dhammā)’ is present just to the extent necessary for knowledge and awareness. And he abides detached, not clinging to anything in the world. That is how a monk abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in terms of the five hindrances.

The chapter on the hindrances is finished.

The section on the aggregates in the contemplation of mind-objects.
commentary_pali:
382. Evaṃ soḷasavidhena cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Apica bhagavatā kāyānupassanāya suddharūpapariggaho kathito, vedanācittānupassanāhi suddhaarūpapariggaho. Idāni rūpārūpamissakapariggahaṃ kathetuṃ ‘‘kathañca, bhikkhave’’tiādimāha. Kāyānupassanāya vā rūpakkhandhapariggahova kathito, vedanānupassanāya vedanākkhandhapariggahova, cittānupassanāya viññāṇakkhandhapariggahova idāni saññāsaṅkhārakkhandhapariggahampi kathetuṃ ‘‘kathañca, bhikkhave’’tiādimāha.

Tattha santanti abhiṇhasamudācāravasena saṃvijjamānaṃ. Asantanti asamudācāravasena vā pahīnattā vā asaṃvijjamānaṃ. Yathā cāti yena kāraṇena kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti. Tañca pajānātīti tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Iti iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

santa Asanta Yathā cā Tañca pajānātī

Tattha subhanimitte ayonisomanasikārena kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti. Subhanimittaṃ nāma subhampi subhanimittaṃ, subhārammaṇampi subhanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāro nāma anupāyamanasikāro uppathamanasikāro anicce niccanti vā, dukkhe sukhanti vā, anattani attāti vā, asubhe subhanti vā manasikāro. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, subhanimittaṃ, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāya uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Subhanimittaṃ Ayonisomanasikāro

Asubhanimitte pana yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Asubhanimittaṃ nāma asubhampi asubhārammaṇampi. Yonisomanasikāro nāma upāyamanasikāro pathamanasikāro anicce aniccanti vā, dukkhe dukkhanti vā, anattani anattāti vā, asubhe asubhanti vā manasikāro. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, asubhanimittaṃ, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa anuppādāya uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa pahānāyā’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Asubhanimittaṃ Yonisomanasikāro

Apica cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattanti asubhanimittassa uggaho, asubhabhāvanānuyogo, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Dasavidhañhi asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi kāmacchando pahīyati, bhāventassāpi indriyesu pihitadvārassāpi catunnaṃ pañcannaṃ ālopānaṃ okāse sati udakaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlatāya bhojanamattaññunopi. Teneva vuttaṃ –

‘‘Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno’’ti. (theragā. 983);

Asubhakammikatissattherasadise asubhabhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassapi kāmacchando pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu dasaasubhanissitasappāyakathāya pahīyati, tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattantī’’ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnakāmacchandassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Paṭighanimitte ayonisomanasikārena pana byāpādassa uppādo hoti. Tattha paṭighampi paṭighanimittaṃ , paṭighārammaṇampi paṭighanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāro sabbattha ekalakkhaṇova. Taṃ tasmiṃ nimitte bahulaṃ pavattayato byāpādo uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, paṭighanimittaṃ , tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā byāpādassa uppādāya uppannassa vā byāpādassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Mettāya pana cetovimuttiyā yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Tattha mettāti vutte appanāpi upacāropi vaṭṭati. Cetovimuttīti appanāva. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇova. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato byāpādo pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, mettā cetovimutti, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā byāpādassa anuppādāya uppannassa vā byāpādassa pahānāyā’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

mettā Cetovimuttī

Apica cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattanti mettānimittassa uggaho mettābhāvanānuyogo kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇā paṭisaṅkhānabahulatā kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇānañhi aññataravasena mettaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati, odhisoanodhisopharaṇavasena mettaṃ bhāventassāpi. ‘‘Tvaṃ etassa kuddho kiṃ karissasi, kimassa sīlādīni vināsetuṃ sakkhissasi, nanu tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attano kammeneva gamissasi, parassa kujjhanaṃ nāma vītaccitaṅgāra tattaaya salākagūthādīni gahetvā paraṃ paharitukāmatāsadisaṃ hoti. Esopi tava kuddho kiṃ karissati, kiṃ te sīlādīni vināsetuṃ sakkhissati, esa attano kammena āgantvā attano kammeneva gamissati, appaṭicchitapaheṇakaṃ viya paṭivātaṃ khittarajomuṭṭhi viya ca etassevesa kodho matthake patissatī’’ti evaṃ attano ca parassa ca kammassakataṃ paccavekkhatopi, ubhayakammassakataṃ paccavekkhitvā paṭisaṅkhāne ṭhitassāpi, assaguttattherasadise mettābhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu mettānissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattantī’’ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa byāpādassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Aratiādīsu ayonisomanasikārena thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti. Tandī nāma kāyālasiyatā. Vijambhitā nāma kāyavinamanā. Bhattasammado nāma bhattamucchā bhattapariḷāho. Cetaso līnattaṃ nāma cittassa līnākāro. Imesu aratiādīsu ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato thinamiddhaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, arati tandī vijambhitā bhattasammado cetaso līnattaṃ, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā thinamiddhassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā thinamiddhassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Arati Tandī Vijambhitā Bhattasammado Cetaso līnattaṃ

Ārambhadhātuādīsu pana yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Ārambhadhātu nāma paṭhamārambhavīriyaṃ. Nikkamadhātu nāma kosajjato nikkhantatāya tato balavataraṃ. Parakkamadhātu nāma paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavataraṃ. Imasmiṃ tippabhede vīriye yonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Tenāha – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā thinamiddhassa anuppādāya, uppannassa vā thinamiddhassa pahānāyā’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Ārambhadhātu Nikkamadhātu Parakkamadhātu

Apica cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattanti – atibhojane nimittaggāho, iriyāpathasamparivattanatā, ālokasaññāmanasikāro, abbhokāsavāso, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Āharahatthaka tatravaṭṭaka alaṃsāṭaka kākamāsaka bhuttavamitakabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhāne nisinnassa hi samaṇadhammaṃ karoto thinamiddhaṃ mahāhatthī viya ottharantaṃ āgacchati, catupañcaālopaokāsaṃ pana ṭhapetvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlassa bhikkhuno taṃ na hotīti evaṃ atibhojane nimittaṃ gaṇhantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Yasmiṃ iriyāpathe thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, tato aññaṃ parivattentassāpi, rattiṃ candālokadīpālokaukkāloke divā sūriyālokaṃ manasikarontassāpi, abbhokāse vasantassāpi, mahākassapattherasadise pahīnathinamiddhe kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhutaṅganissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattantī’’ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa thinamiddhassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Cetaso avūpasame ayonisomanasikārena uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti. Avūpasamo nāma avūpasantākāro, uddhaccakukkuccamevetaṃ atthato. Tattha ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato uddhaccakukkuccaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, cetaso avūpasamo, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā’’ti.

Avūpasamo

Samādhisaṅkhāte pana cetaso vūpasame yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Tenāha – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, cetaso vūpasamo, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa anuppādāya, uppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāyā’’ti.

Apica cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattanti bahussutatā paripucchakatā vinaye pakataññutā vuddhasevitā kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Bāhussaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā dve vā tayo vā cattāro vā pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati. Kappiyākappiyaparipucchābahulassāpi, vinayapaññattiyaṃ ciṇṇavasibhāvatāya pakataññunopi, vuḍḍhe mahallakatthere upasaṅkamantassāpi, upālittherasadise vinayadhare kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu kappiyākappiyanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattantī’’ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīne uddhaccakukkucce uddhaccassa arahattamaggena , kukkuccassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Vicikicchāṭhānīyesu dhammesu ayonisomanasikārena vicikicchāya uppādo hoti. Vicikicchāṭhānīyā dhammā nāma punappunaṃ vicikicchāya kāraṇattā vicikicchāva. Tattha ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato vicikicchā uppajjati. Tenāha – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, vicikicchāṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannāya vā vicikicchāya uppādāya, uppannāya vā vicikicchāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Vicikicchāṭhānīyā dhammā

Kusalādidhammesu yonisomanasikārena panassā pahānaṃ hoti, tenāha – ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā sāvajjānavajjā dhammā sevitabbāsevitabbā dhammā hīnapaṇītā dhammā kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā. Tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro, anuppannāya vā vicikicchāya anuppādāya; uppannāya vā vicikicchāya pahānāyā’’ti.

Apica cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattanti bahussutatā, paripucchakatā, vinaye pakataññutā, adhimokkhabahulatā, kalyāṇamittatā, sappāyakathāti. Bāhussaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā…pe… pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena ca atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati, tīṇi ratanāni ārabbha paripucchābahulassāpi, vinaye ciṇṇavasībhāvassāpi, tīsu ratanesu okappaniyasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhabahulassāpi, saddhādhimutte vakkalittherasadise kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattantī’’ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnāya vicikicchāya sotāpattimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ pañcanīvaraṇapariggaṇhanena attano vā dhammesu, parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha subhanimittaasubhanimittādīsu ayonisomanasikārayonisomanasikāravasena pañcasu nīvaraṇesu vuttāyeva nīharitabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha nīvaraṇapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā nīvaraṇapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Nīvaraṇapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
382. Having explained the Arousing of Mindfulness in regard to consciousness in the sixteenfold way, now, in order to expound the fivefold contemplation of mental objects *dhamma*, he said, “And, how, o *bhikkhus*."

Further, the Blessed One taught the laying hold of pure corporeality or materiality in the instruction on body-contemplation, and in the instruction on the contemplation of feeling and consciousness, the laying hold of the purely spiritual.

Now in order to teach the laying hold of a mixture of the material and the spiritual, he said, “And, how, o *bhikkhus*."

Or in the contemplation on the body the laying hold of the aggregate of corporeality or materiality was spoken of; in the contemplation on feeling, the laying hold of the aggregate of feeling; in the contemplation on mind, the laying hold of the aggregate of consciousness; and now in order to speak of even the laying hold of the aggregates of perception *saṃjñā* and formations *saṃskāra*, he said “And, how, o *bhikkhus*."

There, "existing" means existing by way of constant practice.

"Non-existing" means not existing by way of lack of practice, or because it has been abandoned.

"Just as," means for what reason craving for sensual pleasure *kāmacchanda* arises.

"And he understands that," means he understands that reason.

Thus, the meaning should be understood in all passages by this method.

Existing, non-existing, just as, and he understands that. There, wrong reflection *ayoniso manasikāra* on a sensuously auspicious object causes the arising of craving for sensual pleasure *kāmacchanda*.

"Auspicious sign" *subhanimitta* means either sensuality itself *subha*, or that which produces sensuality, the sensuality-object *subhārammaṇa*.

Wrong reflection *ayoniso manasikāra* means inexpedient reflection *anupāyamanasikāra*, reflection on the wrong track *uppathamanasikāra*. Or it is reflection which considers the impermanent *anicca* as permanent *nicca*, pain *duḥkha* as pleasure *sukha*, non-soul *anatta* as soul *atta*, the bad *asubha* as good *subha*.

Sense-desire *kāmacchanda* arises when that occurs much.

Therefore the Blessed One said that the condition for the arising of fresh sense-desire *kāmacchanda* and for the increase and expansion of existing sense-desire is plentiful wrong reflection on a sensuously auspicious or promising object.

Auspicious sign, wrong reflection

But in the inauspicious object, its abandonment is through right reflection *yoniso manasikāra*.

"Inauspicious sign" *asubhanimitta* means either the inauspicious itself *asubha*, or that which is the object of the inauspicious *asubhārammaṇa*.

Right reflection *yoniso manasikāra* is expedient reflection *upāyamanasikāra*, reflection going on the right track *pathamanasikāra*. It is reflection that considers the facts of impermanence *anicca*, suffering *dukkha*, soullessness *anatta* and of impurity *asubha*, according to reality.

When that occurs much there, sense-desire *kāmacchanda* is knocked out.

Therefore the Blessed One said that the condition for keeping out new sense-desire *kāmacchanda* and for casting out old sense-desire is abundant right reflection on the sensuously inauspicious or unpromising object.

Inauspicious sign, right reflection

Furthermore, six things conduce to the rejection of sensuous desire *kāmacchanda*: taking up the sensuously inauspicious object *asubhanimitta*, application to developing meditation on the sensuously inauspicious *asubhabhāvanā*, guarding the doors of the senses *indriya*, knowing moderation in food *bhojana*, good friendship *kalyāṇamittatā*, and suitable talk *sappāyakathā*.

For when one takes up the tenfold object sensuously inauspicious, impure, or bad *asubhanimitta*, sense-desire is knocked out; also by him who develops it, by him who guards the controlling faculties of sense by closing the six sense doors *indriya*, and by him who knows the measure of food for sustenance, even when there is opportunity for four or five morsels *ālopa*, having drunk water, and by him who is of a sustaining nature in food.

Therefore it was said:

“Having eaten four or five morsels, drink water;

Enough for ease of dwelling is that for the monk who is intent."

(Theragāthā. 983);

Sense-desire is also knocked out for one who frequents a good friend who is like the Elder Tissa, who is devoted to meditation on the sensuously inauspicious object, by suitable talk dependent on the ten inauspicious [objects] *dasāsubhanissita* in places of sitting, etc.; therefore it was said: “Six things conduce to the rejection of sense-desire *kāmacchanda*.”

But through these six things, the yogi understands that sense-desire having been cast out, there is no more arising in the future through the attainment of the path of arahantship.

Indeed, wrong reflection *ayoniso manasikāra* on an object of resentment produces anger *byāpāda*.
There, aversion, too, [is] an aversion-sign; an aversion-object, too, [is] an aversion-sign. Wrong reflection has just the same character everywhere. And when it occurs much in that sign, anger arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "There is, *bhikkhus*, an aversion-sign; frequently giving careless attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will and for the increase and expansion of arisen ill will" (SN 5.232).

But by right reflection on the mind-deliverance of loving-kindness there is abandonment of it [ill-will]. There, when "*mettā*," loving-kindness, is said, both attainment and proximity-concentration are suitable. "*Cetovimuttī*," mind-deliverance, [means] attainment alone. Right reflection has the same character throughout. When it occurs strong there, anger is removed. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “There is, O *bhikkhus*, the liberation of the mind through love. Intense right reflection on love is the condition for keeping out new anger and for throwing out anger that is already in the heart" (SN 5.232).

Moreover, six things conduce to the rejection of ill will: taking up the sign of loving-kindness, application to the cultivation of loving-kindness, investigation of ownership of karma, frequency of reflection, good friendship, and suitable talk. Verily, in one who takes up the love subject of meditation by way of spreading it particularly or separately, anger will be put down. Or if one cultivates the love subject of meditation by way of spreading it generally, without particularization or directional restriction in space, then too anger will be put down. "What will you do to him by becoming angry? Will you be able to destroy things like his virtue? Have you not been born here just by your own actions, and will you not also get reborn hereafter by your own actions? Getting angry with another is comparable to the state of him who wishes to strike another with glowing coals, red-hot crowbar, excreta and such other damaging things after taking them up in his bare hands. And what can another who is angry with you do to you? Can he destroy your virtue or any other similar thing of yours? He, too, has been born here as a result of his actions, and will be reborn hereafter just according to his actions. Like a present not accepted is that anger of his, and like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, that anger of his alights on his own head." In this way, even in one who reflects on one’s own action as one’s own property and also another person’s action as that person's, even in one who reflects on the actions of both as their own and abides in reflection, even in one who keeps the company of good friends sympathetic towards those who delight in the cultivation of loving-kindness like the Elder Assagutta, anger is rejected. It is also rejected by stimulating talk connected with the thought of love when in any one of the four postures. Therefore, it was said, “Six things conduce to the rejection of ill will." However, by these six things, one knows that the ill will that has been rejected is unarisen in the future by the path of the non-returner.

Sloth and Torpor: Through wrong reflection on a state of boredom and the like, sloth and torpor come to be. Lassitude (*tandī*) is bodily laziness. Languidity of body (*vijambhitā*) is the bending of the body torpidly in getting up and in similar actions. Lethargy after a meal (*bhattasammado*) is the intoxication of a meal, the burning from a meal. The mind’s sluggishness (*cetaso līnattaṃ*) is the dullness of the mind. In these [states] of boredom and the like, sloth and torpor come to be in one who frequently practices wrong reflection. Therefore, the Blessed One said that much wrong reflection on boredom, lassitude, languidity of body, lethargy after a meal, and the mind’s sluggishness, is a condition for the production of fresh sloth and torpor and the increase and expansion of sloth and torpor already come into being (SN.
5.232).

*Arati*, *tandī*, *vijambhitā*, *bhattasammado*, *cetaso līnattaṃ*

But by right reflection on the element of inceptive energy, its rejection occurs. *Ārambhadhātu* means initial inceptive energy. *Nikkamadhātu* means stronger than that, owing to going forth from laziness. *Parakkama-dhātu* means still stronger than that, owing to assailing further and further places. By exercising right reflection intensely on this threefold strenuousness sloth and torpor are cast out. Therefore the Blessed One said that the condition for keeping out new sloth and torpor, and for casting out sloth and torpor that is old, is abundant right reflection on the element of inceptive energy, of exertion and of progressive endeavor (SN 5.232).

*Ārambhadhātu*, *nikkamadhātu*, *parakkama-dhātu*

Moreover, six things are conducive to the casting out of sloth and torpor: paying attention to the sign through overeating, changing over from posture to posture, reflecting on the light-perception, living in the open air, sympathetic and helpful companionship and stimulating talk. For sloth and torpor, like a great elephant, comes overwhelming him who, after eating food, whether good or bad, just enough to fill the hand, the bowl or the alms-bowl, or enough to fill a crow’s measure, is seated by night or day, and tries to fulfil the duties of a recluse; but for the bhikkhu who puts aside a space of four or five mouthfuls, drinks water and is of frugal habit, that does not occur. Thus sloth and torpor disappear in him who pays attention to the sign that is overeating. Sloth and torpor disappear in him who changes over from the posture which induces sloth and torpor to another; in him who reflects on the brightness or the light of the moon, a lamp or a torch by night, and on the light or brightness of the sun by day; in him who lives in the open; in him who associates with sympathetic and helpful companions, like the Elder Mahā Kassapa, who have dispelled sloth and torpor; and by stimulating talk connected with a strict recluse-regimen. Therefore it is said: Six things lead to the casting out of sloth and torpor. The *yogī* understands thus: sloth and torpor cast out by these six things are stopped from arising forever in the future by the attainment of the path of arahantship.

Mental agitation and worry arise through wrong reflection on mental agitation. *Avūpasamo* means a state of non-tranquillity; in meaning that is just flurry and worry. Intense wrong reflection on that mental agitation produces flurry and worry. Therefore the Blessed One said that wrong reflection on mental agitation when plentifully done produces fresh flurry and worry and increases and expands flurry and worry already in existence.

*Avūpasamo*

But by right reflection on mental tranquillity designated as concentration, its rejection occurs. Therefore it is said: The condition for the keeping out of fresh mental agitation and worry and the dispelling of agitation and worry already in the mind, is an abundance of right reflection on mental tranquillity.

Six things are conducive to the casting out of agitation and worry: knowledge, questioning, understanding of disciplinary rules; association with those more experienced and older than oneself in the practice of things like virtue; sympathetic and helpful companionship and stimulating talk. In explanation it is said as follows: Agitation and worry disappear in him who learns in the spirit and in the letter one, two, three, four or five collections of Scripture. This is how one gets over agitation and worry by knowledge. Agitation and worry disappear in him who questions much about what is befitting and not befitting, according to the practice of the Sangha. And also in him who has got the mastery of the Discipline due to practical application of and conversance with the nature of the Rule of the Sangha. Then these twin evils disappear in him who goes to the presence of the elders and senior *theras*, and in him who keeps the company of sympathetic and helpful companions, like the Elder Upāli, who is a master of the Discipline. They also disappear by stimulating talk connected with what is befitting and what is not. Therefore it is said: Six things are conducive to the casting out of agitation and worry. The *yogī* understands thus: agitation, however, cast out by these six things finally ceases to arise in the future through the attainment of the path of arahantship, and worry cast out by these things finally ceases to arise in the future through the attainment of the path of the non-returner.

In the case of things which are founded on doubt, doubt arises through wrong reflection. Things which are founded on doubt are known as just doubt owing to the state of being the reason of doubt again and again.
Regarding doubt (vicikicchā):

When wrong reflection (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is frequently practiced concerning that, doubt arises. Therefore, it was said: "Monks, there are things that are the basis of doubt. In that case, frequently applying wrong reflection is a nourishment for the arising of doubt that has not yet arisen, and for the increase and expansion of doubt that has already arisen" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

*Vicikicchāṭhānīyā dhammā* (things that are the basis of doubt):

However, its abandonment occurs by right reflection (*yoniso-manasikāra*) on wholesome qualities (*kusalādidhammesu*). Therefore, it was said: "Monks, there are wholesome and unwholesome qualities (*kusalākusalā dhammā*), blameworthy and blameless qualities (*sāvajjānavajjā dhammā*), qualities to be cultivated and not to be cultivated (*sevitabbāsevitabbā dhammā*), inferior and superior qualities (*hīnapaṇītā dhammā*), qualities with a dark and bright counterpart (*kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā*). In that case, frequently applying right reflection is a nourishment for the non-arising of doubt that has not yet arisen, and for the abandonment of doubt that has already arisen."

And again, six things lead to the abandonment of doubt: being well-learned (*bahussutatā*), questioning (*paripucchakatā*), understanding the nature of the Discipline (*vinaye pakataññutā*), much conviction (*adhimokkhabahulatā*), sympathetic companionship (*kalyāṇamittatā*), and stimulating talk (*sappāyakathā*). Doubt is abandoned even for one who learns one, or...or five Nikāyas by way of the Pali text and by way of the meaning, even for one who is much engaged in questioning concerning the Three Jewels, even for one who has long been familiar with the Discipline, even for one who has much conviction consisting of faith in the Three Jewels, even for one who cultivates sympathetic friends like the venerable Vakkali who is liberated by faith, [and] even by stimulating talk dependent on the qualities of the Three Jewels in places of sitting and lying down, etc. Therefore, it was said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of doubt."

However, one understands that the doubt abandoned by these six things does not arise in the future by the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).

Thus, "internally" (*ajjhattaṃ vā*): in this way, by attending to the five hindrances, one dwells observing phenomena in one's own qualities, or in the qualities of others, or in one's own qualities at times, or in the qualities of others at times. Here, origination and dissolution should be drawn out in the five hindrances just as they were stated by way of wrong reflection and right reflection on attractive signs (*subhanimitta*) and unattractive signs (*asubhanimitta*), etc. From here on, the exposition is just according to the manner already stated. Here, mindfulness which lays hold of the hindrances is the Truth of Suffering. Thus, the portal of deliverance of the *bhikkhu* who lays hold of the hindrances should be understood. The rest is just like that.

Thus, "internally" (*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*).

The chapter on the hindrances is finished.

Explanation of the chapter on the aggregates (*khandhapabba*)

mula_pali:
383. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu – ‘iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā, iti vedanāya samudayo, iti vedanāya atthaṅgamo; iti saññā, iti saññāya samudayo, iti saññāya atthaṅgamo; iti saṅkhārā, iti saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo, iti saṅkhārānaṃ atthaṅgamo, iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti, iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati. ‘Atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya, anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati . Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu.

Khandhapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Dhammānupassanā āyatanapabbaṃ
mula_english:
“Again, monks, a monk abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects with reference to the five aggregates of grasping (pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu).

“And how, monks, does a monk abide contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects with reference to the five aggregates of grasping? Here, monks, a monk understands: ‘Such is material form (rūpaṃ), such its origin (rūpassa samudayo), such its disappearance (rūpassa atthaṅgamo); such is feeling (vedanā), such its origin (vedanāya samudayo), such its disappearance (vedanāya atthaṅgamo); such is perception (saññā), such its origin (saññāya samudayo), such its disappearance (saññāya atthaṅgamo); such are the mental formations (saṅkhārā), such their origin (saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo), such their disappearance (saṅkhārānaṃ atthaṅgamo); such is consciousness (viññāṇaṃ), such its origin (viññāṇassa samudayo), such its disappearance (viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo).’ In this way, he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects internally (ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati), or externally (bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati), or both internally and externally (ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati).

He abides contemplating arising phenomena (samudayadhammānupassī) in mind-objects, he abides contemplating vanishing phenomena (vayadhammānupassī) in mind-objects, he abides contemplating both arising and vanishing phenomena (samudayavayadhammānupassī) in mind-objects.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are mind-objects (atthi dhammā)’ is present just to the extent necessary for knowledge and awareness (ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya). And he abides detached (anissito), not grasping at anything in the world (loke upādiyati).

That is how a monk abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in respect of the five aggregates of grasping (pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu).

The chapter on the aggregates is finished (khandhapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ).

The section on contemplation of mind-objects; the chapter on the sense bases (dhammānupassanā āyatanapabbaṃ).
commentary_pali:
383. Evaṃ pañcanīvaraṇavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni pañcakkhandhavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha pañcasu upādānakkhandhesūti upādānassa khandhā upādānakkhandhā, upādānassa paccayabhūtā dhammapuñjā dhammarāsayoti attho. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana khandhakathā visuddhimagge vuttā.

Iti rūpanti idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito paraṃ rūpaṃ atthīti sabhāvato rūpaṃ pajānāti. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārena pana rūpādīni visuddhimagge khandhakathāyameva vuttāni. Iti rūpassa samudayoti evaṃ avijjāsamudayādivasena pañcahākārehi rūpassa samudayo. Iti rūpassa atthaṅgamoti evaṃ avijjānirodhādivasena pañcahākārehi rūpassa atthaṅgamo. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge udayabbayañāṇakathāya vutto.

Iti rūpa Iti rūpassa samudayo Iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ pañcakkhandhapariggaṇhanena attano vā dhammesu, parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha ‘‘avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo’’tiādīnaṃ pañcasu khandhesu vuttānaṃ paññāsāya lakkhaṇānaṃ vasena nīharitabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha khandhapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā khandhapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Khandhapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
383. Having thus distinguished the contemplation of the Dhamma by way of the five hindrances, he now, in order to distinguish it by way of the five aggregates, says, "Furthermore…"
There, "in the five aggregates of clinging" means aggregates of clinging are aggregates of clinging; it means a mass of Dhammas, a heap of Dhammas, which are the condition for clinging.
This is a brief explanation.
The talk on the aggregates, however, is stated in detail in the Path of Purity (Visuddhimagga).

"Thus is material form": He understands material form according to its nature, [thinking,] "This is material form, so much is material form, there is no more material form than this."
In regard to feeling and the things that come afterwards, the same is the method of exegesis.
This is a brief explanation, but the material form and the rest are stated at length in the Path of Purity in the talk on the aggregates itself.
"Thus is the arising of material form": Thus is the arising of material form in five ways, beginning with the arising of ignorance.
"Thus is the passing away of material form": Thus is the passing away of material form in five ways, beginning with the cessation of ignorance.
In regard to feeling and the things that come afterwards, the same is the method of exegesis.
This is a brief explanation, but the detailed explanation is stated in the Path of Purity in the talk on the knowledge of arising and passing away.

Thus is material form
Thus is the arising of material form
Thus is the passing away of material form

Thus, "internally": Thus, by laying hold of the five aggregates, he dwells contemplating the Dhamma in his own mental objects or in the mental objects of others, or at one time in his own mental objects and at another time in the mental objects of others.
Herein, the origination and dissolution should be brought forward and connected by way of the fifty characteristics of the five aggregates, with the extended application of the words: “From the arising of ignorance the arising of material form comes to be.”
From here on the exposition is just according to the manner already stated.
Indeed, the mindfulness that lays hold of the aggregates is the Truth of Suffering. Thus, the portal of deliverance for the *bhikkhu* who lays hold of the aggregates should be understood.
The rest is as before.

Thus, "internally"
The section on the aggregates is finished.

Explanation of the section on the sense-fields

mula_pali:
384. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu?

‘‘Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhuñca pajānāti, rūpe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Sotañca pajānāti, sadde ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Ghānañca pajānāti, gandhe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Jivhañca pajānāti, rase ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti , yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Kāyañca pajānāti, phoṭṭhabbe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Manañca pajānāti, dhamme ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojanaṃ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṃyojanassa pahānaṃ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṃyojanassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati. ‘Atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya, anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu.

Āyatanapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Dhammānupassanā bojjhaṅgapabbaṃ
mula_english:
384. And further, monks, a monk abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in respect of the six internal and external sense-bases.

And how, monks, does a monk abide contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in terms of the six internal and external sense-bases?

Here, monks, a monk understands the eye (cakṣu), he understands forms (rūpa), and he understands the fetter (saṃyojana) that arises dependent on both; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, and how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.

He knows the ear (śrotra) and knows sounds (śabda). and he knows the fetter (saṃyojana) that arises dependent on both; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, and how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.

He knows the nose (ghāṇa), and knows smells (gandha). and he knows the fetter (saṃyojana) that arises dependent on both; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, and how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.

He knows the tongue (jihvā), and knows tastes (rasa), and he knows the fetter (saṃyojana) that arises dependent on both; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, and how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.

He knows the body (kāya) and knows tangibles (phoṭṭhabba). and he knows the fetter (saṃyojana) that arises dependent on both; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, and how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.

He understands the mind (manas), he understands mind-objects (dharma), and he understands the fetter (saṃyojana) that arises dependent on both; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen fetter, and how there comes to be the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and how there comes to be the future non-arising of the abandoned fetter.

In this way he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects internally, or he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects externally, or he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects both internally and externally. He abides contemplating arising phenomena in mind-objects, he abides contemplating vanishing phenomena in mind-objects, he abides contemplating both arising and vanishing phenomena in mind-objects.

Or else, mindfulness that “there are mind-objects” is present just to the extent necessary for knowledge and awareness. And he abides detached, not grasping at anything in the world.

That is how a bhikkhu abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in terms of the six internal and external bases.

The section on the sense-bases is complete.

The section on contemplation of mind-objects related to the awakening factors.
commentary_pali:
384. Evaṃ pañcakkhandhavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni āyatanavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesūti cakkhu sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhā kāyo manoti imesu chasu ajjhattikesu, rūpaṃ saddo gandho raso phoṭṭhabbo dhammoti imesu chasu bāhiresu. Cakkhuñca pajānātīti cakkhupasādaṃ yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti. Rūpe ca pajānātīti bahiddhā catusamuṭṭhānikarūpañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti. Yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojananti yañca taṃ cakkhuṃ ceva rūpe cāti ubhayaṃ paṭicca. Kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭigha, māna, diṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbataparāmāsa, bhavarāga, issā, macchariya, avijjāsaṃyojananti dasavidhaṃ saṃyojanaṃ uppajjati, tañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti.

Kathaṃ panetaṃ uppajjatīti? Cakkhudvāre tāva āpāthagataṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ kāmassādavasena assādayato abhinandato kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Aniṭṭhārammaṇe kujjhato paṭighasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. ‘‘Ṭhapetvā maṃ ko añño etaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vibhāvetuṃ samattho atthī’’ti maññato mānasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Etaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuvanti gaṇhato diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. ‘‘Etaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ satto nu kho, sattassa nu kho’’ti vicikicchato vicikicchāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. ‘‘Sampattibhave vata no idaṃ sulabhaṃ jāta’’nti bhavaṃ patthentassa bhavarāgasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. ‘‘Āyatimpi evarūpaṃ sīlabbataṃ samādiyitvā sakkā laddhu’’nti sīlabbataṃ samādiyantassa sīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. ‘‘Aho vata taṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ aññe na labheyyu’’nti usūyato issāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Attanā laddhaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ aññassa maccharāyato macchariyasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Sabbeheva sahajātaaññāṇavasena avijjāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati.

Yathā ca anuppannassāti yena kāraṇena asamudācāravasena anuppannassa tassa dasavidhassāpi saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti, tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Yathā ca uppannassāti appahīnaṭṭhena pana samudācāravasena vā uppannassa tassa dasavidhassāpi saṃyojanassa yena kāraṇena pahānaṃ hoti, tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Yathā ca pahīnassāti tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānavasena pahīnassāpi tassa dasavidhassa saṃyojanassa yena kāraṇena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti, tañca pajānāti. Kena kāraṇena panassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti? Diṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsaissāmacchariyabhedassa tāva pañcavidhassa saṃyojanassa sotāpattimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti. Kāmarāgapaṭighasaṃyojanadvayassa oḷārikassa sakadāgāmimaggena, aṇusahagatassa anāgāmimaggena, mānabhavarāgāvijjāsaṃyojanattayassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti. Sotañca pajānāti sadde cātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Apicettha āyatanakathā vitthārato visuddhimagge āyatananiddese vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Yathā ca anuppannassā Yathā ca uppannassā Yathā ca pahīnassā Sotañca pajānāti sadde cā āyatanakathā

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ ajjhattikāyatanapariggaṇhanena attano vā dhammesu bāhirāyatanapariggaṇhanena parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha ‘‘avijjāsamudayā cakkhusamudayo’’ti rūpāyatanassa rūpakkhandhe, arūpāyatanesu manāyatanassa viññāṇakkhandhe, dhammāyatanassa sesakkhandhesu vuttanayena nīharitabbā. Lokuttaradhammā na gahetabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha āyatanapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā āyatanapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Āyatanapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
384. Thus, having divided the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) by way of the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha), now, in order to divide it by way of the sense-bases (*āyatana*), [he] said, “*puna capara*,” and so forth.

Therein, "*chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu*": the eye (cakkhu), the ear (sotaṃ), the nose (ghānaṃ), the tongue (jivhā), the body (kāyo), and the mind (mano)—these are the six internal (*ajjhattika*) sense-bases; form (*rūpaṃ*), sound (*saddo*), smell (*gandho*), taste (*raso*), tactile object (*phoṭṭhabbo*), and mental object (*dhammo*)—these are the six external (*bāhira*) sense-bases.

"*cakkhuñca pajānāti*": he understands the eye faculty (*cakkhupasādaṃ*) according to its distinct function and characteristic (yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena).

"*rūpe ca pajānāti*": he understands external (bahiddhā) form (*rūpañca*) which is caused by the four conditions (catusamuṭṭhānikarūpañca) according to its distinct function and characteristic (*yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena*).

"*yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojana*": “the fetter (*saṃyojana*) that arises dependent on both (ubhayaṃ paṭicca)” means that which arises dependent on both the eye (cakkhuṃ) and forms (rūpe).

The fetter of sense-desire (kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ), resentment (paṭigha), pride (māna), speculative theory (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), belief in rites and ceremonies (sīlabbataparāmāsa), the desire to go on existing (bhavarāga), envy (issā), avarice (macchariya), and the fetter of ignorance (avijjāsaṃyojanaṃ)— thus, the tenfold (dasavidhaṃ) fetter (saṃyojanaṃ) arises, and he understands that according to its distinct function and characteristic (*yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti*).

How does that arise? In the eye-door, when one savors (assādayato) and delights in (abhinandato) an agreeable (iṭṭha) object (ārammaṇaṃ) that has come into the range of perception (āpāthagataṃ) with the enjoyment of sense-desire (kāmassādavasena), the fetter of sense-desire (*kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ*) arises.

When one is angry (kujjhato) at a disagreeable (aniṭṭha) object (ārammaṇe), the fetter of resentment (paṭighasaṃyojanaṃ) arises.

The fetter of pride (mānasaṃyojanaṃ) arises in him who thinks (maññato): “No one but me (ṭhapetvā maṃ ko añño) is able to wisely consider (vibhāvetuṃ samattho atthī) this object (etaṃ ārammaṇaṃ)."

The fetter of speculative theory (diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ) arises in him who takes (gaṇhato) this material form (rūpārammaṇaṃ) to be permanent (niccaṃ) and everlasting (dhuvaṃ).

The fetter of doubt (vicikicchāsaṃyojanaṃ) arises in him who thinks doubtfully (vicikicchato): “Is this material form (*etaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ*) a being (satto nu kho), or a being’s (sattassa nu kho)?"

The fetter of the desire to go on existing (bhavarāgasaṃyojanaṃ) arises in him who wishes for continued existence (bhavaṃ patthentassa) thinking: "To be sure (vata), in a favorable state of existence (sampattibhave) this (idaṃ) will become easy of access (sulabhaṃ jāta)."

The fetter of rites and ceremonies (sīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanaṃ) arises in him who undertakes to perform rites and ceremonies (sīlabbataṃ samādiyantassa) thinking: “In the future (āyatimpi) it will be possible (sakkā laddhu) to obtain such an object as this (evarūpaṃ sīlabbataṃ samādiyitvā) by taking up the observance of rites and ceremonies."

The fetter of envy (issāsaṃyojanaṃ) arises in him who contemplates grudgingly (usūyato): "Should no others (aññe na labheyyu) get that material form (taṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ), it would be good, indeed (aho vata)."

The fetter of avarice (macchariyasaṃyojanaṃ) arises in one who stints for another (aññassa maccharāyato) the material form (rūpārammaṇaṃ) belonging to one (attanā laddhaṃ).

The fetter of ignorance (*avijjāsaṃyojanaṃ*) arises, with all sensuous passion and the like (sabbeheva sahajātaaññāṇavasena), by way of the relation of conascent nescience.

"*yathā ca anuppannassā*": He understands the cause (kāraṇena) owing to which the arising (uppādo hoti) of the non-arisen (anuppannassa) fetter (saṃyojanassa), even of that tenfold one (tassa dasavidhassāpi), had not occurred owing to some cause of non-occurrence (asamudācāravasena).

"*yathā ca uppannassā*": He understands the cause (kāraṇena) owing to which the abandoning (pahānaṃ hoti) of the arisen (uppannassa) fetter (saṃyojanassa), even of that tenfold one (tassa dasavidhassāpi), come to be through occurrence or through previous non-abandoning (appahīnaṭṭhena pana samudācāravasena vā).
