"*yathā ca pahīnassā*": He understands the cause (kāraṇena) owing to which the non-arising (anuppādo hoti) in the future (āyatiṃ) of that (tassa) fetter (*saṃyojanassa*), even of that tenfold one (dasavidhassa), that is abandoned (pahīnassāpi) by way of temporary suppression of its constituent parts (tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānavasena).

By what cause (kena kāraṇena) is its non-arising (anuppādo hoti) in the future (āyatiṃ)? The non-arising (anuppādo hoti) in the future (āyatiṃ) of the fivefold fetter (pañcavidhassa saṃyojanassa) of speculative theory (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), belief in rites and ceremonies (sīlabbataparāmāsa), envy (issā), and avarice (macchariyabhedassa) is by way of the path of stream-winning (*sotāpattimaggena*).

The non-arising (anuppādo hoti) in the future (āyatiṃ) of the twofold (dvayassa) fetter (saṃyojanassa) of sensuous passion (kāmarāga) and resentment (paṭigha) of a gross kind (oḷārikassa) is by way of the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmimaggena*), [and the non-arising] of the subtle residuum which goes along with it (aṇusahagatassa) is by way of the path of never-returning (*anāgāmimaggena*), [and the non-arising] in the future of the threefold (ttayassa) fetter (saṃyojanassa) of pride (māna), the desire to go on existing (bhavarāga), and ignorance (avijjā) is by way of the path of arahantship (*arahattamaggena*).

"*sotañca pajānāti sadde cā*", etc.: The same is the method of exposition in the case of the ear (sotañca) and sounds (sadde).

Moreover, here (*ettha*) the discourse on the sense-bases (*āyatanakathā*) should be understood in detail (vitthārato) just by the method already stated (vuttanayeneva) in the section on the sense-bases (*āyatananiddese*) in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"*yathā ca anuppannassā yathā ca uppannassā yathā ca pahīnassā sotañca pajānāti sadde cā āyatanakathā*": "*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*": Thus (*evaṃ*), contemplating phenomena (dhammānupassī) in phenomena, either internally (*ajjhattikāyatanapariggaṇhanena attano vā dhammesu*) by laying hold of the internal sense-bases, or externally (bāhirāyatanapariggaṇhanena parassa vā dhammesu) by laying hold of the external sense-bases, or in both ways (kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu).

Here (*ettha*) origination and dissolution (samudayavayā) should be brought forward and connected (nīharitabbā) according to the method already stated (vuttanayena) in the aggregate of materiality (*rūpakkhandhe*) for the sense-base of material form (*rūpāyatanassa*) [with the statement], “From the origin of ignorance (avijjāsamudayā) [comes] the origin of the eye (cakkhusamudayo),” in the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandhe*) for the mental sense-base (*manāyatanassa*), and in the remaining aggregates (*sesakkhandhesu*) for the sense-base of mental objects (*dhammāyatanassa*).

The supramundane states (*lokuttaradhammā*) should not be taken (na gahetabbā).

From here on (ito paraṃ) the exposition is just according to the manner already stated (vuttanayameva).

Indeed (kevalañhi), here (idha), the mindfulness which lays hold of the sense-bases (*āyatanapariggāhikā sati*) is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasaccaṃ). Having interpreted (katvā) thus (evaṃ), the portal of deliverance (*niyyānamukhaṃ*) should be known (veditabbaṃ) for the bhikkhu (bhikkhuno) who lays hold of the sense-bases (*āyatanapariggāhakassa*).

The rest (*sesaṃ*) is just like that (tādisameva).

"*iti ajjhattaṃ vā*": The section on the sense-bases (*āyatanapabbaṃ*) is finished (niṭṭhitaṃ).

Explanation of the section on the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā).

mula_pali:
385. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati sattasu bojjhaṅgesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati sattasu bojjhaṅgesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ satisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ satisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa satisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ vīriyasambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ pītisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ pītisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ samādhisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ samādhisambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti , asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya pāripūrī hoti tañca pajānāti.

‘‘Iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati ‘atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati sattasu bojjhaṅgesu.

385. “Again, monks, a monk dwells contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects with regard to the seven factors of enlightenment ( *saptasu bodhyaṅgeṣu*).

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects with regard to the seven factors of enlightenment? Here, monks, if the mindfulness enlightenment factor ( *smṛtisambodhyanga*) is present in himself, he understands: ‘There is the mindfulness enlightenment factor in me’; or if the mindfulness enlightenment factor is absent in himself, he understands: ‘There is no mindfulness enlightenment factor in me’; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen mindfulness enlightenment factor, and how the arisen mindfulness enlightenment factor comes to fulfilment by development.

“If the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor ( *dharmavicayasambodhyanga*) is present in himself, he understands: ‘There is the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor in me’; or if the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor is absent in himself, he understands: ‘There is no investigation-of-states enlightenment factor in me’; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, and how the arisen investigation-of-states enlightenment factor comes to fulfilment by development.

“If the energy enlightenment factor ( *vīryasambodhyanga*) is present in himself, he understands: ‘There is the energy enlightenment factor in me’; or if the energy enlightenment factor is absent in himself, he understands: ‘There is no energy enlightenment factor in me’; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen energy enlightenment factor, and how the arisen energy enlightenment factor comes to fulfilment by development.

“If the rapture enlightenment factor ( *prītisambodhyanga*) is present in himself, he understands: ‘There is the rapture enlightenment factor in me’; or if the rapture enlightenment factor is absent in himself, he understands: ‘There is no rapture enlightenment factor in me’; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen rapture enlightenment factor, and how the arisen rapture enlightenment factor comes to fulfilment by development.

“If the tranquility enlightenment factor ( *praśrabdhisambodhyanga*) is present in himself, he understands: ‘There is the tranquility enlightenment factor in me’; or if the tranquility enlightenment factor is absent in himself, he understands: ‘There is no tranquility enlightenment factor in me’; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen tranquility enlightenment factor, and how the arisen tranquility enlightenment factor comes to fulfilment by development.

“If the concentration enlightenment factor ( *samādhisambodhyanga*) is present in himself, he understands: ‘There is the concentration enlightenment factor in me’; or if the concentration enlightenment factor is absent in himself, he understands: ‘There is no concentration enlightenment factor in me’; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen concentration enlightenment factor, and how the arisen concentration enlightenment factor comes to fulfilment by development.

“If the equanimity enlightenment factor ( *upekṣāsambodhyanga*) is present in himself, he understands: ‘There is the equanimity enlightenment factor in me’; or if the equanimity enlightenment factor is absent in himself, he understands: ‘There is no equanimity enlightenment factor in me’; and he also understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen equanimity enlightenment factor, and how the arisen equanimity enlightenment factor comes to fulfilment by development.

“In this way, he dwells contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects internally, or he dwells contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects externally, or he dwells contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating arising phenomena in mind-objects, he dwells contemplating vanishing phenomena in mind-objects, he dwells contemplating both arising and vanishing phenomena in mind-objects. Or else mindfulness that ‘there are mind-objects ( *dhammā* )’ is established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. That is how, monks, a monk dwells contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects with regard to the seven factors of enlightenment.

The chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment is finished.

commentary_pali:
385. Evaṃ cha ajjhattikabāhirāyatanavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni bojjhaṅgavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha bojjhaṅgesūti bujjhanakasattassa aṅgesu. Santanti paṭilābhavasena saṃvijjamānaṃ. Satisambojjhaṅganti satisaṅkhātaṃ sambojjhaṅgaṃ. Ettha hi sambujjhati āraddhavipassakato paṭṭhāya yogāvacaroti sambodhi. Yāya vā so satiādikāya sattadhammasāmaggiyā sambujjhati kilesaniddāto uṭṭhāti, saccāni vā paṭivijjhati, sā dhammasāmaggī sambodhi. Tassa sambodhissa, tassā vā sambodhiyā aṅganti sambojjhaṅgaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – ‘‘satisaṅkhātaṃ sambojjhaṅga’’nti. Sesasambojjhaṅgesupi imināva nayena vacanattho veditabbo.

Asantanti appaṭilābhavasena avijjamānaṃ. Yathā ca anupannassātiādīsu pana satisambojjhaṅgassa tāva ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī’’ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha satiyeva satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇoyeva. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati.

Asanta Yathā ca anupannassā

Apica cattāro dhammā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti satisampajaññaṃ muṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanatā upaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Abhikkantādīsu hi sattasu ṭhānesu satisampajaññena, bhattanikkhittakākasadise muṭṭhassatipuggale parivajjanena, tissadattattheraabhayattherasadise upaṭṭhitassatipuggale sevanena, ṭhānanisajjādīsu satisamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatāya ca satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Evaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa pana ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā…pe… kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī’’ti evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa

Apica satta dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti paripucchakatā vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattapaṭipādanā duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā paññavantapuggalasevanā gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha paripucchakatāti khandhadhātuāyatanaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgasamathavipassanānaṃ atthasannissitaparipucchābahulatā. Vatthuvisadakiriyāti ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yadā hissa kesanakhalomāni dīghāni honti, sarīraṃ vā ussannadosañceva sedamalamakkhitañca, tadā ajjhattikaṃ vatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Yadā pana cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ duggandhaṃ hoti, senāsanaṃ vā uklāpaṃ, tadā bāhiravatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Tasmā kesādichedāpanena uddhaṃvirecanaadhovirecanādīhi sarīrasallahukabhāvakaraṇena ucchādananahāpanena ca ajjhattikavatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sūcikammadhovanarajanaparibhaṇḍakaraṇādīhi bāhiravatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Etasmiñhi ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi avisade uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ aparisuddhāni dīpakapallavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Visade pana ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi visadaṃ hoti parisuddhāni dīpakapallavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Tena vuttaṃ ‘‘vatthuvisadakiriyā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattatī’’ti.

paripucchakatā Vatthuvisadakiriyā

Indriyasamattapaṭipādanā nāma saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Sace hissa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, itarāni mandāni, tato vīriyindriyaṃ paggahakiccaṃ, satindriyaṃ upaṭṭhānakiccaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ avikkhepakiccaṃ, paññindriyaṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vā, yathā vā manasikaroto balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena hāpetabbaṃ. Vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassanaṃ. Sace pana vīriyindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, atha saddhindriyaṃ adhimokkhakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, na itarāni itarakiccabhedaṃ. Tasmā taṃ passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabbaṃ. Tatrāpi soṇattherassa vatthu dassetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi ekassa balavabhāve sati itaresaṃ attano kiccesu asamatthatā veditabbā.

Indriyasamattapaṭipādanā

Visesato panettha saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samataṃ pasaṃsanti. Balavasaddho hi mandapañño mudhappasanno hoti, avatthusmiṃ pasīdati. Balavapañño mandasaddho kerāṭikapakkhaṃ bhajati, bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hoti. Cittuppādamatteneva kusalaṃ hotīti atidhāvitvā dānādīni akaronto niraye uppajjati. Ubhinnaṃ samatāya vatthusmiṃyeva pasīdati. Balavasamādhiṃ pana mandavīriyaṃ samādhissa kosajjapakkhattā kosajjaṃ abhibhavati. Balavavīriyaṃ mandasamādhiṃ vīriyassa uddhaccapakkhattā uddhaccaṃ abhibhavati. Samādhi pana vīriyena saṃyojito kosajje patituṃ na labhati, vīriyaṃ samādhinā saṃyojitaṃ uddhacce patituṃ na labhati. Tasmā tadubhayaṃ samaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ubhayasamatāya hi appanā hoti.

Apica samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ saddahanto okappento appanaṃ pāpuṇissati. Samādhipaññāsu pana samādhikammikassa ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vipassanākammikassa paññā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ubhinnaṃ pana samatāyapi appanā hotiyeva. Sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭati. Sati hi cittaṃ uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ saddhāvīriyapaññānaṃ vasena uddhaccapātato, kosajjapakkhikena ca samādhinā kosajjapātato rakkhati. Tasmā sā loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu, sabbakammikaamacco viya ca, sabbarājakiccesu sabbattha icchitabbā. Tenāha – ‘‘sati ca pana sabbatthikā vuttā bhagavatā, kiṃ kāraṇā? Cittañhi satipaṭisaraṇaṃ, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā ca sati, na vinā satiyā cittassa paggahaniggaho hotī’’ ti. Duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā nāma khandhādibhede anogāḷhapaññānaṃ dummedhapuggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Paññavantapuggalasevanā nāma samapaññāsalakkhaṇapariggāhikāya udayabbayapaññāya samannāgatapuggalasevanā. Gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā nāma gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya gambhīrapaññāya pabhedapaccavekkhaṇā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evaṃ uppannassa pannassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī’’ti evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa

Apica ekādasa dhammā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇatā ānisaṃsadassāvitā gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇatā piṇḍapātāpacāyanatā dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇatā satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇatā jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti.

Tattha nirayesu pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇato paṭṭhāya mahādukkhānubhavanakālepi, tiracchānayoniyaṃ jālakhipanakumīnādīhi gahitakālepi, pājanakaṇṭakādippahāratunnassa sakaṭavahanādikālepi, pettivisaye anekānipi vassasahassāni ekaṃ buddhantarampi khuppipāsāhi āturībhūtakālepi, kālakañcikaasuresu saṭṭhihatthaasītihatthappamāṇena aṭṭhicammamatteneva attabhāvena vātātapādidukkhānubhavanakālepi na sakkā vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ uppādetuṃ, ayameva te bhikkhu kālo vīriyakaraṇāyāti evaṃ apāyabhayaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi vīriyasambojjhaṅgo uppajjati.

Na sakkā kusītena navalokuttaradhammaṃ laddhuṃ, āraddhavīriyeneva sakkā ayamānisaṃso vīriyassāti evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvinopi uppajjati. Sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhamahāsāvakehi te gatamaggo gantabbo, so ca na sakkā kusītena gantunti evaṃ gamanavīthiṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati. Ye taṃ piṇḍapātādīhi upaṭṭhahanti, ime te manussā neva ñātakā, na dāsakammakarā, nāpi taṃ nissāya jīvissāmāti te paṇītāni cīvarādīni denti. Atha kho attano kārānaṃ mahapphalataṃ paccāsīsamānā denti. Satthārāpi ‘‘ayaṃ ime paccaye paribhuñjitvā kāyadaḷhībahulo sukhaṃ viharissatī’’ti na evaṃ sampassatā tuyhaṃ paccayā anuññātā. Atha kho ‘‘ayaṃ ime paribhuñjamāno samaṇadhammaṃ katvā vaṭṭadukkhato muccissatī’’ti te paccayā anuññātā, so dāni tvaṃ kusīto viharanto na taṃ piṇḍaṃ apacāyissati. Āraddhavīriyasseva hi piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ nāma hotīti evaṃ piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati ayyamittattherassa viya.

Thero kira kassakaleṇe nāma paṭivasati. Tassa ca gocaragāme ekā mahāupāsikā theraṃ puttaṃ katvā paṭijaggati. Sā ekadivasaṃ araññaṃ gacchantī dhītaraṃ āha – ‘‘amma, asukasmiṃ ṭhāne purāṇataṇḍulā, asukasmiṃ sappi, asukasmiṃ khīraṃ, asukasmiṃ phāṇitaṃ, tava bhātikassa ayyamittassa āgatakāle bhattaṃ pacitvā khīrasappiphāṇitehi saddhiṃ dehi, tvañca bhuñjeyyāsi. Ahaṃ pana hiyyo pakkapārivāsikabhattaṃ kañjiyena bhuttāmhī’’ti. Divā kiṃ bhuñjissasi ammā,ti? Sākapaṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā kaṇataṇḍulehi ambilayāguṃ pacitvā ṭhapehi ammā,ti.

Thero cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ nīharantova taṃ saddaṃ sutvā attānaṃ ovadi ‘‘mahāupāsikā kira kañjiyena pārivāsikabhattaṃ bhuñji, divāpi kaṇapaṇṇambilayāguṃ bhuñjissati , tuyhaṃ atthāya pana purāṇataṇḍulādīni ācikkhati, taṃ nissāya kho panesā neva khettaṃ na vatthuṃ na bhattaṃ na vatthaṃ paccāsīsati, tisso pana sampattiyo patthayamānā deti, tvaṃ etissā tā sampattiyo dātuṃ sakkhissasi, na sakkhissasīti, ayaṃ kho pana piṇḍapāto tayā sarāgena sadosena samohena na sakkā gaṇhitu’’nti pattaṃ thavikāya pakkhipitvā gaṇṭhikaṃ muñcitvā nivattitvā kassakaleṇameva gantvā pattaṃ heṭṭhāmañce cīvaraṃ cīvaravaṃse ṭhapetvā ‘‘arahattaṃ apāpuṇitvā na nikkhamissāmī’’ti vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā nisīdi. Dīgharattaṃ appamatto hutvā nivutthabhikkhu vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā purebhattameva arahattaṃ patvā vikasamānamiva padumaṃ mahākhīṇāsavo sitaṃ karontova nisīdi. Leṇadvāre rukkhamhi adhivatthā devatā –

‘‘Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Yassa te āsavā khīṇā, dakkhiṇeyyosi mārisā’’ti. –

Udānaṃ udānetvā ‘‘bhante, piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ tumhādisānaṃ arahantānaṃ bhikkhaṃ datvā mahallakitthiyo dukkhā muccissantī’’ti āha. Thero uṭṭhahitvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā kālaṃ olokento ‘‘pātoyevā’’ti ñatvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ pāvisi.

Dārikāpi bhattaṃ sampādetvā ‘‘idāni me bhātā āgamissati, idāni āgamissatī’’ti dvāraṃ olokayamānā nisīdi. Sā there gharadvāraṃ sampatte pattaṃ gahetvā sappiphāṇitayojitassa khīrapiṇḍapātassa pūretvā hatthe ṭhapesi. Thero ‘‘sukhaṃ hotū’’ti anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sāpi taṃ olokayamānā aṭṭhāsi. Therassa hi tadā ativiya parisuddho chavivaṇṇo ahosi, vippasannāni indriyāni, mukhaṃ bandhanā pavuttatālapakkaṃ viya ativiya virocittha.

Mahāupāsikā araññā āgantvā ‘‘kiṃ, amma, bhātiko te āgato’’ti pucchi. Sā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Upāsikā ‘‘ajja mama puttassa pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ patta’’nti ñatvā ‘‘abhiramati te, amma, bhātā buddhasāsane, na ukkaṇṭhatī’’ti āha.

Mahantaṃ kho panetaṃ satthudāyajjaṃ yadidaṃ satta ariyadhanāni nāma, taṃ na sakkā kusītena gahetuṃ. Yathā hi vippaṭipannaṃ puttaṃ mātāpitaro ‘‘ayaṃ amhākaṃ aputto’’ti paribāhiraṃ karonti, so tesaṃ accayena dāyajjaṃ na labhati, evaṃ kusītopi idaṃ ariyadhanadāyajjaṃ na labhati, āraddhavīriyova labhatīti dāyajjamahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

dāyajjamahattaṃ

Mahā kho pana te satthā, satthuno hi te mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhigaṇhanakālepi abhinikkhamanepi abhisambodhiyampi dhammacakkappavattanayamakapāṭihāriyadevorohanaāyusaṅkhāravossajjanesupi parinibbānakālepi dasasahassilokadhātu akampittha, yuttaṃ nu te evarūpassa satthu sāsane pabbajitvā kusītena bhavitunti evaṃ satthumahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

satthumahattaṃ

Jātiyāpi tvaṃ idāni na lāmakajātiko, asambhinnāya mahāsammatapaveṇiyā āgataukkākarājavaṃse jātosi, suddhodanamahārājassa ca mahāmāyādeviyā ca nattā, rāhulabhaddassa kaniṭṭho, tayā nāma evarūpena jinaputtena hutvā na yuttaṃ kusītena viharitunti evaṃ jātimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

jātimahattaṃ

Sāriputtamahāmoggallānā ceva asīti ca mahāsāvakā vīriyeneva lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhiṃsu, tvaṃ etesaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjasi, na paṭipajjasīti evaṃ sabrahmacārimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

sabrahmacārimahattaṃ

Kucchiṃ pūretvā ṭhitaajagarasadise vissaṭṭhakāyikacetasikavīriye kusītapuggale parivajjantassāpi āraddhavīriye pahitatte puggale sevantassāpi ṭhānanisajjādīsu vīriyuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Pītisambojjhaṅgassa ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī’’ti evaṃ uppādo hoti . Tattha pītiyeva pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā nāma. Tassā uppādakamanasikāro yonisomanasikāro nāma.

Pītisambojjhaṅgassa

Apica ekādasa dhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti buddhānussati, dhamma, saṅgha , sīla, cāga, devatānussati upasamānussati lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā siniddhapuggalasevanatā pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti. Buddhaguṇe anussarantassāpi hi yāva upacārā sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati, dhammasaṅghaguṇe anussarantassāpi, dīgharattaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā rakkhitaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihinopi dasasīlaṃ pañcasīlaṃ pañcavekkhantassāpi, dubbhikkhabhayādīsu paṇītabhojanaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ datvā ‘‘evaṃ nāma adamhā’’ti cāgaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihinopi evarūpe kāle sīlavantānaṃ dinnadānaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, yehi guṇehi samannāgatā devatā devattaṃ pattā, tathārūpānaṃ guṇānaṃ attani atthitaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, samāpattiyā vikkhambhitā kilesā saṭṭhipi sattatipi vassāni na samudācarantīti paccavekkhantassāpi, cetiyadassanabodhidassanatheradassanesu asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve buddhādīsu pasādasinehābhāvena gadrabhapiṭṭhe rajasadise lūkhapuggale parivajjantassāpi, buddhādīsu pasādabahule muducitte siniddhapuggale sevantassāpi, ratanattayaguṇaparidīpake pasādanīyasuttante paccavekkhantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu pītiuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, kāyapassaddhi cittapassaddhi, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī’’ti evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa

Apica satta dhammā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti paṇītabhojanasevanatā utusukhasevanatā iriyāpathasukhasevanatā majjhattapayogatā sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanatā passaddhakāyapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Paṇītañhi siniddhaṃ sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjantassāpi, sītuṇhesu ca utūsu ṭhānādīsu ca iriyāpathesu sappāyautuñca iriyāpathañca sevantassāpi passaddhi uppajjati. Yo pana mahāpurisajātiko sabbautuiriyāpathakkhamo hoti, na taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yassa sabhāgavisabhāgatā atthi, tasseva visabhāge utuiriyāpathe vajjetvā sabhāge sevantassa uppajjati. Majjhattapayogo vuccati attano ca parassa ca kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇā. Iminā majjhattapayogena uppajjati. Yo leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paraṃ viheṭhayamāno vicarati, evarūpaṃ sāraddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ parivajjantassāpi, saṃyatapādapāṇiṃ passaddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu passaddhiuppādanatthāya ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Samādhisambojjhaṅgassa ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, samathanimittaṃ abyagganimittaṃ, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro, anuppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī’’ti evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha samathova samathanimittaṃ avikkhepaṭṭhena ca abyagganimittanti.

Samādhisambojjhaṅgassa

Apica ekādasa dhammā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti vatthuvisadakiriyatā indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā nimittakusalatā samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatā samaye cittassa niggaṇhanatā samaye sampahaṃsanatā samaye ajjhupekkhanatā asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā samāhitapuggalasevanatā jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha vatthuvisadakiriyatā ca indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā ca vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

vatthuvisadakiriyatā indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā

Nimittakusalatā nāma kasiṇanimittassa uggahaṇakusalatā. Samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatāti yasmiṃ samaye atisithilavīriyatādīhi līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayavīriyapītisambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa paggaṇhanaṃ. Samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatāti yasmiṃ samaye āraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa niggaṇhanaṃ. Samaye sampahaṃsanatāti yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānadhigamena vā nirassādaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena saṃvejeti . Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni nāma jāti jarā byādhi maraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti. Ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena ca pasādaṃ janeti, ayaṃ vuccati ‘‘samaye sampahaṃsanatā’’ti.

Nimittakusalatā Samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatā Samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatā Samaye sampahaṃsanatā Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni

Samaye ajjhupekkhanatā nāma yasmiṃ samaye sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadāssa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu na byāpāraṃ āpajjati, sārathi viya samappavattesu assesu. Ayaṃ vuccati – ‘‘samaye ajjhupekkhanatā’’ti. Asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā nāma upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā appattānaṃ vikkhittacittānaṃ puggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Samāhitapuggalasevanā nāma upacārena vā appanāya vā samāhitacittānaṃ sevanā bhajanā payirupāsanā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu samādhiuppādanatthaṃyeva ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evañhi paṭipajjato esa uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

Samaye ajjhupekkhanatā Asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā Samāhitapuggalasevanā Tadadhimuttatā

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa ‘‘atthi, bhikkhave, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī’’ti evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha upekkhāva upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā nāma.

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa

Apica pañca dhammā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti sattamajjhattatā saṅkhāramajjhattatā sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha dvīhākārehi sattamajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti ‘‘tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attanova kammena gamissasi, esopi attanova kammena āgantvā attanova kammena gamissati, tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī’’ti evaṃ kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇena, ‘‘paramatthato sattoyeva natthi, so tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī’’ti evaṃ nissattapaccavekkhaṇena cāti. Dvīhevākārehi saṅkhāramajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti – ‘‘idaṃ cīvaraṃ anupubbena vaṇṇavikāratañceva jiṇṇabhāvañca upagantvā pādapuñchanacoḷakaṃ hutvā yaṭṭhikoṭiyā chaḍḍanīyaṃ bhavissati, sace panassa sāmiko bhaveyya, nāssa evaṃ vinassituṃ dadeyyā’’ti evaṃ assāmikabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena ca, ‘‘anaddhaniyaṃ idaṃ tāvakālika’’nti evaṃ tāvakālikabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena cāti. Yathā ca cīvare, evaṃ pattādīsupi yojanā kātabbā.

sattamajjhattataṃ saṅkhāramajjhattataṃ

Sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatāti ettha yo puggalo gihi vā attano puttadhītādike, pabbajito vā attano antevāsikasamānupajjhāyakādike mamāyati, sahattheneva nesaṃ kesacchedanasūcikammacīvaradhovanarajanapattapacanādīni karoti, muhuttampi apassanto ‘‘asuko sāmaṇero kuhiṃ asuko daharo kuhi’’nti bhantamigo viya ito cito ca oloketi, aññena kesacchedanādīnaṃ atthāya ‘‘muhuttaṃ asukaṃ pesethā’’ti yāciyamānopi ‘‘amhepi taṃ attano kammaṃ na kārema, tumhe naṃ gahetvā kilamessathā’’ti na deti, ayaṃ sattakelāyano nāma.

Sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā

Yo pana cīvarapattathālakakattarayaṭṭhiādīni mamāyati, aññassa hatthena parāmasitumpi na deti, tāvakālikaṃ yācito ‘‘mayampi idaṃ mamāyantā na paribhuñjāma, tumhākaṃ kiṃ dassāmā’’ti vadati, ayaṃ saṅkhārakelāyano nāma. Yo pana tesu dvīsupi vatthūsu majjhatto udāsino, ayaṃ sattasaṅkhāramajjhatto nāma. Iti ayaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo evarūpaṃ sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaṃ ārakā parivajjantassāpi, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu taduppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūri hotīti pajānāti.

saṅkhārakelāyano sattasaṅkhāramajjhatto

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā satta sambojjhaṅge pariggaṇhitvā, parassa vā, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa sambojjhaṅge pariggaṇhitvā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha sambojjhaṅgānaṃ nibbattinirodhavasena veditabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha bojjhaṅgapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā bojjhaṅgapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Bojjhaṅgapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

385. Thus, having divided the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) by way of the six internal and external sense bases, now, in order to divide it by way of the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga), he says beginning with *puna capara*. There, *bojjhaṅgesu* means among the limbs of the awaking mind. *Santa* means existing, being present through attainment. *Satisambojjhaṅga* means the enlightenment factor known as mindfulness (smṛti). Because in these enlightenment factors, the meditator effectively gets enlightened from the time he begins strenuous contemplation on insight, it is called *saṃbodhi*, or complete enlightenment. {10} The sevenfold completeness or harmony, beginning with mindfulness, by which he awakes, effectively rises from the sleep of the defilements, or penetrates the Truths, is *saṃbodhi*. The components of that *saṃbodhi* or of the harmony called *saṃbodhi* are the *saṃbojjhaṅga*, the factors of enlightenment. {11} Hence it was said, “The enlightenment factor known as mindfulness.” In the other factors of enlightenment, the word-meaning should be understood in the same way.

*Asanta* means non-existent, not existing through lack of attainment. *Yathā ca anuppannassā* = “How of the non-arisen.” First, is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. There are things which condition the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and an abundance of right reflection on them is the reason that is conducive to the arising of the non-arisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness and for the increase, the expansion and completion by culture of the arisen enlightenment factor. Thus it comes into being: just mindfulness comprises the things which condition the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Right reflection has the same character throughout. When right reflection occurs plentifully there, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises.

Besides, four things lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor: mindfulness with clear comprehension (smṛti-saṃprajanya), avoiding persons who are confused in mind, cultivation of persons who keep mindfulness ready for application, and inclining towards that. In explanation it is said: Mindfulness arises through mindfulness with clear comprehension in the seven positions beginning with that of “going forwards”;{12} Mindfulness arises through the avoiding of persons who are confused in mind like crows that come cawing to food thrown; through association with persons who keep mindfulness ready for application like the Elder Tissadatta{13} and the Elder Abhaya {14}; and through the state of mind tending for originating mindfulness in all postures, in all. And the bhikkhu knows that the completion by culture of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness brought into being by these four ways takes place by means of the attainment of the path of arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of investigation of mental objects (dharmavicayasambojjhaṅga), “There are karmically good and karmically bad things… right and wrong counterparts of bright and dark things, and an abundance of right reflection on them is the reason conducive to the arising of the non-arisen enlightenment factor of the investigation of mental objects and for the increase, expansion and the completion of culture of that enlightenment factor when it has arisen. {15}

Besides, seven things lead to the arising of this enlightenment factor: Inquiring about the aggregates and so forth; the purification of the basis ; imparting evenness to the controlling faculties; avoiding the ignorant; associating with the wise; reflecting on the profound difference of the hard-to-perceive processes of the aggregates, modes , sense-bases and so forth; and the inclining towards the development of the enlightenment factor of the investigation of mental objects. There, *paripucchakatā* is frequent questioning closely associated with the meaning of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), sense-bases (āyatana), faculties (indriya), strengths (bala), enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga), members of the path (maggāṅga), limbs of jhāna (jhānāṅga), serenity (samatha), and insight (vipaśyanā). *Vatthuvisadakiriyā* is cleansing the internal and the external basis. For when his head hair, nails and body hair are long, or when the body is soaked with sweat, then the internal basis is unclean and unpurified. But when an old dirty smelly robe is worn or when the lodging is dirty, then the external basis is unclean and unpurified. So personal cleanliness should be secured by shaving, hair-cutting, nail-paring, the use of pectoral emetics and of purgatives which make the body light, and by shampooing, bathing and doing other necessary things, at the proper time. In similar way external cleanliness should be brought about by darning, washing and dyeing one’s robes, and by smearing the floor of one’s house with clay and the like to smoothen and clean it, and by doing other necessary things to keep the house clean and tidy. When the internal and external bases are unclean, then the knowledge in the consciousness and consciousness- concomitants that arise is unpurified, like the light of a lamp’s flame that arises with an unpurified lamp-bowl, wick and oil as its support; But when the internal and external bases are clean, then the knowledge in the consciousness and consciousness-concomitants that arise is clean and purified, like the light of a lamp’s flame that arises with a purified lamp bowl, wick and oil as its support. Hence it was said, “Bringing about cleanliness of the basis (vatthuvisadakiriyā) leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of mental objects (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga).”

indriyasamattapaṭipādanā nāma saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samabhāvakaraṇaṃ.
For if his faith faculty (*saddhindriyaṃ*) is strong and the others weak, then the energy faculty (*vīriyindriyaṃ*) cannot perform its function of exerting (*paggahakiccaṃ*), the mindfulness faculty (*satindriyaṃ*) its function of establishing (*upaṭṭhānakiccaṃ*), the concentration faculty (*samādhindriyaṃ*) its function of not distracting (*avikkhepakiccaṃ*), and the understanding faculty (*paññindriyaṃ*) its function of seeing (*dassanakiccaṃ*).
Maintaining balanced faculties is called “the practice of balancing the faculties ( *indriyasamattapaṭipādanā*) of faith (*saddhā*), and the rest.
So in that case the faith faculty should be modified either by reviewing the individual essences of the states concerned, that is, the objects of attention or by not giving them attention in the way in which the faith faculty becomes excessive.
And this is illustrated by the story of the Elder Vakkali.
If however the controlling faculty of energy (*vīriyindriyaṃ*) becomes too powerful then neither will the faculty of faith (*saddhindriyaṃ*) be able to do its work of arousing faith in a settled way in its object nor will the remaining controlling faculties be able to perform their functions.
So in that case the energy faculty should be modified by developing tranquility, and so on.
And this should be illustrated by the story of the Elder Soṇa .
Even thus should the incapacity of the rest of the spiritual faculties to function effectively when one of them has become over-active and powerful, be understood.

visesato panettha saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samataṃ pasaṃsanti.
In particular, here, they praise the balance of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy.
For one strong in faith and weak in understanding has confidence uncritically and groundlessly.
One strong in understanding and weak in faith errs on the side of cunning and is as hard to cure as one sick of a disease caused by medicine.
Such a person thinks that wholesome karma arises with just the intention to do good. Going along the wrong way, by a species of thought beyond the limits of reason, and doing neither almsgiving nor other similar good deeds, he is born in a state of woe.
With the balancing of the two a man has confidence only when there are grounds for it.
Then idleness overpowers one strong in concentration (*samādhi*) and weak in energy (*vīriya*), since concentration (*samādhi*) favours idleness.
Agitation overpowers one strong in energy and weak in concentration (*samādhi*), since energy (*vīriya*) favours agitation.
and concentration (*samādhi*) coupled with energy (*vīriya*) cannot lapse into agitation. So these two should be balanced;
for absorption comes with the balancing of the two.

apica samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati.
Again, concentration and faith should be balanced. One working on concentration needs strong faith,
since it is with such faith and confidence that he reaches absorption.
Then there is balancing of concentration and understanding. One working on concentration needs strong unification,
since that is how he reaches absorption.
and one working on insight needs strong understanding,
since that is how he reaches penetration of characteristics;
but with the balancing of the two he reaches absorption as well.
Strong mindfulness, however, is needed in all instances;
Strong mindfulness is met everywhere since it protects the mind from falling into restlessness belonging to faith, energy and wisdom and from falling into indolence belonging to concentration.
So it is as desirable in all instances as a seasoning of salt in all sauces, as a prime minister in all the king’s business.
Therefore it was said by the Blessed One, “But mindfulness is stated by the Blessed One as essential in all instances. What is the reason? Because mindfulness is a refuge for the mind, and mindfulness is presence for protection, and without mindfulness there is no control or restraint of the mind.”
Turning away from persons of poor wisdom is avoiding from afar dull-witted individuals who do not dive into the distinctions of the aggregates etc.
Association with wise folk is fellowship with persons possessed of the knowledge of rise and fall through the laying hold of all the fifty characteristics.
Profound investigative review of knowledge is the review of the distinctions of profound wisdom that occur in the profound aggregates, etc.

Being intent on that is being intent on a mind that inclines, leans, and tends toward establishing the enlightenment factor of investigation of the Dharma in places of sitting, etc.

Thus, one understands that the completion by culture of the arising wisdom is through the path of *arhatship*.

Avoiding persons of poor wisdom and cultivating persons of wisdom.

The energy enlightenment factor: "There are, monks, the element of exertion, the element of striving, the element of effort; there, thorough attention is made abundant; this is food for the arising of the energy enlightenment factor that has not yet arisen, or for the increase, expansion, culture, and completion of the energy enlightenment factor that has arisen," thus there is arising.

Furthermore, eleven things conduce to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor: reviewing the fear of the lower realms, showing the benefit, reviewing the path to be trodden, making offerings of alms-food, reviewing the greatness of inheritance, reviewing the greatness of the Teacher, reviewing the greatness of birth, reviewing the greatness of those living the holy life, avoiding lazy persons, cultivating energetic persons, and being intent on that.

There, in the hells, even at the time of experiencing great suffering beginning from the cause of the five kinds of bondage, in the animal realm, even when seized by net-casters, worms, etc., even at the time of being pierced by the goad, thorns, etc., and being burdened by cart-drawing, etc., in the realm of the departed, even for many thousands of years, even for one Buddha-interval, even when tormented by hunger and thirst, in the Kālakañcika asuras, even at the time of experiencing suffering from wind, heat, etc., with a self consisting of merely bone and skin to the extent of sixty or eighty cubits, it is not possible to generate the energy enlightenment factor; "This is the time for you, monk, to exert energy," thus, reviewing the fear of the lower realms, the energy enlightenment factor also arises for one who reviews.

It is not possible for the lazy to obtain the nine supramundane *dharmas*; it is only possible for the energetic; this is the benefit of energy. Thus, the energy enlightenment factor also arises for one who shows the benefit.

"The path trodden by all the Buddhas, Private Buddhas, and great disciples is to be trodden by you, and that is not possible for the lazy to tread," thus, the energy enlightenment factor also arises for one who reviews the path to be trodden.

Those who support him with alms-food, etc., these people are neither relatives, nor servants, nor do they give these excellent robes, etc., thinking, "We will live depending on him."

But, expecting great fruit from their actions, they give.

Even the Teacher did not allow these requisites to you, thinking, "Having made use of these requisites, he will live comfortably, with a strong and firm body."

But these requisites were allowed to you thinking, "Having made the ascetic practice, he will be released from the suffering of the round," therefore, now, you, living lazily, will not increase that alms-food.

For, indeed, increase of alms-food is only for the energetic. Thus, the energy enlightenment factor also arises for one who reviews the making of offerings of alms-food, like the venerable Ayyamitta.

The *thera* lived in a cave named Kassaka.

And in the village to which he went for alms, there was a certain great laywoman who, having made the *thera* her son, looked after him.

One day, going to the forest, she said to her daughter: "Dear, in such and such a place there is old rice, in such and such a place there is ghee, in such and such a place there is milk, in such and such a place there is molasses; when your brother Ayyamitta comes, cook food and give it to him together with milk, ghee, and molasses, and you too should eat.

But I ate the cooked stale leftover food with gruel yesterday."

"What will you eat in the day, mother?" "Having put in greens, and having cooked sour gruel with broken rice, keep it, mother."

The *thera*, having robed himself and just as he was taking out his bowl, heard that sound and admonished himself: "The great laywoman ate stale leftover food with gruel, and during the day she will eat gruel made with grain and leaves; but for you, she indicates the old rice, etc.; depending on that, this one expects neither field, nor property, nor food, nor clothing, but she gives, desiring three attainments; will you be able to give those attainments to her, or will you not be able to do so? This alms-food, however, should not be taken by you with passion, with aversion, and with delusion." Having put the bowl in his bag, and having untied the knot, turning back, going to that very Kassaka cave, having placed the bowl on the lower seat and the robe on the robe-rack, resolving on energy, "I will not go out without attaining *arhatship*," he sat down.

Having been earnest for a long time, the recluse, having developed insight, having attained *arhatship* even before mealtime, and the great destroyer of the defilements, smiling like an opening lotus, sat down.

A deity dwelling in a tree at the cave entrance:

"Homage to you, thoroughbred man, homage to you, supreme man;

whose defilements are destroyed, you are worthy of offerings, sir."

Having uttered an exclamation of joy, she said: "Venerable sir, having given alms to the *arhats* like you who have entered for alms, the elderly women will be released from suffering."

The *thera*, having gotten up, having opened the door, observing the time, knowing that it was still early dawn, taking his bowl and robe, entered the village.

That girl too, having prepared the food, thinking, "Now my brother will come, now he will come," sat watching the door.

She, when the *thera* arrived at the house door, taking the bowl, filling it with milk-rice alms mixed with ghee and molasses, placed it in his hands.

The *thera*, having given thanks, saying, "May there be happiness," departed.

That girl too, stood looking at him as he departed.
At that time, the Elder's complexion was exceedingly clear, his senses especially pure, and his face shone brilliantly like a ripe palm fruit freed from its stalk.

The great lay woman came from the forest and asked, "Dear mother, has my brother come?"
She told her everything that had happened.
The lay woman, knowing that her son’s work of renunciation had reached its peak that day, said, “Dear mother, your brother delights in the Buddha’s Dispensation; he is not dissatisfied.”

It is a great inheritance from the Teacher, namely, the seven noble treasures, and it cannot be obtained by the lazy.
Just as parents disown a wayward son, saying, "This is not our son," and he does not receive the inheritance when they die, so too, the lazy do not receive this noble inheritance; only the energetic receive it. Thus, reflection on the greatness of inheritance arises.

Moreover, your Teacher is great. When the Teacher was conceived in his mother's womb, at his renunciation, at his enlightenment, at the turning of the wheel of the Dharma, at the miracle of the twin phenomena, at his descent from the heavens, at the relinquishing of his life force, and at the time of his *parinirvana*, the ten-thousand world system trembled. Is it fitting for you to be lazy after having gone forth into the Dispensation of such a Teacher? Thus, reflection on the greatness of the Teacher arises.

Moreover, by birth, you are not of low birth now. You were born into the lineage of the *Śākya* kings, which has come down in an unbroken line from the Great Elect (*Mahāsammata*). You are the grandson of King Śuddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of Rāhula. Is it fitting for you to be lazy after having become such a son of the Conqueror (*Jina*)? Thus, reflection on the greatness of birth arises.

Moreover, Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna and the eighty great disciples realized the supramundane Dharma through energy alone. You are sharing the holy life with them. Are you not undertaking the path? Thus, reflection on the greatness of those who share the holy life arises.

Even for one who avoids lazy individuals who are like a python that has filled its belly and lies still, and who cultivates energetic individuals who are intent, for one whose mind is inclined and disposed to arouse energy in places for sitting and lying down, diligence arises. The yogi understands that the culture of this enlightenment factor arisen thus comes to completion through the path of arahantship.

Concerning the *pīti-saṃbojjhaṅga*: “There are, monks, things that are conducive to the enlightenment factor of joy. Abundant, systematic attention to them is the food conducive to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of joy and for the increase, expansion, and completion by culture of the enlightenment factor of joy when it has arisen." Thus, its arising occurs.
There, joy itself is called things that are conducive to the enlightenment factor of joy.
Systematic attention, causing its arising, is called systematic attention.

Moreover, eleven things lead to the arising of the joy enlightenment factor: mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, the *Saṃgha*, virtue, generosity, mindfulness of deities, mindfulness of peace, avoidance of rough persons, cultivation of refined persons, reviewing inspiring discourses, and being resolved upon that.

Even for one who recollects the virtues of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, pervading the entire body up to the [level of] access [concentration]. Also, for one who recollects the virtues of the Dharma and the *Saṃgha*, for one who reflects on the precepts of fourfold purity, kept unbroken for a long time, for a householder who reflects on the ten precepts and the five precepts, for one who, in times of famine or fear, gives excellent food to those sharing the holy life and reflects on their generosity, thinking, "Thus, indeed, we have given," for a householder who, at such a time, reflects on the alms given to the virtuous, for one who reflects on possessing the qualities with which the deities, endowed, have attained to divinity, for one who reflects, "The defilements suppressed by attainment do not arise for sixty or seventy years," for one who avoids rough persons who, in seeing *cetiya*s, enlightenment trees, and elders, have a rough manner revealed by acting without respect, and who lack confidence and affection for the Buddha and the like, who are like dirt on a donkey's back, for one who cultivates refined persons who have abundant confidence in the Buddha and the like, and who are mild in mind, for one who reflects on the inspiring *sūtra*s that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem, for one whose mind is inclined and disposed to arouse joy in places for sitting and lying down, joy arises.
The yogi understands that the culture of this enlightenment factor arisen thus comes to completion through the path of arahantship.

Concerning the *passaddhi-saṃbojjhaṅga*: "There are, monks, pliancy of body and pliancy of mind. Abundant, systematic attention to them is the food conducive to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of pliancy, and for the increase, expansion, and completion by culture of the enlightenment factor of pliancy when it has arisen." Thus, its arising occurs.

Moreover, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of pliancy: cultivating fine food, cultivating comfortable weather, cultivating comfortable postures, judgment according to the middle way, avoiding individuals with tense bodies, cultivating individuals with pliable bodies, and resolution upon that.

Indeed, even for one who eats fine, soothing, and agreeable food, pliancy arises from the hot and cold seasons, from cultivating agreeable seasons and postures in places for sitting and the like.
But this is not said with reference to one who, being of great character, is tolerant of all weather conditions and postures.
Pliancy arises for one who has association and dissociation, by avoiding unsuitable weather and postures and by cultivating suitable ones.
Judgment according to the middle way is reflection on one’s own deed as one’s own property and another’s deed as that of others’ property.
By this judgment according to the middle way, it arises.
Pliancy also arises for one who avoids tense-bodied individuals who wander about harming others with sticks and clubs, and for one who cultivates pliant-bodied individuals with restrained feet and hands, and for one whose mind is inclined and disposed to produce pliancy in places for sitting and lying down.
Thus, he understands that the culture of this enlightenment factor comes to completion through the path of arahantship.

The enlightenment factor of concentration: "There are, monks, things that are the sign of quietude and the sign of non-confusion. Therein, frequent right reflection is the nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, and for the increase, expansion, and completion by culture of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration." Thus, its arising occurs.

There the sign of quietude is just the quietude and in the sense of non-distraction is the sign of non-confusion to be taken.

The enlightenment factor of concentration: Moreover, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration: clarity of the object, proper management of the faculties, skill in the sign, at the right time elevating the mind, at the right time restraining the mind, at the right time gladdening the mind, at the right time practicing equanimity, avoiding persons who are not collected in mind, associating with persons who are collected in mind, reviewing the meditative absorption and liberation, and inclination for that.

Therein, clarity of the object and proper management of the faculties should be understood in the manner already stated.

Clarity of the object, proper management of the faculties: Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the kasiṇa sign.

Elevating the mind at the right time: When the mind is sluggish due to excessive sluggishness of effort, etc., at that time elevating it by bringing into being the enlightenment factors of investigation of the Dhamma, effort, and joy.

Elevating the mind at the right time: When the mind is agitated due to excessive arousal of effort, etc., at that time restraining it by bringing into being the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

Gladdening the mind at the right time: When the mind is listless owing to sluggishness in the exercise of understanding or to failure to attain the bliss of peace, then at that time he should stimulate it by reviewing the eight grounds for a sense of urgency.

The eight grounds for a sense of urgency are birth, aging, sickness, and death, the four woeful states, and the five kinds of suffering: suffering rooted in past, suffering rooted in future, suffering rooted in present.

And he generates confidence by reflecting on the qualities of the Triple Gem. This is called "gladdening the mind at the right time".

Skill in the sign, elevating the mind at the right time, elevating the mind at the right time

The enlightenment factor of equanimity: "There are, monks, things that are the basis of the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Therein, frequent right reflection is the nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, and for the increase, expansion, and completion by culture of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity." Thus, its arising occurs.

There equanimity is just the things that are the basis of the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

The enlightenment factor of equanimity: Moreover, five things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: maintaining neutrality towards beings, maintaining neutrality towards formations, avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations, cultivating persons who maintain neutrality towards beings and formations, and inclination for that.

There, in two ways he brings about maintaining neutrality towards beings: "You have come by your own karma and will depart by your own karma; even he has come by his own karma and will depart by his own karma; who then are you attached to?" Thus, by reflection on beings as possessors of their own deeds, and "In the highest sense there is really no living being, so who then are you attached to?" Thus, by reflection on beings as without essence.

In two ways he brings about maintaining neutrality towards formations: "This robe, gradually undergoing change of color and aging, will become a foot-wiper to be discarded at the end of a stick. But if it should belong to a master, he would not allow it to be destroyed in that way." Thus, by reflection on its lack of ownership, and "This is unstable and temporary." Thus, by reflection on its temporary nature.

Just as with the robe, so too the application should be made with the bowl and other things.

Maintaining neutrality towards beings, maintaining neutrality towards formations

Avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations: Here, the person, whether a householder or a monk, is attached to his sons, daughters, disciples, pupils, or preceptors. He himself performs such tasks as cutting their hair, needlework, washing robes, dyeing, receiving alms, and cooking. Not seeing them even for a moment, he looks here and there like a frightened deer, saying "Where is so-and-so novice? Where is so-and-so youth?". Even when he is asked by another to send someone for a moment for the purpose of cutting hair, etc., he does not give [permission], saying "We do not have them do even our own work, you would take them and exhaust them." This is called one who is attached to beings.

Avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations: But he who is attached to his robe, bowl, plate, knife, staff, etc., does not allow another to even touch them. When asked for something temporarily, he says "We do not even enjoy these things that we are attached to, how could we give them to you?". This is called one who is attached to formations.
But whoever among these two things is neutral and indifferent, this is called *sattasaṅkhāramajjhatto*.

Thus, this enlightenment factor of equanimity arises even for one who carefully avoids a person delighting in beings, and for one who cultivates a person who is neutral towards beings, and also for one whose mind is inclined, prone, and directed towards producing that in sitting and lying down, etc.

The yogi understands that the culture of this enlightenment factor arisen thus comes to completion through the path of arahantship.

*Saṅkhārakelāyano, sattasaṅkhāramajjhatto.*

*Iti ajjhattaṃ vā:* Thus, either by taking up the seven enlightenment factors in oneself, or in another, or at one time in oneself, or at one time in another, he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena.

Here, origination and dissolution should be known by way of the origination and dissolution of the enlightenment factors.

From here on the exposition is just according to the manner already stated. {36}

Indeed, the mindfulness that lays hold of the enlightenment factors is the Truth of Suffering. Thus the portal of deliverance for the bhikkhu who lays hold of the enlightenment factors should be understood.

The rest is as before.

*Iti ajjhattaṃ vā*

The Enlightenment Factors Section is finished.

Explanation of the Four Noble Truths Section

mula_pali:
386. ‘‘Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati catūsu ariyasaccesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati catūsu ariyasaccesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘idaṃ dukkha’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

Dukkhasaccaniddeso
mula_english:
“Again, monks, a monk abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in respect of the Four Noble Truths ( *catūsu ariyasaccesu* ).

And how, monks, does a monk abide contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in respect of the Four Noble Truths? Here, monks, a monk understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering ( *idaṃ dukkhaṃ* )’; ‘This is the origin of suffering ( *ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo* )’; ‘This is the cessation of suffering ( *ayaṃ dukkhanirodho* )’; ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering ( *ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā* )’.

The first section for recitation is finished.

Explanation of the Truth of Suffering ( *dukkhasaccaniddeso* ).
commentary_pali:
386. Evaṃ sattabojjhaṅgavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni catusaccavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ tebhūmakadhamme ‘‘idaṃ dukkha’’nti yathāsabhāvato pajānāti, tasseva kho pana dukkhassa janikaṃ samuṭṭhāpikaṃ purimataṇhaṃ ‘‘ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo’’ti, ubhinnaṃ appavattinibbānaṃ ‘‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodho’’ti, dukkhaparijānanaṃ samudayapajahanaṃ nirodhasacchikaraṇaṃ ariyamaggaṃ ‘‘ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadā’’ti yathāsabhāvato pajānātīti attho. Avasesā ariyasaccakathā ṭhapetvā jātiādīnaṃ padabhājanakathaṃ visuddhimagge vitthāritāyeva.

Dukkhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
Thus, having distinguished the contemplation of the Dhamma in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment, he now says "<hi rend="bold">Puna capara</hi>" and so on, in order to distinguish it in terms of the Four Noble Truths.

There, having established "<hi rend="bold">This is suffering, he understands it as it really is</hi>," he understands craving for the three realms as "This is suffering" according to its own nature; he understands the former craving, which is the generator and originator of that very suffering, as "This is the origin of suffering"; he understands the cessation of both, which is non-arising, as "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands the noble path, which is the full knowledge of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, and the realization of its cessation, as "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering," according to its own nature.

The remaining discussion of the Noble Truths, except for the word division concerning birth and so on, has already been extensively explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Explanation of the Discourse on the Truth of Suffering

mula_pali: 387. ‘‘Katamañca , bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ? Jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, maraṇampi dukkhaṃ, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsāpi dukkhā, appiyehi sampayogopi dukkho, piyehi vippayogopi dukkho appiyehi…pe… vippayogo dukkhotipāṭho ceva taṃniddeso ca katthaci na dissati, aṭṭhakathāyaṃpi taṃsaṃvaṇṇanā natthi, yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ, saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhāpañcupādānakkhandhāpi (ka.)dukkhā.
mula_english: 387. "And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering (duḥkhaṃ āryasatyaṃ)? Birth (jāti) is suffering (duḥkhā), aging (jarā) is suffering (duḥkhā), death (maraṇaṃ) is suffering (duḥkhaṃ), sorrow (śoka), lamentation (parideva), pain (duḥkha), grief (daurmanasya), and despair (upāyāsā) are suffering (duḥkhā), association with the unpleasant (appiyehi sampayogo) is suffering (duḥkho), separation from the pleasant (piyehi vippayogo) is suffering (duḥkho), and not getting what one wants (yam picchaṃ na labhati) is suffering (tampi dukkhaṃ). In brief, the five aggregates of clinging (saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā) are suffering (dukkhā)."

mula_pali: 388. ‘‘Katamā ca, bhikkhave, jāti? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jāti sañjāti okkanti abhinibbatti khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, jāti.
mula_english: 388. “And what, monks, is birth (jāti)? Whatever birth, taking birth (sañjāti), descent (okkanti), coming-to-be (abhinibbatti), appearance of aggregates (khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo), & acquisition of sense spheres (āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho) of the various beings in this or that group of beings, that is called birth (jāti).
commentary_pali: 388. Padabhājane pana katamā ca, bhikkhave, jātīti bhikkhave, yā jātipi dukkhāti evaṃ vuttā jāti, sā katamāti evaṃ sabbapucchāsu attho veditabbo. Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānanti idaṃ ‘‘imesaṃ nāmā’’ti niyamābhāvato sabbasattānaṃ pariyādānavacanaṃ. Tamhi tamhi sattanikāyeti idampi sabbasattanikāyapariyādānavacanaṃ jananaṃ jāti savikārānaṃ paṭhamābhinibbattakkhandhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sañjātīti idaṃ tassā eva upasaggamaṇḍitavevacanaṃ. Sā eva anupaviṭṭhākārena okkamanaṭṭhena okkanti. Nibbattisaṅkhātena abhinibbattanaṭṭhena abhinibbatti. Iti ayaṃ catubbidhāpi sammutikathā nāma . Khandhānaṃ pātubhāvoti ayaṃ pana paramatthakathā. Ekavokārabhavādīsu ekacatupañcabhedānaṃ khandhānaṃyeva pātubhāvo, na puggalassa, tasmiṃ pana sati puggalo pātubhūtoti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Āyatanānaṃ paṭilābhoti āyatanāni pātubhavantāneva paṭiladdhāni nāma honti, so tesaṃ pātubhāvasaṅkhāto paṭilābhoti attho.
commentary_english:
388.
In the *padabhājane*. Moreover, monks, what is *jāti*? Monks, that *jāti* which is said to be suffering, what is that? Thus, in all the questions, the meaning should be understood.

"*Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattāna*": This is a term for including all beings because there is no restriction such as "these are their names."

"*Tamhi tamhi sattanikāye*": This too is a term for including all collections of beings. *Jāti* is a term for the first aggregates that have arisen along with their transformations.

"*Sañjātī*": This is a decorated term for that.

That itself, by way of not sitting down, by way of the meaning of entering, is *okkanti*.

Designated as *nibbatti*, by way of the meaning of fully arising, is *abhinibbatti*.

Thus, this fourfold conventional speech is called.

"*Khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo*": This, moreover, is the ultimate discourse.

Among the *ekavokārabhavādīsu*, the arising of the aggregates is only the arising of the aggregates of the one, four, or five kinds, not of the person (*pudgala*). But when that is present, the person has arisen; this is merely a convention.

"*Āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho*": The *āyatana*s, as they arise, are said to have been obtained. That, designated as the arising of those things, is the meaning of obtaining.

mula_pali: 389. ‘‘Katamā ca, bhikkhave, jarā? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jarā jīraṇatā khaṇḍiccaṃ pāliccaṃ valittacatā āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, jarā.
mula_english:
389.

And what, monks, is aging (jarā)? Whatever aging, decrepitude (jīraṇatā), brokenness (khaṇḍiccaṃ), graying (pāliccaṃ), wrinkling (valittacatā), decline of life-force (āyuno saṃhāni), weakening of the faculties (indriyānaṃ paripāko) of the various beings in this or that group of beings (sattānam tamhi tamhi sattanikāye), that is called aging (jarā).
commentary_pali:
389.Jarāti sabhāvaniddeso. Jīraṇatāti ākārabhāvaniddeso. Khaṇḍiccantiādi vikāraniddeso. Daharakālasmiñhi dantā samasetā honti. Teyeva paripaccante anukkamena vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjitvā tattha tattha pattanti. Atha patitañca ṭhitañca upādāya khaṇḍitadantā khaṇḍitā nāma. Khaṇḍitānaṃ bhāvo khaṇḍiccanti vuccati. Anukkamena paṇḍarabhūtāni kesalomāni palitāni nāma. Palitāni sañjātāni assāti palito, palitassa bhāvo pāliccaṃ. Jarāvātappahārena sositamaṃsalohitatāya valiyo tacasmiṃ assāti valittaco, tassa bhāvo valittacatā. Ettāvatā dantakesalomatacesu vikāradassanavasena pākaṭībhūtā pākaṭajarā dassitā.

Yatheva hi udakassa vā vātassa vā aggino vā tiṇarukkhādīnaṃ saṃbhaggapalibhaggatāya vā jhāmatāya vā gatamaggo pākaṭo hoti, na ca so gatamaggo tāneva udakādīni, evameva jarāya dantādīnaṃ khaṇḍiccādivasena gatamaggo pākaṭo, cakkhuṃ ummiletvāpi gayhati, na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarā. Na hi jarā cakkhuviññeyyā hoti. Yasmā pana jaraṃ pattassa āyu hāyati, tasmā jarā ‘‘āyuno saṃhānī’’ti phalūpacārena vuttā. Yasmā daharakāle suppasannāni sukhumampi attano visayaṃ sukheneva ca gaṇhanasamatthāni cakkhādīni indriyāni jaraṃ pattassa paripakkāni ālulitāni avisadāni oḷārikampi attano visayaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthāni honti, tasmā ‘‘indriyānaṃ paripāko’’tipi phalūpacāreneva vuttā.
commentary_english:
389. *Jarā* means a designation of nature.

*Jīraṇatā* means a designation of the state of being.

*Khaṇḍicca* etc. means a designation of change.

In early youth, the teeth are uniform.

These very [teeth], when they mature, gradually undergo changes in color and reach various states.

Then, depending on what has fallen out and what remains, they are called broken teeth (*khaṇḍita-danta*).

The state of having broken teeth is called *khaṇḍicca*.

Gradually, the hairs of the head and body become white; these are called gray hairs (*palita*).

Because they have become gray, they are called *palito*, and the state of *palita* is *pāliccaṃ*.

Because the skin becomes wrinkled (*valī*) due to the striking force of the wind of old age (*jarāvāta-ppahārena*) which has dried up the flesh and blood, it is called wrinkled skin (*valittaco*), and the state of *valittaco* is *valittacatā*.

Thus, apparent aging (*pākaṭajarā*) is shown through the changes seen in the teeth, hair of the head and body, and skin.

Just as the course taken by water, wind, or fire is evident from the damaged and broken state, or the burnt state, of grass, trees, etc., and yet the course that has been taken is not the water, etc., itself, so too the course taken by aging is evident through brokenness of teeth, etc., and it is apprehended by opening the eyes, but the brokenness, etc., themselves are not aging.

Indeed, aging is not cognizable by the eye (*cakkhuviññeyyā*).

Since the life-span (*āyus*) of one who has reached aging dwindles, aging is called “decline of life (*āyuno saṃhānī*)” as a metaphor of its effect.

Since the eye faculty (*cakkhādīni indriyāni*), etc. — which in early youth are quite clear, very easily grasp even subtle objects of their respective domains, and are efficient — become deficient, confused (*ālulitāni*), unclear (*avisadāni*), and unable to grasp even gross (*oḷārikaṃ*) objects when one has reached old age, therefore it is called “weakness of faculties (*indriyānaṃ paripāko*)” also as a metaphor of its effect.

mula_pali: 390. ‘‘Katamañca, bhikkhave, maraṇaṃ? Yaṃ aṭṭhakathā oloketabbā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhā tamhā sattanikāyā cuti cavanatā bhedo antaradhānaṃ maccu maraṇaṃ kālakiriyā khandhānaṃ bhedo kaḷevarassa nikkhepo jīvitindriyassupacchedo, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, maraṇaṃ.
mula_english: 390. "And what, monks, is death (maraṇa)? That which, in whatever beings, of whatever group of beings, is the falling away (cyuti), deceasing (cavanatā), breaking up (bheda), disappearance (antaradhānaṃ), dying (maccu), death (maraṇaṃ), completion of time (kālakiriyā), break up of the aggregates (khandhānaṃ bheda), casting off of the body (kaḷevarassa nikkhepo), interruption in the life faculty (jīvitindriyassupacchedo), this, monks, is called death (maraṇa)."
commentary_pali:
390. Maraṇaniddese yanti maraṇaṃ sandhāya napuṃsakaniddeso, yaṃ maraṇaṃ cutīti vuccati, cavanatāti vuccatīti ayamettha yojanā. Tattha cutīti sabhāvaniddeso. Cavanatāti ākārabhāvaniddeso. Maraṇaṃ pattassa khandhā bhijjanti ceva antaradhāyanti ca adassanaṃ gacchanti, tasmā taṃ bhedo antaradhānanti vuccati. Maccumaraṇanti maccumaraṇaṃ, na khaṇikamaraṇaṃ. Kālakiriyāti maraṇakālakiriyā. Ayaṃ sabbāpi sammutikathāva. Khandhānaṃ bhedoti ayaṃ pana paramatthakathā. Ekavokārabhavādīsu ekacatupañcabhedānaṃ khandhānaṃyeva bhedo, na puggalassa, tasmiṃ pana sati puggalo matoti vohāramattaṃ hoti.

Kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti attabhāvassa nikkhepo. Maraṇaṃ pattassa hi niratthaṃva kaliṅgaraṃ attabhāvo patati, tasmā taṃ kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti vuttaṃ. Jīvitindriyassa upacchedo pana sabbākārato paramatthato maraṇaṃ. Etadeva sammutimaraṇanti pi vuccati. Jīvitindriyupacchedameva hi gahetvā lokiyā ‘‘tisso mato, phusso mato’’ti vadanti.

Kaḷevarassa nikkhepo
commentary_english:
390.
In the explanation of death (*maraṇa-niddeśe*): *yaṃti maraṇaṃ sandhāya napuṃsakaniddeso*, *yaṃ maraṇaṃ cutīti vuccati, cavanatāti vuccatīti ayamettha yojanā* – "regarding death, [there is] a neuter designation; that which is death is called *cuti*; *cavanatā* is said – this is the connection here."
There, *cutī* means designation by nature (*sabhāvaniddeso*).
*Cavanatā* means designation by characteristic nature (*ākārabhāvaniddeso*).
To one who has attained death (*maraṇaṃ pattassa*), the aggregates (*khandhā*) are destroyed (*bhijjanti*), disappear (*antaradhāyanti*), and go to invisibility (*adassanaṃ gacchanti*); therefore, that is called "destruction and disappearance" (*bhedo antaradhānaṃti vuccati*).
*Maccumaraṇaṃti* means continuous death (*maccumaraṇaṃ*), not momentary death (*khaṇikamaraṇaṃ*).
*Kālakiriyāti* means the action of the time of death (*maraṇakālakiriyā*).
This is all conventional language (*sammutikathāva*).
*Khandhānaṃ bhedoti* – this is the ultimate meaning (*paramatthakathā*).
Among those with characteristics such as singularity, etc. (*ekavokārabhavādīsu*), the destruction of the aggregates (*khandhānaṃ*) is itself destruction, not of the person (*puggalassa*); when that exists (*tasmiṃ pana sati*), it is merely a conventional expression (*vohāramattaṃ hoti*) to say "the person is dead" (*puggalo matoti*).

*Kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti* means the abandonment of selfhood (*attabhāvassa nikkhepo*).
For one who has attained death (*maraṇaṃ pattassa*), selfhood (*attabhāvo*) falls away (*patati*) like useless rubbish (*niratthaṃva kaliṅgaraṃ*); therefore, that is called "the rejection of the body" (*kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti vuttaṃ*).
The cutting off (*upacchedo*) of the life faculty (*jīvitindriyassa*) is, in every way (*sabbākārato*), in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), death (*maraṇaṃ*).
This very thing is also called conventional death (*sammutimaraṇaṃti pi vuccati*).
Having taken hold of just the cutting off of the life faculty (*jīvitindriyupacchedameva hi gahetvā*), worldly people (*lokiyā*) say, "Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead" (*tisso mato, phusso mato*tti vadanti).

*Kaḷevarassa nikkhepo*

mula_pali: 391. ‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, soko? Yo kho, bhikkhave, aññataraññatarena byasanena samannāgatassa aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa soko socanā socitattaṃ antosoko antoparisoko, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, soko.
mula_english: Monks, what is sorrow? Monks, whatever sorrow, sorrowing, sadness, inward sorrow, inward sadness of anyone suffering from misfortune, touched by a painful thing, that is called sorrow.
commentary_pali: 391.Byasanenāti ñātibyasanādīsu yena kenaci byasanena. Dukkhadhammenāti vadhabandhādinā dukkhakāraṇena. Phuṭṭhassāti ajjhotthaṭassa abhibhūtassa. Sokoti yo ñātibyasanādīsu vā vadhabandhanādīsu vā aññatarasmiṃ sati tena abhibhūtassa uppajjati socanalakkhaṇo soko. Socitattanti socitabhāvo. Yasmā panesa abbhantare sosento parisosento uppajjati, tasmā antosoko antoparisokoti vuccati.
commentary_english:
"By *byasanenā*," it means by any *byasana* among loss of relatives (*ñātibyasanādi*), and so forth.

"By *dukkadhammenā*," it means by a cause of suffering (*dukkha-kāraṇena*) such as execution (*vadha*), imprisonment (*bandha*), and so forth.

"By *phuṭṭhassā*," it means overwhelmed (*ajjhotthaṭassa*) and overcome (*abhibhūtassa*).

"Sorrow (*śoko*)," it means the sorrow (*śoko*) which arises, having the characteristic of lamentation (*socanalakkhaṇo*), in one who is overcome (*abhibhūtassa*) by either loss of relatives (*ñātibyasanādi*) or execution and imprisonment (*vadhabandhanādi*), and so forth, when that exists.

"By *socitatta*," it means the state of being afflicted (*socitabhāvo*).

Because this dries up (*sosento*) and completely dries up (*parisosento*) internally (*abbhantare*), therefore it is called (*vuccati*) "inner sorrow" (*antośoko*) and "inner complete sorrow" (*antopariśoko*).

mula_pali: 392. ‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, paridevo? Yo kho, bhikkhave, aññataraññatarena byasanena samannāgatassa aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa ādevo paridevo ādevanā paridevanā ādevitattaṃ paridevitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave paridevo.
mula_english: 392. Monks, what is lamentation? Monks, whatever crying, grieving, lamenting, weeping, wailing, lamentation of anyone suffering from misfortune, touched by a painful thing, that is called lamentation.
commentary_pali: 392. ‘‘Mayhaṃ dhītā, mayhaṃ putto’’ti evaṃ ādissa ādissa devanti paridevanti etenāti ādevo. Taṃ taṃ vaṇṇaṃ parikittetvā devanti etenāti paridevo. Tato parā dve tasseva bhāvaniddesā.
commentary_english:
392. "I have a daughter, I have a son," thus, again and again, they lament, therefore it is called *ādevo*.

Praising that, that quality, they lament, therefore it is called *paridevo*.

Thereafter, there are two further explanations of feeling (bhāva).

mula_pali: 393. ‘‘Katamañca , bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ? Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ kāyikaṃ asātaṃ kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ asātaṃ vedayitaṃ, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ.
mula_english: Monks, what is suffering? Monks, whatever bodily pain (kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ), bodily discomfort (kāyikaṃ asātaṃ), painful or uncomfortable feeling born of bodily contact (kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ asātaṃ vedayitaṃ) is, that, monks, is called suffering (dukkhaṃ).
commentary_pali: 393.Kāyikanti kāyapasādavatthukaṃ. Dukkhamanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ. Asātanti amadhuraṃ. Kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhanti kāyasamphassato jātaṃ dukkhaṃ. Asātaṃ vedayitanti amadhuraṃ vedayitaṃ.
commentary_english:
*Kāyika* means having a physical basis.
