*Dukkhaṃ* [means] *duḥkha* due to [its] undesirable nature.

*Asātaṃ* means unpleasant.

*Kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ* means suffering born from physical contact.

*Asātaṃ vedayitaṃ* means unpleasant feeling.

mula_pali: 394. ‘‘Katamañca , bhikkhave, domanassaṃ? Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ cetasikaṃ asātaṃ manosamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ asātaṃ vedayitaṃ, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, domanassaṃ.
mula_english: Monks, what is sadness (*daumanasya*)? Monks, whatever mental pain, mental discomfort, pain or discomfort born of mental contact, that is called sadness.
commentary_pali: 394.Cetasikanti cittasampayuttaṃ. Sesaṃ dukkhe vuttanayameva.
commentary_english:
394. *cetasika* means associated with mind (*cittasampayuttaṃ*).

The rest is as already stated in the section on suffering (*dukkhe vuttanayameva*).

mula_pali: 395. ‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, upāyāso? Yo kho, bhikkhave, aññataraññatarena byasanena samannāgatassa aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa āyāso upāyāso āyāsitattaṃ upāyāsitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, upāyāso.
mula_english: ‘‘And what, monks, is distress (upāyāso)? Whenever, monks, anyone suffering from misfortune is touched by something of a painful nature, that is distress, great distress, affliction with distress, with great distress; this, monks, is called distress (upāyāso).
commentary_pali: 395.Āyāsoti saṃsīdanavisīdanākārappatto cittakilamatho. Balavataraṃ āyāso upāyāso. Tato parā dve attattaniyābhāvadīpakā bhāvaniddesā.
commentary_english: 395. āyāsoti: weariness is the mental fatigue consisting of sinking and collapsing. A stronger weariness is upāyāsa. After that, two further instructions on mental development elucidate the absence of self and what belongs to self ( *ātman* and *ātmānīya* ).

mula_pali: 396. ‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho? Idha yassa te honti aniṭṭhā akantā amanāpā rūpā saddā gandhā rasā phoṭṭhabbā dhammā, ye vā panassa te honti anatthakāmā ahitakāmā aphāsukakāmā ayogakkhemakāmā, yā tehi saddhiṃ saṅgati samāgamo samodhānaṃ missībhāvo, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho.
mula_english: "396. Furthermore, monks, what is the suffering of association with the unpleasant (appiyehi sampayogo dukkho)? Here, whatever unwanted (aniṭṭhā), disliked (akantā), unpleasant (amanāpā) sights (rūpā), sounds (saddā), smells (gandhā), tastes (rasā), tangibles (phoṭṭhabbā), or mental objects (dhammā) there are; or whoever wishes for their harm (anatthakāmā), injury (ahitakāmā), discomfort (aphāsukakāmā), or insecurity (ayogakkhemakāmā); the encounter (saṅgati), meeting (samāgamo), union (samodhānaṃ), mixing (missībhāvo) with them—this is called, monks, the suffering of association with the unpleasant (appiyehi sampayogo dukkho)."

mula_pali: 397. ‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, piyehi vippayogo dukkho? Idha yassa te honti iṭṭhā kantā manāpā rūpā saddā gandhā rasā phoṭṭhabbā dhammā, ye vā panassa te honti atthakāmā hitakāmā phāsukakāmā yogakkhemakāmā mātā vā pitā vā bhātā vā bhaginī vā mittā vā amaccā vā ñātisālohitā vā, yā tehi saddhiṃ asaṅgati asamāgamo asamodhānaṃ amissībhāvo, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, piyehi vippayogo dukkho.
mula_english: Monks, what is the suffering of separation from the loved? Here, whoever has desirable, pleasing, attractive sights (rūpa), sounds (sadda), smells (gandha), tastes (rasa), tangibles (phoṭṭhabba), or mind-objects (dhamma); or whoever encounters well-wishers (atthakāmā), wishers of good (hitakāmā), of comfort (phāsukakāmā), of security (yogakkhemakāmā), mother (mātā) or father (pitā) or brother (bhātā) or sister (bhaginī) or friends (mittā) or colleagues (amaccā) or blood-relations (ñātisālohitā), and then is deprived of such concourse (asaṅgati), intercourse (asamāgamo), connection (asamodhānaṃ), or union (amissībhāvo), that, monks, is called being separated from the loved (piyehi vippayogo dukkho).

mula_pali: 398. ‘‘Katamañca , bhikkhave, yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ? Jātidhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati – ‘aho vata mayaṃ na jātidhammā assāma, na ca vata no jāti āgaccheyyā’ti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ. Jarādhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati – ‘aho vata mayaṃ na jarādhammā assāma, na ca vata no jarā āgaccheyyā’ti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ. Byādhidhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati ‘aho vata mayaṃ na byādhidhammā assāma, na ca vata no byādhi āgaccheyyā’ti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ. Maraṇadhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati ‘aho vata mayaṃ na maraṇadhammā assāma, na ca vata no maraṇaṃ āgaccheyyā’ti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ. Sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammānaṃ, bhikkhave, sattānaṃ evaṃ icchā uppajjati ‘aho vata mayaṃ na sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammā assāma, na ca vata no sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammā āgaccheyyu’nti. Na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ, idampi yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ.
mula_english:
398.
"And what, monks, is the suffering of not getting what one wants (yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ)? In beings subject to birth (jātidhammānaṃ sattānaṃ), monks, the wish arises, ‘Oh that we were not subject to birth (na jātidhammā assāma), and that birth (jāti) might not come to us (na ca jāti āgaccheyyā)!’

But this cannot be gained by wishing (na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ). That is not getting what one wants (yampicchaṃ na labhati) as suffering (tampi dukkhaṃ).

In beings subject to aging (jarādhammānaṃ sattānaṃ), monks, the wish arises, ‘Oh that we were not subject to aging (na jarādhammā assāma), and that aging (jarā) might not come to us!’

But this cannot be gained by wishing (na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ). That is not getting what one wants (yampicchaṃ na labhati) as suffering (tampi dukkhaṃ).

In beings subject to illness (byādhidhammānaṃ sattānaṃ), monks, the wish arises, ‘Oh that we were not subject to illness (na byādhidhammā assāma), and that illness (byādhi) might not come to us!’

But this cannot be gained by wishing (na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ). That is not getting what one wants (yampicchaṃ na labhati) as suffering (tampi dukkhaṃ).

In beings subject to death (maraṇadhammānaṃ sattānaṃ), monks, the wish arises, ‘Oh that we were not subject to death (na maraṇadhammā assāma), and that death (maraṇaṃ) might not come to us!’

But this cannot be gained by wishing (na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ). That is not getting what one wants (yampicchaṃ na labhati) as suffering (tampi dukkhaṃ).

In beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair (sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammānaṃ sattānaṃ), monks, the wish arises, ‘Oh that we were not subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair (na sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammā assāma), and that sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair (sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammā) might not come to us!’

But this cannot be gained by wishing (na kho panetaṃ icchāya pattabbaṃ). That is not getting what one wants (yampicchaṃ na labhati) as suffering (tampi dukkhaṃ)."
commentary_pali: 398.Jātidhammānanti jātisabhāvānaṃ. Icchā uppajjatīti taṇhā uppajjati. Aho vatāti patthanā. Na kho panetaṃ icchāyāti evaṃ jātiyā anāgamanaṃ vinā maggabhāvanaṃ na icchāya pattabbaṃ. Idampīti etampi upari sesāni upādāya pikāro. Yampicchanti yenapi dhammena alabbhaneyyavatthuṃ icchanto na labhati, taṃ alabbhaneyya vatthumhi icchanaṃ dukkhaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.
commentary_english:
"***jātidhammāna***nti" means *jāti* nature.

"***icchā uppajjatī***ti" means *taṇhā* arises.

"***aho vatā***ti" means desire.

"***na kho panetaṃ icchāyā***ti" means thus, without the path practice, not returning by means of *jāti* is not attainable by desire.

"***idampī***ti" means even this, taking the remainder into account, is a *pikāro*.

"***yampiccha***nti" means by whatever *dhamma* one desiring an unattainable thing does not obtain it, that desire for an unattainable thing is suffering (*dukkha*).

This method applies to all the other cases.

mula_pali:
399. ‘‘Katame ca, bhikkhave, saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā? Seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, saṅkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ.

Samudayasaccaniddeso
mula_english:
Monks, what in brief, are the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering (pañcupādānakkhandhā duhkha)? They are: the aggregate of material form as an object of clinging (rūpupādānakkhandha), the aggregate of feeling as an object of clinging (vedanupādānakkhandha), the aggregate of perception as an object of clinging (saññupādānakkhandha), the aggregate of mental formations as an object of clinging (saṅkhārupādānakkhandha), and the aggregate of consciousness as an object of clinging (viññāṇupādānakkhandha). These, monks, are called, in brief, the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering (dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ).

Explanation of the Truth of Origin
commentary_pali:
399. Khandhaniddese rūpañca taṃ upādānakkhandho cāti rūpupādānakkhandho evaṃ sabbattha.

Samudayasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
Section 399.
In the *khandha*-analysis, rūpa and that which is the aggregate of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) is the *rūpupādānakkhandha*; thus everywhere.

Explanation of the analysis of the truth of arising (*samudayasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā*).

mula_pali:
400. ‘‘Katamañca , bhikkhave, dukkhasamudayaṃ dukkhasamudayo (syā.) ariyasaccaṃ? Yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobbhavikā ponobhavikā (sī. pī.) nandīrāgasahagatā nandirāgasahagatā (sī. syā. pī.) tatratatrābhinandinī, seyyathidaṃ – kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhā.

‘‘Sā kho panesā, bhikkhave, taṇhā kattha uppajjamānā uppajjati, kattha nivisamānā nivisati? Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Kiñca loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ? Cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati. Sotaṃ loke…pe… ghānaṃ loke… jivhā loke… kāyo loke… mano loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Rūpā loke… saddā loke… gandhā loke… rasā loke… phoṭṭhabbā loke… dhammā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ loke… sotaviññāṇaṃ loke… ghānaviññāṇaṃ loke… jivhāviññāṇaṃ loke… kāyaviññāṇaṃ loke… manoviññāṇaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Cakkhusamphasso loke… sotasamphasso loke… ghānasamphasso loke… jivhāsamphasso loke… kāyasamphasso loke… manosamphasso loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Cakkhusamphassajā vedanā loke… sotasamphassajā vedanā loke… ghānasamphassajā vedanā loke… jivhāsamphassajā vedanā loke… kāyasamphassajā vedanā loke… manosamphassajā vedanā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Rūpasaññā loke… saddasaññā loke… gandhasaññā loke… rasasaññā loke… phoṭṭhabbasaññā loke… dhammasaññā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Rūpasañcetanā loke… saddasañcetanā loke… gandhasañcetanā loke… rasasañcetanā loke… phoṭṭhabbasañcetanā loke… dhammasañcetanā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Rūpataṇhā loke… saddataṇhā loke… gandhataṇhā loke… rasataṇhā loke… phoṭṭhabbataṇhā loke… dhammataṇhā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Rūpavitakko loke… saddavitakko loke… gandhavitakko loke… rasavitakko loke… phoṭṭhabbavitakko loke… dhammavitakko loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati.

‘‘Rūpavicāro loke… saddavicāro loke… gandhavicāro loke… rasavicāro loke… phoṭṭhabbavicāro loke… dhammavicāro loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ.

Nirodhasaccaniddeso
mula_english:
400. "And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering ( *duḥkhasamudayaṃ āryasatyaṃ*)? It is that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) which gives rise to rebirth, bound up with pleasure and lust, finding fresh delight now here, now there: that is to say, craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).

"But where, monks, does this craving arise, and where does it establish itself? Wherever there is what is likable and agreeable in the world, there this craving arises, and there it establishes itself.

"And what is endearing & alluring in terms of the world? The eye (*cakṣu*) in the world is agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells. The ear (*śrotra*) ... the nose (*ghāṇa*) ... the tongue (*jihvā*) ... the body (*kāya*) ... the mind (*manas*) in the world is agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Forms (*rūpa*) in the world... sounds (*śabda*) ... smells (*gandha*) ... tastes (*rasa*) ... tangible objects (*sparśa*) ... ideas (*dharma*) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) ... ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) ... nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*) ... tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*) ... body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) ... mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in the world is agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Eye-contact (*cakṣu-saṃsparśa*) ... ear-contact (*śrotra-saṃsparśa*) ... nose-contact (*ghrāṇa-saṃsparśa*) ... tongue-contact (*jihvā-saṃsparśa*) ... body-contact (*kāya-saṃsparśa*) ... mind-contact (*mano-saṃsparśa*) in the world is agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Feeling born of eye-contact (*cakṣu-saṃsparśa-jā vedanā*) ... feeling born of ear-contact (*śrotra-saṃsparśa-jā vedanā*) ... feeling born of nose-contact (*ghrāṇa-saṃsparśa-jā vedanā*) ... feeling born of tongue-contact (*jihvā-saṃsparśa-jā vedanā*) ... feeling born of body-contact (*kāya-saṃsparśa-jā vedanā*) ... feeling born of mind-contact (*mano-saṃsparśa-jā vedanā*) in the world is agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Perception of forms (*rūpasaṃjñā*) ... perception of sounds (*śabdasaṃjñā*) ... perception of smells (*gandhasaṃjñā*) ... perception of tastes (*rasasaṃjñā*) ... perception of tangible objects (*sparśasaṃjñā*) ... perception of ideas (*dharmasaṃjñā*) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Intention for forms (*rūpasaṃcetanā*) ... intention for sounds (*śabdasaṃcetanā*) ... intention for smells (*gandhasaṃcetanā*) ... intention for tastes (*rasasaṃcetanā*) ... intention for tangible objects (*sparśasaṃcetanā*) ... intention for ideas (*dharmasaṃcetanā*) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Craving for forms (*rūpatṛṣṇā*) ... craving for sounds (*śabdatṛṣṇā*) ... craving for smells (*gandhatṛṣṇā*) ... craving for tastes (*rasatṛṣṇā*) ... craving for tangible objects (*sparśatṛṣṇā*) ... craving for ideas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Thought directed at forms (*rūpavitarka*) ... thought directed at sounds (*śabdavitarka*) ... thought directed at smells (*gandhavitarka*) ... thought directed at tastes (*rasavitarka*) ... thought directed at tangible objects (*sparśavitarka*) ... thought directed at ideas (*dharmavitarka*) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

"Evaluation of forms (*rūpavicāra*) ... evaluation of sounds (*śabdavicāra*) ... evaluation of smells (*gandhavicāra*) ... evaluation of tastes (*rasavicāra*) ... evaluation of tangible objects (*sparśavicāra*) ... evaluation of ideas (*dharmavicāra*) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable, and there this craving arises, and there it dwells.

This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayaṃ āryasatyaṃ*)."

Explanation of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatyanirdeśa*).
commentary_pali:
400.Yāyaṃ taṇhāti yā ayaṃ taṇhā. Ponobbhavikāti punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punobbhavo, punobbhavo sīlaṃ assāti ponobbhavikā. Nandīrāgena saha gatāti nandīrāgasahagatā. Nandīrāgena saddhiṃ atthato ekattameva gatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatratatrābhinandinīti yatra yatra attabhāvo, tatra tatra abhinandinī. Rūpādīsu vā ārammaṇesu tatra tatra abhinandinī, rūpābhinandinī sadda, gandha, rasa, phoṭṭhabba, dhammābhinandinīti attho. Seyyathidanti nipāto. Tassa sā katamā ceti attho. Kāme taṇhā kāmataṇhā, pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Bhave taṇhā bhavataṇhā, bhavapatthanāvasena uppannassa sassatadiṭṭhisahagatassa rūpārūpabhavarāgassa ca jhānanikantiyā cetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vibhave taṇhā vibhavataṇhā, ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Idāni tassā taṇhāya vatthuṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ sā kho panesātiādimāha. Tattha uppajjatīti jāyati. Nivisatīti punappunaṃ pavattivasena patiṭṭhahati. Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpanti yaṃ lokasmiṃ piyasabhāvañceva madhurasabhāvañca. Cakkhu loketiādīsu lokasmiñhi cakkhādīsu mamattena abhiniviṭṭhā sattā sampattiyaṃ patiṭṭhitā attano cakkhuṃ ādāsatalādīsu nimittaggahaṇānusārena vippasannaṃ pañcapasādaṃ suvaṇṇavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇisīhapañjaraṃ viya maññanti, sotaṃ rajatapanāḷikaṃ viya, pāmaṅgasuttaṃ viya ca maññanti, ‘‘tuṅganāsā’’ti laddhavohāraṃ ghānaṃ vaṭṭitvā ṭhapitaharitālavaṭṭaṃ viya maññanti, jivhaṃ rattakambalapaṭalaṃ viya mudusiniddhamadhurasadaṃ maññanti, kāyaṃ sālalaṭṭhiṃ viya, suvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya ca maññanti, manaṃ aññesaṃ manena asadisaṃ uḷāraṃ maññanti. Rūpaṃ suvaṇṇakaṇikārapupphādivaṇṇaṃ viya, saddaṃ mattakaravīka kokilamandadhamitamaṇivaṃsanigghosaṃ viya, attanā paṭiladdhāni catusamuṭṭhānikagandhārammaṇādīni ‘‘kassaññassa evarūpāni atthī’’ti maññanti. Tesaṃ evaṃ maññamānānaṃ tāni cakkhādīni piyarūpāni ceva sātarūpāni ca honti. Atha nesaṃ tattha anuppannā ceva taṇhā uppajjati , uppannā ca taṇhā punappunaṃ pavattivasena nivisati. Tasmā bhagavā ‘‘cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjatī’’tiādimāha. Tattha uppajjamānāti yadā uppajjamānā hoti, tadā ettha uppajjatīti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha.

sā kho panesā uppajjatī Nivisatī Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa Cakkhu loke uppajjamānā

Nirodhasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
400. *yāyaṃ taṇhā* means this craving which is this craving.

*ponobbhavikā* means that which causes rebirth, rebirth is virtue, *ponobbhavikā* possesses virtue.

*nandīrāgena saha gatāti* means accompanied by delight and greed, *nandīrāgasahagatā*.

*nandīrāgena saddhiṃ atthato ekattameva gatāti vuttaṃ hoti* means that it is identical in meaning with delight and greed.

*tatratatrābhinandinī* means concerned with this and that: wherever personality is generated there is concern with that.

*rūpādīsu vā ārammaṇesu tatra tatra abhinandinī, rūpābhinandinī sadda, gandha, rasa, phoṭṭhabba, dhammābhinandinīti attho* means concerned with this and that in forms, etc., or objects, rejoicing in form, sound, odor, taste, tactile object, mental object.

*seyyathida*nti is a particle.

*tassa sā katamā ceti attho* means what is that?

*kāme taṇhā kāmataṇhā,* means craving in desire is desire-craving; this is a name for the greed that has the five sense qualities as its objects.

*bhave taṇhā bhavataṇhā,* means craving in existence is existence-craving; this term is an epithet for the attachment to existence in the realms of form and the formless, which arises through wanting to be reborn and is accompanied by the eternalist view and delight in absorption (*dhyāna*).

*vibhave taṇhā vibhavataṇhā,* means craving in non-existence is non-existence-craving; this term is an epithet for the greed accompanied by the annihilationist view.

Now, to show in detail the basis of that craving, he said, "*sā kho panesā*," and so forth.

There, *uppajjati* means it is born.

*nivisatī* means it becomes repeatedly established through continuity.

*yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa* means whatever in the world is of an endearing and pleasurable nature.

*cakkhu loke* etc., means in the world, beings are attached with possessiveness to the eye, etc., established in prosperity. They consider their own eye—clear, possessing the five kinds of luminosity, like a jewel cage opened in a golden airplane—in accordance with how they apprehend signs in mirrors, etc. They consider the ear like a silver pipe, and they consider the nose, which has gained the designation "high-nosed," like a circle of orpiment placed in a circle. They consider the tongue like a red blanket, soft, smooth, and of sweet taste. They consider the body like a *sāla* rod, and they consider the mind, unlike the minds of others, magnificent.

Form is like the color of golden *kaṇikāra* flowers, etc. Sound is like the sound of a drunk *karavīka* bird, a cuckoo, the soft sound of a blown jeweled flute. They think, "Others do not have such things," the four elements, the object of smell, etc., which they have obtained for themselves.

In this way, those who think in this way, those eyes, etc., are endearing and pleasurable.

Then, craving, which has not yet arisen in them, arises; and craving, which has arisen, repeatedly dwells through continuity.

Therefore, the Blessed One said, "The eye in the world is agreeable and pleasurable: therein this craving arises, therein it dwells," and so forth.

There, *uppajjamānā* means when it is in the process of arising, then craving arises in that.

This method applies to all the other cases .

*sā kho panesā, uppajjati, nivisatī, yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa, cakkhu loke, uppajjamānā*

Explanation of the discourse on the truth of cessation.

mula_pali:
401. ‘‘Katamañca , bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhaṃ dukkhanirodho (syā.) ariyasaccaṃ? Yo tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo.

‘‘Sā kho panesā, bhikkhave, taṇhā kattha pahīyamānā pahīyati, kattha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati? Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Kiñca loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ? Cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati. Sotaṃ loke…pe… ghānaṃ loke… jivhā loke… kāyo loke… mano loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Rūpā loke… saddā loke… gandhā loke… rasā loke… phoṭṭhabbā loke… dhammā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ loke… sotaviññāṇaṃ loke… ghānaviññāṇaṃ loke… jivhāviññāṇaṃ loke… kāyaviññāṇaṃ loke… manoviññāṇaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Cakkhusamphasso loke… sotasamphasso loke… ghānasamphasso loke… jivhāsamphasso loke… kāyasamphasso loke… manosamphasso loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Cakkhusamphassajā vedanā loke… sotasamphassajā vedanā loke … ghānasamphassajā vedanā loke… jivhāsamphassajā vedanā loke… kāyasamphassajā vedanā loke… manosamphassajā vedanā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Rūpasaññā loke… saddasaññā loke… gandhasaññā loke… rasasaññā loke… phoṭṭhabbasaññā loke… dhammasaññā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Rūpasañcetanā loke… saddasañcetanā loke… gandhasañcetanā loke… rasasañcetanā loke… phoṭṭhabbasañcetanā loke… dhammasañcetanā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Rūpataṇhā loke… saddataṇhā loke… gandhataṇhā loke… rasataṇhā loke… phoṭṭhabbataṇhā loke… dhammataṇhā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Rūpavitakko loke… saddavitakko loke… gandhavitakko loke… rasavitakko loke… phoṭṭhabbavitakko loke… dhammavitakko loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati.

‘‘Rūpavicāro loke… saddavicāro loke… gandhavicāro loke… rasavicāro loke… phoṭṭhabbavicāro loke… dhammavicāro loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ , etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ.

Maggasaccaniddeso
mula_english:
401. "And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering (duḥkhanirodhaṃ āryasatyaṃ)? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very thirst (tṛṣṇā), its abandonment, relinquishment, liberation, and detachment.

"And where, monks, is this thirst abandoned, where does it cease? Wherever in the world there is what is agreeable and pleasurable (priyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ), there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"And what in the world is agreeable and pleasurable? The eye (cakṣu) in the world is agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases. The ear (śrotra) in the world... the nose (ghāṇa) in the world... the tongue (jihvā) in the world... the body (kāya) in the world... the mind (manas) in the world is agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Forms (rūpa) in the world... sounds (śabda) in the world... smells (gandha) in the world... tastes (rasa) in the world... tactile objects (sparśa) in the world... mental objects (dharma) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñānaṃ) in the world... ear-consciousness (śrotravijñānaṃ) in the world... nose-consciousness (ghāṇavijñānaṃ) in the world... tongue-consciousness (jihvāvijñānaṃ) in the world... body-consciousness (kāyavijñānaṃ) in the world... mind-consciousness (manovijñānaṃ) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Eye-contact (cakṣuḥsamsparśa) in the world... ear-contact (śrotrasamsparśa) in the world... nose-contact (ghāṇasamsparśa) in the world... tongue-contact (jihvāsamsparśa) in the world... body-contact (kāyasamsparśa) in the world... mind-contact (manasamsparśa) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Feeling born of eye-contact (cakṣuḥsamsparśajā vedanā) in the world... feeling born of ear-contact (śrotrasamsparśajā vedanā) in the world... feeling born of nose-contact (ghāṇasamsparśajā vedanā) in the world... feeling born of tongue-contact (jihvāsamsparśajā vedanā) in the world... feeling born of body-contact (kāyasamsparśajā vedanā) in the world... feeling born of mind-contact (manasamsparśajā vedanā) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Perception of form (rūpasaṃjñā) in the world... perception of sound (śabdasaṃjñā) in the world... perception of smell (gandhasaṃjñā) in the world... perception of taste (rasasaṃjñā) in the world... perception of tactile object (sparśasaṃjñā) in the world... perception of mental object (dharmasaṃjñā) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Volition regarding form (rūpasaṃcetanā) in the world... volition regarding sound (śabdasaṃcetanā) in the world... volition regarding smell (gandhasaṃcetanā) in the world... volition regarding taste (rasasaṃcetanā) in the world... volition regarding tactile object (sparśasaṃcetanā) in the world... volition regarding mental object (dharmasaṃcetanā) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Craving for form (rūpataṇhā) in the world... craving for sound (śabdataṇhā) in the world... craving for smell (gandhataṇhā) in the world... craving for taste (rasataṇhā) in the world... craving for tactile object (sparśataṇhā) in the world... craving for mental object (dharmataṇhā) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Thinking about form (rūpavitarka) in the world... thinking about sound (śabdavitarka) in the world... thinking about smell (gandhavitarka) in the world... thinking about taste (rasavitarka) in the world... thinking about tactile object (sparśavitarka) in the world... thinking about mental object (dharmavitarka) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

"Pondering on form (rūpavicāra) in the world... pondering on sound (śabdavicāra) in the world... pondering on smell (gandhavicāra) in the world... pondering on taste (rasavicāra) in the world... pondering on tactile object (sparśavicāra) in the world... pondering on mental object (dharmavicāra) in the world are agreeable and pleasurable; there this thirst is abandoned, there it ceases.

This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering (duḥkhanirodhaṃ āryasatyaṃ)."

*Explanation of the Truth of the Path*
commentary_pali:
401.Asesavirāganirodhotiādīni sabbāni nibbānavevacanāneva. Nibbānañhi āgamma taṇhā asesā virajjati nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ ‘‘tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho’’ti vuccati. Nibbānañca āgamma taṇhā cajiyati paṭinissajjiyati vimuccati na allīyati, tasmā nibbānaṃ ‘‘cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo’’ti vuccati. Ekameva hi nibbānaṃ, nāmāni panassa sabbasaṅkhatānaṃ nāmapaṭipakkhavasena anekāni honti. Seyyathidaṃ, asesavirāgo asesanirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo taṇhakkhayo anuppādo appavattaṃ animittaṃ appaṇihitaṃ anāyūhanaṃ appaṭisandhi anupapatti agati ajātaṃ ajaraṃ abyādhi amataṃ asokaṃ aparidevaṃ anupāyāsaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭhanti.

Idāni maggena chinnāya nibbānaṃ āgamma appavattipattāyapi ca taṇhāya yesu vatthūsu tassā uppatti dassitā, tattheva abhāvaṃ dassetuṃ sā kho panesātiādimāha. Tattha yathā puriso khette jātaṃ tittaalābuvalliṃ disvā aggato paṭṭhāya mūlaṃ pariyesitvā chindeyya, sā anupubbena milāyitvā apaññattiṃ gaccheyya. Tato tasmiṃ khette tittaalābu niruddhā pahīnāti vucceyya, evameva khette tittaalābu viya cakkhādīsu taṇhā. Sā ariyamaggena mūlacchinnā nibbānaṃ āgamma appavattiṃ gacchati. Evaṃ gatā pana tesu vatthūsu khette tittaalābu viya na paññāyati.

sā kho panesā

Yathā ca aṭavito core ānetvā nagarassa dakkhiṇadvāre ghāteyyuṃ, tato aṭaviyaṃ corā matāti vā māritāti vā vucceyyuṃ, evaṃ aṭaviyaṃ corā viya cakkhādīsu taṇhā. Sā dakkhiṇadvāre corā viya nibbānaṃ āgamma niruddhattā nibbāne niruddhā. Evaṃ niruddhā panetesu vatthūsu aṭaviyaṃ corā viya na paññāyati, tenassā tattheva nirodhaṃ dassento ‘‘cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhatī’’tiādimāha.

Maggasaccaniddesavaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
401. "Asesavirāganirodho," and so forth, are all synonyms for *nirvāṇa*. For, having reached *nirvāṇa*, craving is completely extinguished and ceases. Therefore, that is called "the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving." And having reached *nirvāṇa*, craving is relinquished, abandoned, and liberated; it does not cling. Therefore, *nirvāṇa* is called "relinquishment, abandonment, liberation, non-attachment." Indeed, *nirvāṇa* is one, but its names are many, according to the opposing aspects of all conditioned things. Namely, complete fading away, complete cessation, relinquishment, abandonment, liberation, non-attachment, destruction of passion, destruction of hatred, destruction of delusion, destruction of craving, non-arising, non-occurrence, signless, undirected, non-accumulation, non-rebirth, non-reappearance, no-destiny, unborn, unaging, without disease, deathless, without sorrow, without lamentation, without tribulation, uncorrupted.

Now, in order to show the absence in those things in which the arising of craving, cut off by the path and attained to non-occurrence having reached *nirvāṇa*, was shown, he says, beginning with "sā kho panesā." There, just as a man, seeing a bitter gourd vine growing in a field, might cut it, seeking out the root from the top, and it would gradually wither away and go to non-cognition; then it would be said, "The bitter gourd in that field is stopped, abandoned"; even so, craving in the eye and so forth is like the bitter gourd in the field. Cut off at the root by the noble path, it goes to non-occurrence having reached *nirvāṇa*. But, having gone thus, it is not perceived in those things, like the bitter gourd in the field.

sā kho panesā Just as having brought thieves from the forest, they might kill them at the southern gate of the city, then it would be said, "The thieves are dead or killed in the forest"; even so, craving in the eye and so forth is like the thieves in the forest. Because of being stopped having reached *nirvāṇa*, like the thieves at the southern gate, it is stopped in *nirvāṇa*. But, having been stopped thus, it is not perceived in these things, like the thieves in the forest. Therefore, showing its cessation right there, he says, beginning with "The eye in the world is agreeable and pleasurable, therein this craving is abandoned, therein it ceases."

Explanation of the Discourse on the Truth of the Path

mula_pali:
402. ‘‘Katamañca, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo sammāvācā sammākammanto sammāājīvo sammāvāyāmo sammāsati sammāsamādhi.

‘‘Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sammādiṭṭhi? Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dukkhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammādiṭṭhi.

‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāsaṅkappo? Nekkhammasaṅkappo abyāpādasaṅkappo avihiṃsāsaṅkappo, ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhave, sammāsaṅkappo.

‘‘Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sammāvācā? Musāvādā veramaṇī veramaṇi (ka.) pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇī pharusāya vācāya veramaṇī samphappalāpā veramaṇī, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāvācā.

veramaṇi (ka.)

‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammākammanto? Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī adinnādānā veramaṇī kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammākammanto.

‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāājīvo? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako micchāājīvaṃ pahāya sammāājīvena jīvitaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāājīvo.

‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāvāyāmo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati; uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāvāyāmo.

‘‘Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sammāsati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; citte cittānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāsati.

‘‘Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhi? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati, sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave , sammāsamādhi. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ.

adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ
mula_english:
402. “And what, monks, is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*), right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*), right speech (*sammā-vācā*), right action (*sammā-kammanta*), right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*), right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*), right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*), right concentration (*sammā-samādhi*).

“And what, monks, is right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*)? It is, monks, the knowledge of suffering (*dukkha*), the knowledge of the origin of suffering (*dukkha-samudaya*), the knowledge of the cessation of suffering (*dukkha-nirodha*), and the knowledge of the way of practice leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadā*). This is called right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*).

“And what, monks, is right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*)? The intention of renunciation (*nekkhammasaṅkappa*), the intention of non-ill-will (*abyāpādasaṅkappa*), the intention of harmlessness (*avihiṃsāsaṅkappa*). This is called right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*).

“And what, monks, is right speech (*sammā-vācā*)? Abstaining from lying (*musāvādā veramaṇī*), from divisive speech (*pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇī*), from abusive speech (*pharusāya vācāya veramaṇī*), and from idle chatter (*samphappalāpā veramaṇī*). This is called right speech (*sammā-vācā*).

“And what, monks, is right action (*sammā-kammanta*)? Abstaining from killing (*pāṇātipātā veramaṇī*), abstaining from stealing (*adinnādānā veramaṇī*), abstaining from sexual misconduct (*kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī*). This is called right action (*sammā-kammanta*).

“And what, monks, is right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*)? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes a living by right livelihood. This is called right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*).

“And what, monks, is right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*)? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, endeavors, stirs up energy, exerts his mind, and strives to prevent the arising of unarisen evil unwholesome mental states; he generates desire, endeavors, stirs up energy, exerts his mind, and strives to overcome evil unwholesome mental states that have arisen; he generates desire, endeavors, stirs up energy, exerts his mind, and strives to produce unarisen wholesome mental states; he generates desire, endeavors, stirs up energy, exerts his mind, and strives to maintain wholesome mental states that have arisen, not to let them fade, to increase them, to develop them, and to bring them to perfection. This is called right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*).

“And what, monks, is right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*)? Here, monks, a monk abides contemplating the body in the body (*kāye kāyānupassī viharati*), ardent (*ātāpī*), clearly aware (*sampajāno*), and mindful (*satimā*), having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he abides contemplating feelings in feelings (*vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati*), ardent, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he abides contemplating mind in mind (*citte cittānupassī viharati*), ardent, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he abides contemplating mind-objects in mind-objects (*dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati*), ardent, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*).

“And what, monks, is right concentration (*sammā-samādhi*)? Here, monks, quite secluded from sense pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a monk enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second *jhāna*, which has internal assurance and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading of rapture, he remains equanimous, mindful, and alert, and experiences pleasure with the body. He enters and dwells in the third *jhāna*, of which the noble ones declare, 'Equanimous and mindful, one has a pleasant abiding.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain—as with the earlier disappearance of elation and distress—he enters and remains in the fourth *jhāna*, which has purity of mindfulness through equanimity, neither pleasure nor pain (*adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ*). This is called right concentration (*sammā-samādhi*).

This, monks, is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
commentary_pali:
402.Ayamevāti aññamaggapaṭikkhepanatthaṃ niyamanaṃ. Ariyoti taṃ taṃ maggavajjhehi kilesehi ārakattā ariyabhāvakarattā ca ariyo. Dukkhe ñāṇantiādinā catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ. Tattha purimāni dve saccāni vaṭṭaṃ, pacchimāni vivaṭṭaṃ. Tesu bhikkhuno vaṭṭe kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso hoti, vivaṭṭe natthi abhiniveso. Purimāni hi dve saccāni ‘‘pañcakkhandhā dukkhaṃ, taṇhā samudayo’’ti evaṃ saṅkhepena ca ‘‘katame pañcakkhandhā, rūpakkhandho’’tiādinā nayena vitthārena ca ācariyassa santike uggaṇhitvā vācāya punappunaṃ parivattento yogāvacaro kammaṃ karoti. Itaresu pana dvīsu saccesu nirodhasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ, maggasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpanti evaṃ savanena kammaṃ karoti. So evaṃ karonto cattāri saccāni ekapaṭivedheneva paṭivijjhati ekābhisamayena abhisameti. Dukkhaṃ pariññāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, samudayaṃ pahānapaṭivedhena, nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyāpaṭivedhena, maggaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati. Dukkhaṃ pariññābhisamayena…pe… maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayena abhisameti. Evamassa pubbabhāge dvīsu saccesu uggahaparipucchāsavanadhāraṇasammasanapaṭivedho hoti, dvīsu pana savanapaṭivedhoyeva. Aparabhāge tīsu kiccato paṭivedho hoti, nirodhe ārammaṇapaṭivedho. Paccavekkhaṇā pana pattasaccassa hoti. Ayañca ādikammiko, tasmā sā idha na vuttā.

Imassa ca bhikkhuno pubbe pariggahato ‘‘dukkhaṃ parijānāmi, samudayaṃ pajahāmi, nirodhaṃ sacchikaromi, maggaṃ bhāvemī’’ti ābhogasamannāhāramanasikārapaccavekkhaṇā natthi, pariggahato paṭṭhāya hoti. Aparabhāge pana dukkhaṃ pariññātameva…pe… maggo bhāvitova hoti. Tattha dve saccāni duddasattā gambhīrāni, dve gambhīrattā duddasāni. Dukkhasaccañhi uppattito pākaṭaṃ, khāṇukaṇṭakapahārādīsu ‘‘aho dukkha’’nti vattabbatampi āpajjati. Samudayampi khāditukāmatābhuñjitukāmatādivasena uppattito pākaṭaṃ. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhato pana ubhayampi gambhīraṃ. Iti tāni duddasattā gambhīrāni. Itaresaṃ pana dvinnaṃ dassanatthāya payogo bhavaggagahaṇatthaṃ hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya avīciphusanatthaṃ pādappasāraṇaṃ viya satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭipādanaṃ viya ca hoti. Iti tāni gambhīrattā duddasāni. Evaṃ duddasattā gambhīresu gambhīrattā ca duddasesu catūsu saccesu uggahādivasena pubbabhāgañāṇuppattiṃ sandhāya idaṃ dukkhe ñāṇantiādi vuttaṃ. Paṭivedhakkhaṇe pana ekameva taṃ ñāṇaṃ hoti.

dukkhe ñāṇa

Nekkhammasaṅkappādayo kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāviramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu tīsu ṭhānesu uppannassa akusalasaṅkappassa padapacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamāno ekova kusalasaṅkappo uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāsaṅkappo nāma.

sammāsaṅkappo

Musāvādāveramaṇiādayopi musāvādādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu catūsu ṭhānesu uppannāya akusaladussīlyacetanāya padapacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāvācā nāma .

sammāvācā

Pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādayopi pāṇātipātādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesu tīsu ṭhānesu uppannāya akusaladussīlyacetanāya akiriyato padapacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati, ayaṃ sammākammanto nāma.

sammākammanto

Micchāājīvanti khādanīyabhojanīyādīnaṃ atthāya pavattitaṃ kāyavacīduccaritaṃ. Pahāyāti vajjetvā. Sammāājīvenāti buddhapasatthena ājīvena. Jīvitaṃ kappetīti jīvitappavattiṃ pavatteti. Sammāājīvopi kuhanādīhi viramaṇasaññānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesuyeva sattasu ṭhānesu uppannāya micchājīvadussīlyacetanāya padapacchedato anuppattisādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva kusalaveramaṇī uppajjati, ayaṃ sammāājīvo nāma.

Micchāājīva Pahāyā Sammāājīvenā Jīvitaṃ kappetī sammāājīvo

Anuppannānanti ekasmiṃ vā bhave tathārūpe vā ārammaṇe attano na uppannānaṃ. Parassa pana uppajjamāne disvā ‘‘aho vata me evarūpā pāpakā akusaladhammā na uppajjeyyu’’nti evaṃ anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya. Chandaṃ janetīti tesaṃ anuppādakapaṭipattisādhakaṃ vīriyachandaṃ janeti. Vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti vīriyaṃ pavatteti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti vīriyena cittaṃ paggahitaṃ karoti. Padahatīti kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca aṭṭhi ca avasissatūti padahanaṃ pavatteti.

Anuppannāna Chandaṃ janetī Vāyamatī Vīriyaṃ ārabhatī Cittaṃ paggaṇhātī Padahatī

Uppannānanti samudācāravasena attano uppannapubbānaṃ. Idāni tādise na uppādessāmīti tesaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānanti appaṭiladdhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ. Uppannānanti tesaṃyeva paṭiladdhānaṃ. Ṭhitiyāti punappunaṃ uppattipabandhavasena ṭhitatthaṃ. Asammosāyāti avināsanatthaṃ. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti uparibhāvāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya. Bhāvanāya pāripūriyāti bhāvanāya paripūraṇatthaṃ. Ayampi sammāvāyāmo anuppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ anuppādanādicittānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana imesuyeva catūsu ṭhānesu kiccasādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānaṃ ekameva kusalavīriyaṃ uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāvāyāmo nāma.

Uppannāna Anuppannānaṃ kusalāna Uppannāna Ṭhitiyā Asammosāyā Bhiyyobhāvāyā Vepullāyā Bhāvanāya pāripūriyā sammāvāyāmo

Sammāsatipi kāyādipariggāhakacittānaṃ nānattā pubbabhāge nānā, maggakkhaṇe pana catūsu ṭhānesu kiccasādhanavasena maggaṅgaṃ pūrayamānā ekāva sati uppajjati. Ayaṃ sammāsati nāma.

sammāsati

Jhānāni pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi nānā, pubbabhāge samāpattivasena nānā, maggakkhaṇe nānāmaggavasena. Ekassa hi paṭhamamaggo paṭhamajjhāniko hoti, dutiyamaggādayopi paṭhamajjhānikā vā dutiyajjhānādīsu aññatarajhānikā vā. Ekassapi paṭhamamaggo dutiyādīnaṃ aññatarajhāniko hoti, dutiyādayopi dutiyādīnaṃ aññatarajjhānikā vā paṭhamajjhānikā vā. Evaṃ cattāropi maggā jhānavasena sadisā vā asadisā vā ekaccasadisā vā honti. Ayaṃ panassa viseso pādakajjhānaniyamena hoti.

Pādakajjhānaniyamena tāva paṭhamajjhānalābhino paṭhamajjhānā vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno maggo paṭhamajjhāniko hoti. Maggaṅgabojjhaṅgāni panettha paripuṇṇāneva honti. Dutiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno dutiyajjhāniko hoti. Maggaṅgāni panettha satta honti. Tatiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa uppanno tatiyajjhāniko. Maggaṅgāni panettha satta , bojjhaṅgāni cha honti. Esa nayo catutthajjhānato vuṭṭhāya yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ.

Āruppe catukkapañcakajjhānaṃ uppajjati, tañca lokuttaraṃ, no lokiyanti vuttaṃ, ettha kathanti? Etthāpi paṭhamajjhānādīsu yato vuṭṭhāya sotāpattimaggaṃ paṭilabhitvā arūpasamāpattiṃ bhāvetvā so āruppe uppanno, taṃ jhānikāvassa tattha tayo maggā uppajjanti. Evaṃ pādakajjhānameva niyameti.

Keci pana therā ‘‘vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamentī’’ti vadanti. Keci ‘‘puggalajjhāsayo niyametī’’ti vadanti. Keci ‘‘vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā niyametī’’ti vadanti. Tesaṃ vādavinicchayo visuddhimagge vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanādhikāre vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhīti ayaṃ pubbabhāge lokiyo aparabhāge lokuttaro sammāsamādhīti vuccati.

Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sammāsamādhī

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā cattāri saccāni pariggaṇhitvā, parassa vā, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa cattāri saccāni pariggaṇhitvā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha catunnaṃ saccānaṃ yathāsambhāvato uppattinivattivasena veditabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha catusaccapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā saccapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ, sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vā

Catusaccapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.
commentary_english:
402. " *Ayameva*" means a determining [factor] for the purpose of rejecting other paths. " *Ariyo*" means noble, because he is far from the defilements that are the faults of that path, and because he makes one noble. "*Dukkhe ñāṇa*" etc. shows the four truths as the basis for practice. There, the former two truths are the round, and the latter are the turning away from the round. In these, a *bhikkhu* has an inclination towards the round as the basis for practice, but there is no inclination towards turning away from the round. The former two truths, having learned from a teacher in brief, "the five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin," and in detail in the manner of "*katame pañcakkhandhā, rūpakkhandho*" etc., the *yogāvacara* does the practice, repeatedly reciting the words. But in the other two truths, he does the practice by hearing "*nirodhasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ, maggasaccaṃ iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ manāpaṃ*." Doing so, he penetrates the four truths with a single penetration, he comprehends with a single comprehension. He penetrates suffering with the penetration of thorough knowledge, he penetrates the origin with the penetration of abandoning, he penetrates cessation with the penetration of realization, he penetrates the path with the penetration of cultivation. He comprehends suffering with the comprehension of thorough knowledge…pe… he comprehends the path with the comprehension of cultivation. Thus, in the former part, he has the penetration of learning, questioning, hearing, holding, reflecting, and penetration in the two truths, but in the two, only the penetration of hearing. In the latter part, there is penetration in three ways, in cessation there is penetration of the object. But reviewing is of the attained truth. And this is the first practice, therefore it is not said here. And for this *bhikkhu*, formerly, from grasping, there is no reviewing in the way of application, coordination, attention, "*dukkhaṃ parijānāmi, samudayaṃ pajahāmi, nirodhaṃ sacchikaromi, maggaṃ bhāvemī*," but it is from the time of grasping. But in the latter part, suffering is thoroughly known…pe… the path is cultivated. There, two truths are difficult to see because of [their] reality, two are difficult to see because of [their] depth. For the truth of suffering is evident from its arising, and it also incurs the obligation to say "*aho dukkha*" in injuries from stumps, thorns, etc. The origin is also evident from its arising, in terms of the desire to eat, the desire to enjoy, etc. But in terms of the penetration of characteristics, both are deep. Thus, those are difficult to see because of [their] reality and deep. But for seeing the other two, the effort is like stretching out the hand to grasp the summit of existence, like stretching out the foot to touch *avīci*, and like placing the tip of a hair split into a hundred pieces on [another] tip. Thus, those are difficult to see because of [their] depth. Thus, in the four truths that are difficult to see because of [their] reality and deep, and difficult to see because of [their] depth, "*dukkhe ñāṇa*" etc. is said in reference to the arising of knowledge in the former part in terms of learning etc. But at the moment of penetration, that knowledge is only one. "*Dukkhe ñāṇa*" Renunciation-thought etc. are different in the former part because of the difference in the perceptions of abstaining from sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness, but at the moment of the path, only one skillful thought arises, filling the limb of the path in the manner of establishing non-arising from cutting off the cause of unskillful thought that arose in these three places. This is called "*sammāsaṅkappo*" (right intention). "*Sammāsaṅkappo*" Abstaining from false speech etc. are also different in the former part because of the difference in the perceptions of abstaining from false speech etc., but at the moment of the path, only one skillful abstaining arises, filling the limb of the path in the manner of establishing non-arising from cutting off the cause of unskillful immoral intention that arose in these four places. This is called "*sammāvācā*" (right speech). "*Sammāvācā*" Abstaining from killing etc. are also different in the former part because of the difference in the perceptions of abstaining from killing etc., but at the moment of the path, only one skillful abstaining arises, filling the limb of the path in the manner of establishing non-arising from cutting off the cause of unskillful immoral intention that arose in these three places through non-action. This is called "*sammākammanto*" (right action). "*Sammākammanto*" "*Micchāājīva*" (wrong livelihood) means wrong conduct of body and speech that is engaged in for the sake of food etc. "*Pahāya*" means having avoided. *Sammāājīvenā* means by a right way of livelihood that is praised by the Buddhas. *Jīvitaṃ kappetī* means he carries on the continuity of his life. Right livelihood, too, is diverse in its preliminary stage due to the variety of intentions to abstain from deceit and so on. However, at the moment of the path, the single wholesome abstinence that arises in these very seven places, fulfilling the path factor in terms of accomplishing non-occurrence by cutting off the basis of wrong livelihood and bad moral conduct consciousness, is called *sammāājīvo* (right livelihood). *Micchāājīva pahāya sammāājīvenā jīvitaṃ kappetī sammāājīvo* *Anuppannāna*nti means for those evil, unwholesome qualities of *dhammas* that have not arisen for oneself in a certain existence or in a corresponding object, thinking, "Oh, may such evil, unwholesome qualities never arise in me!" Seeing them arising in another, *dhammānaṃ anuppādāya*—for the non-arising of those evil, unwholesome qualities. *Chandaṃ janetī* means he generates zeal ( *chanda*), energetic zeal ( *vīriyachandaṃ*), for accomplishing the practice that prevents their arising. *Vāyamatī* means he makes an effort. *Vīriyaṃ ārabhatī* means he initiates energy. *Cittaṃ paggaṇhātī* means he makes his mind uplifted with energy. *Padahatī* means he initiates striving, [thinking,] "Let only skin, sinew, and bone remain!" *Anuppannāna chandaṃ janetī vāyamatī vīriyaṃ ārabhatī cittaṃ paggaṇhātī padahatī* *Uppannāna*nti means for those that have previously arisen for oneself in terms of habitual practice. *Tesaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti*—he generates zeal for abandoning them, [thinking,] "Now I will not let them arise in such a way!" *Anuppannānaṃ kusalāna*nti means for those wholesome [qualities] such as the first jhāna, etc., that have not been attained. *Uppannāna*nti means for those very [qualities] that have been attained. *Ṭhitiyā*ti means for their stability, in the sense of lasting in terms of the continuity of repeated arising. *Asammosāyā*ti means for their non-disappearance. *Bhiyyobhāvāyā*ti means for the state of being higher. *Vepullāyā*ti means for the state of being extensive. *Bhāvanāya pāripūriyā*ti means for the fulfillment of cultivation. This right effort ( *sammāvāyāmo*), too, is diverse in its preliminary stage due to the variety of minds regarding the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome qualities, etc. However, at the moment of the path, the single wholesome energy that arises in these very four places, fulfilling the path factor in terms of accomplishing the task, is called *sammāvāyāmo* (right effort). *Uppannāna anuppannānaṃ kusalāna uppannāna ṭhitiyā asammosāyā bhiyyobhāvāyā vepullāyā bhāvanāya pāripūriyā sammāvāyāmo* Right mindfulness ( *sammāsati*), too, is diverse in its preliminary stage due to the variety of minds that take up the body, etc. However, at the moment of the path, the single mindfulness that arises in the four places, fulfilling the path factor in terms of accomplishing the task, is called *sammāsati* (right mindfulness). *Sammāsati* The *jhānas* are diverse both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path. In the preliminary stage, they are diverse in terms of attainment; at the moment of the path, they are diverse according to the diversity of paths. For the first path of one [person] is jhāna-related to the first jhāna. The second path and so on can be jhāna-related to the first jhāna or to any jhāna among the second jhāna and so on. For even the first path of one [person] can be jhāna-related to any jhāna among the second and so on; the second and so on can be jhāna-related to any jhāna among the second and so on, or to the first jhāna. Thus, all four paths, in terms of jhāna, can be similar or dissimilar or similar in one respect. But this is his distinction due to governance by the basic jhāna. In governance by the basic jhāna, the path that arises for one who has gained the first jhāna, when he emerges from the first jhāna and is contemplating, is jhāna-related to the first jhāna. The path factors and enlightenment factors are entirely complete here. The path that arises for one who emerges from the second jhāna and is contemplating is jhāna-related to the second jhāna. Here there are seven path factors. The path that arises for one who emerges from the third jhāna and is contemplating is jhāna-related to the third jhāna. Here there are seven0394"/>, and the enlightenment factors are six. This is the method: from the fourth *jhāna* up to the peak of existence (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).

formless Four- or fivefold *jhāna* arises; and that is supramundane, not mundane, it is said. What is here? Here also, from the first *jhāna*, having risen, having attained the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), having developed the formless attainment (*arūpasamāpatti*), he arises in the formless realm; the *jhānika* certainly has three paths arising there. Thus, equanimity governs only the path.

Some elders, however, say, "The aggregates (*khandhā*) that are the object of insight (*vipassanā*) govern." Some say, "Personal inclination governs." Some say, "Emerging insight (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*) governs." The resolution of their arguments should be understood just by the method already stated in the section on emerging insight (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*) in the *Visuddhimagga*.

This is called, *bhikkhus*, right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*)—this is called mundane right concentration in the former part, and supramundane right concentration in the latter part.

This is called, *bhikkhus*, right concentration

Thus, internally—thus, either one's own four truths (*cattāri saccāni*) having grasped, or another's, or at one time one's own, at another time another's four truths having grasped, in phenomena, contemplating phenomena, he dwells. Herein, the arising and dissolution of the four truths should be understood according to possibility by way of arising and ceasing. From here on, it is just according to the manner already stated. Because, indeed, here, mindfulness is the exclusive approhender of the four truths, and suffering is truth, thus having made a *yojana*, the means of escape for the *bhikkhu* who apprehends the truth should be understood; the rest is just the same.

Thus, internally

The section on the four truths is finished.

mula_pali:
403. ‘‘Iti ajjhattaṃ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati. ‘Atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati, na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati catūsu ariyasaccesu.

Saccapabbaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Dhammānupassanā niṭṭhitā.
mula_english:
“In this way, he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects internally, or he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects externally, or he abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects both internally and externally. He abides contemplating arising phenomena in mind-objects, he abides contemplating vanishing-phenomena in mind-objects, he abides contemplating both arising and vanishing phenomena in mind-objects. Or else, mindfulness that “there are mind-objects” is present just to the extent necessary for knowledge and awareness. And he abides detached, not grasping at anything in the world. That is how a *bhikkhu* abides contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects in terms of the Four Noble Truths.

The chapter on truth is finished.

Contemplation of mind-objects is finished.

mula_pali:
404. ‘‘Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya sattavassāni, tassa dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme aññā; sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā.

‘‘Tiṭṭhantu, bhikkhave, sattavassāni. Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya cha vassāni…pe… pañca vassāni… cattāri vassāni… tīṇi vassāni… dve vassāni… ekaṃ vassaṃ… tiṭṭhatu, bhikkhave, ekaṃ vassaṃ. Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya sattamāsāni, tassa dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme aññā; sati vā upādisese anāgāmitā.

‘‘Tiṭṭhantu , bhikkhave, satta māsāni. Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya cha māsāni…pe… pañca māsāni… cattāri māsāni… tīṇi māsāni … dve māsāni… ekaṃ māsaṃ… aḍḍhamāsaṃ… tiṭṭhatu, bhikkhave, aḍḍhamāso. Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya sattāhaṃ, tassa dvinnaṃ phalānaṃ aññataraṃ phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme aññā; sati vā upādisese anāgāmitāti.
mula_english:
404. “Monks (bhikkhave), if anyone should develop these four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) in this way for seven years (sattavassāni), one of two fruits (*phala*) can be expected for him: either knowledge (*aññā*) right here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-returning (*anāgāmitā*).

“Let alone seven years (sattavassāni), monks (bhikkhave). If anyone should develop these four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) in this way for six years… for five years… for four years… for three years… for two years… for one year… Let alone one year, monks (bhikkhave).

Monks (bhikkhave), if anyone should develop these four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) in this way for seven months (sattamāsāni), one of two fruits (*phala*) can be expected for him: either knowledge (*aññā*) right here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-returning (*anāgāmitā*).

“Let alone seven months (satta māsāni), monks (bhikkhave). If anyone should develop these four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) in this way for six months… for five months… for four months… for three months… for two months… for one month… for half a month… Let alone half a month (aḍḍhamāso), monks (bhikkhave).

Monks (bhikkhave), if anyone should develop these four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) in this way for seven days (sattāhaṃ), one of two fruits (*phala*) can be expected for him: either knowledge (*aññā*) right here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-returning (*anāgāmitā*).”
commentary_pali:
404. Ettāvatā ānāpānapabbaṃ catuiriyāpathapabbaṃ catusampajaññapabbaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ catudhātuvavatthānaṃ navasivathikā vedanānupassanā cittānupassanā nīvaraṇapariggaho khandhapariggaho āyatanapariggaho bojjhaṅgapariggaho saccapariggahoti ekavīsati kammaṭṭhānāni. Tesu ānāpānaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ navasivathikāti ekādasa appanākammaṭṭhānāni honti. Dīghabhāṇakamahāsīvatthero pana ‘‘navasivathikā ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttā’’ti āha. Tasmā tassa matena dveyeva appanākammaṭṭhānāni, sesāni upacārakammaṭṭhānāni. Kiṃ panetesu sabbesu abhiniveso jāyatīti? Na jāyati. Iriyāpathasampajaññanīvaraṇabojjhaṅgesu hi abhiniveso na jāyati, sesesu jāyatīti. Mahāsīvatthero panāha ‘‘etesupi abhiniveso jāyati. Ayañhi ‘atthi nu kho me cattāro iriyāpathā udāhu natthi, atthi nu kho me catusampajaññaṃ udāhu natthi, atthi nu kho me pañcanīvaraṇā udāhu natthi, atthi nu kho me sattabojjhaṅgā udāhu natthī’ti evaṃ pariggaṇhāti. Tasmā sabbattha abhiniveso jāyatī’’ti.

Yo hi koci, bhikkhaveti yo hi koci, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā upāsako vā upāsikā vā. Evaṃ bhāveyyātiādito paṭṭhāya vuttena bhāvanānukkamena bhāveyya. Pāṭikaṅkhanti paṭikaṅkhitabbaṃ icchitabbaṃ avassaṃbhāvīti attho. Aññāti arahattaṃ. Sati vā upādiseseti upādānasese vā sati aparikkhīṇe. Anāgāmitāti anāgāmibhāvo.

Yo hi koci, bhikkhave Evaṃ bhāveyyā Pāṭikaṅkha Aññā Sati vā upādisese Anāgāmitā

Evaṃ sattannaṃ vassānaṃ vasena sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ dassetvā puna tato appatarepi kāle dassento tiṭṭhantu, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Sabbampi cetaṃ majjhimassa veneyyapuggalassa vasena vuttaṃ, tikkhapaññaṃ pana sandhāya ‘‘pātova anusiṭṭho sāyaṃ visesaṃ adhigamissati, sāyaṃ anusiṭṭho pāto visesaṃ adhigamissatī’’ti vuttaṃ. Iti bhagavā ‘‘evaṃ niyyānikaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāsana’’nti dassetvā ekavīsatiyāpi ṭhānesu arahattanikūṭena desitaṃ desanaṃ niyyātento ‘‘ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo…pe… iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta’’nti āha. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti. Desanāpariyosāne pana tiṃsa bhikkhusahassāni arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsūti.

tiṭṭhantu, bhikkhave

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
404. With this, the following twenty-one subjects of meditation have been stated: breathing (*ānāpāna*), the modes of deportment (*catuiriyāpatha*), mindfulness and clear comprehension (*catusampajañña*), the thirty-two parts of the body (*dvattiṃsākāra*), the determination of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*), the nine cemetery contemplations (*navasivathikā*), contemplation of feeling (*vedanānupassanā*), contemplation of consciousness (*cittānupassanā*), laying hold on the hindrances (*nīvaraṇapariggaha*), laying hold on the aggregates (*khandhapariggaha*), laying hold on the sense-bases (*āyatanapariggaha*), laying hold on the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅgapariggaha*), and laying hold on the truths (*saccapariggaha*).

Among these, breathing, the thirty-two parts, and the nine cemetery contemplations are eleven subjects of meditation which produce full absorption (*appanākammaṭṭhānāni*).

The Dīgha-bhāṇaka Mahāsīvatthera, however, said, "The nine cemetery contemplations (*navasivathikā*) are stated by way of contemplation of misery (*ādīnavānupassanāvasena*)."

Therefore, according to his view, only two subjects—those of breathing and the thirty-two parts—produce full absorption (*appanākammaṭṭhānāni*); the rest produce only partial absorption (*upacārakammaṭṭhānāni*).

Is there attachment in all of these? No, there is not.

Indeed, there is no attachment in the modes of deportment, mindfulness and clear comprehension, the hindrances and the enlightenment factors, but there is attachment in the rest.

Mahāsīvatthera, however, says, "There is attachment even in these.

For this person ascertains thus: 'Do I have the four modes of deportment or do I not? Do I have mindfulness and clear comprehension or do I not? Do I have the five hindrances or do I not? Do I have the seven enlightenment factors or do I not?'

Therefore, there is attachment everywhere."

"If anyone, monks (*yo hi koci bhikkhave*)" means if any monk (*bhikkhu*) or nun (*bhikkhunī*) or layman (*upāsako*) or laywoman (*upāsikā*).

"Thus he should develop (*evaṃ bhāveyyā*)" means he should develop in the order of development stated from the beginning.

"Expected (*pāṭikaṅkha*)" means to be expected, to be desired, necessarily so, is the meaning.

"Knowledge (*aññā*)" means the state of an *arhat* (*arahattaṃ*).

"While the residue of existence remains (*sati vā upādisese*)" means while the residue of clinging remains (*upādānasese*) or is not exhausted (*aparikkhīṇe*).

"*Anāgāmitā*" means the state of a Non-Returner (*anāgāmibhāvo*).

If anyone, monks, should develop thus, it is to be expected that, while the residue of existence remains, it leads to *anāgāmitā*. Showing the state of leading outwards of the Dispensation (*sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ*) in dependence on seven years, and again showing it in a shorter time than that, he says, "May they remain, monks (*tiṭṭhantu, bhikkhave*)," and so forth.

All of this was stated in dependence on a person of middling teachability (*majjhimassa veneyyapuggalassa vasena*), but with reference to one of sharp wisdom (*tikkhapaññaṃ*), it was said, "If advised in the morning, he will attain distinction in the evening; if advised in the evening, he will attain distinction in the morning."

Thus, the Blessed One (*bhagavā*), having shown that "Thus, monks, my Dispensation leads outwards (*evaṃ niyyānikaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāsana*)," bringing to a close the teaching (*desanaṃ*) that was crowned with *arhatship* (*arahattanikūṭena*) in twenty-one places, and bringing it out, said, "This is the only way, monks (*ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo*)…pe… In this regard, what was said, this was said in dependence on that (*idametaṃ paṭicca vutta*)."

The rest is clear in meaning.

At the conclusion of the discourse (*desanāpariyosāne*), thirty thousand monks were established in *arhatship*.

May they remain, monks.

Thus ends the commentary on the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* in the *Sumangalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

mula_pali:
405. ‘‘Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya ñāyassa adhigamāya nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya yadidaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhānāti. Iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta’’nti. Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.
mula_english:
405. "Monks, this is the direct path, the only way (ekāyano maggo), for the purification of beings (sattānaṃ visuddhiyā), for overcoming sorrow and lamentation (sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya), for the cessation of suffering and grief (dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya), for attaining the right knowledge (ñāyassa adhigamāya), and for the realization of *nirvāṇa* (nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya)—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (cattāro satipaṭṭhānāti)."

It is with reference to this that it was said (iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta’’nti).

This is what the Blessed One (bhagavā) said (idamavoca bhagavā).

The monks (bhikkhū), delighted (attamanā), rejoiced in the Blessed One's (bhagavato) words (bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti).

The Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ), the ninth (navamaṃ), is concluded (niṭṭhitaṃ).

mula_pali:
406. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā kumārakassapo kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi yena setabyā nāma kosalānaṃ nagaraṃ tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ āyasmā kumārakassapo setabyāyaṃ viharati uttarena setabyaṃ siṃsapāvane sīsapāvane (syā.). Tena kho pana samayena pāyāsi rājañño setabyaṃ ajjhāvasati sattussadaṃ satiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ sadhaññaṃ rājabhoggaṃ raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinnaṃ rājadāyaṃ brahmadeyyaṃ.

Pāyāsirājaññavatthu
mula_english:
Thus have I heard. On one occasion, the venerable Kumārakassapa, while wandering in Kosala, arrived together with a large Saṅgha of monks, about five hundred monks, at a town of the Kosalas named Setabyā.

There the venerable Kumārakassapa was staying near Setabyā in the *śiṃśapā* (rosewood) forest to the north of Setabyā.

At that time, Prince Payāsi was residing at Setabyā, a populous place, full of grass, timber, water, and grain, a royal possession given by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift, a *brahmadeyya* (brahmin grant).

The subject of Prince Payāsi.
commentary_pali:
406.Evaṃme sutanti pāyāsirājaññasuttaṃ. Tatrāyamapubbapadavaṇṇanā – āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ. Kumārakassapoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kumārakāle pabbajitattā pana bhagavatā ‘‘kassapaṃ pakkosatha, idaṃ phalaṃ vā khādanīyaṃ vā kassapassa dethā’’ti vutte ‘‘katarakassapassā’’ti. ‘‘Kumārakassapassā’’ti evaṃ gahitanāmattā tato paṭṭhāya vuḍḍhakālepi ‘‘kumārakassapo’’ tveva vuccati. Apica rañño posāvanikaputtattāpi taṃ kumārakassapoti sañjāniṃsu.

Ayaṃ panassa pubbayogato paṭṭhāya āvibhāvakathā – thero kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle seṭṭhiputto ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ citrakathiṃ ekaṃ attano sāvakaṃ etadagge ṭhapentaṃ disvā bhagavato sattāhaṃ dānaṃ datvā ‘‘ahampi bhagavā anāgate ekassa buddhassa ayaṃ thero viya citrakathī sāvako bhavāmī’’ti patthanaṃ katvā puññāni karonto kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tadā kira parinibbutassa bhagavato sāsane osakkante pañca bhikkhū nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā pabbataṃ āruyha samaṇadhammaṃ akaṃsu. Saṅghatthero tatiyadivase arahattaṃ patto, anuthero catutthadivase anāgāmī ahosi, itare tayo visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkontā devaloke nibbattā.

Tesaṃ ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devesu ca manussesu ca sampattiṃ anubhavantānaṃ eko takkasilāyaṃ rājakule nibbattitvā pakkusāti nāma rājā hutvā bhagavantaṃ uddissa pabbajitvā rājagahaṃ uddissa āgacchanto kumbhakārasālāyaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā anāgāmiphalaṃ patto. Eko ekasmiṃ samuddapaṭṭane kulaghare nibbattitvā nāvaṃ āruyha bhinnanāvo dārucīrāni nivāsetvā lābhasampattiṃ patto ‘‘ahaṃ arahā’’ti cittaṃ uppādetvā ‘‘na tvaṃ arahā, gaccha, satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchā’’ti atthakāmāya devatāya codito tathā katvā arahattaphalaṃ patto.

Eko rājagahe ekissā kuladārikāya kucchimhi uppanno. Sā ca paṭhamaṃ mātāpitaro yācitvā pabbajjaṃ alabhamānā kulagharaṃ gantvā gabbhaṃ gaṇhi . Gabbhasaṇṭhitampi ajānanti sāmikaṃ ārādhetvā tena anuññātā bhikkhunīsu pabbajitā, tassā gabbhanimittaṃ disvā bhikkhuniyo devadattaṃ pucchiṃsu. So ‘‘assamaṇī’’ti āha. Dasabalaṃ pucchiṃsu. Satthā upālittheraṃ sampaṭicchāpesi. Thero sāvatthinagaravāsīni kulāni visākhañca upāsikaṃ pakkosāpetvā sodhento ‘‘pure laddho gabbho, pabbajjā arogā’’ti āha. Satthā ‘‘suvinicchitaṃ adhikaraṇa’’nti therassa sādhukāramadāsi. Sā bhikkhunī suvaṇṇabimbasadisaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃ gahetvā rājā pasenadi kosalo posāpesi. ‘‘Kassapo’’ti cassa nāmaṃ katvā aparabhāge alaṅkaritvā satthu santikaṃ netvā pabbājesi. Iti naṃ rañño posāvanikaputtattāpi ‘‘kumārakassapo’’ti sañjāniṃsūti. Taṃ ekadivasaṃ andhavane samaṇadhammaṃ karontaṃ atthakāmā devatā pañhe uggahāpetvā ‘‘ime pañhe bhagavantaṃ pucchā’’ti āha. Thero pañhe pucchitvā pañhavissajjanāvasāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Bhagavāpi taṃ citrakathikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

Setabyāti tassa nagarassa nāmaṃ. Uttarena setabyanti setabyato uttaradisāya. Rājaññoti anabhisittakarājā. Diṭṭhigatanti diṭṭhiyeva. Yathā gūthagataṃ muttagatanti vutte na gūthādito aññaṃ atthi, evaṃ diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigataṃ. Itipi natthīti taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ apadisitvā evampi natthīti vadati. Purā…pe… saññāpetīti yāva na saññāpeti.

Setabyā Uttarena setabya Rājañño Diṭṭhigata Itipi natthī Purā…pe… saññāpetī

Candimasūriyaupamāvaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
406. Thus have I heard. This is from the Pāyāsi-rājañña-sutta.

Here is an explanation of the words: *Āyasmā* is a term of endearment. *Kumārakassapa* was his name. Because he went forth in his youth, when the Blessed One said, “Call Kassapa, give this fruit or food to Kassapa,” [people asked,] “Which Kassapa?” Because he was known as “Kumārakassapa,” from then on, even in old age, he was called “Kumārakassapa.” Moreover, because he was the king’s adopted son, they recognized him as Kumārakassapa.

This is the story of his manifestation from a previous endeavor: It seems that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was the son of a wealthy man. One day, seeing the Blessed One placing a certain disciple of his, a skilled speaker, at the forefront, he gave alms to the Blessed One for seven days, and made the aspiration: “May I also, in the future, become a disciple of a Buddha, a skilled speaker like this elder.” Making merit, he was not able to bring about a distinction, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa.

It seems that at that time, when the dispensation of the Blessed One was declining after his complete extinction, five monks tied a ladder and climbed a mountain, and performed the ascetic life. The Saṅghathera attained arahantship on the third day, the Anuthera became a non-returner on the fourth day, and the other three, being unable to bring about a distinction, were reborn in the world of the gods.

Of these, after experiencing prosperity among gods and humans for an era of Buddhas, one was reborn in a royal family in Takkasilā and, becoming a king named Pukkusāti, went forth dedicating himself to the Blessed One, and, coming towards Rājagaha, hearing the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma in a potter's hall, attained the fruit of non-returning.

One was reborn in a family in a coastal city, went aboard a ship, had his ship wrecked, put on bark clothes, and attained gain and prosperity, generated the thought, “I am an Arhat,” was urged by a deity who desired his welfare, “You are not an Arhat, go, approach the Teacher and ask a question,” did so, and attained the fruit of arahantship.

One was born in Rājagaha in the womb of a certain woman from a good family. She, first asking her parents [for permission] to go forth, not obtaining it, went to a family home and conceived a child. Not knowing that she was pregnant, she pleased her husband and, being permitted by him, went forth among the nuns. Seeing the sign of the pregnancy, the nuns asked Devadatta. He said, "She is not an ascetic." They asked the One with Ten Powers. The Teacher had Upālitthera investigate. The elder, summoning the families living in Sāvatthinagara and the female lay follower Visākha, investigating, said, "The pregnancy was conceived before, the going forth is healthy." The Teacher gave his approval to the elder, saying, "The matter is well decided." That nun gave birth to a son resembling a golden statue. Taking him, King Pasenadi Kosala raised him. Naming him "Kassapa," later, having him adorned, he took him to the Teacher and had him go forth. Thus, because he was the adopted son of the king, they recognized him as "Kumārakassapa."

One day, while he was practicing the ascetic life in the Andhavana, a deity desiring his welfare had him learn some questions and said, “Ask the Blessed One these questions.” The elder, asking the questions, at the end of the answers to the questions, attained arahantship. The Blessed One also placed him at the forefront of the monks who were skilled speakers.

*Setabyā* is the name of that city. *Uttarena Setabyā* means to the north of Setabyā. *Rājañño* means an unanointed king.
*Diṭṭhigata* means simply *diṭṭhi* (view).

Just as, when it is said "gone to excrement" (*gūthagataṃ*), "gone to urine" (*muttagataṃ*), there is nothing other than excrement, so *diṭṭhigata* is simply *diṭṭhi*.

"*Itipi natthi*" means having pointed out that particular cause, he says, "Even in this way, it does not exist."

"*Purā...pe...saññāpetī*" means as long as he does not make [it] known.

Explanation of the simile of the moon and the sun.

mula_pali: 407. Tena kho pana samayena pāyāsissa rājaññassa evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti – ‘‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ sukaṭakkaṭānaṃ (sī. pī.) kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’’ti. Assosuṃ kho setabyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā – ‘‘samaṇo khalu bho kumārakassapo samaṇassa gotamassa sāvako kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi setabyaṃ anuppatto setabyāyaṃ viharati uttarena setabyaṃ siṃsapāvane. Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ kumārakassapaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato – ‘paṇḍito byatto medhāvī bahussuto cittakathī kalyāṇapaṭibhāno vuddho buddho (syā. ka.) ceva arahā ca. Sādhu kho pana tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ dassanaṃ hotī’’’ti.
