Note: vīsatidhā (perhaps).

Note: ophuni (perhaps).

Then that fire-tending ( *aggiko*) ascetic (*jaṭilo*) went to his hermitage ( *assamo*) in the country (*janapade*), having finished that task (*karaṇīyaṃ tīretvā*); having gone to that boy ( *taṃ dārakaṃ*) he said this ( *etadavoca*) – ‘Why, dear ( *tāta*), has the fire (*aggi*) not gone out ( *na nibbuto* )?’ ‘Here, dear ( *tāta*), the fire ( *aggi*) went out ( *nibbāyi*) on me, while I was indulging in play (*khiḍḍāpasutassa*).

Then I thought ( *etadahosi*) – “Father ( *pitā* ) said this ( *avaca*) to me ( *maṃ*): ‘Dear ( *tāta*), tend ( *paricareyyāsi*) the fire (*aggiṃ*)! And don't ( *mā ca te*) let the fire ( *aggi*) go out ( *nibbāyi*)! If ( *sace ca te*) the fire (*aggi*) should go out ( *nibbāyeyya*), here ( *ayaṃ*) is an axe ( *vāsī*), these ( *imāni*) are sticks ( *kaṭṭhāni*), this ( *idaṃ*) is a fire-stick set ( *araṇisahitaṃ*), having produced ( *nibbattetvā*) the fire ( *aggiṃ*), you should tend ( *paricareyyāsi*) the fire (*aggiṃ*)!’”

“What if I now ( *yaṃnūnāhaṃ*) produce ( *nibbattetvā*) the fire (*aggiṃ*) and tend ( *paricareyya’’nti*) the fire (*aggiṃ*)?”

Then I ( *ahaṃ*), dear ( *tāta*), chopped ( *tacchiṃ*) the fire-stick set ( *araṇisahitaṃ*) with an axe ( *vāsiyā*) – “Perhaps ( *appeva nāma*) I will obtain ( *adhigaccheyya’’nti*) the fire ( *aggiṃ*)!”

But I did not ( *nevāhaṃ*) obtain ( *adhigacchiṃ*) the fire (*aggiṃ*).

I split ( *phālesiṃ*) the fire-stick set ( *araṇisahitaṃ*) in two ( *dvidhā*), I split ( *phālesiṃ*) it in three ( *tidhā*), I split ( *phālesiṃ*) it in four ( *catudhā*), I split ( *phālesiṃ*) it in five ( *pañcadhā*), I split ( *phālesiṃ*) it in ten ( *dasadhā*), I split ( *phālesiṃ*) it in a hundred ( *satadhā*) pieces, I made ( *akāsiṃ*) small pieces ( *sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ*), having made ( *karitvā*) small pieces ( *sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ*), I pounded ( *koṭṭesiṃ*) it in a mortar ( *udukkhale*), having pounded ( *koṭṭetvā*) it in a mortar ( *udukkhale*), I winnowed ( *opuniṃ*) it in a great wind ( *mahāvāte*) – “Perhaps ( *appeva nāma*) I will obtain ( *adhigaccheyya’’nti*) the fire ( *aggiṃ*)!”

But I did not ( *nevāhaṃ*) obtain ( *adhigacchi’’’nti*) the fire (*aggiṃ*)!”

Then that fire-tending ( *aggikassa*) ascetic (*jaṭilassa*) thought ( *etadahosi*) – “Since ( *yāva*) this boy ( *ayaṃ dārako*) is stupid ( *bālo abyatto*), how ( *kathañhi nāma*) will he search ( *gavesissatī’ti*) for the fire ( *aggiṃ*) in an unfitting way ( *ayoniso*)?”

While he ( *tassa*) was looking on ( *pekkhamānassa*), having taken ( *gahetvā*) the fire-stick set ( *araṇisahitaṃ*), having produced ( *nibbattetvā*) the fire ( *aggiṃ*), he said this ( *etadavoca*) to that boy ( *taṃ dārakaṃ*) – “Dear ( *tāta*), the fire ( *aggi*) should be produced ( *nibbattetabbo*) in this way ( *evaṃ kho*). But not ( *na tveva*) as you ( *tvaṃ*) searched ( *gavesī’ti*) for the fire ( *aggiṃ*) in a stupid ( *bālo abyatto*) and unfitting way ( *ayoniso*)!”

“In just the same way ( *evameva kho tvaṃ*), prince ( *rājañña*), you, being stupid ( *bālo abyatto*) will search ( *gavesissasi*) for the next world ( *paralokaṃ*) in an unfitting way ( *ayoniso*).

Prince ( *rājañña*), give up ( *paṭinissajjetaṃ*), give up ( *paṭinissajjetaṃ*) this evil ( *pāpakaṃ*) viewpoint ( *diṭṭhigataṃ*), prince ( *rājañña*)! May it not ( *mā te ahosi*) be for long ( *dīgharattaṃ*) for your harm ( *ahitāya*) and suffering ( *dukkhāyā’’ti*)!”
commentary_pali: 428.Aggikoti aggiparicārako. Āpādeyyanti nipphādeyyaṃ, āyuṃ vā pāpuṇāpeyyaṃ. Poseyyanti bhojanādīhi bhareyyaṃ. Vaḍḍheyyanti vaḍḍhiṃ gameyyaṃ. Araṇīsahitanti araṇīyugaḷaṃ.
commentary_english:
428.
"Aggiko" means the fire-attendant ( *aggiparicārakaḥ*).
"Āpādeyya" means "may I accomplish," or "may I cause [him] to obtain life" (*āyuṃ vā pāpuṇāpeyyaṃ*).
"Poseyya" means "may I fill with food, etc." (*bhojanādīhi bhareyyaṃ*).
"Vaḍḍheyya" means "may I attain growth" (*vaḍḍhiṃ gameyyaṃ*).
"Araṇīsahita" means a pair of *araṇī* woods (*araṇīyugaḷaṃ*).

mula_pali:
429. ‘‘Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho nevāhaṃ sakkomi idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ. Rājāpi maṃ pasenadi kosalo jānāti tirorājānopi – ‘pāyāsi rājañño evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – ‘‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’’ti. Sacāhaṃ, bho kassapa, idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjissāmi, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘yāva bālo pāyāsi rājañño abyatto duggahitagāhī’ti. Kopenapi naṃ harissāmi, makkhenapi naṃ harissāmi, palāsenapi naṃ harissāmī’’ti.

Dve satthavāhaupamā
mula_english:
429. ‘Even though you say this, Reverend Kassapa, still I cannot bear to give up this evil opinion. King Pasenadi of Kosala knows my opinions, and so do kings abroad. ‘Prince Pāyāsi holds such views and says this: “There is no other world, there are no beings reborn spontaneously, there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions.”’ If I give it up, Reverend Kassapa, they will say: “What a fool Prince Pāyāsi is, how stupidly he grasps at wrong views!” I will stick to this view out of anger, contempt and spite!’

Two similes of caravan leaders.
commentary_pali: 429.Tirorājānopīti tiroraṭṭhe aññasmimpi janapade rājāno jānanti. Abyattoti avisado acheko. Kopenapīti ye maṃ evaṃ vakkhanti, tesu uppajjanakena kopenapi etaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ harissāmi pariharissāmīti gahetvā vicarissāmi. Makkhenāti tayā vuttayuttakāraṇamakkhalakkhaṇena makkhenāpi. Palāsenāti tayā saddhiṃ yugaggāhalakkhaṇena palāsenāpi.
commentary_english:
429. "Tirorājānopī" means in Tiroraṭṭha, also in another country, the kings know.

"Abyatto" means not agitated, not cut off.

"Kopenapī" means, "Those who will speak to me in this way, I will take away and completely remove this viewpoint with anger that arises," having taken [it], I will wander.

"Makkhenā" means by you, with the characteristic of deceitfulness due to what is said and fitting, also by deceit.

"Palāsenā" means by you, together with the characteristic of seizing a pair, also by Palasa.

mula_pali:
430. ‘‘Tena hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, mahāsakaṭasattho sakaṭasahassaṃ puratthimā janapadā pacchimaṃ janapadaṃ agamāsi. So yena yena gacchi, khippaṃyeva pariyādiyati tiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ haritakapaṇṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana satthe dve satthavāhā ahesuṃ eko pañcannaṃ sakaṭasatānaṃ, eko pañcannaṃ sakaṭasatānaṃ. Atha kho tesaṃ satthavāhānaṃ etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho mahāsakaṭasattho sakaṭasahassaṃ; te mayaṃ yena yena gacchāma, khippameva pariyādiyati tiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ haritakapaṇṇaṃ. Yaṃnūna mayaṃ imaṃ satthaṃ dvidhā vibhajeyyāma – ekato pañca sakaṭasatāni ekato pañca sakaṭasatānī’ti. Te taṃ satthaṃ dvidhā vibhajiṃsu vibhajesuṃ (ka.) ekato pañca sakaṭasatāni, ekato pañca sakaṭasatāni. Eko satthavāho bahuṃ tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca āropetvā satthaṃ payāpesi pāyāpesi (sī. pī.). Dvīhatīhapayāto kho pana so sattho addasa purisaṃ kāḷaṃ lohitakkhaṃ lohitakkhiṃ (syā.) sannaddhakalāpaṃ āsannaddhakalāpaṃ (syā.) kumudamāliṃ allavatthaṃ allakesaṃ kaddamamakkhitehi cakkehi bhadrena rathena paṭipathaṃ āgacchantaṃ’, disvā etadavoca – ‘kuto, bho, āgacchasī’ti? ‘Amukamhā janapadā’ti. ‘Kuhiṃ gamissasī’ti? ‘Amukaṃ nāma janapada’nti. ‘Kacci, bho, purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho’ti? ‘Evaṃ, bho, purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho, āsittodakāni vaṭumāni, bahu tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca. Chaḍḍetha, bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatha, mā yoggāni kilamitthā’ti.

‘‘Atha kho so satthavāho satthike āmantesi – ‘ayaṃ, bho, puriso evamāha – ‘‘purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho, āsittodakāni vaṭumāni, bahu tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca. Chaḍḍetha, bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatha, mā yoggāni kilamitthā’’ti. Chaḍḍetha, bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi satthaṃ payāpethā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bho’ti kho te satthikā tassa satthavāhassa paṭissutvā chaḍḍetvā purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni lahubhārehi sakaṭehi satthaṃ payāpesuṃ. Te paṭhamepi satthavāse na addasaṃsu tiṇaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā udakaṃ vā. Dutiyepi satthavāse… tatiyepi satthavāse… catutthepi satthavāse… pañcamepi satthavāse… chaṭṭhepi satthavāse… sattamepi satthavāse na addasaṃsu tiṇaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā udakaṃ vā. Sabbeva anayabyasanaṃ āpajjiṃsu. Ye ca tasmiṃ satthe ahesuṃ manussā vā pasū vā, sabbe so yakkho amanusso bhakkhesi. Aṭṭhikāneva sesāni.

‘‘Yadā aññāsi dutiyo satthavāho – ‘bahunikkhanto kho, bho, dāni so sattho’ti bahuṃ tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca āropetvā satthaṃ payāpesi. Dvīhatīhapayāto kho pana so sattho addasa purisaṃ kāḷaṃ lohitakkhaṃ sannaddhakalāpaṃ kumudamāliṃ allavatthaṃ allakesaṃ kaddamamakkhitehi cakkehi bhadrena rathena paṭipathaṃ āgacchantaṃ, disvā etadavoca – ‘kuto, bho, āgacchasī’ti? ‘Amukamhā janapadā’ti. ‘Kuhiṃ gamissasī’ti? ‘Amukaṃ nāma janapada’nti. ‘Kacci, bho, purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho’ti? ‘Evaṃ, bho, purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho. Āsittodakāni vaṭumāni, bahu tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca. Chaḍḍetha , bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatha, mā yoggāni kilamitthā’ti.

‘‘Atha kho so satthavāho satthike āmantesi – ‘ayaṃ, bho, ‘‘puriso evamāha – purato kantāre mahāmegho abhippavuṭṭho, āsittodakāni vaṭumāni, bahu tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca udakañca. Chaḍḍetha, bho, purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, lahubhārehi sakaṭehi sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatha; mā yoggāni kilamitthā’’ti. Ayaṃ bho puriso neva amhākaṃ mitto, na ñātisālohito, kathaṃ mayaṃ imassa saddhāya gamissāma. Na vo chaḍḍetabbāni purāṇāni tiṇāni kaṭṭhāni udakāni, yathābhatena bhaṇḍena satthaṃ payāpetha. Na no purāṇaṃ chaḍḍessāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bho’ti kho te satthikā tassa satthavāhassa paṭissutvā yathābhatena bhaṇḍena satthaṃ payāpesuṃ. Te paṭhamepi satthavāse na addasaṃsu tiṇaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā udakaṃ vā. Dutiyepi satthavāse… tatiyepi satthavāse… catutthepi satthavāse… pañcamepi satthavāse… chaṭṭhepi satthavāse… sattamepi satthavāse na addasaṃsu tiṇaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ vā udakaṃ vā. Tañca satthaṃ addasaṃsu anayabyasanaṃ āpannaṃ. Ye ca tasmiṃ satthepi ahesuṃ manussā vā pasū vā, tesañca aṭṭhikāneva addasaṃsu tena yakkhena amanussena bhakkhitānaṃ.

‘‘Atha kho so satthavāho satthike āmantesi – ‘ayaṃ kho, bho, sattho anayabyasanaṃ āpanno, yathā taṃ tena bālena satthavāhena pariṇāyakena. Tena hi, bho, yānamhākaṃ satthe appasārāni paṇiyāni, tāni chaḍḍetvā, yāni imasmiṃ satthe mahāsārāni paṇiyāni, tāni ādiyathā’ti. ‘Evaṃ, bho’ti kho te satthikā tassa satthavāhassa paṭissutvā yāni sakasmiṃ satthe appasārāni paṇiyāni, tāni chaḍḍetvā yāni tasmiṃ satthe mahāsārāni paṇiyāni, tāni ādiyitvā sotthinā taṃ kantāraṃ nitthariṃsu, yathā taṃ paṇḍitena satthavāhena pariṇāyakena. Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, bālo abyatto anayabyasanaṃ āpajjissasi ayoniso paralokaṃ gavesanto seyyathāpi so purimo satthavāho. Yepi tava te (ka.) sotabbaṃ saddhātabbaṃ saddahātabbaṃ (pī. ka.) maññissanti, tepi anayabyasanaṃ āpajjissanti, seyyathāpi te satthikā. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña , pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ; paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā’’ti.

te (ka.) saddahātabbaṃ (pī. ka.)
mula_english:
430. ‘Well then, Prince *rājañña*, I will give you a parable *upamā*.

Because some wise people understand what is said by means of parables *upamā*.

Once, Prince *rājañña*, a great caravan *mahāsakaṭasattha* of a thousand carts was travelling from east to west.

And wherever they went, they rapidly consumed all the grass *tiṇa*, wood *kaṭṭha*, water *udaka* and greenstuff *haritakapaṇṇa*.

Now this caravan *sattha* had two leaders *satthavāhā*, each in charge of five hundred carts.

And they thought: “This is a great caravan *mahāsakaṭasattha* of a thousand carts. Wherever we go we use up all the supplies.

Perhaps we should divide the caravan *sattha* into two groups of five hundred carts each”.

So they divided that caravan *sattha* into two, five hundred carts in each.

Then one of the leaders *satthavāha* collected plenty of grass *tiṇa*, wood *kaṭṭha* and water *udaka*, and set off.

After two or three days’ journey this leader *sattha* saw a dark, red-eyed man coming towards him wearing a quiver and a wreath of white water-lilies, with his clothes and hair all wet, driving a donkey-chariot whose wheels were splashed with mud. On seeing this man, the leader said: “Where do you come from, sir *bho*?” “From such and such a district *janapada*”.

“Where are you going?” “To such and such a district *janapada*”.

“Has there been much rainfall in the jungle *kantāra* ahead?” “Yes, sir *bho*, there has been much rainfall in the jungle *kantāra* ahead; there are pools full of water *udaka*, and plenty of grass *tiṇa* and wood *kaṭṭha* and water *udaka*.”

Throw away the grass *tiṇāni*, wood *kaṭṭhāni* and water *udakāni* you have already got, sir *bho*! You will make rapid progress with lightly-laden carts, so do not tire your draught-oxen!”

Then the leader *satthavāha* said to the carters *satthika*: “This man says that there has been much rainfall in the jungle *kantāra* ahead; there are pools full of water *udaka*, and plenty of grass *tiṇa* and wood *kaṭṭha* and water *udaka*.

Throw away the grass *tiṇāni*, wood *kaṭṭhāni* and water *udakāni* you have already got, sir *bho*! You will make rapid progress with lightly-laden carts, so do not tire your draught-oxen!”

Throw away the grass *tiṇāni*, wood *kaṭṭhāni* and water *udakāni*…”, and advised him to throw away his stocks of grass *tiṇa*, wood *kaṭṭha* and water *udaka*.

“Yes, sir *bho*”, said the carters *satthikā* to that leader *satthavāhassa*, agreeing with him, and throwing away their old grass *tiṇāni*, wood *kaṭṭhāni* and water *udakāni*, they set off with lightly-laden carts.

But at the first camping-place *satthavāsa* they did not find any grass *tiṇa*, wood *kaṭṭha* or water *udaka*.

nor at the second, the third, fourth, fifth, sixth or seventh camping-place *satthavāsa*, they did not find any grass *tiṇa*, wood *kaṭṭha* or water *udaka*.

and thus they all came to ruin and destruction *anaya-byasana*.

And whatever there was of them, men *manussa* and cattle *pasū*, they were all gobbled up by that *yakkha*- spirit *amanussa*,

and only their bones *aṭṭhika* remained.

‘And when the leader *satthavāha* of the second caravan was sure the first caravan had gone forward far enough, he stocked up with plenty of grass *tiṇa*, wood *kaṭṭha* and water *udaka*.

After two or three days’ journey this leader *sattha* saw a dark, red-eyed man coming towards him wearing a quiver *sannaddha-kalāpa* and a wreath of white water-lilies *kumudamāli*, with his clothes and hair all wet, driving a donkey-chariot whose wheels were splashed with mud. On seeing this man, the leader said: “Where do you come from, sir *bho*?” “From such and such a district *janapadā*”.

“Where are you going?” “To such and such a district *janapadā*”.

“Has there been much rainfall in the jungle *kantāre* ahead?” “Yes, sir *bho*, there has been much rainfall in the jungle *kantāre* ahead.
[There are] pools with water poured into them, and much grass, wood, and water.

Throw away the old grass, wood, and water, sir! Go quickly, quickly with lightly-laden carts, and do not tire your draught animals!

Then the caravan leader addressed the carters: “This man says, ‘Ahead in the desert, a great cloud has rained, there are pools with water poured into them, and much grass, wood, and water.’

Throw away the old grass, wood, and water, sir! Go quickly, quickly with lightly-laden carts, and do not tire your draught animals!”

This man is not our friend or relative, so why should we go trusting his word?

You should not throw away the old grass, wood, and water. Let the caravan proceed with the goods as they are."

“We will not throw away the old [supplies]!”

“So be it, sir,” the carters replied to the caravan leader. They proceeded with the goods as they were.

At the first encampment they did not see grass, wood, or water.

At the second encampment… at the third encampment… at the fourth encampment… at the fifth encampment… at the sixth encampment… at the seventh encampment they did not see grass, wood, or water.

They saw that the caravan had met with misfortune and disaster.

And they saw the bones of those men and cattle in that caravan who had been devoured by a *yakṣa* demon, an inhuman being.

Then the caravan leader addressed the carters: “This caravan has met with misfortune and disaster, just as it was for that foolish caravan leader without guidance.

Therefore, sirs, let us throw away the goods of little value in our caravan and take the goods of great value from that caravan."

“So be it, sir,” the carters replied to the caravan leader. They threw away the goods of little value in their own caravan, took the goods of great value in that caravan, and safely crossed the desert, just as [they were led by] that wise caravan leader with guidance.

Just so, O prince, being foolish and unwise, you will meet with misfortune and disaster, seeking the next world in an improper way, just like that former caravan leader.

Those who think that anything you say is worth listening to and trusting will also meet with misfortune and disaster, just like those carters.

Give up, O prince, this evil view; give up, O prince, this evil view.

Do not let it cause you harm and suffering for a long time!
commentary_pali:
430.Haritakapaṇṇanti yaṃ kiñci haritakaṃ, antamaso allatiṇapaṇṇampi na hotīti attho. Sannaddhakalāpanti sannaddhadhanukalāpaṃ. Āsittodakāni vaṭumānīti paripuṇṇasalilā maggā ca kandarā ca. Yoggānīti balibadde.

Bahunikkhantaroti bahunikkhanto ciranikkhantoti attho. Yathābhatena bhaṇḍenāti yaṃ vo tiṇakaṭṭhodakabhaṇḍakaṃ āropitaṃ, tena yathābhatena yathāropitena, yathāgahitenāti attho.

bahunikkhanto Yathābhatena bhaṇḍenā

Appasārānīti appagghāni. Paṇiyānīti bhaṇḍāni.

Appasārānī Paṇiyānī

Gūthabhārikādiupamāvaṇṇanā
commentary_english:
430. "Haritakapaṇṇa" means whatever is green, even to the point of a fresh grass leaf, does not exist; this is the meaning.

"Sannaddhakalāpa" means a tied-on quiver of bows.

"Āsittodakāni vaṭumānī" means completely full of water, both roads and caves.

"Yoggānī" means oxen.

"Bahunikkhantaroti" means "bahunikkhanto," someone who has been gone a long time; this is the meaning.

"Yathābhatena bhaṇḍenā" means that which is loaded with grass, wood, and water vessels, with whatever is loaded, with whatever is put on, with whatever is taken; this is the meaning.

"Bahunikkhanto," "yathābhatena bhaṇḍenā," "appasārānī" means things of little value.

"Paṇiyānī" means goods.

"Appasārānī," "paṇiyānī," description of the comparison to a dung-load etc.

mula_pali:
431. ‘‘Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho nevāhaṃ sakkomi idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ. Rājāpi maṃ pasenadi kosalo jānāti tirorājānopi – ‘pāyāsi rājañño evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – ‘‘itipi natthi paro loko…pe… vipāko’’’ti. Sacāhaṃ, bho kassapa, idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjissāmi, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘yāva bālo pāyāsi rājañño, abyatto duggahitagāhī’ti. Kopenapi naṃ harissāmi, makkhenapi naṃ harissāmi, palāsenapi naṃ harissāmī’’ti.

Gūthabhārikaupamā
mula_english:
‘Even though you say this, Reverend Kassapa, still I cannot bear to give up this evil opinion. King Pasenadi of Kosala knows me, and so do the kings of outlying regions: "Prince Pāyāsi holds such a view, such an opinion: ‘There is no other world…and so on…[no] result [of deeds].’" If I give up this evil opinion, Reverend Kassapa, people will say of me: “What a fool is Prince Pāyāsi, how inept, how grasping at wrong views!” I will cling to it out of anger, out of contempt, out of spite!’

The Simile of Carrying Dung

mula_pali: 432. ‘‘Tena hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi. Upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, aññataro sūkaraposako puriso sakamhā gāmā aññaṃ gāmaṃ agamāsi. Tattha addasa pahūtaṃ sukkhagūthaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi – ‘ayaṃ kho pahuto sukkhagūtho chaḍḍito, mama ca sūkarabhattaṃ sūkarānaṃ bhakkho (syā.); yaṃnūnāhaṃ ito sukkhagūthaṃ hareyya’nti. So uttarāsaṅgaṃ pattharitvā pahūtaṃ sukkhagūthaṃ ākiritvā bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā sīse ubbāhetvā uccāropetvā (ka. sī. ka.) agamāsi. Tassa antarāmagge mahāakālamegho pāvassi. So uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ yāva agganakhā gūthena makkhito gūthabhāraṃ ādāya agamāsi. Tamenaṃ manussā disvā evamāhaṃsu – ‘kacci no tvaṃ, bhaṇe, ummatto, kacci viceto, kathañhi nāma uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ yāva agganakhā gūthena makkhito gūthabhāraṃ harissasī’ti. ‘Tumhe khvettha, bhaṇe, ummattā, tumhe vicetā, tathā hi pana me sūkarabhatta’nti. Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, gūthabhārikūpamo gūthahārikūpamo (sī. pī.) maññe paṭibhāsi. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā’’ti.
mula_english: 432. “Well then, Prince, I will give you a parable. For some wise men understand what is said by means of parables. Once, Prince, a certain swineherd was going from his own village to another village. There he saw a heap of dry dung that had been thrown away. When he saw it, he thought: ‘Here is a lot of dry dung that has been thrown away, and this is food for my pigs; I should take this dry dung from here.’ And he spread out his upper robe, gathered up a lot of dry dung, tied it into a bundle, put it on his head, and went on. On his way, a great unseasonable rain cloud burst. And he went on, smeared with oozing, dripping dung right down to his fingernails, carrying his load of dung. When people saw him, they said: ‘Surely you are mad, sir? Surely you are crazy? Why are you carrying that load of dung, smeared with oozing, dripping dung right down to your fingernails?’ ‘But this is food for my pigs!’ Just so, Prince, you remind me of someone carrying a load of dung. Prince, give up this evil viewpoint (pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ), give it up! Do not let it cause you misfortune and suffering for a long time!”
commentary_pali: 432.Mamaca sūkarabhattanti mama ca sūkarānaṃ idaṃ bhattaṃ. Uggharantanti upari gharantaṃ. Paggharantanti heṭṭhā parissavantaṃ. Tumhe khvettha bhaṇeti tumhe kho ettha bhaṇe. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Tathā hi pana me sūkarabhattanti tathā hi pana me ayaṃ gūtho sūkarānaṃ bhattaṃ.
commentary_english:
432.

*mama ca sūkarabhatta* means this food is mine and the pigs'.
*uggharanta* means dripping above.
*paggharanta* means dripping below.
*tumhe khvettha bhaṇe* means you say here.
Or, this is the reading.
*tathā hi pana me sūkarabhatta* means this excrement is my and the pigs’ food.

mula_pali:
433. ‘‘Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho nevāhaṃ sakkomi idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ. Rājāpi maṃ pasenadi kosalo jānāti tirorājānopi – ‘pāyāsi rājañño evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – ‘‘itipi natthi paro loko…pe… vipāko’’ti. Sacāhaṃ, bho kassapa, idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjissāmi, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘yāva bālo pāyāsi rājañño abyatto duggahitagāhī’ti. Kopenapi naṃ harissāmi, makkhenapi naṃ harissāmi, palāsenapi naṃ harissāmī’’ti.

Akkhadhuttakaupamā
mula_english:
433. ‘Even though you say this, Reverend Kāśyapa (Kassapa), still I cannot bear to give up this evil opinion (pāpakaṃ dṛṣṭigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ). King Prasenajit (Pasenadi) of Kosala (Kosala) knows me, and so do other kings, [thinking:] “Prince (Rājañño) Pāyāsi holds such views and opinions: ‘There is no other world… etc. (paro loko…pe… vipāko’ti).’" If I give it up, Reverend Kāśyapa, they will say: “What a fool Prince Pāyāsi is, how stupidly he grasps at wrong views (abyatto duggahitagāhī)!” I will stick to this view out of anger (kopenapi), contempt (makkhenapi) and spite (palāsenapi)!'

The Simile of the Dishonest Dice Player (akkhadhuttakaupamā).

mula_pali:
434. ‘‘Tena hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi, upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, dve akkhadhuttā akkhehi dibbiṃsu. Eko akkhadhutto āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilati. Addasā kho dutiyo akkhadhutto taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilantaṃ, disvā taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ etadavoca – ‘tvaṃ kho, samma, ekantikena jināsi, dehi me, samma, akkhe pajohissāmī’ti. ‘Evaṃ sammā’ti kho so akkhadhutto tassa akkhadhuttassa akkhe pādāsi. Atha kho so akkhadhutto akkhe visena paribhāvetvā taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ etadavoca – ‘ehi kho, samma, akkhehi dibbissāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ sammā’ti kho so akkhadhutto tassa akkhadhuttassa paccassosi. Dutiyampi kho te akkhadhuttā akkhehi dibbiṃsu. Dutiyampi kho so akkhadhutto āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilati. Addasā kho dutiyo akkhadhutto taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ dutiyampi āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilantaṃ, disvā taṃ akkhadhuttaṃ etadavoca –

‘‘Littaṃ paramena tejasā, gilamakkhaṃ puriso na bujjhati;

Gila re gila pāpadhuttaka gili re pāpadhuttaka (ka.), pacchā te kaṭukaṃ bhavissatīti.

gili re pāpadhuttaka (ka.)

‘‘Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, akkhadhuttakūpamo maññe paṭibhāsi. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ; paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā’’ti.
mula_english:
“As to that, Prince, I shall give you a simile, for some wise men here understand the meaning of a statement by means of a simile.

Once there were two gamblers using nuts as dice. One of them, whenever he got the unlucky dice (*kali*), swallowed it. The other noticed what he was doing, and said: “Well, my friend (*samma*), you’re the winner all right! Give me the dice and I will make an offering of them.” “All right”, said the first, and gave them to him. Then that one filled the dice with poison and then said: “Come on, let’s have a game!” “All right”, said the first, agreed. they played again, and once again the one player, whenever he got the unlucky dice (*kali*), swallowed it. The other noticed what he was doing, and said:

“Anointed with the greatest power, a man does not understand the swallowed dice;
Swallow, cheat, and swallow well — Bitter it will be like hell!”

Prince, you speak just like the gambler in my parable. Prince, give up this evil viewpoint (*pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ*), give it up! Do not let it cause you misfortune and suffering for a long time!’
commentary_pali: 434.Āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilatīti āgatāgataṃ parājayaguḷaṃ gilati. Pajjohissāmīti pajjohanaṃ karissāmi, balikammaṃ karissāmīti attho. Akkhehi dibbissāmāti guḷehi kīḷissāma. Littaṃ paramena tejasāti paramatejena visena littaṃ.
commentary_english:
434. "She swallows the *kali* that has come and gone" means she swallows the *parājaya-guḷa* that has come and gone.

"I will illuminate" means I will perform illumination; the meaning is I will perform the rite of offering (*balikamma*).

"*Akkhehi dibbissāmā*" means we will play with dice (*guḷehi kīḷissāma*).

"*Littaṃ paramena tejasā*" means smeared with supreme energy (*paramatejena visena littaṃ*).

mula_pali:
435. ‘‘Kiñcāpi bhavaṃ kassapo evamāha, atha kho nevāhaṃ sakkomi idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjituṃ. Rājāpi maṃ pasenadi kosalo jānāti tirorājānopi – ‘pāyāsi rājañño evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhī – ‘‘itipi natthi paro loko…pe… vipāko’’ti. Sacāhaṃ, bho kassapa, idaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ paṭinissajjissāmi, bhavissanti me vattāro – ‘yāva bālo pāyāsi rājañño abyatto duggahitagāhī’ti. Kopenapi naṃ harissāmi, makkhenapi naṃ harissāmi, palāsenapi naṃ harissāmī’’ti.

Sāṇabhārikaupamā
mula_english:
‘Even though you say this, Reverend Kassapa, I am still unable to relinquish this evil view. King Pasenadi of Kosala, and even kings in foreign lands, know of me, [know of] Prince Pāyāsi's doctrine and view that "There is no other world…and no fruition of deeds well done or ill done." If I were to relinquish this evil view, Reverend Kassapa, people would say of me, "Prince Pāyāsi is a mere boy, inexperienced, and grasps wrongly held views." I will cling to this view out of anger, scorn, and spite!’

Section on the simile of the hemp carrier.

mula_pali:
436. ‘‘Tena hi, rājañña, upamaṃ te karissāmi, upamāya midhekacce viññū purisā bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājānanti. Bhūtapubbaṃ, rājañña, aññataro janapado vuṭṭhāsi. Atha kho sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘āyāma, samma, yena so janapado tenupasaṅkamissāma, appeva nāmettha kiñci dhanaṃ adhigaccheyyāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ sammā’ti kho sahāyako sahāyakassa paccassosi. Te yena so janapado, yena aññataraṃ gāmapaṭṭaṃ gāmapajjaṃ (syā.), gāmapattaṃ (sī.) tenupasaṅkamiṃsu , tattha addasaṃsu pahūtaṃ sāṇaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘idaṃ kho, samma, pahūtaṃ sāṇaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, tena hi, samma, tvañca sāṇabhāraṃ bandha, ahañca sāṇabhāraṃ bandhissāmi, ubho sāṇabhāraṃ ādāya gamissāmā’ti. ‘Evaṃ sammā’ti kho sahāyako sahāyakassa paṭissutvā sāṇabhāraṃ bandhitvā te ubho sāṇabhāraṃ ādāya yena aññataraṃ gāmapaṭṭaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Tattha addasaṃsu pahūtaṃ sāṇasuttaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yassa kho, samma, atthāya iccheyyāma sāṇaṃ, idaṃ pahūtaṃ sāṇasuttaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Tena hi, samma, tvañca sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍehi, ahañca sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍessāmi, ubho sāṇasuttabhāraṃ ādāya gamissāmā’ti. ‘Ayaṃ kho me, samma, sāṇabhāro dūrābhato ca susannaddho ca, alaṃ me tvaṃ pajānāhī’ti. Atha kho so sahāyako sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍetvā sāṇasuttabhāraṃ ādiyi.

‘‘Te yena aññataraṃ gāmapaṭṭaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Tattha addasaṃsu pahūtā sāṇiyo chaḍḍitā, disvā sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yassa kho , samma, atthāya iccheyyāma sāṇaṃ vā sāṇasuttaṃ vā, imā pahūtā sāṇiyo chaḍḍitā. Tena hi, samma, tvañca sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍehi, ahañca sāṇasuttabhāraṃ chaḍḍessāmi, ubho sāṇibhāraṃ ādāya gamissāmā’ti . ‘Ayaṃ kho me, samma, sāṇabhāro dūrābhato ca susannaddho ca, alaṃ me, tvaṃ pajānāhī’ti. Atha kho so sahāyako sāṇasuttabhāraṃ chaḍḍetvā sāṇibhāraṃ ādiyi.

‘‘Te yena aññataraṃ gāmapaṭṭaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Tattha addasaṃsu pahūtaṃ khomaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā…pe… pahūtaṃ khomasuttaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ khomadussaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ kappāsaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ kappāsikasuttaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ kappāsikadussaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ ayaṃ ayasaṃ (syā.) chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ lohaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ tipuṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ sīsaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ sajjhaṃ sajjhuṃ (sī. syā. pī.) chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā… pahūtaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ, disvā sahāyako sahāyakaṃ āmantesi – ‘yassa kho, samma, atthāya iccheyyāma sāṇaṃ vā sāṇasuttaṃ vā sāṇiyo vā khomaṃ vā khomasuttaṃ vā khomadussaṃ vā kappāsaṃ vā kappāsikasuttaṃ vā kappāsikadussaṃ vā ayaṃ vā lohaṃ vā tipuṃ vā sīsaṃ vā sajjhaṃ vā, idaṃ pahūtaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ. Tena hi, samma, tvañca sāṇabhāraṃ chaḍḍehi, ahañca sajjhabhāraṃ sajjhubhāraṃ (sī. syā. pī.) chaḍḍessāmi, ubho suvaṇṇabhāraṃ ādāya gamissāmā’ti. ‘Ayaṃ kho me, samma, sāṇabhāro dūrābhato ca susannaddho ca, alaṃ me tvaṃ pajānāhī’ti. Atha kho so sahāyako sajjhabhāraṃ chaḍḍetvā suvaṇṇabhāraṃ ādiyi.

ayasaṃ (syā.) sajjhuṃ (sī. syā. pī.) sajjhubhāraṃ (sī. syā. pī.)

‘‘Te yena sako gāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Tattha yo so sahāyako sāṇabhāraṃ ādāya agamāsi, tassa neva mātāpitaro abhinandiṃsu, na puttadārā abhinandiṃsu, na mittāmaccā abhinandiṃsu, na ca tatonidānaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ adhigacchi. Yo pana so sahāyako suvaṇṇabhāraṃ ādāya agamāsi, tassa mātāpitaropi abhinandiṃsu, puttadārāpi abhinandiṃsu, mittāmaccāpi abhinandiṃsu, tatonidānañca sukhaṃ somanassaṃ adhigacchi. ‘‘Evameva kho tvaṃ, rājañña, sāṇabhārikūpamo maññe paṭibhāsi. Paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ; paṭinissajjetaṃ, rājañña, pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyā’’ti.

Saraṇagamanaṃ
mula_english:
436. Then, O king, I will make a simile for you, for some wise men here understand the meaning of a statement by means of a simile.

Once, O king, the inhabitants of a certain district migrated. Then one man said to his friend: “Come along, friend, let’s go to that neighborhood, we might find something valuable!”

“Very well,” his friend replied.

So they went to that district, and came to a village street. And there they saw a pile of hemp that had been thrown away, and one said: “Here’s some hemp. You make a bundle, I’ll make a bundle, and we’ll both carry it off.”

The other agreed, and they did so. Then, coming to another village street, they found some hemp-thread, and one said: “This pile of hemp-thread is just what we wanted the hemp for.

Let’s each throw away our bundle of hemp, and we’ll go on with a load of hemp-thread each.”

“I’ve brought this load of hemp a long way and it’s well tied up. That will do for me — you do as you like!”

So his companion threw away the hemp and took the hemp-thread.

They came to another village street. There they saw a large quantity of hemp cloth discarded, and having seen [it], one companion said to the other companion: “Friend, for whatever purpose we would want hemp, or hemp thread, this large quantity of hemp cloths is discarded.

Therefore, friend, you throw away your hemp load, and I will throw away my hemp thread load, and we will both take a hemp cloth load and go.”

“This hemp load of mine, friend, has been brought from afar, and is well secured, enough with me, you figure it out.”

Then that companion, having discarded the hemp thread load, took the hemp cloth load.

They came to another village street. There they saw a pile of flax that had been thrown away, and so on... a pile of linen-thread that had been thrown away…, a pile of linen-cloth that had been thrown away…, a pile of cotton that had been thrown away…, a pile of cotton-thread that had been thrown away…, a pile of cotton-cloth that had been thrown away…, a pile of iron that had been thrown away…, a pile of copper that had been thrown away…, a pile of tin that had been thrown away…, a pile of lead that had been thrown away…, a pile of silver that had been thrown away…, a pile of gold that had been thrown away. Then one said: “This pile of gold is just what we wanted the hemp, hemp-thread, hemp- cloth, flax, linen-thread, linen-cloth, cotton, cotton-thread, cot­ton-cloth, iron, copper, tin, lead, silver for.

You throw away your load of hemp and I’ll throw away my load of silver, and we’ll both go on with a load of gold each.”

“I’ve brought this load of hemp a long way and it’s well tied up. That will do for me — you do as you like!”

And this companion threw away the load of silver and took the load of gold.
ayasaṃ (syā.)
sajjhuṃ (sī. syā. pī.)

sajjhubhāraṃ (sī. syā. pī.)

‘‘Then they came back to their own village.

And there the one who brought a load of hemp (*sāṇabhāraṃ*) gave no pleasure to his parents, nor to his wife and children, nor to his friends and colleagues, and he did not even get any joy or happiness (*sukhaṃ somanassaṃ*) from it himself.

But the one who came back with a load of gold (*suvaṇṇabhāraṃ*) pleased his parents, his wife and children, his friends and colleagues, and he derived joy and happiness (*sukhaṃ somanassaṃ*) from it himself as well.

‘Prince, you speak just like the hemp-bearer in my parable.

Prince, give up this evil viewpoint (*pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ*), give it up!

Do not let it cause you misfortune and suffering for a long time!’

Taking Refuge.
commentary_pali:
436.Gāmapaṭṭanti vuṭṭhitagāmapadeso vuccati. ‘‘Gāmapada’’ntipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Sāṇabhāranti sāṇavākabhāraṃ. Susannaddhoti subaddho. Tvaṃ pajānāhīti tvaṃ jāna. Sace gaṇhitukāmosi, gaṇhāhīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Khomanti khomavākaṃ. Ayanti kāḷalohaṃ. Lohanti tambalohaṃ. Sajjhanti rajataṃ. Suvaṇṇanti suvaṇṇamāsakaṃ. Abhinandiṃsūti tussiṃsu.

Khoma Aya Loha Sajjha Suvaṇṇa Abhinandiṃsū
commentary_english:
436. *Gāmapaṭṭa* means a region that is known as a village. "Gāmapada" is also a reading, this is the meaning. *Sāṇabhāra* means a load of hemp fiber. *Susannaddho* means well-bound. *Tvaṃ pajānāhī* means you should know. If you are desirous of taking it, it means, take it.

*Khoma* means flax. *Aya* means black iron. *Loha* means copper. *Sajjha* means silver. *Suvaṇṇa* means a gold *māsaka*. *Abhinandiṃsū* means they rejoiced.

*Khoma*, *aya*, *loha*, *sajjha*, *suvaṇṇa*, *abhinandiṃsū*

mula_pali:
437. ‘‘Purimeneva ahaṃ opammena bhoto kassapassa attamano abhiraddho. Api cāhaṃ imāni vicitrāni pañhāpaṭibhānāni sotukāmo evāhaṃ bhavantaṃ kassapaṃ paccanīkaṃ kātabbaṃ amaññissaṃ. Abhikkantaṃ, bho kassapa, abhikkantaṃ, bho kassapa. Seyyathāpi, bho kassapa, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti evamevaṃ bhotā kassapena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ, bho kassapa, taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammañca, bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ kassapo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gataṃ.

‘‘Icchāmi cāhaṃ, bho kassapa, mahāyaññaṃ yajituṃ, anusāsatu maṃ bhavaṃ kassapo, yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā’’ti.

Yaññakathā
mula_english:
437. Just as before, I was delighted and pleased with Reverend Kassapa’s parable. And I would not have thought of treating Reverend Kassapa, who is capable of such diverse and wonderful expressions and insights, as an opponent. Excellent, Reverend Kassapa, excellent! It is as if, Reverend Kassapa, someone were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms. Just so has the Dhamma been expounded in many ways by Reverend Kassapa. And I, Reverend Kassapa, go to the Blessed Gotama for refuge, and to the Dharma, and to the Sangha of monks. May Reverend Kassapa remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, as long as I have breath and life.

I wish, Reverend Kassapa, to perform a great sacrifice (mahāyañña). Instruct me, Reverend Kassapa, how this may be to my lasting benefit and happiness."

Account of the Sacrifice (yaññakathā).
commentary_pali: 437.Attamanoti sakamano tuṭṭhacitto. Abhiraddhoti abhippasanno. Pañhāpaṭibhānānīti pañhupaṭṭhānāni. Paccanīkaṃ kattabbanti paccanīkaṃ paṭiviruddhaṃ viya kattabbaṃ amaññissaṃ, paṭilomagāhaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsinti attho.
commentary_english:
437. *attamano* means "with his own mind," "with a contented heart."
*abhiraddho* means "greatly pleased".
*pañhāpaṭibhānānī* means "questions that are the basis".
*paccanīkaṃ kattabba* means "the opposite should be done," meaning "I would not think of doing the opposite, something contradictory; having grasped the opposite way, he stood."

mula_pali:
438. ‘‘Yathārūpe kho, rājañña, yaññe gāvo vā haññanti ajeḷakā vā haññanti, kukkuṭasūkarā vā haññanti, vividhā vā pāṇā saṃghātaṃ āpajjanti, paṭiggāhakā ca honti micchādiṭṭhī micchāsaṅkappā micchāvācā micchākammantā micchāājīvā micchāvāyāmā micchāsatī micchāsamādhī, evarūpo kho, rājañña, yañño na mahapphalo hoti na mahānisaṃso na mahājutiko na mahāvipphāro. Seyyathāpi, rājañña, kassako bījanaṅgalaṃ ādāya vanaṃ paviseyya. So tattha dukkhette dubbhūme avihatakhāṇukaṇṭake bījāni patiṭṭhāpeyya khaṇḍāni pūtīni vātātapahatāni asāradāni asukhasayitāni. Devo ca na kālena kālaṃ sammādhāraṃ anuppaveccheyya. Api nu tāni bījāni vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ viruḷhiṃ (moggalāne) vepullaṃ āpajjeyyuṃ, kassako vā vipulaṃ phalaṃ adhigaccheyyā’’ti? ‘‘No hidaṃ na evaṃ (syā. ka.) bho kassapa’’. ‘‘Evameva kho, rājañña, yathārūpe yaññe gāvo vā haññanti, ajeḷakā vā haññanti, kukkuṭasūkarā vā haññanti, vividhā vā pāṇā saṃghātaṃ āpajjanti, paṭiggāhakā ca honti micchādiṭṭhī micchāsaṅkappā micchāvācā micchākammantā micchāājīvā micchāvāyāmā micchāsatī micchāsamādhī, evarūpo kho , rājañña, yañño na mahapphalo hoti na mahānisaṃso na mahājutiko na mahāvipphāro.

‘‘Yathārūpe ca kho, rājañña, yaññe neva gāvo haññanti, na ajeḷakā haññanti, na kukkuṭasūkarā haññanti, na vividhā vā pāṇā saṃghātaṃ āpajjanti, paṭiggāhakā ca honti sammādiṭṭhī sammāsaṅkappā sammāvācā sammākammantā sammāājīvā sammāvāyāmā sammāsatī sammāsamādhī, evarūpo kho, rājañña, yañño mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso mahājutiko mahāvipphāro. Seyyathāpi, rājañña, kassako bījanaṅgalaṃ ādāya vanaṃ paviseyya. So tattha sukhette subhūme suvihatakhāṇukaṇṭake bījāni patiṭṭhapeyya akhaṇḍāni apūtīni avātātapahatāni sāradāni sukhasayitāni. Devo ca kālena kālaṃ sammādhāraṃ anuppaveccheyya. Api nu tāni bījāni vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjeyyuṃ, kassako vā vipulaṃ phalaṃ adhigaccheyyā’’ti? ‘‘Evaṃ, bho kassapa’’. ‘‘Evameva kho, rājañña, yathārūpe yaññe neva gāvo haññanti, na ajeḷakā haññanti, na kukkuṭasūkarā haññanti, na vividhā vā pāṇā saṃghātaṃ āpajjanti, paṭiggāhakā ca honti sammādiṭṭhī sammāsaṅkappā sammāvācā sammākammantā sammāājīvā sammāvāyāmā sammāsatī sammāsamādhī, evarūpo kho, rājañña, yañño mahapphalo hoti mahānisaṃso mahājutiko mahāvipphāro’’ti.

Uttaramāṇavavatthu
mula_english:
438. ‘Prince, when a sacrifice (*yajña*) is made at which oxen (*gāvaḥ*) are slain, or goats (*ajeḷakā*), fowl or pigs (*kukkuṭasūkarāḥ*), or various creatures (*pāṇā*) are slaughtered, and the participants have wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), wrong thought (*micchāsaṅkappā*), wrong speech (*micchāvācā*), wrong action (*micchākammantā*), wrong livelihood (*micchāājīvā*), wrong effort (*micchāvāyāmā*), wrong mindfulness (*micchāsatī*) and wrong concentration (*micchāsamādhī*), then that sacri­fice (*yajña*) is of no great fruit (*mahapphalo*) or profit, it is not very brilliant (*mahājutiko*) and has no great radiance (*mahāvipphāro*).

Suppose, Prince, a farmer (*kassako*) went into the forest (*vanaṃ*) with plough (*bījanaṅgalaṃ*) and seed (*bījāni*), and there, in an untilled place (*dukkhette*) with poor soil (*dubbhūme*) from which the stumps had not been uprooted (*avihatakhāṇukaṇṭake*), were to sow seeds (*bījāni*) that were broken (*khaṇḍāni*), rotting (*pūtīni*), ruined by wind and heat (*vātātapahatāni*), stale (*asāradāni*), and not properly embedded in the soil (*asukhasayitāni*), and the rain-god (*devo*) did not send proper showers (*sammādhāraṃ*) at the right time (*kālaṃ*) — would those seeds (*bījāni*) germinate, develop (*vuddhiṃ*) and increase (*vepullaṃ*), and would the farmer (*kassako*) get an abundant crop (*vipulaṃ phalaṃ*)?’’ “No, sir (*bho kassapa*).”

‘In the same way, Prince, at a sacrifice (*yajña*) at which oxen (*gāvaḥ*) are slain, or goats (*ajeḷakā*), fowl or pigs (*kukkuṭasūkarāḥ*), or various creatures (*pāṇā*) are slaughtered, and the participants have wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), wrong thought (*micchāsaṅkappā*), wrong speech (*micchāvācā*), wrong action (*micchākammantā*), wrong livelihood (*micchāājīvā*), wrong effort (*micchāvāyāmā*), wrong mindfulness (*micchāsatī*) and wrong concentration (*micchāsamādhī*), then that sacrifice (*yajña*) is of no great fruit (*mahapphalo*) or profit, it is not very brilliant (*mahājutiko*) and has no great radiance (*mahāvipphāro*).

But when none of these creatures are put to death, and the participants have right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), right thought (*sammāsaṅkappā*), right speech (*sammāvācā*), right action (*sammākammantā*), right livelihood (*sammāājīvā*), right effort (*sammāvāyāmā*), right mindfulness (*sammāsatī*), right concentration (*sammāsamādhī*), then that sacri­fice (*yajña*) is of great fruit (*mahapphalo*) and profit, it is brilliant (*mahājutiko*) and of great radiance (*mahāvipphāro*).

Suppose, Prince, a farmer (*kassako*) went into the forest (*vanaṃ*) with plough (*bījanaṅgalaṃ*) and seed (*bījāni*), and there, in a well-tilled place (*sukhette*) with good soil (*subhūme*) from which the stumps had been uprooted (*suvihatakhāṇukaṇṭake*), were to sow seeds (*bījāni*) that were not broken (*akhaṇḍāni*), rotting (*apūtīni*), ruined by wind and heat (*avātātapahatāni*), or stale (*sāradāni*), and were firmly embedded in the soil (*sukhasayitāni*), and the rain-god (*devo*) were to send proper showers (*sammādhāraṃ*) at the right time (*kālaṃ*) — would those seeds (*bījāni*) germinate, develop (*vuddhiṃ*) and increase (*vepullaṃ*), and would the farmer (*kassako*) get an abundant crop (*vipulaṃ phalaṃ*)?’’ “Yes, sir (*evaṃ, bho kassapa*).”

‘In the same way, Prince, at a sacrifice (*yajña*) at which no oxen (*gāvo*) are slain, nor goats (*ajeḷakā*), fowl or pigs (*kukkuṭasūkarāḥ*), nor various creatures (*pāṇā*) are slaughtered, and the participants have right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), right thought (*sammāsaṅkappā*), right speech (*sammāvācā*), right action (*sammākammantā*), right livelihood (*sammāājīvā*), right effort (*sammāvāyāmā*), right mindfulness (*sammāsatī*) and right concentration (*sammāsamādhī*), then that sacrifice (*yajña*) is of great fruit (*mahapphalo*) and profit, it is brilliant (*mahājutiko*) and of great radiance (*mahāvipphāro*).’

Uttaramāṇavavatthu
commentary_pali:
438.Saṅghātaṃ āpajjantīti saṅghātaṃ vināsaṃ maraṇaṃ āpajjanti. Na mahapphaloti vipākaphalena na mahapphalo hoti. Na mahānisaṃsoti guṇānisaṃsena mahānisaṃso na hoti. Na mahājutikoti ānubhāvajutiyā mahājutiko na hoti. Na mahāvipphāroti vipākavipphāratāya mahāvipphāro na hoti. Bījanaṅgalanti bījañca naṅgalañca. Dukkhetteti duṭṭhukhette nissārakhette. Dubbhūmeti visamabhūmibhāge. Patiṭṭhāpeyyāti ṭhapeyya. Khaṇḍānīti chinnabhinnāni. Pūtīnīti nissārāni. Vātātapahatānīti vātena ca ātapena ca hatāni pariyādinnatejāni. Asārādānīti taṇḍulasārādānarahitāni palālāni. Asukhasayitānīti yāni sukkhāpetvā koṭṭhe ākiritvā ṭhapitāni, tāni sukhasayitāni nāma. Etāni pana na tādisāni. Anuppaveccheyyāti anupaveseyya, na sammā vasseyya, anvaddhamāsaṃ anudasāhaṃ anupañcāhaṃ na vasseyyāti attho. Api nu tānīti api nu evaṃ khettabījavuṭṭhidose sati tāni bījāni aṅkuramūlapattādīhi uddhaṃ vuddhiṃ heṭṭhā virūḷhiṃ samantato ca vepullaṃ āpajjeyyunti . Evarūpo kho rājañña yaññoti evarūpaṃ rājañña dānaṃ parūpaghātena uppāditapaccayatopi dāyakatopi pariggāhakatopi avisuddhattā na mahapphalaṃ hoti.

Evarūpo kho rājañña yaññoti evarūpaṃ rājaññadānaṃ aparūpaghātena uppannapaccayatopi aparūpaghātitāya sīlavantadāyakatopi sammādiṭṭhiādiguṇasampannapaṭiggāhakatopi mahapphalaṃ hoti. Sace pana guṇātirekaṃ nirodhā vuṭṭhitaṃ paṭiggāhakaṃ labhati, cetanā ca vipulā hoti, diṭṭheva dhamme vipākaṃ detīti.
commentary_english:
438. *saṅghātaṃ āpajjantī* means they undergo striking together, destruction, and death.

*na mahapphalo* means it is not greatly fruitful in terms of resultant fruit (vipāka-phala).

*na mahānisaṃso* means it is not of great advantage in terms of the advantage of qualities (guṇānisaṃsa).

*na mahājutiko* means it is not greatly radiant in terms of the radiance of power (ānubhāva-juti).

*na mahāvipphāro* means it is not of great expansion in terms of the expansion of result (vipāka-vipphāra).

*bījanaṅgala* means both seed (bīja) and plough (naṅgala).

*dukkhette* means in a bad field, in an unproductive field.

*dubbhūme* means in an uneven place.

*patiṭṭhāpeyyā* means he should establish.

*khaṇḍānī* means broken and divided.

*pūtīnī* means without essence.

*vātātapahatānī* means struck by wind and heat, the brilliance is exhausted.

*asārādānī* means stalks devoid of the essence of rice grains (taṇḍula-sāra).

*asukhasayitānī* means those that have been dried, scattered in a storehouse, and established; those are called comfortably situated.

These, however, are not like that.

*anuppaveccheyyā* means he should not provide, he should not rain well, he should not rain for half a month, or for ten days, or for five days. This is the meaning.

*api nu tānī* means, but now, even when there is a fault of field, seed, and rain, will those seeds attain growth upward by sprout, root, leaf, etc., and downward by sprouting, and fullness all around?

*evarūpo kho rājañña yañño* means, O king, such a sacrifice is not greatly fruitful because of the impurity of the means of production produced by injury to others (parūpaghātena), of the giver, and of the recipient.

*evarūpo kho rājañña yañño* means, O king, such a sacrifice is greatly fruitful because of the means of production arising without injury to others, and because of the giver having morality (śīlavant), and because of the recipient being endowed with qualities such as right view (sammādiṭṭhi).

But if he obtains a recipient who has arisen from cessation with a superior quality, and his intention is vast, then it gives result in this very life.

mula_pali: 439. Atha kho pāyāsi rājañño dānaṃ paṭṭhapesi samaṇabrāhmaṇakapaṇaddhikavaṇibbakayācakānaṃ . Tasmiṃ kho pana dāne evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ dīyati kaṇājakaṃ bilaṅgadutiyaṃ, dhorakāni thorakāni (sī. pī.), corakāni (syā.) ca vatthāni guḷavālakāni guḷagāḷakāni (ka.). Tasmiṃ kho pana dāne uttaro nāma māṇavo vāvaṭo byāvaṭo (sī. pī.) ahosi. So dānaṃ datvā evaṃ anuddisati – ‘‘imināhaṃ dānena pāyāsiṃ rājaññameva imasmiṃ loke samāgacchiṃ, mā parasmi’’nti. Assosi kho pāyāsi rājañño – ‘‘uttaro kira māṇavo dānaṃ datvā evaṃ anuddisati – ‘imināhaṃ dānena pāyāsiṃ rājaññameva imasmiṃ loke samāgacchiṃ, mā parasmi’’’nti. Atha kho pāyāsi rājañño uttaraṃ māṇavaṃ āmantāpetvā etadavoca – ‘‘saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, tāta uttara, dānaṃ datvā evaṃ anuddisasi – ‘imināhaṃ dānena pāyāsiṃ rājaññameva imasmiṃ loke samāgacchiṃ, mā parasmi’’’nti? ‘‘Evaṃ, bho’’. ‘‘Kissa pana tvaṃ, tāta uttara, dānaṃ datvā evaṃ anuddisasi – ‘imināhaṃ dānena pāyāsiṃ rājaññameva imasmiṃ loke samāgacchiṃ, mā parasmi’nti? Nanu mayaṃ, tāta uttara, puññatthikā dānasseva phalaṃ pāṭikaṅkhino’’ti? ‘‘Bhoto kho dāne evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ dīyati kaṇājakaṃ bilaṅgadutiyaṃ, yaṃ bhavaṃ pādāpi pādāsi (ka.) na iccheyya samphusituṃ chupituṃ (pī. ka.), kuto bhuñjituṃ, dhorakāni ca vatthāni guḷavālakāni, yāni bhavaṃ pādāpi acittikataṃ (ka.) na iccheyya samphusituṃ, kuto paridahituṃ. Bhavaṃ kho panamhākaṃ piyo manāpo, kathaṃ mayaṃ manāpaṃ amanāpena saṃyojemā’’ti? ‘‘Tena hi tvaṃ, tāta uttara, yādisāhaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjāmi, tādisaṃ bhojanaṃ paṭṭhapehi. Yādisāni cāhaṃ vatthāni paridahāmi, tādisāni ca vatthāni paṭṭhapehī’’ti. ‘‘Evaṃ, bho’’ti kho uttaro māṇavo pāyāsissa rājaññassa paṭissutvā yādisaṃ bhojanaṃ pāyāsi rājañño bhuñjati, tādisaṃ bhojanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Yādisāni ca vatthāni pāyāsi rājañño paridahati, tādisāni ca vatthāni paṭṭhapesi.
mula_english:
Then Prince Pāyāsi established a charity for ascetics ( *śramaṇa* ) and Brahmins ( *brāhmaṇa* ), wayfarers, beggars and the needy.

And there, in that charity, such food was given out as broken rice with sour gruel, and also rough clothing with ball-fringes.

And in that charity, a young Brahmin called Uttara was put in charge of the distribution.

Referring to it, he said: ‘Through this generosity, may I be associated with Prince Pāyāsi in this world, but not in the next.’

And Prince Pāyāsi heard of his words,

Then Prince Pāyāsi sent for Uttara and asked him if he had said that.

‘Is it true, Uttara, that you, having given alms, made such a pronouncement, "Through this almsgiving, may I meet Pāyāsi, the prince, in this very world, and never in the next!"?’

‘Yes, Lord.’

‘But why did you say such a thing?

Why did you, kind Uttara, having given alms, make such a pronouncement, "Through this almsgiving, may I meet Pāyāsi, the prince, in this very world, and never in the next!"? Surely, kind Uttara, we are seekers of merit, hoping for the fruit of generosity alone!’

‘In your honor's almsgiving, such food is given: broken rice with *bilaṅga* gruel, which your honor would not even wish to touch—how much less to eat! And coarse cloths with ball fringes, which your honor would not wish even to touch—how much less to wear!

Lord, you are kind and gentle to us, so how can we reconcile such kindness and gentleness with unkindness and roughness?’

‘‘Then, kind Uttara, prepare food such as I eat.

And prepare clothes such as I wear.’

‘Very good, Lord’, said Uttara to Prince Pāyāsi, and he prepared food such as Prince Pāyāsi ate.

And he prepared clothes such as Prince Pāyāsi wore.
commentary_pali: 439. Imaṃ pana therassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā pāyāsirājañño theraṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ therassa mahādānaṃ datvā tato paṭṭhāya mahājanassa dānaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Taṃ sandhāya atha kho pāyāsi rājaññotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kaṇājakanti sakuṇḍakaṃ uttaṇḍulabhattaṃ. Bilaṅgadutiyanti kañjikadutiyaṃ. Dhorakāni ca vatthānīti thūlāni ca vatthāni. Guḷavālakānīti guḷadasāni, puñjapuñjavasena ṭhitamahantadasānīti attho. Evaṃ anuddisatīti evaṃ upadisati. Pādāpīti pādenapi.
commentary_english:
439. Having heard this Dhamma talk of the Elder, King Pāyāsi invited the Elder, gave a great gift to the Elder for a week, and from then on, he established giving to the general public.

With reference to that, "Then, King Pāyāsi," etc., was said.

There, *kaṇājaka* means rice gruel with condiments.

*bilaṅgadutiya* means with sour gruel as the second item.

*dhorakāni ca vatthāni* means thick cloths.

*guḷavālakānī* means molasses fringes, meaning large fringes that stand in the manner of heaps.

*evaṃ anuddisatī* means thus he advises.

*pādāpī* means even by foot.

mula_pali:
440. Atha kho pāyāsi rājañño asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā asahatthā dānaṃ datvā acittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajji suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ. Yo pana tassa dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo. So sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā sahatthā dānaṃ datvā cittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajji devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ.

Pāyāsidevaputto
mula_english:
440. Then, Payasi (Pāyāsi) the prince, having given a charity grudgingly (asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā), not with his own hands (asahatthā dānaṃ datvā), without proper concern (acittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā), like something casually tossed aside (apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā), after death, at the breaking-up of the body (kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā), was reborn in the company of the Four Great Kings (cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajji) in the empty Serisaka mansion (suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ).

But Uttara (uttaro nāma māṇavo), a young Brahmin, was put in charge of that distribution (yo pana tassa dāne vāvaṭo ahosi).

He, having given charity ungrudgingly (sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā), with his own hands (sahatthā dānaṃ datvā), with proper concern (cittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā), not as something carelessly cast aside (anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā), after death, at the breaking-up of the body (kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā), was reborn in a good place (sugatiṃ), a heavenly realm (saggaṃ lokaṃ), in the company of the Thirty-Three Gods (devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajji).

Payasidevaputta
commentary_pali: 440.Asakkaccanti saddhāvirahitaṃ assaddhadānaṃ. Asahatthāti na sahatthena. Acittīkatanti cittīkāravirahitaṃ, na cittīkārampi paccupaṭṭhāpetvā na paṇītacittaṃ katvā adāsi. Apaviddhanti chaḍḍitaṃ vippatitaṃ. Suññaṃ serīsakanti serīsakaṃ nāma ekaṃ tucchaṃ rajatavimānaṃ upagato. Tassa kira dvāre mahāsirīsarukkho, tena taṃ ‘‘serīsaka’’nti vuccati.
commentary_english:
440. *Asakkacca* means giving without faith, devoid of faith (*saddhā*).

*Asahatthā* means not with one's own hand.

*Acittīkata* means devoid of consideration; without even establishing consideration, he gave without making his mind pure.

*Apaviddha* means discarded, rejected.

*Suññaṃ serīsaka*—he approached a certain empty silver mansion called Serīsaka.

It is said that at its door was a large *sirīsaka* tree; therefore, it is called "Serīsaka."

mula_pali:
441. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā gavampati abhikkhaṇaṃ suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ divāvihāraṃ gacchati. Atha kho pāyāsi devaputto yenāyasmā gavampati tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ gavampatiṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho pāyāsiṃ devaputtaṃ āyasmā gavampati etadavoca – ‘‘kosi tvaṃ, āvuso’’ti? ‘‘Ahaṃ, bhante, pāyāsi rājañño’’ti. ‘‘Nanu tvaṃ, āvuso, evaṃdiṭṭhiko ahosi – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’’’ti? ‘‘Saccāhaṃ, bhante, evaṃdiṭṭhiko ahosiṃ – ‘itipi natthi paro loko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko’ti. Api cāhaṃ ayyena kumārakassapena etasmā pāpakā diṭṭhigatā vivecito’’ti. ‘‘Yo pana te, āvuso, dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo, so kuhiṃ upapanno’’ti? ‘‘Yo me, bhante, dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo, so sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā sahatthā dānaṃ datvā cittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapanno devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ. Ahaṃ pana, bhante, asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā asahatthā dānaṃ datvā acittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapanno suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ. Tena hi, bhante gavampati, manussalokaṃ gantvā evamārocehi – ‘sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ detha, sahatthā dānaṃ detha, cittīkataṃ dānaṃ detha, anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ detha. Pāyāsi rājañño asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā asahatthā dānaṃ datvā acittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapanno suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ. Yo pana tassa dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo, so sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā sahatthā dānaṃ datvā cittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapanno devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyata’’’nti.

Atha kho āyasmā gavampati manussalokaṃ āgantvā evamārocesi – ‘‘sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ detha, sahatthā dānaṃ detha, cittīkataṃ dānaṃ detha, anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ detha. Pāyāsi rājañño asakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā asahatthā dānaṃ datvā acittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā apaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapanno suññaṃ serīsakaṃ vimānaṃ. Yo pana tassa dāne vāvaṭo ahosi uttaro nāma māṇavo, so sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā sahatthā dānaṃ datvā cittīkataṃ dānaṃ datvā anapaviddhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapanno devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyata’’nti.

Pāyāsisuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.

Mahāvaggo niṭṭhito.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Mahāpadāna nidānaṃ, nibbānañca sudassanaṃ;

Janavasabha govindaṃ, samayaṃ sakkapañhakaṃ;

Mahāsatipaṭṭhānañca, pāyāsi dasamaṃ bhave satipaṭṭhānapāyāsi, mahāvaggassa saṅgaho (sī. pī.) satipaṭṭhānapāyāsi, mahāvaggoti vuccatīti (syā.).

satipaṭṭhānapāyāsi, mahāvaggassa saṅgaho (sī. pī.) satipaṭṭhānapāyāsi, mahāvaggoti vuccatīti (syā.)

Mahāvaggapāḷi niṭṭhitā.
mula_english:
441. At that time, the Venerable Gavampati was accustomed to go to the empty Serisaka mansion for his midday rest.

Then, the deva Pāyāsi approached the Venerable Gavampati; having approached, after respectfully greeting the Venerable Gavampati, he stood to one side.

As Pāyāsi the deva was standing to one side, the Venerable Gavampati said this to him: "Who are you, friend?" "I am Pāyāsi, your majesty," he said.

"Surely, friend, you held such a view as this: 'There is no other world, there are no beings reborn spontaneously, there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions'?" "Indeed, venerable sir, I held such a view: 'There is no other world, there are no beings reborn spontaneously, there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions.'

But I was converted from that evil view by the Noble Kumārakassapa."

"Where is Uttara, the young man who managed your almsgiving, friend?" "Uttara, the young man who managed my almsgiving, venerable sir, by carefully giving alms, giving alms with his own hands, giving alms with proper concern, not giving alms carelessly, at the breaking up of the body, after death, has been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Thirty-Three Gods.

But I, venerable sir, by giving alms carelessly, not giving alms with my own hands, giving alms without proper concern, giving alms carelessly, at the breaking up of the body, after death, have been reborn in the company of the Four Great Kings in the empty Serisaka mansion.

Therefore, venerable Gavampati, go to the human world and announce this: ‘Give alms carefully, give alms with your own hands, give alms with proper concern, give alms unreservedly.

Pāyāsi, your majesty, by giving alms carelessly, not giving alms with your own hands, giving alms without proper concern, giving alms carelessly, at the breaking up of the body, after death, has been reborn in the company of the Four Great Kings in the empty Serisaka mansion.

Uttara, the young man who managed his almsgiving, by carefully giving alms, giving alms with his own hands, giving alms with proper concern, not giving alms carelessly, at the breaking up of the body, after death, has been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Thirty-Three Gods.’"

Then the Venerable Gavampati went to the human world and announced this: "Give alms carefully, give alms with your own hands, give alms with proper concern, give alms unreservedly.

Pāyāsi, your majesty, by giving alms carelessly, not giving alms with your own hands, giving alms without proper concern, giving alms carelessly, at the breaking up of the body, after death, has been reborn in the company of the Four Great Kings in the empty Serisaka mansion.

Uttara, the young man who managed his almsgiving, by carefully giving alms, giving alms with his own hands, giving alms with proper concern, not giving alms carelessly, at the breaking up of the body, after death, has been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Thirty-Three Gods."

The Pāyāsi Sutta, the tenth, is finished.

The Great Division is finished.

Its summary:

Mahāpadāna, Nidāna, Nibbāna, and Sudassana;

Janavasabha, Govinda, Samaya, Sakkapañhaka;

Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna, and Pāyāsi is the tenth.

The Great Division Text is finished.
commentary_pali:
441.Āyasmāgavaṃpatīti thero kira pubbe manussakāle gopāladārakānaṃ jeṭṭhako hutvā mahato sirīsassa mūlaṃ sodhetvā vālikaṃ okiritvā ekaṃ piṇḍapātikattheraṃ rukkhamūle nisīdāpetvā attanā laddhaṃ āhāraṃ datvā tato cuto tassānubhāvena tasmiṃ rajatavimāne nibbatti. Sirīsarukkho vimānadvāre aṭṭhāsi. So paññāsāya vassehi phalati, tato paññāsa vassāni gatānīti devaputto saṃvegaṃ āpajjati. So aparena samayena amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle manussesu nibbattitvā satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā arahattaṃ patto. Pubbāciṇṇavasena pana divāvihāratthāya tadeva vimānaṃ abhiṇhaṃ gacchati, taṃ kirassa utusukhaṃ hoti. Taṃ sandhāya ‘‘tena kho pana samayena āyasmā gavaṃpatī’’tiādi vuttaṃ.

Sosakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvāti so parassa santakampi dānaṃ sakkaccaṃ datvā. Evamārocesīti ‘‘sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ dethā’’tiādinā nayena ārocesi. Tañca pana therassa ārocanaṃ sutvā mahājano sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā devaloke nibbatto. Pāyāsissa pana rājaññassa paricārakā sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvāpi nikantivasena gantvā tasseva santike nibbattā. Taṃ kira disācārikavimānaṃ vaṭṭaniaṭaviyaṃ ahosi. Pāyāsidevaputto ca ekadivasaṃ vāṇijakānaṃ dassetvā attano katakammaṃ kathesīti.

So sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā Evamārocesī

Iti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

Pāyāsirājaññasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Niṭṭhitā ca mahāvaggassatthavaṇṇanā.

Mahāvaggaṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.
commentary_english:
441. The venerable Gavampati: It seems that in a former life, that elder, as the eldest of the cowherd boys, having cleared the base of a great *sirīsa* tree, sprinkled sand, seated an alms-mendicant (*piṇḍapātika*) elder at the foot of the tree, and given the food (*āhāra*) he had obtained himself, after death, through the power of that [deed], was reborn in that silver mansion (*rajatavimāna*).

A *sirīsa* tree stood at the gate of the mansion.

It bears fruit for fifty years, and the god (*devaputta*) experiences agitation when fifty years have passed.

At another time, having been reborn among humans at the time of our Blessed One, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching (*dhamma-katha*), he attained Arhatship (*arahattaṃ patto*).

Due to his past habit, he frequently goes to that same mansion for the sake of the day's dwelling (*divāvihāratthāya*); it is his seasonal bliss (*utusukhaṃ hoti*).

With reference to that, it was said: "Then, on that occasion, the venerable Gavampati," and so forth.

He so, having given alms respectfully (*sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā*), that is, he, even with property belonging to another, gave alms respectfully (*sakkaccaṃ datvā*).

He announced thus (*evamārocesī*), that is, he announced in a manner beginning with "Give alms respectfully (*sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ dethā*)."

And the great multitude, having heard that announcement of the elder, having given alms respectfully (*sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā*), was reborn in the world of the gods (*devaloke nibbatto*).

The attendants of Pāyāsi the prince (*rājañña*), even having given alms respectfully (*sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvāpi*), having gone by way of desire (*nikantivasena*), were reborn in the presence of that same one.

That wandering mansion (*disācārikavimāna*) was in Vaṭṭaniaṭavi.

And Pāyāsidevaputta, one day, having shown it to the merchants, told of his past deed, it is said.

He so, having given alms respectfully (*sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ datvā*), he announced thus (*evamārocesī*).

Thus ends the commentary on the Pāyāsi-rājañña Sutta in the Sūmaṅgalavilāsinī, commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.

And finished is the meaning-commentary of the Mahāvagga.

The Mahāvagga commentary is finished.
